What is Model Routing in AI?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sources indicate that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Recent findings suggest that "Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages. Most AI apps send both to the same large model and pay large-model prices for each one.

According to recent reports, model routing fixes that. A router looks at each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it, and keeps the expensive model for the requests that need it.

In this guide we'll cover what model routing is, how routers decide, and what it saves. Then we'll build a small router in about 60 lines of JavaScript and run it over 200 customer messages. At one setting it matched a large model's accuracy for about a third of the cost. At another it came within a point and a half for 89% less.

Model routing in AI is the practice of sending each request to the model best suited to it, instead of sending every request to one model. A router sits between your app and a pool of models, reads each request, and picks a model based on what you care about: cost, speed, or quality.

It has been revealed that you'll also see it called AI model routing, LLM routing, or LLM model routing. They all mean the same thing. The pool might be a small and a large model from one provider, or models from several providers behind one API.

The idea rests on one observation: most requests are easy. A small model answers them as well as a large one, in a fraction of the time and for a fraction of the price. The router's whole job is finding the hard ones.

The diagram below reveals a typical AI model routing architecture.

Model routing works in three steps: the router reads the request, decides which model should answer it, and forwards the request to that model. The middle step is where routers differ. Routing tools decide which model to use in one of four ways.

Industry observers note that rule-based routing uses rules you write by hand. Requests from free-strategy consumers go to a small model. Anything tagged as code goes to a coding model. Prompts over a certain length go to a model with a bigger context window. It's simple, predictable, and free to run, but the rules only know what you thought of in advance.

According to recent reports, intelligent model routing uses a model to make the decision. A small, fast classifier reads each request and predicts which model in the pool will answer it well. You'll also see it called smart or dynamic model routing.

Two more terms come up here. Task-aware routing picks a model by the kind of job, like summarising, coding, or answering a support question. Context-aware routing also looks at what surrounds the request, like the conversation so far, the user, or the tools available.

The big platforms work this way. Microsoft describes its Foundry model router as "a trained language model" that picks a model for each prompt in real time. Google indicates Gemini Notebook uses its fresh Decisions API as a real-time router, serving everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency. I've tested the Google Decisions API against Jev on the same messages we'll use below.

Cascade routing tries the cheapest model first and only moves up when the answer isn't good enough. The usual test is confidence: if the cheap model is sure, keep its answer. If it isn't, send the request to a stronger model. It's also called confidence-based routing, and it's what we'll build below.

A cascade needs no separate classifier, because the first model's own confidence does the routing. The trade-off is that escalated requests pay for two models and wait for both.

Fallback routing is about staying up, not saving money. If a model times out, hits a rate limit, or its provider has an outage, the router sends the request to the next model on a list. Most production routers combine fallbacks with one of the three methods above.

The main benefits of model routing in AI systems are lower cost, faster responses, and fewer outages, without giving up quality on the hard requests.

It has been revealed that we'll build a cascade router for a job every support tool has: sorting customer messages. Each message gets one of ten labels, like atm support or request refund.

The test set is 200 messages from Banking77, a public set of banking support messages: ten labels, 20 messages each. They're the same 200 messages from my zero shot classification test, which is where the single-model numbers below come from.

In a recent development, put both keys in a .env file and run the examples with node --env-file=.env. It's the same setup as in my guide to getting a YouTube API key.

Create router.mjs. The first function sends the message to Jev with one multiple-choice question, and returns the label Jev picked along with its confidence:.

In a recent development, confidence runs from 0 to 1. When nearly all the probability sits on one label, it's close to 1. When Jev is torn between two labels, it drops.

The second function asks Claude Opus 5.5 the same question. The output_config block limits the answer to one of our labels, so there's no free text to parse. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema explains how that works.

The router itself is about a dozen lines:.

According to recent reports, if Jev is at least 80% confident, its answer goes straight back. If not, Claude answers instead. And if Claude fails, the router falls back to Jev's answer, because a shaky answer beats an error page.

Try it on an easy message and a harder one:.

Jev was sure about the lost card. On the ATM question it leaned towards card acceptance with a confidence of 0.64, so the router asked Claude, which got it right.

Because cheap, strong, and threshold are options, the same function routes between any two models.

Model routing reduces AI costs by keeping easy requests on a cheap model and paying for the expensive one only when it's needed. Here's what that looked like on our 200 messages, starting with each model on its own:.

Opus gets six more messages right out of 200, and costs more than 120 times as much.

Now the router, at four confidence thresholds:.

Recent findings suggest that speed improved too. At the 0.8 threshold, the messages Jev kept came back in a median of 227 ms. The ones that escalated took about 2.1 seconds, because they waited for both models.

A note on method: I ran every message through both models once and saved the answers, then replayed the router over them at each threshold. That's how you compare thresholds without paying for the same test four times.

Then I ran the router live to check. At 0.95 it scored the same 95.0% and sent 61 messages to Opus. At 0.8 it scored 93.5% and sent 20, a point under the replay. Two answers moved: one of Jev's confidence scores landed at 0.82 instead of 0.78, just over the line, and Opus changed its answer on one message. Scores near the threshold shift a little between runs, so leave yourself a margin.

It has been revealed that the choice of cheap model matters less than you'd think. With Google's Gemini Decision 1 in first place instead of Jev, a 0.7 threshold reached the same 95% for US$0.28 per 1,000 messages.

Industry observers note that model routing can cost a little quality, and the threshold decides how much. In our test the gap to Opus ranged from nothing at 0.95 to two points at 0.7.

Sources indicate that the loss comes from one place: answers the cheap model got wrong while feeling sure. At the 0.8 threshold, Jev kept five wrong answers because its confidence was above the line. Opus got four of those five wrong as well, so only one was a real loss: "Do all ATMs take this card?", which Jev filed under card acceptance with a confidence of 0.91.

Escalating isn't risk-free either. On one message, Jev had the right label with a confidence of 0.44, and Opus overruled it with the wrong one.

To optimize costs using AI model routing, measure first, route second, and keep measuring. These six steps cover LLM model routing cost optimization for any pair of models:.

In a recent development, the return is easy to estimate once you know the split. If nine in ten requests stay on a model that costs 1% as much, the bill drops by about 89%, which is what we measured.

According to recent reports, several inference providers have multi-model routing built in, and most AI gateway platforms support model routing too, so you don't have to write your own. As of November 2026, these are the top model routing solutions for AI apps. Each name links to the tool's model routing docs:.

Hosted model routing platforms for large language models decide for you, which is the fastest way to start. A hand-built router like ours takes more work, but you choose the signal and you can see why every request went where it did.

An LLM router is the component that does model routing for large language models. It can be a function in your own code, like the one in this guide, a hosted model such as Microsoft Foundry's model router, or a feature of an AI gateway.

In a recent development, smart model routing is another name for intelligent model routing: a model, not a hand-written rule, decides where each request goes. Dynamic model routing means the same thing.

Sources indicate that the ROI of AI model routing depends on how much of your traffic a cheaper model can handle. In our test, a 0.8 threshold kept 89.5% of messages on the cheap model and cut the cost per 1,000 messages from US$1.96 to US$0.22, for about a point of accuracy. The build was about 60 lines of code.

Recent findings suggest that openRouter's auto model routing works through its Auto Router. You set the model to openrouter/auto, and a decision model picks a model and a reasoning effort for each request. You pay the standard rate of whichever model it selects, with no extra fee.

According to recent reports, openClaw model routing is a primary model plus an ordered list of fallbacks. In the OpenClaw model routing configuration you set agents.defaults.model.primary and agents.defaults.model.fallbacks, and an agent can override the fallback list. When a model fails, OpenClaw first rotates auth profiles on the same provider, then moves to the next model on the list, as its model failover docs describe. That makes it fallback routing, not cost-based routing.

An AI gateway simplifies model routing by putting every model behind one API, one set of keys, and one place for logs. Your app calls the gateway, and the routing rules live in config instead of code, so changing a model doesn't need a deploy.

Mid-stream failover is when a router switches models after a streamed response has already started, because the first model failed partway through. It's the hardest kind of failover, because the user has already seen part of an answer. Many routers only fail over before the first token arrives and return an error after that, so check what your gateway does.

Latest Update: PRX Part 3 — Training a Text-to-Image Model in 24h!

📅 03 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the last two posts (Part 1 and Part 2), we explored a wide range of architectural and training tricks for diffusion models.
  • In this post, we want to answer a much more practical question:.
  • What happens when we combine all the tricks that worked?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the last two posts (Part 1 and Part 2), we explored a wide range of architectural and training tricks for diffusion models. We tried to evaluate each idea in isolation, measuring throughput, convergence speed, and final image quality, and tried to understand what actually moves the needle.

In this post, we want to answer a much more practical question:.

What happens when we combine all the tricks that worked?

Instead of optimizing one dimension at a time, we’ll stack the most promising ingredients together and see how far we can push performance under a strict compute budget.

To make things concrete, we’re doing a 24-hour speedrun:.

This is very far from the early diffusion days, where training competitive models could cost millions of dollars. The goal here is to demonstrate how much the field has evolved and how far careful engineering can take you in just a single day of training.

According to recent reports, this speedrun is not just a fun experiment. It will likely serve as the foundation for our large-scale training recipe going forward.

Alongside the results, we’re also open-sourcing our code (Github link), which contains:.

So you can reproduce, modify, and extend everything yourself.

Now let’s walk through what went into this 24h run.

We use the x-prediction formulation from Back to Basics: Let Denoising Generative Models Denoise [Li and He, 2025]. As seen in Part 2, this enables training directly in pixel space and eliminates the need for a VAE altogether. We use a patch size of 32 and use a 256-dimensional bottleneck in the initial token projection layer. This design keeps the sequence length under control, making pixel-space training computationally manageable even at higher resolutions.

At 512px, the sequence length is:.

(512/32)2=256 (512 / 32)^2 = 256 (512/32)2=256.

At 1024px, the sequence length becomes:.

(1024/32)2=1024 (1024 / 32)^2 = 1024 (1024/32)2=1024.

Instead of following the usual 256px → 512px → 1024px schedule, we start directly at 512px and then fine-tune at 1024px.

With controlled token counts and modern hardware, pixel-space training is no longer prohibitive. It is simply a cleaner and more direct formulation.

One very nice side effect of predicting x0x_0x0​ directly in pixel space is that we can reuse a whole toolbox from classical computer vision.

It has been revealed that when your model outputs latents, perceptual supervision becomes awkward. You either have to decode back to pixels or define losses in a learned latent space that may or may not align with human perception. Once you predict pixels directly, everything becomes straightforward again. You can plug in perceptual losses exactly as they were originally designed.

Sources indicate that we take inspiration from the paper PixelGen: Pixel Diffusion Beats Latent Diffusion with Perceptual Loss [Ma et al.], where the authors introduce additional perceptual objectives on top of the diffusion loss. They show that adding perceptual signals can noticeably improve convergence speed and final visual quality.

For this 24h run, we add two auxiliary losses:.

Industry observers note that the idea is simple: In addition to the standard flow matching objective, we encourage the predicted clean image to match the target image in a perceptual feature space. LPIPS captures low-level perceptual similarity, while DINO features provide a stronger semantic signal.

Recent findings suggest that we keep the same overall idea as the paper, but we tweaked a few details. In our experiments, we empirically found that it worked better to:.

These are small implementation details, but in our setting they consistently gave better results.

We used a weight of 0.1 for the LPIPS loss and 0.01 for the DINO perceptual loss, matching the values recommended in the original paper.

These losses are lightweight compared to the main transformer forward pass, and in our setup they add only a small overhead while providing a consistent quality boost.

To make each step cheaper, we use token routing with TREAD [Krause et al., 2025]), which randomly selects a fraction of tokens and lets them bypass a contiguous chunk of transformer blocks, then re-injects them later so nothing is dropped.

According to recent reports, we picked TREAD over SPRINT (Park et al., 2025) mostly for simplicity, and because the extra complexity of SPRINT did not feel worth the fairly small additional compute savings in our setting (sequence length 64 vs. 128 with TREAD at 512px).

Following the TREAD recipe, we route 50% of the tokens from the 2nd block to the penultimate block of the transformer.

Routed models can look worse under vanilla CFG, especially when undertrained, so we implemented a simple self-guidance scheme inspired by Guiding Token-Sparse Diffusion Models (Krause et al., 2025), which guides using a dense vs. routed conditional prediction instead of relying on an unconditional branch.

We used REPA [Yu et al., 2024] for representation alignment.

According to recent reports, for the teacher, we went with DINOv3 [Siméoni et al. 2025] since it gave the best quality improvements in our previous experiments.

Concretely, we apply the alignment loss once,at the 8th transformer block with a loss weight of 0.5.

Since we combine REPA with TREAD routing, we only compute the alignment loss on the non-routed tokens, meaning the tokens that actually go through the blocks where we apply the loss. This keeps the REPA signal consistent and avoids comparing features for tokens that skipped the computation path.

We used the Muon optimizer, using the FSDP implementation from muon_fsdp_2, since it revealed a clear improvement over Adam in our previous runs.

It has been revealed that muon is only applied to 2D parameters (basically matrices). Everything else (biases, norms, embeddings, etc.) is optimized with Adam, which is why the config has two parameter groups.

We trained on three publicly available synthetic datasets:.

The schedule is basically: go fast at 512, then sharpen at 1024:.

We also keep an EMA of the weights for sampling and eval:.

Below are the evaluation curves we tracked throughout the run and a few sample grids from the final checkpoint:.

It has been revealed that for a one day training run, this is already a pretty solid place to be. The model is not flawless yet (you can still spot some texture glitches, occasional weird anatomy, and it can get a bit shaky on very hard prompts), but it is clearly usable. Prompt following is strong, the overall aesthetic is consistent, and the 1024 stage mostly does what we want: sharpen details without breaking composition.

In a recent development, the key takeaway is that we're very close. The remaining challenges look more like undertraining artifacts and limited data diversity than signs of a structural flaw in the recipe. The failure modes are consistent with what you’d expect from a model that simply hasn’t seen enough varied data yet. With more compute and broader coverage, this exact setup should continue improving in a fairly predictable way.

Zooming out, this speed run also highlights how far diffusion training has come. By combining pixel-space training, efficient routing, representation alignment, and lightweight perceptual guidance, you can now get a meaningful model in about a day on a budget that would have sounded unrealistic not that long ago.

This 24h run is just a starting point, not the finish line. Next, we will keep pushing the same recipe with a bit more scale and iterate on the dataset mix and captioning.

All the code and configs behind this speedrun, as well as the full experimental framework used throughout Part 1 and Part 2, are available in the PRX repository: https://github.com/Photoroom/PRX.

Industry observers note that while we don’t redistribute the exact training datasets used in this run, the pipeline is fully configurable and designed to be easily adapted to your own data. You can plug in different datasets, tweak individual components (TREAD, REPA, perceptual losses, Muon, etc.), and run controlled experiments with minimal friction. Our goal is to make this a practical playground for fast diffusion research, and we hope the community will use it to explore, benchmark, and iterate on these techniques in their own setups.

According to recent reports, if you made it this far, thank you for reading. We would also love to have you join our Discord community, where we share PRX progress and results, and discuss anything diffusion and text-to-image related.

Sources indicate that goodbye for now, and stay tuned for the next round of experiments! 🚀.

Sources indicate that this speedrun was inspired by several recent efforts exploring fast and low-cost training of diffusion models. If you're interested in speedrunning text-to-image models, we encourage you to check out the following works:.

Yeah, definitely not possible on consumer hardware… yet :D That’s also why we added the $1500 tag.

Regarding releasing the captions, we hadn’t really thought about that. If you think it would be valuable for the community, we can work on releasing them as well.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In this post, we'll walk through how Modular Diffusers works — from the familiar API to run a modular pipeline, to building fully custom blocks and composing them into your own workflow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that modular Diffusers introduces a new way to build diffusion pipelines by composing reusable blocks. Instead of writing entire pipelines from scratch, you can mix and match blocks to create workflows tailored to your needs! This complements the existing DiffusionPipeline class with a more flexible, composable alternative.

In this post, we'll walk through how Modular Diffusers works — from the familiar API to run a modular pipeline, to building fully custom blocks and composing them into your own workflow. We'll also show how it integrates with Mellon, a node-based visual workflow interface that you can use to wire Modular Diffusers blocks together.

Here is a simple example of how to run inference with FLUX.2 Klein 4B using pre-built blocks:.

You get the same results as with a standard DiffusionPipeline, but the pipeline is very different under the hood: it's composed of flexible blocks — text encoding, image encoding, denoising, and decoding — that you can inspect directly:.

Each block is self-contained with its own inputs and outputs. You can run any block independently as its own pipeline, or add, remove, and swap blocks freely — they dynamically recompose to work with whatever blocks remain. Use .init_pipeline() to convert blocks into a runnable pipeline, and .load_components() to load the model weights.

For more on block types, composition patterns, lazy loading, and memory management with ComponentsManager, check out the Modular Diffusers documentation.

Modular Diffusers really shines when creating your own blocks. A custom block is a Python class that defines its components, inputs, outputs, and computation logic — and once defined, you can plug it into any workflow.

Here's an example block that extracts depth maps from images using Depth Anything V2.

In a recent development, let's use this block with Qwen's ControlNet workflow. Extract the ControlNet workflow and insert the depth block at the beginning:.

Blocks in a sequence share data automatically: the depth block's control_image output flows to downstream blocks that need it, and its image input becomes a pipeline input since no earlier block provides it.

You can publish your custom block to the Hub so anyone can load it with trust_remote_code=True. We've created a template to get you started — check out the Building Custom Blocks guide for the full walkthrough.

The DepthProcessorBlock from this post is published at diffusers/depth-processor-custom-block — you can load and use it directly:.

We've published a collection of ready-to-use custom blocks here.

ModularPipeline.from_pretrained works with any existing Diffusers repo out of the box, but Modular Diffusers also introduces a new kind of repo: the Modular Repository.

A modular repository is able to reference components from their original model repos. For example, diffusers/flux2-bnb-4bit-modular contains a quantized transformer and loads the remaining components from the original repo.

Modular repositories can also host custom pipeline blocks as Python code and visual UI configurations for tools like Mellon — all in one place.

The community has already started building complete pipelines with Modular Diffusers and publishing them on the Hub, with model weights and ready-to-run code.

Teams can build novel architectures, package them as blocks, and publish the entire pipeline on the Hub for anyone to use with ModularPipeline.from_pretrained.

Check out the full collection of community pipelines for more.

In a recent development, 💡 Mellon is in early development and not ready for production use yet. Consider this a sneak peek of how the integration works!

Industry observers note that mellon is a node graph interface integrated with Modular Diffusers. If you're familiar with node-based tools like ComfyUI, you'll feel right at home — but there are some key differences:.

Sources indicate that this integration is possible because every block exposes the same properties (inputs, intermediate_outputs, expected_components). This consistent API means Mellon can automatically generate a node's UI from any block definition and compose blocks into higher-level nodes.

It has been revealed that for example, diffusers/FLUX.2-klein-4B-modular contains a pipeline definition, component references, and a mellon_pipeline_config.json — all in one repo. Load it in Python with ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("diffusers/FLUX.2-klein-4B-modular") or in Mellon to create either a single-node or multi-node workflow.

Here's a quick example. We add a Gemini prompt expansion node — hosted as a modular repo at diffusers/gemini-prompt-expander-mellon — to an existing text-to-image workflow:.

In a recent development, gemini expands your short prompt into a detailed description before generating the image. No code, no configuration — just a Hub repo id.

Sources indicate that this is just one example. For a detailed walkthrough, check out the Mellon x Modular Diffusers guide. You can also check out this video!

Industry observers note that modular Diffusers brings the composability and flexibility the community has been asking for, without compromising the features that make Diffusers powerful. It's still early — we want your input to shape what comes next. Give it a try and tell us what works, what doesn't, and what's missing.

According to recent reports, elementor made your site easy to build. It may also be making it slow. Here's how to move a site onto the Block Editor without breaking URLs, losing content or dropping out of Google.

Recent findings suggest that page builders solved a real problem. Before the Block Editor matured, they were the easiest way to give clients drag-and-drop layouts. Many of those sites are still running today, and a lot of them are slow on phones.

In a recent development, the data backs that up. According to the HTTP Archive Core Web Vitals Technology Report for June 2026, 36.8% of Elementor sites pass Core Web Vitals on mobile. Sites built with the Block Editor pass 53.0% of the time. That's correlation, not proof, since hosting and setup matter too. But in my experience, it matches what happens when you remove the builder from a slow site.

According to recent reports, my reason for migrating sites off Elementor is simple: **page builders make websites heavy. **Having said that, Elementor has improved a lot. Its performance settings, Flexbox Containers, and asset-loading options cut much of the bloat, and a carefully tuned Elementor site can pass Core Web Vitals. But tuning only goes so far. You’re still shipping the builder’s framework, wrapper markup and scripts, and every plugin or Elementor enhancement is a chance for the speed to slip again.

For small business sites that don’t need drag-and-drop editing, rebuilding the same design on the WordPress Block Editor (Gutenberg) removes that weight at the source, without changing what the client sees.

Recent findings suggest that this guide follows the order I use. It assumes you're comfortable with WordPress admin, WP-CLI and a staging site. If you need to set those up first, SitePoint's guide to the ultimate WordPress development environment covers the tooling.

Not every Elementor site needs to move. Migration makes sense when:.

It's harder to justify when the site leans on Elementor Pro features you'd need to replace, such as complex popups, dynamic loops or WooCommerce templates. Those can all be rebuilt, but the job gets bigger fast.

You can't prove a migration worked without "before" numbers. Capture these on the live site first.

Crawl the site with a tool such as Screaming Frog, and export every indexable URL with its title, meta description, H1 and canonical tag. You can also pull published pages and posts with WP-CLI:.

It has been revealed that run Google PageSpeed Insights, which uses Lighthouse for its lab scores, on the homepage and two or three key templates. Save the mobile lab scores and, if the site has enough traffic, the field data from real people.

Export the last three months of pages and queries from Google Search Console. That's what you'll compare against after launch.

Industry observers note that elementor stores each page's layout as JSON in the elementordata post meta field, and marks builder pages with elementoredit_mode. This command lists every page that uses the builder:.

Then list everything else Elementor controls, which is easy to miss:.

In a recent development, on the small business sites I've migrated, the inventory usually turns up more than the owner expects. The pages are the easy part. The surprises are saved templates nobody remembers creating, a popup still running on every page, add-on widgets from plugins that were installed once and forgotten, and contact forms that live inside Elementor Pro rather than a form plugin. Finding those before the rebuild saves a broken launch.

Work on a staging copy. Install a block theme, such as Twenty Twenty-Five or a lightweight starter theme, and move the Elementor global styles into theme.json. That way colors, fonts and spacing are defined once, instead of in every widget.

Sources indicate that copy the hex values and font names from Elementor's Site Settings so the fresh site matches the old one. Rebuild the header and footer as template parts in the Site Editor. If you'd rather write a theme yourself, SitePoint's series on building a WordPress theme from scratch covers the basics.

According to recent reports, most Elementor sites repeat the same few sections: a hero, a services grid, testimonials and a call to action. Build each one once as a block pattern, then reuse it on every page. Patterns are plain block markup, so you don't need React to write them, whatever you may have heard about React and WordPress development.

In a block theme, any PHP file in the /patterns folder with a header comment is registered automatically:.

Industry observers note that for page content, there's a useful shortcut. Elementor saves a plain HTML copy of each page into post_content. Open a page in the Block Editor, and the old content usually appears in a Classic block. Choose Convert to blocks, then delete the leftovers and rebuild the layout with your patterns. It keeps the copy and images, so you only redo the design.

Sources indicate that the difference indicates up in the page source. Here's typical front-end markup for a single heading on an Elementor page, using the older section and column layout:.

And the same heading as a block:.

Newer Elementor versions with Flexbox containers and the optimized markup settings trim some of those wrappers, but most older sites still carry all of them. Multiply that by every element on every page, and the weight adds up.

Recent findings suggest that to speed up this step, I built a free Elementor to Gutenberg converter. Paste in a page's elementordata JSON from Step 2, and it returns block markup you can paste into the Block Editor's code editor. It handles headings, text, images, buttons, spacers, dividers and column layouts, and lists anything it can't convert, such as forms and popups, for you to rebuild by hand. It runs entirely in your browser, so the page data never leaves your computer.

The code is rarely what holds a migration up. Content is. Once clients see their site being rebuilt, many decide it's time to rewrite their pages too, and the project ends up waiting on copywriters and approvals. My fix is to separate the two: migrate the existing content as it is, launch, then patch the copy afterwards. That keeps the speed and SEO gains on schedule, and it means any ranking change can be traced to either the migration or the new copy, not both at once.

This is the step that decides whether rankings hold.

To spot-check a redirect or a status code from the command line:.

When staging matches the live site, deploy it. Then:.

Leave the old elementordata meta in place for a few weeks, in case you need to roll back. Once you're confident, take a backup and remove it to shrink the database.

According to recent reports, run PageSpeed Insights again straight away for lab scores. Field data takes longer: the Chrome UX Report uses a rolling 28-day window, so give it a month before judging real-user results. Compare Search Console clicks for the same period before and after launch.

It has been revealed that in my migrations, the biggest change is usually page weight and loading time, because the builder's CSS, JavaScript and wrapper markup are gone. What doesn't always improve is server response time. If the site is on slow shared hosting, the first byte still arrives late, and that needs a hosting fix, not a rebuild. Search traffic should hold steady if the URLs and metadata were protected. If it drops, the Step 5 crawl comparison is the first place to look.

Moving off Elementor isn't a one-click job, but it isn't a full redesign either. Record a baseline, inventory what the builder controls, rebuild with patterns, and protect every URL. Most of the speed gain comes from removing code the site never needed. For what to tackle after that, see these practical web performance techniques. Most of the risk comes from rushing the SEO checks. Done carefully, the client gets the same site, a faster one, and an editor that comes with WordPress itself.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, in synchronous control pipelines, while the VLA is running inference, the arm is idle awaiting commands leading to oscillatory behavior and delayed corrections.
  • Bringing VLA models to embedded platforms is not a matter of model compression, but a complex systems engineering problem requiring architectural decomposition, latency-aware scheduling, and hardware-aligned execution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Authors: Enzo Ruedas, Tess Boivin.

Sources indicate that recent advances in Large Language Models have enabled the transition from text-only reasoning to multimodal systems. First, with the integration of visual perception in Vision–Language Models (VLMs), and more recently with the generation of robot actions in Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models. Deploying these models on embedded robotic platforms remains a challenge due to tight constraints in terms of compute, memory, and power, as well as real-time control requirements.

In a recent development, in synchronous control pipelines, while the VLA is running inference, the arm is idle awaiting commands leading to oscillatory behavior and delayed corrections. To tackle that, asynchronous Inference can enable smooth and continuous motion by dissociating generation from execution. However, to be effective, the end-to-end inference latency must remain shorter than the action execution duration. This temporal constraint therefore sets an upper limit on the model's throughput.

Bringing VLA models to embedded platforms is not a matter of model compression, but a complex systems engineering problem requiring architectural decomposition, latency-aware scheduling, and hardware-aligned execution. Addressing these challenges is essential to translate recent advances in multimodal foundation models into practical and deployable embedded robotic systems.

This guide presents NXP’s hands‑on best practices for recording reliable robotic datasets, fine‑tuning VLA policies (ACT and SmolVLA), and hightlights the real-time performance that NXP i.MX 95 SoC achieves after optimization.

In a recent development, high‑quality, consistent data beats “more but messy” data. This section turns hard‑earned lessons into concrete checklists and schemas.

In our case, we recorded a dataset for the task: "Put the tea bag in the mug.".

Moving from scene‑only views to mixed viewpoints increases the global accuracy, but the more cameras you have the more the latency is impacted. Therefore, you must choose right compromise. In our case that balance was reached with 3 cameras:.

It has been revealed that we strongly recommend using a gripper-mounted camera. It consistently improves success rates on fine manipulation tasks by providing a close, task-relevant viewpoint. Importantly, it is also the camera that most effectively enforces correct data collection practices, allowing the operator to rely exclusively on the robot’s perception rather than observing the scene directly.

When installing a gripper camera, we recommend securing the cable with Velcro or a strain-relief guide to prevent it from obstructing the field of view or becoming disconnected during motion.

Simple hardware tweaks like heat‑shrink tubing over gripper claws increase friction, reduce roughness, reduce slippage during episodes, and increase task success rate (fewer “almost success” episodes), improving policy learning stability.

When recording a dataset, you should:.

Vary episodes distribution: Divide your workspace into starting-position clusters, and record at least 10 episodes per cluster. Add diversity by changing the object position and rotation.

e.g. we partitioned the robot arm’s reachable workspace into 11 clusters, each measuring 10 × 10 cm.

Differentiate training & validation sets: Policies can easily overfit on the training set, so make sure that the validation set is unseen by the model.

e.g. we removed cluster 6 from the training set.

Recent findings suggest that record the most movements you can: Small VLA models exhibit limited generalization on unseen motion. Therefore, record episodes that cover the wider ranges of degrees of freedom.

Recent findings suggest that e.g. we grasped the tea bag either in horizontal or vertical position.

Anticipate failure: Sometimes the policy will not reach the object the first time and will have to "go back to it". We noticed that having 20% of all episodes that corresponds to the case of going back to the object help the model improve overall success rate.

According to recent reports, e.g. around 20% of our training set corresponds to recovery episodes.

This mirrors best practices across VLA papers and community guides. Here are 3 examples of data diversity within the same cluster:.

It has been revealed that starting positions 1 and 2 correspond to different positions within the same cluster. In contrast, during the recovery episode, the robot does not begin in "starting mode"; but is instead already near the mug and should proceed directly to retrieve the tea bag from that location.

The range providing the best trade-off between accuracy, generalization, and motion smoothness across both the training and validation sets was found for ACT (100 actions per chunk) within a 100k-160k training steps. For SMolVLA training (50 actions per chunk), the trade‑off appears after many more training steps. We found that continuing training slightly past the point where the model begins to overfit tends to improve overall accuracy.

Rule of thumb: choose final checkpoint by evaluating success on both training and validation set, not by training loss.

It has been revealed that the i.MX 95 SoC integrates 6× Arm Cortex‑A55, a Cortex‑M7 and a Cortex M33 MCU, a Mali GPU, a fresh NXP ISP, and the eIQ® Neutron NPU, targeting efficient, secure edge inference with multi‑camera support and strong I/O. [nxp.com].

Instead of running the models as one monolithic graph, we decompose the VLA graph into logical stages: encoders, decoders, and action experts. Therefore, allowing each component to be optimized, scheduled, and deployed independently.

Industry observers note that this separation allows per-block optimizations. The impact of each block quantization can be measured to choose the best tradeoff between latency and accuracy. Also, isolating the action expert from the VLM was ideal to run it at lower frequency.

Sources indicate that in order to optimize the inference for i.MX 95 SoC, we explored several quantization techniques on different blocks. We found that quantizing the vision encoder and LLM prefill had limited impact on accuracy, whereas quantization of the denoising flow in the action expert significantly degrades performance.This behaviour is expected, as quantization errors are accumulating across iterative denoising steps.

That is why we decided to keep this block at higher precision to preserve stability, while on the other blocks, we explored various quantization configurations, from 8-bit mixed precision to 4-bit quantization, depending on the layers.

With Asynchronous Inference, action generation runs in parallel with execution:.

This increases effective control frequency, reduces observation staleness, and improves recovery behavior.

On embedded platforms such as the i.MX 95 SoC, asynchronous inference is essential — but only effective if inference latency is kept under the action horizon budget: inference time < execution time.

Our immediate objective is to improve task accuracy with SmolVLA (ONNX FP32). We have already established a baseline and measured an optimized on-board inference latency of 6.15 s.

  • Industry observers note that with over 200 merged PRs and over 50 fresh contributors since v0.4.0, LeRobot v0.5.0 is our biggest release yet — expanding in every direction at once.
  • LeRobot v0.5.0 adds full Unitree G1 humanoid support (whole-body control models), new policies –including Pi0-FAST autoregressive VLAs and Real-Time Chunking for responsive inference–, and streaming video encoding that eliminates wait times between recording episodes.
  • LeRobot v0.5.0 dramatically expands the roster of supported hardware — from arms and mobile robots to a full humanoid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that with over 200 merged PRs and over 50 fresh contributors since v0.4.0, LeRobot v0.5.0 is our biggest release yet — expanding in every direction at once. More robots (including our first humanoid), more policies (including the comeback of autoregressive VLAs), faster datasets, simulation environments you can load straight from the Hub, and a modernized codebase running on Python 3.12 and Transformers v5. Whether you're training policies in simulation or deploying them on real hardware, v0.5.0 has something for you.

LeRobot v0.5.0 adds full Unitree G1 humanoid support (whole-body control models), new policies –including Pi0-FAST autoregressive VLAs and Real-Time Chunking for responsive inference–, and streaming video encoding that eliminates wait times between recording episodes. The release also introduces EnvHub for loading simulation environments from the Hugging Face Hub, NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena integration, and a major codebase modernization with Python 3.12+, Transformers v5, and third-party policy plugins.

LeRobot v0.5.0 dramatically expands the roster of supported hardware — from arms and mobile robots to a full humanoid.

The biggest hardware addition in this release: full Unitree G1 humanoid support. This is LeRobot's first humanoid integration, and it's comprehensive:.

The G1 integration represents a major step toward general-purpose robotics within LeRobot — moving beyond tabletop arms into full-body embodied AI. Try it out yourself by following the documentation.

It has been revealed that we've added support for the OpenArm robot and its companion OpenArm Mini teleoperator. OpenArm is a capable robot arm with full LeRobot integration, and the Mini serves as its natural teleoperation device. Both support bi-manual configurations, enabling dual-arm setups for more complex manipulation tasks. Check it out in the documentation.

The hardware ecosystem keeps growing:.

New motor controller support via CAN (Controller Area Network) bus opens the door to higher-performance actuators:.

These additions mean LeRobot can now drive a wider variety of professional-grade actuators beyond the existing Dynamixel and Feetech ecosystem.

This release brings six new policies and techniques into LeRobot, pushing the boundaries of what's possible with open-source robot learning.

It has been revealed that pi0-FAST brings autoregressive Vision-Language-Action models to LeRobot with FAST (Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization). Unlike the flow-matching approach of Pi0, Pi0-FAST uses an autoregressive action expert (based on Gemma 300M) that generates discretized action tokens, enabling:.

Real-Time Chunking is an inference-time technique from Physical Intelligence that makes flow-matching policies dramatically more responsive. Instead of waiting for a full action chunk to finish before replanning, RTC continuously blends latest predictions with in-progress actions, producing smoother and more reactive behavior.

RTC is not a standalone policy — it's an enhancement that plugs into existing flow-matching policies (Pi0 family, SmolVLA & Diffusion). Configure it via --policy.rtc_config.enabled=true.

This is a game-changer for real-world deployment where latency matters. Read the original paper for the technical details and our documentation.

Wall-X is a new VLA policy built on Qwen2.5-VL with flow-matching action prediction. It combines the strong vision-language understanding of Qwen2.5-VL with a flow-matching head for cross-embodiment robotic control.

It has been revealed that X-VLA brings a Florence2-based VLA to LeRobot. Built on Microsoft's Florence-2 vision-language model, X-VLA offers an alternative backbone for VLA policies, expanding the diversity of foundation models available for robot learning. Check out the training guide for setup instructions and the base model.

SARM (Stage-Aware Reward Modeling) tackles one of the hardest problems in robot learning: long-horizon tasks. Instead of using a single global linear progress signal over the whole episode, it models progress in a stage-aware manner by predicting both the task stage and the progress within that stage. This makes it much easier to train policies for complex, multi-step manipulation tasks. Start experimenting with it by following the documentation.

You can now fine-tune large VLAs using LoRA (and other PEFT methods) without modifying the core training pipeline. PEFT configuration lives at the policy level, making it straightforward to adapt massive foundation models to your specific robot and task with a fraction of the compute. Learn more reading the documentation.

The dataset pipeline gets major performance improvements in this release, making both data collection and training significantly faster.

Sources indicate that previously, recording a dataset meant waiting after each episode for video encoding to finish. No more. With streaming video encoding, frames are encoded in real-time as they're captured — meaning zero wait time between episodes. Just finish one episode and immediately start the next.

Streaming encoding also supports hardware encoder auto-detection, so if your system has a GPU-accelerated video encoder, LeRobot will use it automatically:.

Streaming encoding performance can vary significantly depending on your hardware and recording setup (number of cameras, resolution, etc.). Make sure to review the streaming video encoding documentation before enabling it.

Under the hood, we've fixed key data access bottlenecks and overhauled image processing:.

The dataset editing toolkit continues to grow:.

EnvHub is a fresh way to use simulation environments in LeRobot: load them directly from the Hugging Face Hub. Instead of installing environment packages locally and wiring up registration, you can now point LeRobot at a Hub repository and it handles everything — downloading the environment code, registering it with Gymnasium, and making it available for training and evaluation.

Hub environments use HubEnvConfig, which downloads and executes remote make_env functions:.

Industry observers note that this lowers the barrier for sharing custom simulation environments with the community. Package your environment, push it to the Hub, and anyone can train on it. Check out the documentation to learn more. Here's an example to get started: LeIsaac x LeRobot EnvHub tutorial.

It has been revealed that we've integrated NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena, bringing GPU-accelerated simulation to LeRobot. IsaacLab-Arena provides a collection of manipulation tasks running on NVIDIA's Isaac Sim, offering massively parallel environment instances for fast reinforcement learning. The integration includes dedicated pre/post-processing steps and full compatibility with LeRobot's training pipeline. Check out the documentation.

This release modernizes the codebase:.

Sources indicate that beyond these headline features, v0.5.0 includes hundreds of bug fixes, documentation improvements, CI/CD enhancements, and quality-of-life improvements across the entire codebase. From better type checking to more robust test infrastructure, we're investing in the foundations that make LeRobot reliable and maintainable as it scales.

In a recent development, we want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community — contributors, users, and collaborators alike — for helping LeRobot grow into what it is today. Every bug report, PR, and discussion makes this project better.

According to recent reports, stay tuned for more to come 🤗 Get started here! – The LeRobot team ❤️.

Ulysses Sequence Parallelism: Training with Million-Token Contexts

📅 09 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1488 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Training large language models on long sequences has become essential for building capable AI systems.
  • Ulysses Sequence Parallelism (part of the Arctic Long Sequence Training (ALST) protocol from Snowflake AI Research) provides an elegant solution by distributing the attention computation across multiple GPUs through attention head parallelism.
  • The attention mechanism in transformers scales quadratically with sequence length.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Training large language models on long sequences has become essential for building capable AI systems. As models are increasingly used for tasks like document analysis, code understanding, complex reasoning, and RAG workloads, the need to process sequences of hundreds of thousands—or even millions—of tokens has grown dramatically. To put this in perspective, an average book is roughly 250k tokens, so training on multi-document contexts or book-length inputs requires handling sequences well beyond what fits on a single GPU. However, training with such long contexts presents significant memory challenges: the attention computation scales quadratically with sequence length, rapidly exceeding GPU memory for contexts beyond tens of thousands of tokens.

Ulysses Sequence Parallelism (part of the Arctic Long Sequence Training (ALST) protocol from Snowflake AI Research) provides an elegant solution by distributing the attention computation across multiple GPUs through attention head parallelism. In this post, we'll explore how Ulysses works and how it's been integrated across the Hugging Face ecosystem—from Accelerate to the Transformers Trainer and TRL's SFTTrainer.

The attention mechanism in transformers scales quadratically with sequence length. For a sequence of length n n n, standard attention requires O(n2) O(n^2) O(n2) FLOPs and O(n2) O(n^2) O(n2) memory to compute and store the attention score matrix. Optimized implementations like FlashAttention reduce the memory to O(n) O(n) O(n) by tiling the computation and never materializing the full attention matrix—but the O(n2) O(n^2) O(n2) compute remains. For very long sequences (32k+ tokens), even with FlashAttention, training still pushes the limits of single-GPU memory.

Consider these scenarios where long-context training is essential:.

Traditional data parallelism doesn't help here—each GPU still needs to process the full sequence inside the attention block. We need a way to split the sequence itself across multiple devices.

Ulysses Sequence Parallelism (SP), introduced in the DeepSpeed Ulysses paper, takes a clever approach: in addition to splitting on the sequence dimension, it also partitions the attention heads across GPUs.

Sequence Sharding: The input sequence is split along the sequence dimension across P P P GPUs. Each GPU i i i holds tokens [i⋅n/P,(i+1)⋅n/P) [i \cdot n/P, (i+1) \cdot n/P) [i⋅n/P,(i+1)⋅n/P).

QKV Projection: Each GPU computes the query, key, and value projections for its local sequence chunk.

All-to-All Communication: An all-to-all collective operation redistributes the data so that each GPU holds all sequence positions after the projections, but only for a subset of attention heads.

Local Attention: Each GPU computes attention for its assigned heads using standard attention mechanisms (FlashAttention or SDPA).

All-to-All Communication: Another all-to-all operation reverses the redistribution, returning to sequence-sharded format.

Output Projection: Each GPU computes the output projection for its local sequence chunk.

Sources indicate that the key insight is that attention heads are independent—each head can be computed separately. By trading sequence locality for head locality, Ulysses enables efficient parallelization with relatively low communication overhead.

Ulysses requires two all-to-all operations per attention layer, with total communication volume of O(n⋅d/P) O(n \cdot d / P) O(n⋅d/P) per GPU, where:.

Ring Attention communicates O(n⋅d) O(n \cdot d) O(n⋅d) per GPU — a factor of P P P more — via P−1 P-1 P−1 sequential point-to-point transfers around the ring. Ulysses also benefits from lower latency because all-to-all can exploit full bisectional bandwidth in a single collective step, whereas Ring Attention serializes over P−1 P-1 P−1 hops.

Accelerate provides the foundation for Ulysses sequence parallelism through its ParallelismConfig class and DeepSpeed integration.

When you call accelerator.prepare(), Ulysses is automatically set up:.

With Ulysses, each GPU computes loss on different parts of the sequence. The losses must be aggregated properly, weighted by the number of valid tokens per rank. If you're using the Transformers Trainer or TRL's SFTTrainer, this is handled automatically—the code below is only needed when writing a custom Accelerate training loop:.

The weighted loss aggregation ensures correct gradients when tokens are unevenly distributed across ranks (e.g., when some ranks contain only padding or masked out prompt tokens).

Sources indicate that both Ulysses and Ring Attention use position_ids instead of attention_mask for causal masking during training. A 4D attention mask at these sequence lengths would be just as prohibitive as the attention scores themselves—at 128k tokens, that's another ~1TB tensor. Position IDs achieve the same causal behavior with O(n) O(n) O(n) memory instead of O(n2) O(n^2) O(n2). During evaluation/inference, DeepSpeed's SP attention layer can bypass the SP operations entirely (via disable_in_eval) and fall back to the model's default attention implementation.

The Transformers Trainer provides seamless Ulysses integration through TrainingArguments.parallelism_config. It handles all the SP-specific details automatically—dataloader wrapping, sequence sharding, and loss aggregation—so you don't need to write any of the custom loss code shown above.

Balance SP and DP for your GPU count:.

Remember: dp_replicate_size × dp_shard_size × sp_size = num_processes.

If your desired model architecture is supported by Liger-Kernel, it is fully compatible with Ulysses SP and can be enabled with a single flag:.

In a recent development, the main memory saving comes from FusedLinearCrossEntropy which avoids materializing the full logits tensor during loss calculation. The savings grow with longer sequences where the logits tensor is larger.

Additionally, you can enable TiledMLP to further extend sequence length — like FusedLinearCrossEntropy, it saves working memory by tiling large matrix operations.

You don't need to worry about manually balancing tokens across SP ranks—the loss aggregation code handles uneven distributions gracefully (including ranks with zero valid tokens). With random batching over a reasonably sized dataset, the distribution evens out statistically over training.

Recent findings suggest that to quantify the benefits of Ulysses SP, we trained Qwen3-4B on the Gutenberg English streaming dataset using TRL's SFTTrainer. All experiments ran on H100 80GB GPUs with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, CPU optimizer offloading, gradient checkpointing, and flash-attn2 as the attention backend.

The benchmark runs in the table above use the same global batch size (8 micro-batches), cosine learning-rate schedule, and seed, so those benchmark loss curves are directly comparable.

To verify SP-vs-DP loss equivalence, we ran controlled 4-GPU A/B experiments with identical seed, model, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and data order.

For fair comparison, GAS must scale with SP:.

Measured over 20 steps on 4 GPUs in controlled equivalence harnesses:.

Industry observers note that takeaway: under matched token budget, SP and non-SP match on canonical token-normalized loss. The remaining difference is in trainer-reported logging (loss), not in the underlying cross-entropy objective.

Industry observers note that at 8K tokens, DP=4 and SP=4 use nearly the same memory per GPU (~22 GB with ZeRO-3). The advantage of SP is that it enables scaling to much longer sequences: at 96K tokens (12x longer), peak memory is 66 GB — still within the H100's 80 GB capacity. At 128K, the model OOMs, establishing the practical limit for this configuration. DP=4 without SP cannot scale beyond 8K for this model.

At the same sequence length (8K), SP=4 has comparable throughput to the single-GPU baseline — the all-to-all communication overhead is minimal on NVLink-connected GPUs. The real benefit comes from longer sequences: as sequence length grows, the quadratic attention computation dominates over communication and other overheads, making each training step increasingly compute-efficient. Each step also processes proportionally more tokens, so throughput scales with sequence length. At 64K, SP=4 processes 13,396 tokens/second — 3.7x the baseline.

Recent findings suggest that these results use only 4 GPUs with SP=4. With 8 GPUs (SP=8), you can push to even longer sequences — up to 256K+ tokens — or use 2D parallelism (SP=4, DP=2) to combine long-context training with data-parallel throughput.

Use flash_attention_2 for Ampere GPUs, or flash_attention_3 for Hopper GPUs. Wait for flash_attention_4 on Blackwell 🕰.

Sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

The code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Set three environment variables:.

Industry observers note that before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

Recent findings suggest that the 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint claims so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

Industry observers note that the trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:.

Two design choices are worth calling out.

According to recent reports, use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:.

Most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Industry observers note that every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

The defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:.

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:.

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Sources indicate that now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":.

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Recent findings suggest that don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

According to recent reports, don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF reveals what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

According to recent reports, retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

In a recent development, A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:.

Since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

According to recent reports, in the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

Sources indicate that in the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Recent findings suggest that across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:.

Industry observers note that the send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

Keep the Tokens Flowing: Lessons from 16 Open-Source RL Libraries

📅 10 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6149 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR -- For those of you who don't have time to read 5,000 words about async RL plumbing (we get it, you have models to train):.
