#34937. Latest Update: State of Open Source on Hugging Face: Spring 2026

📅 17 Mar 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2789 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: State of Open Source on Hugging Face: Spring 2026

📅 17 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This post examines how the open source AI landscape has shifted across competition, geography, technical trends, and emerging communities over the past year.
  • Recent findings suggest that this post builds on an earlier analysis conducted mid-2025, available here, which examined what the Hugging Face Community is building.
  • Activity in the open source AI ecosystem has rapidly grown, with the number of consumers, model, and dataset repositories all close to doubling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post examines how the open source AI landscape has shifted across competition, geography, technical trends, and emerging communities over the past year. We primarily examine community activity on Hugging Face across many types of metrics to give a holistic view of the ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that this post builds on an earlier analysis conducted mid-2025, available here, which examined what the Hugging Face Community is building. We recommend reading additional perspectives on the open source ecosystem in and outside of Hugging Face from the Data Provenance Initiative, Interconnects, OpenRouter and a16z, and MIT and the Linux Foundation. As the Hugging Face ecosystem is distributed, analyses are a combination of Hugging Face and community members' work, each of which is appropriately credited.

Activity in the open source AI ecosystem has rapidly grown, with the number of consumers, model, and dataset repositories all close to doubling. In 2025, Hugging Face grew to 13 million users, more than 2 million public models, and over 500,000 public datasets. This growth signals more than increased interest in open source; it reflects a shift toward active participation, with users increasingly creating derivative artifacts such as fine-tuned models, adapters, benchmarks, and applications rather than only consuming pre-trained systems.

Data from Hugging Face | Hugging Face's two million models and counting: Graph and story by AI World.

The ecosystem remains highly concentrated. Approximately half of the models on Hugging Face have less than 200 total downloads, and the top 200 most downloaded models, or 0.01% of models, comprise 49.6% of all downloads.

Specialized communities form around particular domains, languages, or problem areas, and often show sustained engagement and reuse even when their overall download counts are modest. Open source AI is best understood as a collection of overlapping sub-ecosystems rather than a single uniform market.

It has been revealed that more companies, both large and small, are building on open source. Over 30% of the Fortune 500 now maintain verified accounts on Hugging Face. Startups frequently use open models as default components: Thinking Machines built its Tinker model options entirely on open weights, while popular IDEs such as VSCode and Cursor support both open and closed models. Established American companies such as Airbnb have increased their engagement with the open ecosystem, and Hugging Face has seen more legacy companies upgrading their organizational subscriptions over the course of 2025.

Massive Tech companies are frequently creating newly introduced repositories on Hugging Face Hub; visualized side-by-side, the strong increase in repository growth highlights investment over time. NVIDIA has emerged as the strongest contributor.

Data from Hugging Face | Big Tech Is All-In On Open-Source AI, Graph and story by AI World.

Industry observers note that studies of open software more broadly suggest that the downstream value created by open artifacts far exceeds the cost of producing them. Similar dynamics are emerging in AI, where open models are reused, adapted, and specialized across thousands of downstream applications. Organizations that rely exclusively on closed systems often incur higher costs and face reduced flexibility in deployment and customization.

All-time downloads over the past four years show clear frontrunner regions in model popularity. The U.S. and China have historically been top contributors, with the UK, Germany, and France as secondary in popularity. Models developed by individual people or distributed organizations without a clear geographic base account for about half of all platform downloads.

In a recent development, data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Longpre et al. “Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem”.

The geographic composition of the open source ecosystem has fundamentally changed. Hugging Face data highlights China surpassing the U.S. in monthly downloads and overall downloads. In the past year, Chinese models swiftly accounted for the plurality or 41% of downloads.

Data and Graph from Hugging Face.

Industry's share of overall development fell from around 70% before 2022 to roughly 37% in 2025. Meanwhile, independent or unaffiliated developers rose from 17% to 39% of all downloads over the same period, at times accounting for more than half of total usage. Individuals and small collectives focused on quantizing, adapting, and redistributing base models. These intermediaries now steer a meaningful portion of what typical customers can run and how innovations spread through the ecosystem.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Longpre et al. “Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem”.

In a recent development, different regions contribute in different ways. The United States and Western Europe have historically dominated through large industry labs (Google, Meta, OpenAI, Stability AI), while China has increasingly led on both releases and adoption. France, Germany, and the UK continue to contribute through research organizations, national AI initiatives, and specialized model families. Ecosystems supporting a variety of contributors and organizational forms tend to produce more widely adopted artifacts.

In a recent development, popular models from startups were more widespread. Competitive countries were France and South Korea. Notably, the fourth most popular entity for developing latest trending models were individual users, not organizations. Creating competitive models at a user level is more accessible than ever before.

Data and Graph from Hugging Face.

Sources indicate that of the newly created models in 2025, the majority of trending models were either developed in China or derivative of a model developed in China. The most popular models were developed by large organizations, predominantly from the U.S. and China. For more on the Chinese AI ecosystem, read our three part series reflecting on the changes in one year since the "DeepSeek Moment", with one on strategic changes, two on architectural changes, and three on organizations and the future.

It has been revealed that in 2025, China’s AI ecosystem steered heavily into open source, following the viral release of DeepSeek’s R1 model in January. The number of competitive Chinese organizations releasing models and the number of repositories on Hugging Face skyrocketed. Baidu went from zero releases on the Hub in 2024 to over 100 in 2025. ByteDance and Tencent each increased releases by eight to nine times. Organizations that had previously favored closed approaches, including Baidu and MiniMax, shifted decisively toward open releases.

Data and Graph from Hugging Face.

A similar number of popular U.S. organizations have consistently contributed a higher volume of repositories over time. Meta and its former Facebook research organization account for a significant proportion of open releases, as does Google to a lesser extent.

Data and Graph from Hugging Face.

Next to each other, the steep upward trajectory of repository growth among popular Chinese organizations emerges as a key strategic difference.

Data and Graph from Hugging Face.

Recent findings suggest that open source AI is increasingly tied to questions of sovereignty. Open weight models allow governments and public institutions to fine-tune systems on local data under national legal frameworks. Models that can be deployed on domestic hardware reduce reliance on foreign-controlled cloud infrastructure. Transparency around model architecture, training processes, and evaluation supports regulatory review and public accountability. Read more about the open source approach to sovereignty here.

Sources indicate that at the national level, governments are taking action. South Korea's National Sovereign AI Initiative released mid-2025 named national champions LG AI Research, SK Telecom, Naver Cloud, NC AI, and Upstage to produce competitive domestic models. Three models from South Korea trended simultaneously on Hugging Face Hub in February 2026. In March 2026, In 2026, South Korea and U.S. startup Reflection AI unveiled a data center partnership, also bringing frontier open weight models to South Korea.

Switzerland's Swiss AI initiative and various EU-funded projects reflect similar priorities. The UK's principle of "public money, public code" has influenced several government-backed AI initiatives.

Hugging Face Trending Page February 2026.

These investments in open-source and open weight AI are already paying dividends for countries with thriving AI training ecosystems of their own, as we see that models and datasets are typically most used in the regions where they're developed; with developers often turning to the models that best represent their languages and reflect similar technical and application requirements.

Data and Graph from Hugging Face.

In a recent development, most liked models on the Hub show community attention, in terms of ability to go back to or reference the model or general popularity. While this metric does not always reflect usage, the attention collected over time can show signals of interest. In one year, the most liked models went from predominantly U.S.-developed from Meta’s Llama family, to an international mix with China’s DeepSeek-R1 at the top.

Data and Graphic from Hugging Face.

Recent findings suggest that while determining the value of scientific contributions can be determined by many metrics, our upvote feature on the Hub shows papers from large AI organizations be widely appreciated by community members. Notably, the most upvoted papers are from large organizations, mostly from the U.S. and China. The majority of the top organizations are Chinese Massive Tech companies, with ByteDance sharing a high volume of high impact papers.

Space by Hugging Face | PaperVerse Explorer.

Recent findings suggest that of Hugging Face's Daily Papers, a set of papers curated by Hugging Face's AK, papers that reference model and dataset creation, showing the most open source adoption, are generally diverse. Prominent takeaways show medical papers being influential, while Substantial Tech's influence is sparse.

Data from Hugging Face | Graphic and story by AI World.

In a recent development, how our community members choose to build on models, whether via fine-tuning, merging, or other methods, reflects model popularity and usability. Alibaba as an organization has more derivative models than both Google and Meta combined, with the Qwen family constituting more than 113,000 derivative models. When including all models that tag Qwen, that number balloons to over 200,000 models.

Data and Graph from Hugging Face.

Model development has increasingly emphasized accessibility alongside scale. Smaller models are downloaded and deployed at far higher rates than very large systems, reflecting practical constraints around cost, latency, and hardware availability.

This small-model dominance occurs in part because far more models are released at that size. But even when normalizing for this, the data from the ATOM Project's Relative Adoption Metric highlights that the median top-10 models from 1-9B parameters are only downloaded about 4x more than models above 100B. Automated systems and CI pipelines further inflate small model download counts, but the trend toward smaller, deployable models is real.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Article by ATOM.

Sources indicate that engagement with open models tends to peak almost immediately after release, then slow. Mean engagement duration is approximately 6 weeks. Continuous improvement and frequent updates have become critical for maintaining relevance. DeepSeek's successive releases (V3, R1, V3.2) kept it competitive even as challengers emerged. Organizations that stagnate in development tend to lose share quickly to those with frequent updates or domain-specific fine-tunes.

It has been revealed that data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Choksi et al. "The Brief and Wondrous Life of Open Models".

The mean size of downloaded open models rose from 827M parameters in 2023 to 20.8B in 2025, driven largely by quantization and mixture-of-experts architectures. The median, however, increased only marginally, from 326M to 406M parameters. This divergence indicates that high-end LLM consumers are pulling up the mean while underlying small-model usage remains stable.

In a recent development, data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Longpre et al. "Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem".

In a recent development, performance differences between frontier models and smaller systems often narrow rapidly through fine-tuning and task-specific adaptation. On the Hub, models with hundreds of millions of parameters support search, tagging, and document processing workflows, while models in the single-digit billions are widely used for coding, reasoning, and multimodal tasks. As a result, most major model developers now release families of models spanning a range of sizes. The rise of capable small models shifts autonomy closer to the edge, reducing dependency on centralized cloud providers.

Open source AI development is closely linked to hardware trends. Most models are optimized for NVIDIA GPUs, but support for AMD hardware continues to expand. Stability AI model collections now optimize for both NVIDIA and AMD platforms. Libraries increasingly target both, and tooling has improved to make cross-hardware deployment more straightforward. In 2025 Hugging Face introduced the Kernel Hub to load and run kernels optimized for NVIDIA and AMD GPUs.

In parallel, Chinese open models are being released with explicit support for domestically developed chips. Alibaba has invested in inference-focused chip architectures designed to fill Chinese data centers with hardware capable of running open source models locally.

While access to compute remains a core necessity across the board for development and deployment of AI models, open-source and open-weight models are helping break away from an ecosystem where it becomes the be-all and end-all, with increasingly more models at all levels of performance pushing efficiency from 10x to 1000x lower costs than flagship AI models the largest developers.

Data and Graphic from Hugging Face.

Still, the question of infrastructure investment for open source remains urgent. Public funding for data centers capable of training and serving open models has become a growing policy discussion, particularly in Europe and the UK. The gap between the compute resources available to large closed-model companies and those accessible to the open source community continues to shape what is feasible in open development.

Sources indicate that robotics has emerged as one of the fastest-growing sub-communities on Hugging Face. The numbers are striking: robotics datasets grew from 1,145 in 2024 to 26,991 in 2025, climbing from rank 44 to the single largest dataset category on the Hub in just three years. For comparison, text generation, the second-largest category, had only around 5,000 datasets in 2025.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Story by AI World.

It has been revealed that community-contributed datasets span everything from household manipulation tasks to autonomous driving. The largest multimodal dataset for spatial intelligence, Learning to Drive (L2D), was released through a LeRobot collaboration with Yaak. Datasets like RoboMIND, with over 107,000 real-world trajectories across 479 distinct tasks and multiple robot embodiments, provide the kind of scale and diversity needed for training generalizable robotic policies.

According to recent reports, hugging Face's acquisition of Pollen Robotics opened open source robotic sales to both industry and academic labs, as well as everyday hobbyists. LeRobot, Hugging Face's open source robotics library that provides models, datasets, and tools for real-world robotics in PyTorch, covering imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and vision-language-action models, experienced rapid growth. Over the past year, its GitHub repository stars nearly tripled.

Data from GitHub | Graphic from star-history.com.

Scientific research has become another particularly active area. Open models and datasets are increasingly used for protein folding, molecular dynamics, drug discovery, and scientific data analysis. All frontier AI companies now have dedicated science teams, though much current focus remains on literature discovery rather than direct experimentation.

Space by Hugging Face | Science Release Heatmap.

Community-led projects have formed around shared research goals, often involving hundreds of contributors working across institutions and disciplines. These efforts highlight the role of open source as a mechanism for coordinating large-scale, interdisciplinary work that would be difficult to organize through traditional academic or corporate structures alone.

The open source AI ecosystem continues to evolve through a combination of global participation, technical specialization, and institutional adoption. Several trends are likely to define the next phase.

The geographic rebalancing of power is accelerating. Western organizations increasingly seek commercially deployable alternatives to Chinese models, creating urgency around efforts like OpenAI's GPT-OSS, AI2's OLMo, and Google's Gemma to offer competitive open options from US and European developers. Whether these efforts can match the adoption momentum of Qwen and DeepSeek will be a defining question of 2026.

It has been revealed that the growth of sub-communities in robotics and science suggests that open source AI is expanding beyond language and image generation into the physical and experimental domains. The infrastructure, norms, and coordination mechanisms developed around text and image models are being adapted for new modalities and use cases.

For researchers, developers, companies, and governments, open source remains a foundational layer for building, evaluating, and governing AI systems. With increasing agent deployments, open-source and its interoperability will be key for agents to thrive. Its trajectory over the past year makes one thing clear: the open source ecosystem is where much of the practical work of AI development, adaptation, and deployment takes place, and its influence on the broader AI landscape continues to grow.

AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:.

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free plan is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app consumers, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every plan, Free included.

Industry observers note that base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Recent findings suggest that bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

Bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

In a recent development, replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Industry observers note that core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Recent findings suggest that bubble is a visual builder that targets the browser as well as native iOS and Android, with an AI agent that drafts pages and logic before you refine them by hand. One editor covers the design, the database, the logic and the privacy rules behind each page.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web plans run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

In a recent development, retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

In a recent development, v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

v0's Free proposal gives new customers $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Industry observers note that figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Industry observers note that figma's Starter strategy is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

Recent findings suggest that the questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real tech giant data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human consumers.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

Recent findings suggest that the caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

📅 20 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1758 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you are building a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system, you have likely hit this wall: Everything works… until it doesn’t.
  • In a recent development, with a single GPU and less than a day of training time, you can transform a general-purpose embedding model into one that truly understands your domain, no manual labeling required.
  • By the end of this post, you’ll know how to:📄 Generate training data from domain documents without labeled data🎯 Use hard negative mining for effective contrastive training🔗 Improve embedding quality with multi-hop queries⚙️ Fine-tune a bi-encoder embedding model📊 Evaluate whether fine-tuning improves retrieval🚀 Deploy the fine-tuned model in your pipeline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you are building a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system, you have likely hit this wall: Everything works… until it doesn’t. General-purpose embedding models are trained to understand the internet; not your contracts, manufacturing logs, proprietary chemical formulations or internal taxonomy. They capture broad semantic similarity, but they do not understand the fine-grained distinctions that matter in your domain. Fine-tuning an embedding model can improve the performance of your retrieval pipeline when off-the-shelf models fail to effectively capture domain-specific nuances. Despite how critical embeddings are to RAG performance, the process remains surprisingly fragmented, the skills required are specialized, and the time investment is daunting.

In a recent development, with a single GPU and less than a day of training time, you can transform a general-purpose embedding model into one that truly understands your domain, no manual labeling required. To help you hit the ground running, we are also releasing a ready-to-use synthetic training dataset generated from NVIDIA's public documentation using this exact pipeline. Using this data and the recipe, we saw over 10% improvement in both Recall@10 and NDCG@10. Atlassian applied this recipe to fine-tune on their JIRA dataset, increasing Recall@60 from 0.751 to 0.951, a 26% improvement - on a single GPU.

By the end of this post, you’ll know how to:📄 Generate training data from domain documents without labeled data🎯 Use hard negative mining for effective contrastive training🔗 Improve embedding quality with multi-hop queries⚙️ Fine-tune a bi-encoder embedding model📊 Evaluate whether fine-tuning improves retrieval🚀 Deploy the fine-tuned model in your pipeline.

In this tutorial, we will finetune the base model Llama-Nemotron-Embed-1B-v2 - a 1-billion-parameter embedding model that balances quality and inference cost. To get started, follow this setup guide.

Fine-tuning an embedding model requires thousands of (query, relevant document) pairs. Most use cases don’t have this data readily available. Creating it manually is expensive, slow, and often biased by the annotator’s personal interpretation of what’s “relevant.”Instead of labeling data by hand, you can use an LLM (nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b) to read your documents and automatically generate high-quality synthetic question–answer pairs.

Behind the scenes, this runs a four-stage synthetic data generation (SDG) pipeline powered by NeMo Data Designer:.

According to recent reports, the thermal design power (TDP) of the H100 GPU is 700W in SXM form factor. The cooling solution must maintain junction temperature below 83°C under sustained workloads. Liquid cooling is recommended for dense deployments exceeding 4 GPUs per node, as air cooling cannot dissipate sufficient heat in standard 2U chassis configurations.

Notice the difference: the first question is a simple factual lookup. The second requires multi-hop, causal reasoning. The pipeline generates both types, with configurable complexity levels (2–5) and hop counts (1–3). Each QA pair then undergoes quality evaluation, receiving sub-scores for relevance, accuracy, context support, and clarity, along with an overall score. Only pairs that meet the threshold are included in training.

Sources indicate that if you train an embedding model with only positive pairs (query + correct document), it learns to distinguish obviously different documents but fails on the hard cases — passages that look relevant but are not the right answer. In a real retrieval system, these near-misses are exactly the documents that cause bad answers. Hard negative mining finds these confusing passages so the model can learn to tell them apart.

The above command runs three sub-steps automatically:.

Recent findings suggest that the generated QA pairs are split into training (80%) and test (20%) sets. The test set is formatted as a BEIR-compatible benchmark for standardized evaluation in Step 5.

Using the base embedding model, the pipeline:.

Recent findings suggest that the result: hard negatives are the most similar non-positive passages that still fall safely below the positive-score ceiling. They are passages the current model considers highly relevant but that are not the labeled answer.

Recent findings suggest that why this works: Training on easy negatives (completely unrelated passages) teaches the model nothing newly introduced. Training on hard negatives forces it to learn the subtle distinctions that matter in your domain. For example, in a medical corpus, a question about "metformin dosage for Type 2 diabetes" might have hard negatives about "metformin side effects" or "insulin dosage for Type 1 diabetes" — close but critically different. The 95% margin ceiling prevents the miner from selecting passages that are too close to the positive, which could actually be correct answers that simply weren't labeled during SDG.

Multi-hop questions reference multiple positive documents. For example, a question like "How does the thermal management system in Section 3.2 relate to the power constraints described in Section 5.1?" has two positive passages.

Recent findings suggest that unrolling creates one training example per (query, positive document) pair, so the contrastive loss sees each positive independently. A question with 2 positive documents becomes 2 training examples, each with the same hard negatives but a different positive.

The final output is a training-ready JSON file:.

It has been revealed that standard embedding fine-tuning generates one question per passage and trains the model to match them. This works for simple factual lookups, but real users ask complex questions that span multiple documents or sections. If the model has only seen single-hop training data, it will struggle to retrieve all the relevant passages for these complex queries.

The SDG pipeline generates questions at 1 to 3 hops by default:.

Each hop is tracked with its own context summary and segment IDs, so the training data preserves the full reasoning chain. After unrolling (Step 2c), each (question, relevant passage) pair becomes an independent training signal, teaching the model that all of these passages are relevant to the multi-hop query.

The fine-tuned model learns to retrieve contextually related documents, not just lexically similar ones.

The training uses a biencoder architecture with contrastive loss.

The temperature of 0.02 is deliberately aggressive, it produces a very sharp probability distribution. This works well because the hard negatives from Step 2 are high-quality: they are genuinely confusing passages that the model needs strong gradients to learn to distinguish.

If ckpt_every_steps is omitted from the config, checkpoint frequency is set automatically:.

This means you can start with a small corpus (50–100 documents) for a quick proof-of-concept and scale up later without manually tuning checkpoint settings.

Did fine-tuning actually help? Let’s find out by running a standardized evaluation comparing the base model against the fine-tuned checkpoint on the held-out test set:.

The evaluation uses the BEIR framework and computes four standard information retrieval metrics at k = 1, 5, 10, and 100:.

A successful fine-tune typically results in a 10% improvement in nDCG@10 and Recall@10 within <1 day.

Results using Retrieval Synthetic NVDocs:.

The pipeline makes it easy to iterate:.

Recent findings suggest that this recipe has been validated on real enterprise data by Atlassian. They applied this pipeline to fine-tune Llama-Nemotron-Embed-1B-v2 on a public Jira dataset using a single NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU, following the same stages described above.

According to recent reports, recall@60 jumped from 0.751 to 0.951 — a 26.7% gain.The fine-tuned model retrieves the correct document within the top 60 results for 95.1% of queries, up from 75.1% with the base model. For a retrieval system underpinning Jira search, this directly translates into more relevant results for millions of owners. Find more details in their blog post Advancing semantic search for millions of Rovo users.

A PyTorch checkpoint is great for evaluation but too slow for production. The final two stages convert the model and serve it behind an API.

Industry observers note that this exports the fine-tuned checkpoint to ONNX (opset 17). Optionally, it compiles a TensorRT engine for maximum inference throughput, with configurable optimization profiles for batch size (1–64) and sequence length (3–256):.

The exported model is deployed inside an NVIDIA NIM container — a production-ready inference microservice exposing an OpenAI-compatible /v1/embeddings endpoint:.

Once running, any client can call it:.

Because NIM serves an OpenAI-compatible API, you can drop it into any existing RAG pipeline that uses the embeddings API format — no code changes needed.

The pipeline includes a NIM accuracy verification step that runs the same BEIR evaluation against the deployed endpoint:.

This catches any accuracy loss from the ONNX/TensorRT conversion. Metrics that match within tolerance (0.03 for @1, 0.01 for @5+) are marked with a check; deviations beyond conversion noise are flagged.

The full embedding fine-tuning pipeline can be run in six commands, from raw documents to a deployed model.

Sources indicate that total: under a day, with most time being hands-off training. For a small corpus (~500 documents), the entire pipeline completes in about 2–3 hours.

Industry observers note that the pipeline can run end-to-end, but each stage can also be executed independently depending on your starting point. For example, if you have raw documents, you can begin with synthetic data generation (SDG), while datasets that already include hard negatives can skip earlier steps and go directly to fine-tuning. Since every stage uses standard formats such as JSON, BEIR, and ONNX, it’s easy to integrate custom components or reuse intermediate outputs in other workflows. The recipe is also flexible in how it runs, supporting execution on a local machine, inside Docker containers, or on Slurm-based clusters.

In a recent development, if you have domain documents and some time in your hand, you can generate your first batch of synthetic training data today! The full pipeline - from documents to a deployed, domain-adapted embedding model - runs in under a day on a single GPU. You can start with our ready-made nvidia/Retrieval-Synthetic-NVDocs-v1 dataset to try the pipeline right away. Let us know what you build.Star the repos for Nemotron, NeMo Data Designer and NeMo Automodel if you find them useful.

Industry observers note that thank you Nvidia for this. Could you please make it possible, even if not the default, to call a "locally" / internally deployed LLM (OpenAI compatible endpoint) for the SDG phase ? The whole point of self-hosting a fine-tuned embedding model, appart from accurracy, is that the organization's data never leave the premises. Thanks.

Thanks for the feedback. We will add the support in the next release of the recipe.

The domain-specific evaluation and the thread's point about keeping sensitive data local are both notable. Before choosing whether to fine-tune an embedding model, a useful control is a lexical baseline on the same held-out domain queries, including paraphrase-heavy and exact-identifier slices. We explored BM25 + semantic reranking here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). Our reranking experiment uses a hosted API, so it doesn't satisfy a strict no-data-leaves-premises requirement; we haven't compared it with this recipe.

#34933. A New Framework for Evaluating Voice Agents (EVA)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

A New Framework for Evaluating Voice Agents (EVA)

📅 24 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that conversational voice agents present a distinct evaluation challenge: they must simultaneously satisfy two objectives — accuracy (completing the user's task correctly and faithfully) and conversational experience (doing so naturally, concisely, and in a way appropriate for spoken interaction).
  • In a recent development, we introduce EVA, an end-to-end evaluation framework for conversational voice agents that evaluates complete, multi-turn spoken conversations using a realistic bot-to-bot architecture.
  • In a recent development, we also provide benchmark results for 20 cascade and audio-native systems, such as speech-to-speech (S2S) models and Large Audio Language Models (LALMs).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that conversational voice agents present a distinct evaluation challenge: they must simultaneously satisfy two objectives — accuracy (completing the user's task correctly and faithfully) and conversational experience (doing so naturally, concisely, and in a way appropriate for spoken interaction). These objectives are deeply intertwined: mishearing a confirmation code renders perfect LLM reasoning meaningless, a wall of options overwhelms a caller who can't skim spoken output, and delayed responses can pass every accuracy check while remaining unusable in practice. Existing frameworks treat these as separate concerns — evaluating task success or conversational dynamics, but not both.

In a recent development, we introduce EVA, an end-to-end evaluation framework for conversational voice agents that evaluates complete, multi-turn spoken conversations using a realistic bot-to-bot architecture. EVA produces two high-level scores, EVA-A (Accuracy) and EVA-X (Experience), and is designed to surface failures along each dimension. EVA is the first to jointly score task success and conversational experience. We release EVA with an initial airline dataset of 50 scenarios covering flight rebooking, cancellation handling, vouchers, and more — the first in a planned series of domains.

In a recent development, we also provide benchmark results for 20 cascade and audio-native systems, such as speech-to-speech (S2S) models and Large Audio Language Models (LALMs). Our biggest finding is that there is a consistent Accuracy-Experience tradeoff; agents that perform well on task completion tend to deliver worse user experiences, and vice versa.

It has been revealed that the field currently lacks a framework that evaluates the full quality of voice agent interactions, as most existing efforts assess individual components in isolation. For example, AudioBench, SD-Eval, VoxEval, Kimi-Audio-Evalkit, VoiceBench and VoxDialogue evaluate core speech understanding capabilities for Speech-to-Text (STT) — transcription, paralinguistics, acoustic cues — but remain confined to single-turn, non-interactive settings. On the other hand, EmergentTTS-Eval and SHEET assess perceived speech quality using subjective listening tests (e.g., Mean Opinion Score). Beyond speech perception, FD-Bench, Talking Turns, Full-Duplex-Bench provide deeper analyses of conversational dynamics — interruptions, backchanneling, turn-taking — yet evaluate these in isolation from task-oriented tool use, leaving the relationship between dialogue quality and agentic capability unexamined. More recent efforts, notably VoiceAgentBench and CAVA, take steps towards evaluating the agentic capabilities of commercial voice agent systems, including tool-calling and complex instruction-following. However, these voice-agentic capabilities are not evaluated within complete conversational workflows that voice agents must navigate in practice: from initial user request through multi-step tool orchestration to final task resolution.

The lack of frameworks that jointly capture accuracy and experience underscores the need for a framework that treats voice agent quality as an integrated whole. This means evaluating not only whether the task succeeded, but whether the agent communicated accurately, concisely, and naturally throughout, and surfacing how these dimensions trade off against one another in realistic deployment conditions.

End-to-end evaluation reveals interaction dynamics that are not apparent at the component level: whether the agent interrupts people during natural pauses in speech, whether it recovers smoothly when a user corrects a transcription error, or whether high latency disrupts the conversational flow enough to prompt users to repeat themselves or abandon the task entirely.

Recent findings suggest that EVA simulates multi-turn spoken conversations over live audio in which the agent must invoke appropriate tools, adhere to task-specific policies, and reach a deterministically verifiable end state. EVA evaluates voice agents using a bot-to-bot audio architecture composed of five core components:.

Industry observers note that user Simulator — A conversational AI configured with a specific goal and persona that plays the role of a caller. It operates in audio using high-quality Text-to-Speech (TTS) models, ensuring the evaluation captures representative speech-understanding challenges in natural-sounding conversational speech and realistic turn-taking dynamics.

Voice Agent — The voice agent being evaluated, built with Pipecat, an open-source Python framework for real-time voice applications. EVA supports both cascade architectures (STT → LLM → TTS) and audio-native models (S2S or LALM → TTS).

Recent findings suggest that tool Executor — The engine that provides deterministic, reproducible tool responses via custom Python functions. It dynamically queries and modifies a predefined per-scenario database.

Validators — A set of validation metrics that check that conversations are complete and that the user faithfully reproduced the intended behavior and speech, with no human annotation required. Any conversation that fails in this validation step is regenerated, ensuring that only valid, correctly executed conversations enter evaluation. This stands in contrast to approaches that rely on post-hoc human labeling to identify simulator errors.

Metrics Suite — A suite of metrics evaluates the voice agent using the conversation recording, transcript, and tool call logs.

Each test case (scenario) in our framework is an evaluation record, structured to make tests reproducible:.

Sources indicate that we release EVA with a synthetic airline dataset of 50 scenarios and 15 tools, spanning IRROPS rebooking, voluntary itinerary changes, cancellations, same-day standby, and compensation vouchers. Scenarios are designed to test temporal reasoning, policy-following, constraint satisfaction, and named-entity handling.

EVA evaluates voice agents across two fundamental dimensions, EVA-A for accuracy, and EVA-X for experience. EVA also includes a set of diagnostic metrics. Unlike the primary metrics, these are not used directly to compare or rank models — rather, they offer granular insight into why a model scores the way it does, helping identify and understand specific failure modes (e.g., ASR, speech synthesis, etc.). We report pass@k (the probability that at least one of k runs succeeds) and pass^k (the probability that all k runs succeed) across three trials per scenario (k = 3), capturing both peak performance and behavioral consistency.

EVA uses two evaluation methods: deterministic code-based metrics, which compute scores directly from structured data and are fast; and LLM-as-Judge metrics, which use Large Language Models (LLMs) to assess qualitative aspects of the conversation, or Large Audio Language Models (LALM) to evaluate speech directly. Each judge-based metric uses the model that performs best on a curated evaluation dataset for that specific metric.

Task completion alone is a necessary but insufficient measure of accuracy. An agent can reach the correct end state while fabricating a policy detail, misreading a confirmation code aloud, or hallucinating a flight number mid-conversation. These failures are invisible to a binary pass/fail check but directly harm customers. EVA-A therefore measures three dimensions of accuracy:.

Recent findings suggest that turn-taking timing matters, but it tells only part of the story. An agent can have perfect timing while overwhelming a caller with a wall of spoken options they cannot skim, or repeatedly asking for information already given. These failures degrade the experience without ever involving a mistimed response. EVA-X therefore measures three dimensions of experience:.

We evaluated 20 systems — proprietary and open-source, cascade and audio-native — and find a consistent accuracy-experience tradeoff: agents that perform well on task completion tend to deliver worse user experiences, and vice versa — a tradeoff invisible to benchmarks that score only task completion. No single configuration dominates both axes, confirming that accuracy and experience must be measured jointly.

Sources indicate that additionally, we identified named entity transcription as a dominant failure mode. A single misheard character can cascade into an authentication failure and a full conversation breakdown. Also, multi-step workflows break agents in predictable ways. Rebooking a flight while preserving ancillary services — seats, baggage — is the dominant complexity breaker across all configurations. Finally, we observed that additional calibration is needed for real-world use cases. The gap between pass@3 and pass^3 is substantial across all configurations. Even agents that can complete a task often cannot do so consistently, which is critical for real-world success.

EVA is designed to provide rigorous, end-to-end evaluation of conversational voice agents, but several limitations are important to acknowledge, across the framework, data, and metrics dimensions:.

It has been revealed that metrics — LLM-as-judge models carry inherent biases and may favor certain response styles independent of quality, with additional risk of systematic bias when the evaluated and judge models share a provider. While we validate our judges against labeled datasets and report accuracy measurements on our website, these alignment scores do not eliminate systematic bias entirely. Additionally, task completion is measured as binary, which does not capture partial credits and may understate the relative quality of systems that fail gracefully versus catastrophically.

It has been revealed that simulation — The current release covers 50 English-language scenarios in a single domain (airline); results may not generalize to other domains, languages, or accents. Also, the user simulator may not perfectly replicate real caller behavior (e.g., disfluencies, hesitations, emotions) or guarantee full policy adherence.

Framework — The user simulator relies on a single commercial provider whose voice characteristics may systematically favor certain ASR systems, and the bot-to-bot pipeline — including audio format conversions and real-time audio interfaces — may not fully represent production deployments. Also, full reproduction requires commercial API access, and latency measurements will vary across providers and infrastructure.

In a recent development, on the evaluation side, we proposal to add prosodic quality assessment (pronunciation, rhythm, expressiveness) — at the moment an open problem after finding very low alignment between LALM-as-Judge and human judgments. We also plan robustness testing under noisy conditions, diverse accents, multilingual customers, and varied speaker behaviors, alongside affect-aware evaluation of how agents respond to user distress. In terms of data, we are developing additional domain datasets — each with distinct policy structures, named entity profiles, and conversational dynamics — and more complex scenarios involving compound requests, multi-step follow-ups, and longer conversational memory. On the tooling front, we will release a results and error analysis application that automatically identifies errors per metric and model, surfaces representative examples for exploration, and generates structured summaries of each model’s strengths and weaknesses. Finally, we intend to expand the leaderboard continuously to provide an up-to-date assessment of voice agent capabilities across the field.

View more details about limitations and our upcoming roadmap here.

Core contributors include Tara Bogavelli, Gabrielle Gauthier Melançon, Katrina Stankiewicz, Oluwanifemi Bamgbose, Hoang Nguyen, Raghav Mehndiratta, and Hari Subramani.

According to recent reports, we also thank Lindsay Brin, Akshay Kalkunte, Joseph Marinier, Jishnu Nair, and Aman Tiwari for their careful data review and thoughtful contributions to the framework, and Fanny Riols, Anil Madamala, Sridhar Nemala, and Srinivas Sunkara for their management, leadership, and support throughout. We also extend our thanks to the PAVA and CLAE ServiceNow teams, whose prior work on evaluations and voice agents provided valuable inspiration for this project.

A woman has revealed that she completed seven marathons in 2026 despite being pregnant for a few of them, admitting that it was a bit “bizarre” at times.

Industry observers note that for a lot of people, running a marathon is a goal that they work towards for months, if not years. Some want to set an impressive time, while others just want to be able to say they’ve completed the 26.2 miles.

In the case of Deirdre Keane, the 38-year-old is a seasoned long-distance runner, completing more than 60 marathons to this point. However, throughout 2026, she has been running marathons with an additional hurdle to deal with: she has been pregnant throughout.

“I knew how bizarre it was to be running a marathon at 34 weeks, but I also knew how fit I was and self-aware of my body at this point,” she told the Associated Press, admitting it is a “very unusual” challenge, but noted that she isn’t the first woman to do so.

As per the AP, the 38-year-old had signed up for 11 races in 2026, including the seven major marathons: Berlin, Boston, Chicago, London, New York, Sydney and Tokyo.

Industry observers note that “I was like, this is going to be my last hurrah before settling down and becoming pregnant, becoming a mother,” Keane added. However, she didn’t discover she was pregnant until after running the Tokyo marathon, when she noticed her pace had started to slip.

“I don’t think she thought I would do them towards the end, especially being so pregnant at Upcoming York. But I am very stubborn and determined,” Keane added. “Plus, I got lucky; I was feeling good. So I was able to do it.”.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Recent findings suggest that AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

This guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

• A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

Industry observers note that • Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

In a recent development, • Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

• Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

According to recent reports, • Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it claims it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

Limitations and gaps: the page shows different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your blueprint. It claims to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

Industry observers note that GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

Strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and claims other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The company’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and initiative prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

Copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it says it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

Recent findings suggest that limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid initiative prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, indicates very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Recent findings suggest that turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Sources indicate that strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

Sources indicate that limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

Sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

In a recent development, strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page indicates false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

In a recent development, limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

The table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

Recent findings suggest that • Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

Sources indicate that • Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

• Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

It has been revealed that • Moving targets. Fresh models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

• Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

OpenAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

Recent findings suggest that most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

• Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

Sources indicate that • Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and update as new models appear.

• Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

Recent findings suggest that • Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Which Tool Fits Which Situation?

Industry observers note that because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

from dataclasses import dataclass.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control.

group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical".

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):.

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function.""".

flagged = detect(s.text) >= threshold.

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0}).

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through.

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged.

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan").

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan").

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}").

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2.

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),.

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),.

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),.

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),.

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

• Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

Recent findings suggest that • Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

• Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

• Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

Sources indicate that • Protect privacy. Do not paste confidential or personal text into a tool unless you have checked how it handles data.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

According to recent reports, they can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

Yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

According to recent reports, sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

Industry observers note that A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

A university in China has rolled out a $5 million surveillance system that actually checks if people are paying attention in class.

It has been revealed that plenty of schools across the globe have embraced technology in their classrooms. Some of these have been as simple as letting kids use iPads and computers, while other schools are fully focused on teaching students about AI. Others are even using AI-powered robots to help them teach.

So, these days, it can be pretty difficult to slack off, not pay attention to what your teacher is saying, and then grab some notes from your friend.

Over in China, though, things have been taken to the next level when it comes to checking on who is actually paying attention to the lessons.

As per the South China Morning Post, Nanjing University, in Jiangsu province, has rolled out a smart classroom system that monitors students in different ways.

The system, which cost just under $5 million, tracks attendance and lateness, but is also able to check the “head-raising rate” of students as well. If you’re not looking up at the teacher and paying attention, the system will recognise that and count it against you.

According to SCMP, some students have rallied against the system on social media, forcing the university to scrap the tracking of head-raising rates. However, that hasn’t stopped other schools from going ahead with it.

SCMP noted that the China University of Mining and Technology in Jiangsu tracks the “classroom status” of students. This identified students who checked their phones during class, as well as flagging some as being asleep – even though they had been collecting notes.

It has been revealed that good morning. Today I’m rewatching Tenet to better picture Robert Pattinson in his new role, sighing over the inevitability of delivery drones triggering PTSD symptoms, and laugh-cringing at some of these Bit.ly link hijack stories from the weekend. Plus, prayers to anyone who had to find a last-minute hotel room during last week’s flying nightmare.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous concerns here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

In the immediate fallout of Jensen Huang’s humiliating resignation from Nvidia, coverage will focus on how the company plans to continue without its beloved former CEO, the world’s biggest champion of open-source AI and the proliferation of GPUs across borders. But in the long term, there’s an argument to be made that Google will be one of the largest winners of the shake-up, with a market opening up to competition outside of Nvidia’s CUDA moat.

While Colette Kress, the interim CEO, is unlikely to make any drastic changes to the company’s roadmap, the reality is that Nvidia’s competitors in the semiconductor space have desperately been working to unseat the market leader, and without Jensen at the helm, customers may be more likely to pursue alternatives.

For years, Google has offered its TPUs, or Tensor Processing Units, as a solution for AI training and inference, but they’ve been largely locked to its Google Cloud infrastructure. That’s changing now that the firm is opening up sales to third parties and has unveiled it will bring TPU capacity to Oracle’s cloud beginning in 2027.

Google’s latest generation of TPUs is specialized; here’s how the firm describes the lineup in its recent announcement post:.

While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning (inference), TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack.

Google isn’t comparing its fresh TPUs directly to Nvidia’s offerings, and clock-for-clock, even the most powerful TPU 8i Max doesn’t touch Vera Rubin for sheer performance. But this generation should be much more competitive for a few reasons: it’s more power efficient in certain configurations, and Google made it easier to translate coding workflows optimized for CUDA to work with its TPUs.

In a recent development, back in October, Google open-sourced TorchTPU, which it co-developed with Meta’s PyTorch team, to let developers use familiar PyTorch workflows on TPUs with minimal code changes. That won’t make every custom CUDA operation portable or eliminate performance tuning, but reducing the effort required to try an alternative may change the buying decision. Customers don’t need to abandon Nvidia outright for Google to increase its TPU market share, or for Nvidia to face more pressure on price.

Alongside Broadcom and MediaTek, Google is taking on the Nvidia behemoth, and in the short term, it will almost certainly see a large upside in sentiment. But in the longer term, with scaling pressure lowering margins for Nvidia, Google’s specialized and more efficient TPUs may be a primary beneficiary of this sea change. They could also offset a slowdown in Search as Google’s shift to Cloud continues apace.

Over the past few days, the one-two punch of Microsoft’s 365/Exchange outage and the FAA’s ground stop shows just how vulnerable everyone is to the effects of seemingly brittle tech infrastructure.

Industry observers note that the FAA describes a flood of connection attempts that destabilized its telecommunications network, affecting aircraft communications and radar feeds. Investigators identified sites in Arkansas and Texas that were undergoing router and wire replacements, but even days after the stop was lifted, there’s still no clear underlying cause.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, the Microsoft 365 outage lasted about 30 hours, with service restored to the remaining customers and regions late Friday. Microsoft says that a “latent defect” introduced into its network code in a July enhancement wasn’t triggered until a few days ago, when high loads led to cascading failures across the company’s servers worldwide.

While neither AI nor cyberattacks were to blame, individually and together the two outages add urgency to getting companies to shore up their defenses and redundancies in a world where we’re overly reliant on digital systems.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Similar to a recent iPhone feature, Google appears to be working on “Fast Switch” as a way to share one SIM and phone number on two Android phones at once, and it sounds pretty cool.

Through the SIM Manager app on Android, the folks over at Android Authority noticed strings that tell a pretty clear story.

A new feature called “Android Fast Switch” would let you “use your phone number on up to two phones,” with the SIM automatically switching to “whichever phone you unlock.”.

“Android Fast Switch” sounds nearly identical to Handoff on iPhone, a feature that lets iPhone owners share one SIM between two iPhones and swiftly switch devices on the fly.

Industry observers note that other strings explicitly say that you can “Use a SIM on two phones” and specify that both devices would need to be logged into the same Google account. One phone would be the “Primary” with the other as a “companion.”.

There are still plenty of unknown details here, including what data might sync between devices as well as how carriers will respond. On iPhone, carriers either charge extra for this feature ($5 at T-Mobile, $10 at Verizon), or don’t support it at all (AT&T). We also don’t know what devices may be supported – this could easily end up as a Pixel-only affair.

This would make my decision to buy device like Clicks Communicator much easier.

As per usual with these early teardowns, though, the actual launch of a feature like this could be weeks, months, or even years away. Still, the idea itself is rather exciting.

Industry observers note that iPhone’s Handoff feature always sounded useful, but I personally always questioned why it would be useful on iPhone. With so little variety in hardware, the utility of switching between two iPhones seems somewhat dubious, outside of perhaps using a Mini or Air as a situational device alongside a Pro device.

Sources indicate that on Android, the combinations are endless. It all just depends on what devices Google supports. What devices would you switch between?
