GTA 6 is finally here, and for many, the allure of taking a sick day to sneak in some extra game time is proving too strong. In fact, some workplaces, like this California-based car company, gave employees the day off to play.

Industry observers note that an army unit in the United States even offered troops a four-day pass to play GTA 6 as part of their incentives to re-enlist, with 20 soldiers taking up the offer. Then there was a KFC in Australia that hosted a funeral for a fake person, just so customers have a valid reason to take the day off work.

However, a school in the UK is desperately trying to keep students in school by using a minibus to catch those who try to skip class in order to play Rockstar’s latest open-world outing.

According to ITV News, Ninestiles Academy in Birmingham has sent staff into the local community in a minibus to bring pupils to school during GTA 6’s launch week.

“We have been working hard to make this a particularly engaging and positive week for our learners, with a range of activities designed to encourage strong attendance,” mentioned principal Alex Hughes.

“This has included careers-focused assemblies and information events, colleagues visiting the local community in our school minibus to help bring learners into school and a prize draw for everyone who achieves 100% attendance across the week.”.

School offers students $85 prize if they don’t skip for GTA 6.

Professor cancels homework and exams during GTA 6 launch week.

KFC is hosting a fake funeral so GTA 6 fans can take the day off.

Ninestiles has not mentioned whether any pupils brought in by minibus missed class because they were playing GTA 6, but its more direct approach to tackling convenient absences around GTA 6’s launch is just one of several ways schools have responded.

Another school in England offered students the chance to win an $85 Amazon voucher for attending on launch day, while a professor in Spain actually canceled homework and postponed an exam to give students more time to play.

TRL v1.0: Post-Training Library Built to Move with the Field

📅 31 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2210 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we’re releasing TRL v1.0, and it marks a real shift in what TRL is.
  • TRL now implements more than 75 post-training methods.
  • TRL is built for a field that doesn’t sit still.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we’re releasing TRL v1.0, and it marks a real shift in what TRL is. What started as a research codebase has become a dependable library people build on, with clearer expectations around stability. This isn't just a version bump. It reflects the reality that TRL now powers production systems, and embraces that responsibility.

TRL now implements more than 75 post-training methods. But coverage isn’t the goal by itself. What matters is making these methods easy to try, compare, and actually use in practice. The design of the library wasn’t decided upfront. It is the result of years of iteration — the first commit goes back more than six years — and it has been shaped by everything the field threw at it: latest algorithms, new models, shifting paradigms. Over time, this pressure forced the codebase toward a very specific design. Parts of it might look unusual at first, but like in many evolutionary codebases, they exist for a reason.

TRL is built for a field that doesn’t sit still. So the question is not how to design the perfect abstraction. It is how to make stable software in a domain that keeps invalidating its own assumptions. This is what we tried to solve in TRL v1.0, and this post explains how.

Post-training has not evolved as a smooth refinement of one recipe. It has moved through successive centers of gravity, each changing not just the objective, but the shape of the stack.

PPO [Schulman et al., (2017); Ziegler et al., (2019)] made one architecture look canonical: a policy, a reference model, a learned reward model, sampled rollouts, and an RL loop.

It has been revealed that then DPO-style methods such as the original DPO [Rafailov et al., (2023)], ORPO [Hong et al., (2024)], and KTO [Ethayarajh et al., (2024)] cut through that stack: preference optimization could work without a separate reward model, value model, or any online RL. Components that had looked fundamental suddenly looked optional.

RLVR-style methods such as GRPO [Shao et al., (2024)] shifted the center again. On tasks like math, code, and tool use, rewards often come from verifiers or deterministic checks rather than learned reward models. Sampling and rollouts matter again, but the objects in the loop are no longer quite the ones PPO libraries were designed around.

Sources indicate that the lesson is not just that methods change. The definition of the core keeps changing with them. Strong assumptions here have a short half-life. This is probably why no post-training library is really stable yet.

So what does it mean to build a library for a field that won't sit still? The answer is counterintuitive: don't try to capture the essence of what's stable today. Instead, design around what could change. Reward models illustrate why: they looked essential in PPO, became optional in DPO, and came back as verifiers in RLVR methods — structures that could be deterministic functions rather than learned models. Any abstraction built around their original form would have been obsolete twice over by now. The library survives by recognizing that strong assumptions have a short life, and by making that changeability central to how the codebase is organized.

This is the environment in which TRL is downloaded 3 million times a month, and in which major downstream projects treat it as stable infrastructure. The field keeps shifting the ground, and at the same time, those users need things not to break.

It has been revealed that TRL didn’t make a deliberate decision to become a library. It found out it already was one. Projects like Unsloth and Axolotl — with thousands of owners between them — had built directly on top of TRL’s trainers and APIs. A breaking change in TRL propagated instantly into their stacks. A renamed argument, a shifted default, a restructured output — any of these became someone else’s incident. The shift had already happened. v1.0 is the moment TRL acknowledged it explicitly.

Recent findings suggest that the unusual thing about TRL’s stability model is not what it guarantees, it is what it tolerates alongside those guarantees. Stable and experimental coexist within the same package, with explicitly different contracts. The stable core follows semantic versioning. The experimental layer makes no such promises — it is where newly introduced methods land while they are still being evaluated, and where the API can move fast to keep up with the field.

Industry observers note that this isn’t a compromise. It’s a response to a specific constraint: the field produces upcoming methods faster than any of them can earn stability. Refusing to add immature methods would make TRL irrelevant within months. Adding them all to stable would break every downstream project every time an algorithm turned out not to work as expected.

Promotion from experimental to stable isn’t automatic. What matters is the ratio between maintenance cost and actual usage. Some methods earn their place because the community uses them heavily. Others become viable because we can make them cheap enough to maintain — and the design of the codebase is what makes that possible.

In practice, the stable surface includes trainers for SFT, DPO, Reward modeling, RLOO, and GRPO, along with their close variants. The experimental surface is broader and moves faster; for an up-to-date view, the best reference is the TRL documentation.

According to recent reports, the breaking changes needed to reach v1.0 were distributed deliberately across the 0.x releases. Migration from the last 0.x version is minimal — see the migration guide.

In a domain where patterns keep changing, the temptation is to build flexible abstractions that can accommodate anything. Our answer was the opposite: limit abstractions to the strict minimum — while recognizing that this “minimum” is almost always overestimated.

In practice, this translates into a very local approach to code:.

Industry observers note that the goal is not to eliminate structure altogether — shared utilities still exist — but to avoid imposing abstractions where the domain itself is not yet stable. For instance, rather than defining a common base class for offline trainers, we prefer independent implementations when their future evolution is uncertain.

It has been revealed that judges are a good example of what happens when we don’t follow this principle. Early on, we introduced a Judge abstraction to unify the various ways of evaluating model outputs. It looked reasonable at the time. In practice, it was never really used — the abstraction didn’t match how people actually approached evaluation, and it added indirection without adding value. It still lives in the repo, mostly as legacy. In hindsight, shipping the concrete implementations without the unifying abstraction would have served users better.

This approach favors explicit and modifiable usage over rigid frameworks: less magic, but more control. It comes with an obvious cost: code duplication. While often seen as an anti-pattern, in this context it has proven not only acceptable, but effective. Contrary to intuition, it remains manageable in practice with a small but consistent discipline: keeping deltas between implementations minimal and avoiding unnecessary divergence. Like in the Transformers design philosophy, we accept duplication and local explicitness by design. The motivations largely coincide, with some nuance in focus.

According to recent reports, this is easier to see than to describe. Compare RLOO and GRPO: large parts of their implementation are duplicated almost line for line. That is not accidental, and it is not dead weight. These methods are close enough that keeping their code paths aligned makes them easier to read, easier to evolve, and cheaper to maintain.

In a recent development, the goal of this comparison is not to argue that TRL should be judged as best on every axis. It should not. Some systems are built for maximum throughput (like PipelineRL), some are optimized for a narrower slice of the problem (like LLaMA-Factory), and some offer a more opinionated development experience in a specific environment (like Tinker). TRL occupies a different place in the ecosystem: it is a general-purpose post-training library that tries to keep the API and the code as simple as the domain allows, while combining broad method coverage, deep Hugging Face integration, a relatively low infrastructure burden, and an explicit stability contract.

Libraries like Unsloth and Axolotl are not included here because they build on top of TRL rather than sitting beside it in the comparison; in that sense, many of their users are also TRL users indirectly.

Some rows are factual (GitHub stars, Last release, Last commit), others are qualitative judgments (Semver stability).

Recent findings suggest that taken together, these comparisons point to a clear role for TRL: a general-purpose library designed to keep breadth, simplicity, integration, and stability in the same place. Its full downstream footprint is hard to measure, since most deployments are private and reverse dependencies are largely invisible, but the available signals already show that TRL operates at a distinctly different scale.

By now, the logic of v1.0 should be clear: it is not a claim that post-training has stabilized. On the contrary, it is an acknowledgment that the field will keep shifting, and that we're confident that the library has the right shape to absorb whatever comes next. The question is not what comes after v1.0, but what’s next for v1.0.

Industry observers note that today, GRPO in TRL is primarily used through a synchronous loop: generate rollouts, score them, then step the optimizer. That shape is simple and dependable, but it ties throughput to the slowest stage and leaves performance on the table at scale.

The fix is conceptually simple: generation and training don't need to be lock-stepped. We already have an early asynchronous GRPO design, and the next step is to harden it. The core idea is to decouple generation and training, letting generation run continuously on dedicated inference resources while training consumes a steady stream of scored trajectories, with buffering, backpressure, and clear policy-version accounting. This improves utilization and scales across GPUs and nodes. Other libraries already offer forms of asynchronous RL, but bringing it to TRL would make this style of training available through broader integrations, simpler APIs, and a much lower barrier to adoption.

The next candidates include KTO and newer distillation trainers such as SDFT, SDPO, and possibly GOLD or GKD. As discussed in Section 2, before moving them to stable, the goal is to minimize code differences across implementations and monitor sustained community interest relative to maintenance cost.

Sources indicate that TRL supports large-scale training, including multi-node runs and larger models; the next step is to make this path significantly more robust and easier to operate in production. That includes stronger guarantees around distributed stability, clearer scaling defaults, and deeper support for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), especially expert parallelism, where routing, load balancing, and memory behavior become critical.

According to recent reports, training is still too often driven by vibes. Loss curves go down, reward curves go up, a few samples look better than before, and people convince themselves the run is working. When it fails, they scroll through logs, compare runs by eye, and guess. That is already a weak interface for humans. For agents, it is worse: it is barely an interface at all.

According to recent reports, one of the most important directions for TRL is to make training legible to software, not just to people. That means going beyond dashboards and raw metrics to produce explicit signals: is the policy improving, collapsing, over-optimizing the verifier, drifting off-distribution, or plateauing? The goal is for TRL to surface these patterns automatically, explain them clearly, and turn them into actions.

The plan is to embed heuristics directly into the training loop and emit structured, actionable warnings — the kind a beginner can act on immediately and an agent can parse:.

Not just logging what happened — reasoning about what it means and what to do next. Useful for beginners who need guardrails, and for agents that need a training stack they can actually automate.

Recent findings suggest that post-training doesn't converge. It shifts, and the next shift is already coming.

Sources indicate that v1.0 is not a claim that things have settled. It's an acknowledgment that they haven't yet, and a commitment that the library can be relied on anyway. Six years of evolving alongside the field — and alongside the hundreds of contributors who made it possible — shaped a design we're confident is ready for what comes next, whatever that turns out to be. The community and the downstream projects had already assumed that stability — v1.0 makes it real.

Migration from the last 0.x release is minimal, and the migration guide covers everything. If you're fresh, now is a good time to start.

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick is already being asked about GTA 7, despite GTA 6 only being days old.

Rockstar released GTA 6 on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, ending a 13-year wait for a new numbered Grand Theft Auto.

But while players are only just getting their first look at Vice City and the rest of Leonida, some are already looking ahead to the next entry in the series.

On launch day, Zelnick joined the TBPN podcast to talk about the release, and was asked early on about when GTA 7 could drop, to which he answered: “Once you get through several hundred hours of the most incredible fun you’ve ever heard, ask the question again.”.

Later in the interview, he was asked about the sequel again and how major the map could be, given that GTA 6 covers a huge city and a surrounding state.

“Theoretically, GTA 7 could just be a live version of the entire world, right?” one of the hosts asked, with Zelnick clearly amused by the question.

In a recent development, “We at Take-Two just went live with GTA 6 on November 19,” he jokingly replied. “Let me check my watch. Oh, it’s still November 19. And you’re asking a question about GTA 7. I mean guys, really?”.

Jordi: "Theoretically, GTA 7 could just be a live version of the entire world, right?"@StraussZelnick, the CEO behind GTA 6: "We went live with GTA 6 on November 19. Let me check my watch. Oh, it's still November 19. And you're asking a question about GTA 7." pic.twitter.com/sHdVawdln2.

He then mentioned a quote his father used to say about past achievements being “yesterday’s headlines,” but then quipped: “It’s not even yesterday.”.

In a recent development, with GTA 6 only just arriving, it will likely be years before we get any concrete information about its potential follow-up. However, Zelnick has hinted that Rockstar’s future games won’t take as long to make.

Plus, we still have GTA 6 Online to look forward to, which should tide players over until GTA 7.

#34922. XREAL Aura Initial Review: Taking Android XR out of the headset, but who is it for?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2337 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

XREAL Aura Initial Review: Taking Android XR out of the headset, but who is it for?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2337 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We all kind of want to be Tony Stark, don’t we?
  • XREAL isn’t upcoming to the mixed reality space.
  • According to recent reports, XREAL Aura is a two-part device.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We all kind of want to be Tony Stark, don’t we? Almost everyone can relate to that futuristic sense of wonder that comes from the movies where we see digital elements being interacted with through a simple wave of the hand. To date, that’s only really been replicable through massive ol’ headsets like Apple’s Vision Pro or the various Meta Quest sets. But with XREAL Aura, Android XR brings that feeling to something far easier to actually use, but my one remaining question is who this product is for.

XREAL isn’t upcoming to the mixed reality space. The organization has been building some of the best example of optical see-through XR glasses. These aren’t quite like a VR headset because they actually let you see the world around you, not through a camera, but by simply making the lenses themselves see-through. I’ve tried these in the past and, while they’re great for mirroring a tablet or laptop for bigger screen (especially on airplanes), I did feel they were missing something.

But first, let’s talk hardware.

According to recent reports, XREAL Aura is a two-part device. There are the glasses themselves which include two displays, one for each eye, and electrochromic dimming on the lenses to control just how much of the outer world you’re seeing. It’s wildly different from a typical VR headset, while also having most of the same benefits. Unlike most other XREAL glasses, Aura has built-in world-facing cameras used for hand and spatial tracking, as well as being able to be used as a camera for things like scanning QR codes, Gemini Live, or simply taking a quick picture (there’s no privacy light here, but the bulkier-than-normal design compared to standard glasses is more than enough a dead giveaway that the “perv glasses” dilemma doesn’t really apply in my opinion).

The other half of the formula is a wired puck that provides battery power and the brains of Android XR. There’s no screen on the puck, just a status light, and it has USB-C out for the glasses as well as USB-C in for power and/or external devices. It also has a fingerprint sensor (are you hearing this Android tablet makers??) and a touchpad, the latter used as a secondary, far subtler input method within Android XR to supplement hand tracking.

According to recent reports, together, these two make a wonderful package for building a true mixed reality experience. The displays are plenty bright for even the brightest indoor conditions (frankly, it’d be insane to use these outside in my opinion, though a wide-open plane window may present a challenge), and the electrochromic dimming does a great job of blocking out most, but not quite all of the world around you. If you’re looking to be fully cut off from reality as you would with a VR headset, these aren’t for you. I did find some display elements, like smaller text, a little tough to focus my eyes on at times, but I have a feeling that’s more so me being overdue for an eye exam than it is the glasses themselves. There’s virtually no flicker in my usage, with only bright white backgrounds occasionally being a little overbearing, and everything is smooth with the 120Hz refresh rate.

Where this hardware really shines compared to a typical VR headset is in its design, and it’s what makes XREAL a perfect partner for Android XR. The glasses themselves weigh in at 95 grams, a mere fifth of the Meta Quest 3 and Samsung’s Galaxy XR, and up to 700 grams less than Apple’s Vision Pro. It’s comfortable for much longer periods of time and not nearly as annoying to actually put on either, as it just feels like putting on a pair of bulky sunglasses. They look a little goofy, obviously, but far less so than a full-on VR headset like any of those mentioned above. This is also the only one of those I consider “mixed reality” thanks to the see-through lenses. Apple and Samsung constantly talk about Vision Pro and Galaxy XR as if they’re mixed reality, but a camera feed is explicitly not true reality. But XREAL’s glasses still aren’t quite just augmented reality, because they’re not just letting you see that digital world through a tiny window, they’re quite literally overlaying everything on top of the real world around you. The illusion is somewhat broken by the limited 70-degree field-of-view and the fact that darker backgrounds often look a little funky when there are light sources in the real world in front of you, but I can say with confidence that this is my favorite version of this experience – the speakers are pretty good too, topping it all off.

And that brings us to Android XR.

Google’s platform introduced on Samsung’s Galaxy XR headset earlier this year, and it’s all pretty familiar on XREAL Aura. The Android-based experience opens up to a floating launcher of your favorite apps that mostly open up into floating windows in front of you. You can use hand gestures to move everything around or interact with UI elements, and every app I tried worked perfectly well. The gestures can be hit or miss at times, especially the one for going back to the home screen (having this as a long-press that you have to physically look at your hand for gets annoying when doing anything remotely fast-paced, but thankfully the top button is a dedicated home shortcut), but it works well and everything is designed fairly intuitively. A floating cursor shows where you are aiming with a pinch acting as a tap on a touchscreen, and you can move things around in your space as if they’re real objects. There’s a sense of depth throughout the entire experience.

Some apps open to fully immersive experiences, but these are still in the minority. XREAL touts that there are around 150 experiences launching alongside Aura, but it’s definitely still early days here. Apps like Google TV should obviously be ready for a full format like that but, most things, like the Google Docs app which I’m typing this review in right now, just act as if they’re on independent displays floating around you.

In a recent development, like Googlebook, Android XR is also still struggling to figure out the best app experience for each user. Most things are mobile apps, including Google Chrome which is just the standard Android version from your phone. It’s fine in most cases, but I found this restrictive seeing as I can get a ton done in a browser, but fighting mobile optimization is a frustrating way to interact with a window that can be as significant as a TV if you want it to. Meanwhile, the Spotify app is weirdly the web version which is horribly optimized for interacting with hand gestures. I’d have rather had the mobile version here. Another quirk I found was notifications, which pop up at the top of the display and quite literally on top of whatever you’re doing. Something they were invasive, and having to physically reach out to dismiss them is a little annoying. I’m sure there are workflows to help make this less of a distraction, but I’d almost rather have notifications turned off entirely.

There’s also Gemini, which is core to the experience here. A quick “Hey Google” triggers a Gemini Live session for answering questions, and you can share what you’re seeing to give additional context. It’s way faster than switching between apps to get a quick search done, but there are friction points here, especially if you’re just asking a single question. Gemini answers quickly and leaves the conversation going, great for follow-up queries, bad if you’re done because the UI controls go away, which leaves you to tell Gemini to end the session which, every time, it asks for secondary confirmation you want to end. Google, if I say “end the session,” I think that should be more than sufficient proof I want to end the session. Luckily, a long-press of the top home button fixes that headache, but I still hate that I either need to use a physical control, or basically have to fight an AI to end a conversation that I started hands-free.

Industry observers note that performance is excellent. Everything is smooth and quick, probably thanks in part to XREAL’s use of 12GB of RAM alongside Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite chip.

But how do you actually use a product like this?

Industry observers note that that’s the question I found myself asking when I first spun up XREAL Aura and started to learn its ins and outs. See, other XREAL glasses have an extremely straightforward use case. Plug in the external device of your choice, get it on a bigger screen. Simple, easy, obvious. I found this helpful in travel primarily, with a bigger display for my MacBook feeling nice for tasks like video editing, while the main value came in just having a very comfortable way to watch a movie on a flight from my connected tablet.

Both of those use cases are valid on XREAL Aura. You can plug a USB-C device into the puck to get that wired mirroring through an Android XR window, and it works super well. Having Android XR alongside that mirroring also opens the door to added functionality, like having extra windows off to the side for perhaps a media app or reference document if you run out of room on the wired device. As just one example, I kept Spotify and Slack open in side windows while using Aura with my MacBook Air for an afternoon of writing articles.

I think Android XR makes Aura an absolute powerhouse for media consumption, as you can just download content directly to the device (256GB of storage in the base model) for a flight, or even just use streaming apps if you have Wi-Fi. I couldn’t find any 3D content during my brief review period (nothing in my Google TV library was compatible, apparently), but that’s also on the table. Genuinely, I cannot wait to use these on my next long flight.

But outside of those, I think a lot of the other scenarios start to fall apart.

By far the most popular use case for virtual/mixed reality has been gaming. XREAL Aura has a ton of potential here and I’m really excited to try out Project Hail Mary: Journey to the Stars on this, but the fact that these are simply glasses restricts a lot of what you can do. Any major movements could easily result in the glasses slipping or even falling off, whereas a VR headset is much more secure. Stationary immersive gaming has potential, and XREAL’s Gamesir controller collab highlights promise, but I’m just not sold on these as a replacement to something like Meta Quest seeing as the latter already has a deep catalog of games and a much more affordable price.

The other use case is productivity, one I’m also not entirely sold on. As mentioned, this entire post was written in Aura, and I’m not sure I benefitted much from that experience versus just using a normal laptop or desktop computer. My workflow was having Google Docs up in the center, typing on a physical keyboard (only a psycho could use the virtual keyboard for anything beyond the shortest messages or passwords) with reference documents in Chrome off to my right and Slack on my left, with the occasional “Hey Google” command helping to find information on the fly (such as the weight comparison earlier). It all works well, but I think Android XR is inherently limited by its reliance mostly on mobile apps, and also just by the use of gestures. You can use a mouse or trackpad, of course, but at that point you might as well just use a laptop.

Industry observers note that XREAL Aura is for a very specific customer from my point of view. Wired mirroring is still very much the strong suit here, with Android XR’s apps and offline video giving these utility outside of just relying on another device. That was my problem with previous XREAL glasses, because the experience just varies wildly depending on what’s connected. Aura’s puck and Android XR experience solves every complaint I had about previous models, while expanding very much on what it can do.

Further limiting matters is the price. $1,279, in my book, is actually a mostly fair price for this, especially given the RAMageddon of it all. XREAL 1+ Pro come in around $600 and is utterly useless without a secondary device. XREAL Aura more or less doubles the price, but includes the best possible version of that secondary device while also giving you the added camera sensors that are only available as add-ons for other hardware. Don’t get me wrong, it’s still pricey, but I don’t think it’s unfair either, especially not when one of the main competitors for this sort of experience is still $3,600 (which still sounds insane two years later, even for Apple).

We’ll have far more to say about XREAL Aura in a long-term review from our Nick Sutrich, but the verdict on day one is that Android XR has really solved the biggest problem for XREAL, while XREAL has solved a lot of major problems for Android XR, all while being an overall win for the user at the end of the day. Not so often we get a storybook ending like that in tech anymore, and I’m all here for it.

Industry observers note that don’t forget, XREAL Aura is $200 off – so $1,099 – through the end of December. Much more worth it at that price.

Most Chinese-brand Android phones don’t like it when you use a 3rd-party launcher, but the ColorOS 17 upgrade may be changing that.

Recent findings suggest that if I hop on a phone from Oppo, Vivo, Honor, or most other Chinese brands and try to use a 3rd-party launcher, I’m definitely not going to like how the phone operates. Often, there’s a weird delay when navigating back home or opening the Overview multitasking screen. Sometimes, Overview doesn’t work at all, essentially forcing you back to the default launcher that shipped with the phone.

Recent findings suggest that but one Reddit user says Oppo is doing things differently in the ColorOS 17 update. According to their experience, the delay and other concerns with 3rd-party launchers are completely solved. OnePlus’s OxygenOS doesn’t have the same issues, so it’s good to see that OnePlus owners who are still set to receive ColorOS 17 in the near future won’t feel like their phones are losing a valuable feature.

Chinese Android brands like Oppo, Vivo, Xiaomi, Realme, and several others often outshine Western brands in many ways, but they’ve always had one annoying weakness: software. Whether it’s the number of updates a phone receives, overall quality, or another specific problem, Chinese brands often build very different visions of Android than Google, Samsung, Motorola, or Nothing.

Industry observers note that the value and hardware prowess these phones usually deliver help outshine software weaknesses, and these companies have been steadily improving software over the past year or two to meet the demands of a more Westernized audience. Companies like Honor now offer 7 years of software updates, and ColorOS is widely regarded as the best Android skin next to Samsung’s One UI in many circles. That’s great news for everyone, especially in an age where fewer smartphone companies compete for your hard-earned dollars.

Training mRNA Language Models Across 25 Species for $165

📅 31 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By OpenMed, Open-Source Agentic AI for Healthcare & Life Sciences.
  • According to recent reports, TL;DR: We built an end-to-end protein AI pipeline covering structure prediction, sequence design, and codon optimization.
  • According to recent reports, imagine going from a therapeutic protein concept to a synthesis-ready, codon-optimized DNA sequence in an afternoon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By OpenMed, Open-Source Agentic AI for Healthcare & Life Sciences.

According to recent reports, TL;DR: We built an end-to-end protein AI pipeline covering structure prediction, sequence design, and codon optimization. After comparing multiple transformer architectures for codon-level language modeling, CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 emerged as the clear winner with a perplexity of 4.10 and a Spearman CAI correlation of 0.40, significantly outperforming ModernBERT. We then scaled to 25 species, trained 4 production models in 55 GPU-hours, and built a species-conditioned system that no other open-source project offers. Complete results, architectural decisions, and runnable code below.

According to recent reports, imagine going from a therapeutic protein concept to a synthesis-ready, codon-optimized DNA sequence in an afternoon. That is the pipeline OpenMed set out to build, and this post documents the process from start to finish.

In Part I, we mapped the landscape of protein AI: the architectures powering structure prediction, the open-source tools available for protein design, and the ecosystem of models from AlphaFold to ESMFold. That was a survey. This is the build.

At OpenMed, we set out to build a complete pipeline that takes a protein idea from concept to expression-ready DNA. That means three stages: predict the 3D structure of a protein, design amino acid sequences that fold into that structure, and optimize the underlying DNA codons so the protein actually expresses in the target organism. Along the way, we ran extensive experiments comparing transformer architectures for codon optimization, scaled our best model to 25 species, and built tooling that ties it all together.

This is not a polished success story. It is a transparent account of what worked, what surprised us, and what we would do differently, with runnable code and full results at every step.

Industry observers note that the pipeline has three components, each addressing a different stage of the protein engineering workflow described in Part I. Structure prediction determines what shape a protein takes. Sequence design determines which amino acids will produce that shape. Codon optimization determines which DNA will produce those amino acids efficiently in a living cell.

The mRNA optimization work is where we invested the most effort, and where we have the most to share. The folding and design components use established tools (ESMFold from Meta, ProteinMPNN from the Baker Lab, both covered in depth in Part I). The codon optimization component is entirely ours: latest models, new training infrastructure, new evaluation metrics.

It has been revealed that in Part I, we surveyed the protein AI landscape and noted that most biological language models are adaptations of NLP architectures. The open question was which architecture. BERT variants dominate protein modeling (ESM-2, ProtTrans), but codon sequences have different statistical properties than both natural language and amino acid sequences. Codons are triplets drawn from a small 64-token alphabet, with strong positional dependencies and species-specific usage biases. We needed to find out what works from first principles.

The core question: which transformer architecture works best for codon-level language modeling?

This matters because codon optimization is crucial for therapeutic mRNA, vaccines, and recombinant protein production. The genetic code is degenerate: the same protein can be encoded by astronomically many different DNA sequences, but some codon arrangements express 100x better than others. The Pfizer-BioNTech COVID vaccine, for example, was codon-optimized for human expression. We wanted to build a model that could learn these preferences directly from natural coding sequences, rather than relying on hand-crafted frequency tables.

We started with a small CodonBERT baseline (6M params, following Sanofi's published architecture) and scaled up through two families: ModernBERT, which represented the latest efficiency innovations from the NLP community, and RoBERTa, the proven workhorse behind Meta's ESM protein language models.

The choice of RoBERTa was deliberate. As we discussed in Part I, Meta's ESM-2 (which powers ESMFold) is itself a RoBERTa variant trained on protein sequences. We hypothesized that the same architecture family that learned amino acid patterns might also learn codon patterns. ModernBERT was the counterpoint: a 2024 architecture with RoPE embeddings, Flash Attention, and alternating local/global attention layers, representing everything the NLP community had learned since RoBERTa's 2019 release.

Industry observers note that to ensure a fair comparison, every model was trained on identical data with the same evaluation protocol. We used 250,000 coding sequences (CDS) from E. coli RefSeq, covering chromosome and complete assembly accessions. This is a clean, well-annotated dataset where codon usage patterns are well-characterized in the literature, giving us ground truth to validate against.

According to recent reports, our tokenizer maps each codon to a single token: 64 codons plus 5 special tokens (PAD, UNK, CLS, SEP, MASK) for a 69-token vocabulary. This is intentionally minimal. Unlike BPE tokenizers used in NLP, where subword boundaries are statistically learned, codon boundaries are biologically defined. Every three nucleotides encode one amino acid. Our tokenizer respects this.

Training ran on 4 A100 GPUs (80GB) with FSDP sharding, using 15,000 to 25,000 steps depending on model size. All models used masked language modeling (MLM) with 15% masking rate, the same objective used by ESM-2 for protein sequences.

Recent findings suggest that the result was unambiguous: RoBERTa outperformed ModernBERT by 6x on perplexity (4.01 vs 26.24). This was not a marginal difference. ModernBERT, despite its modern attention patterns and efficient architecture, fundamentally underperformed the classic RoBERTa design on codon sequences.

According to recent reports, 1. Pre-trained NLP weights do not transfer to biology.

Industry observers note that we initialized ModernBERT from its published English-language checkpoint, expecting the learned attention patterns to provide a useful starting point. They did not. Our best explanation: ModernBERT's pre-training on English text instilled inductive biases (subword frequency distributions, positional attention patterns) that actively interfere with learning codon statistics. RoBERTa, initialized randomly and trained purely on biological data, had no such baggage. This aligns with what the field has seen more broadly: ESM-2 and ProtTrans both train from scratch on biological data rather than fine-tuning from NLP checkpoints.

Recent findings suggest that 2. Hyperparameter tuning unlocked biological alignment.

Recent findings suggest that this was the most surprising and practically important finding of the exploration. Compare CodonRoBERTa-large v1 and v2:.

Recent findings suggest that same architecture. Same data. Same number of parameters. The only differences: half the learning rate and a longer warmup (2,000 steps vs 1,000). Yet v2's predicted codon likelihoods are 16x better correlated with real biological codon preferences, as measured by Codon Adaptation Index.

According to recent reports, the perplexity actually got slightly worse (4.10 vs 4.01), which means v2 is marginally less accurate at predicting the exact masked codon. But it is dramatically better at predicting codons that biology actually uses. The slower training schedule let the model settle into representations that capture genuine biological signal rather than overfitting to surface statistics.

According to recent reports, this is a crucial insight for anyone training biological language models: MLM loss alone does not measure biological relevance. Domain-specific metrics are essential. In our case, CAI correlation turned out to be the metric that separates a useful model from a technically impressive but biologically meaningless one.

3. The base model is remarkably efficient.

CodonRoBERTa-base (92M params) achieved nearly identical perplexity to the large model (4.01 vs 4.10) with 3.4x fewer parameters and proportionally less training time. Its CAI correlation (0.219) is lower than v2's (0.404), but still well above the baseline and ModernBERT. For teams without access to multi-GPU clusters, the base model is a practical choice that captures most of the codon modeling performance at a fraction of the cost.

Recent findings suggest that in Part I, we described the three-stage workflow that most computational protein engineering projects follow: predict structure, design sequences, optimize codons. Here we run each stage with real data and report what we actually got.

ESMFold architecture. The model parses a single amino acid sequence through the ESM-2 encoder, then predicts 3D coordinates via a folding trunk and structure module. Figure from Bertoline et al., Biomolecules 2024, CC-BY 4.0.

As covered in Part I, ESMFold is Meta's single-sequence structure predictor. It uses ESM-2, a 15-billion-parameter protein language model trained on 65 million UniRef sequences, as its backbone. The key advantage over AlphaFold 2 is speed: ESMFold skips the computationally expensive multiple sequence alignment (MSA) step and predicts structures directly from a single amino acid sequence. That makes it seconds per protein instead of hours.

Recent findings suggest that the tradeoff is accuracy. ESMFold achieves ~0.87 TM-score on CASP14 targets vs. AlphaFold's ~0.92. For rapid prototyping and candidate screening, that gap is acceptable. When a pipeline generates 100 designed sequences and needs to refold all of them to check viability, speed matters more than the last few percentage points of accuracy.

We ran ESMFold on 30 protein chains sourced from the Protein Data Bank. These are real experimental structures with known ground truth, spanning sequence lengths from 211 to 519 residues. The set deliberately includes both easy targets (single-domain proteins) and challenging ones (chains from a multi-chain ribosomal complex, PDB 7K00) to stress-test the model.

According to recent reports, the PTM scores are solid: anything above 0.5 suggests the model has the overall topology correct, and our average of 0.79 indicates high confidence in the predicted folds. The pLDDT scores are lower than published ESMFold benchmarks, which initially concerned us. The explanation turned out to be our test set composition: the ribosomal chains from 7K00 are part of a large multi-chain complex, and ESMFold (which predicts single chains in isolation) cannot model the inter-chain contacts that stabilize these structures. For single-domain proteins in our set, pLDDT scores were consistently above 70.

Recent findings suggest that each prediction takes ~10-30 seconds on an A100. The output includes:.

ProteinMPNN architecture. (A) The encoder processes backbone atom distances; the decoder autoregressively generates amino acid sequences. (B) Random decoding order improves diversity. (C) Tied positions enable symmetric and multi-state design. Figure from Dauparas et al., Science 2022, CC-BY 4.0.

It has been revealed that as we described in Part I, protein design is the inverse of protein folding. Folding goes sequence to structure: given amino acids, predict the 3D shape. Inverse folding goes the other way: given a target 3D shape, find amino acid sequences that will fold into it.

Sources indicate that proteinMPNN, from David Baker's lab at the University of Washington, is the current gold standard for this task. It was published in Science in 2022 and has since been validated experimentally: designed sequences fold into their target structures at rates far exceeding random or earlier computational methods. The architecture treats the protein backbone as a graph, where nodes are amino acid positions and edges connect spatially proximate residues (K-nearest neighbors in 3D). A message-passing neural network propagates information through this graph, then autoregressively generates a sequence one residue at a time.

We ran ProteinMPNN on PDB structure 7K00 (a large multi-chain ribosomal complex):.

Here's what the output looks like:.

The first line is the native (natural) sequence extracted from the crystal structure. Subsequent lines are ProteinMPNN's designed variants. At temperature 0.1 (low randomness), the model recovers ~42% of the original amino acids, purely from 3D geometry. This is a strong result: it means the model independently rediscovered nearly half the residues that evolution selected, using only the backbone coordinates as input.

In a recent development, several practical notes from running ProteinMPNN. Scores are negative log-likelihoods, so lower is better. The 42% recovery rate is typical for well-resolved structures and consistent with the original paper's benchmarks. Higher sampling temperatures produce more diverse but riskier sequences. For real design work, the most powerful feature is partial design: catalytic residues, binding site amino acids, or any positions with known functional importance can be fixed in place, while ProteinMPNN redesigns only the scaffold around them. This is the standard approach for engineering a more stable version of an enzyme without disrupting its active site.

This is where the pipeline transitions from existing tools to our own models. ESMFold and ProteinMPNN are established, well-validated software that we integrated. Codon optimization is where we built something new.

Codon usage frequencies vary dramatically between organisms. These heatmaps compare codon preferences across E. coli, yeast, and CHO cells, the three expression hosts covered by our multi-species models. Figure from Kim et al., J. Microbiol. Biotechnol. 2025, CC-BY 4.0.

The genetic code is degenerate: most amino acids are encoded by multiple codons. Leucine, for example, has six: TTA, TTG, CTT, CTC, CTA, and CTG. All six produce the same amino acid in the final protein. Methionine and tryptophan are the exceptions, with only one codon each.

It has been revealed that this redundancy means that for any given protein, there are astronomically many DNA sequences that encode it. A typical 300-amino-acid protein has roughly 10^150 possible codon combinations. They all produce the same amino acid chain, but they do not all produce the same amount of protein. Codon choice affects translation speed (because tRNA molecules are not equally abundant for all codons), mRNA stability (because the nucleotide sequence affects how swiftly the transcript degrades), co-translational folding (because translation pauses at rare codons give the protein time to fold), and immune recognition (because the innate immune system in mammalian cells can distinguish native from foreign mRNA patterns). In practice, bad codon choices can reduce protein expression by 100x. This is why every mRNA vaccine, every recombinant protein therapeutic, and every gene therapy vector goes through codon optimization.

In a recent development, the scale of the codon optimization problem. For a typical mRNA, there are over 10^600 possible codon sequences encoding the same protein. The challenge is finding the arrangement that maximizes expression. Figure from Zhang et al. (LinearDesign), Nature 2023, CC-BY 4.0.

The classical method is simple: measure which codons appear most frequently in highly-expressed genes of the target organism, then replace every codon with the most frequent synonym. This is codified as the Codon Adaptation Index (CAI), a per-sequence score that measures how closely the codon usage matches the organism's preferred distribution.

Industry observers note that CAI-based optimization works, but it is crude. It treats each codon position independently, ignoring the sequence context. It produces repetitive sequences (the same "optimal" codon used everywhere for a given amino acid), which can cause ribosome stalling and mRNA secondary structure problems. And it misses complex dependencies: the optimal codon at position 50 might depend on what codons are at positions 48 and 52, which a frequency table cannot capture.

According to recent reports, we reframe codon optimization as a language modeling problem. Instead of looking up frequencies in a table, we train a transformer on hundreds of thousands of natural coding sequences using masked language modeling (MLM), the same pre-training objective used by BERT, RoBERTa, and Meta's ESM protein models. The model sees a codon sequence with 15% of positions masked and learns to predict the missing codons from context.

Recent findings suggest that what the model learns, implicitly, is the grammar of codon usage: which codon patterns appear in nature, which codons tend to co-occur, and how preferences shift depending on the surrounding sequence context. This is fundamentally richer than a frequency table because the model captures long-range dependencies across the entire coding sequence.

After our architecture exploration (see above), CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 emerged as the winner:.

Evaluating a codon language model is not straightforward. As we learned from the v1/v2 comparison above, a model can have excellent perplexity (accurately predicting masked codons) while having poor biological alignment (predicting codons that nature does not actually prefer). We evaluate on three complementary axes:.

According to recent reports, 1. Perplexity measures how well the model predicts masked codons, computed as the exponentiated cross-entropy loss. A perplexity of 4.10 means the model is, on average, choosing between ~4 equally likely codons at each masked position. Given that most amino acids have 2-6 synonymous codons, this indicates the model has learned meaningful preferences rather than guessing uniformly. Lower is better. CodonRoBERTa-large-v2: 4.10.

2. CAI Correlation (Spearman) measures whether a model's predicted codon likelihoods align with known biological codon usage preferences. We compute the Codon Adaptation Index for each test sequence, then correlate it with the model's pseudo-log-likelihood score. A positive correlation means the model assigns higher probability to sequences that biology actually uses. This is the metric that matters most for practical codon optimization, because it directly measures whether the model has learned biologically relevant patterns vs. just statistical ones. CodonRoBERTa-large-v2: 0.404 (p < 10^-20).

3. Synonymous Recovery asks: when the model predicts a codon for a masked position, does it at least get the amino acid right? Even if it picks the wrong synonym (e.g., CTT instead of CTC for leucine), predicting the correct amino acid shows the model understands the protein-level constraint. CodonRoBERTa-large-v2: 12.1% top-1 synonymous.

Putting it all together across our model variants:.

Sources indicate that the RoBERTa family dominates across the board. For production use, CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 is the clear choice: it has the strongest biological alignment (CAI 0.404) while maintaining competitive perplexity. For teams with limited compute, CodonRoBERTa-base delivers nearly the same perplexity at 3.4x fewer parameters. ModernBERT underperformed substantially, which we attribute to its NLP-pretrained weights interfering with codon pattern learning.

Single-species codon optimization is useful, but limited. Every organism has its own codon usage biases shaped by millions of years of evolution. E. coli favors different codons than human cells, which favor different codons than yeast. A model trained only on E. coli data will not produce optimal codons for human expression.

Sources indicate that the industry standard is to use separate CAI tables for each organism. We wanted something better: a single model that understands codon usage across organisms, can be conditioned on a target species, and can transfer knowledge from data-rich organisms (human, with 145k annotated coding sequences) to data-poor ones (E. coli, with 9k). After establishing CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 as our best architecture on single-species data, we built this system.

Assembling a multi-species codon dataset is not as simple as downloading a few genomes. Each organism lives in a different NCBI RefSeq assembly, with different annotation quality, different CDS boundaries, and different sequence conventions. We wrote an automated pipeline that downloads CDS sequences from 25 organisms, validates them (checking for proper start/stop codons, length divisible by 3, no internal stops), labels each sequence with a species token, and splits into train/test sets with stratification by species.

The final dataset spans three domains of biotechnology relevance:.

Recent findings suggest that the coverage is deliberate: bacteria are the workhorse of recombinant protein production, yeast dominates industrial biomanufacturing, and mammalian cells (especially CHO and human) are required for therapeutic proteins and mRNA vaccines. These 25 organisms collectively cover the vast majority of real-world codon optimization use cases.

A model that sees sequences from 25 different organisms needs to know which organism it is looking at. We solved this by extending our 69-token codon vocabulary with 25 species tokens, creating a 94-token system. Each sequence is prepended with its species token (e.g., [HUMAN], [ECOLI], [YEAST]), so the model learns species-specific codon preferences within a single shared architecture.

Industry observers note that this design has three advantages. First, it enables species-conditioned generation: the same model produces human-optimal or E. coli-optimal codons depending on which species token is prepended. Second, it enables cross-species transfer learning: universal codon patterns (like avoiding certain dinucleotides, or preferring GC-rich codons in GC-rich genomes) are shared across all species, while species-specific preferences are captured by conditioning on the species token. Third, the 94-token vocabulary is backward-compatible with our 69-token single-species models, since the first 69 tokens are identical.

Industry observers note that the universal base model is a 311.9M-parameter RoBERTa-large, identical in architecture to our single-species v2 but with the expanded 94-token vocabulary. It was trained for 48 hours on 4 A100 GPUs using the full 362k-sequence multispecies dataset.

The test perplexity of 24.9 is higher than our single-species model's 4.01, which might look like a regression. It is not. The multispecies model must learn distinct codon preferences for 25 different organisms, each with its own evolutionary history and tRNA pools. A bacterium like M. tuberculosis (65% GC content) uses completely different codons than human cells (41% GC). The model is solving a fundamentally harder problem, and the perplexity reflects that. What matters is whether species-specific fine-tuning can recover performance, and it does.

The universal base model is a generalist. For production use, specialists perform better. OpenMed's fine-tuning strategy starts from the multispecies checkpoint and trains further on a single species at a lower learning rate (2e-5 vs 5e-5), preserving cross-species knowledge while specializing the model's predictions for one organism.

Training all three priority species:.

The most vital result here is the HUMAN model: at 24.3 perplexity, it is the only specialist that beats the universal base, making it our production model for therapeutic mRNA applications. But the ECOLI result is arguably more interesting from a research perspective. With only 8,547 training sequences (compared to 131k for human), the E. coli specialist still improved over the multispecies base. This validates the transfer learning hypothesis: training on 25 species first, then fine-tuning on a small species-specific dataset, works better than training on the small dataset alone. For the many organisms where annotated CDS data is scarce, this approach opens the door to reasonable codon optimization without needing tens of thousands of species-specific sequences.

Industry observers note that the CHO model showed slight degradation (25.5 vs 24.9), which we attribute to insufficient training steps. ECOLI got 5,000 steps for 8.5k sequences (0.59 steps per sequence), while CHO got 10,000 steps for 42.5k sequences (0.24 steps per sequence). A rerun with 15,000 steps should close this gap. All three specialists fine-tuned in just 7 hours total, leveraging the 48-hour investment in the multispecies base.

After 55 hours of training, we have:.

All models will be released on Hugging Face under the OpenMed organization. The naming convention follows OpenMed/{model-name} for direct use with from_pretrained().

OpenMed/CodonRoBERTa-large-human (311.9M params).

OpenMed/CodonRoBERTa-large-ecoli (311.9M params).

OpenMed/CodonRoBERTa-large-cho (311.9M params).

OpenMed/CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 (312M params).

OpenMed/CodonRoBERTa-base (92M params).

For therapeutic mRNA (Moderna, BioNTech-style vaccines):.

For industrial protein production:.

According to recent reports, the multi-species suite covers the three pillars of applied codon optimization. For therapeutic mRNA, the HUMAN specialist model optimizes codons for expression in human cells, directly applicable to vaccine design (Moderna and BioNTech both codon-optimize their mRNA constructs) and gene therapy vectors. For recombinant protein production, the ECOLI specialist handles the most common bacterial expression host, while the CHO specialist covers the mammalian cell line used to produce most monoclonal antibodies and biopharmaceuticals. For organisms not covered by a specialist, the multispecies base model accepts any of the 25 species tokens and generates organism-appropriate codons.

The transfer learning result is particularly relevant for the broader community. Many industrially key organisms (non-model bacteria, insect cells, plant cells) have limited annotated CDS data. Our results with E. coli (8.5k sequences, improved over base) suggest that multispecies pre-training followed by small-scale fine-tuning is a viable path for these organisms, without requiring the tens or hundreds of thousands of sequences that training from scratch demands.

Industry observers note that the full project consumed 55 GPU-hours on 4 A100 80GB GPUs (~$165 at AWS spot pricing), produced ~150 GB of models and checkpoints across 4 training runs, and covers 381,283 CDS sequences from 25 species downloaded from NCBI RefSeq. All models use the same 311.9M-parameter architecture, are saved in safetensors format for fast loading, and run inference on a single GPU with 16GB+ VRAM. Everything is released under Apache 2.0.

It has been revealed that the modern computational protein design workflow. Structure generation (top) produces backbone coordinates; sequence optimization (bottom) finds amino acid sequences that fold into the target shape. Our pipeline adds a third step: codon optimization for expression. Figure from Kortemme, Cell 2024, CC-BY 4.0.

In a recent development, in Part I, we described the protein engineering loop as a cycle of prediction, design, and optimization. Here is what that looks like in practice with OpenMed's pipeline. Each step feeds into the next, and the entire computational phase runs in an afternoon on a single GPU.

Consider a concrete scenario: engineering a more stable version of a therapeutic enzyme that degrades too promptly in the bloodstream.

Industry observers note that step 1: Fold (ESMFold). Predict the structure of the starting sequence to understand its active site and identify regions that might be destabilized. ESMFold returns a 3D structure in PDB format, per-residue confidence scores (pLDDT) highlighting uncertain regions, and an overall topology confidence metric (PTM).

Recent findings suggest that step 2: Design (ProteinMPNN). Keep the active site fixed but redesign the scaffold for improved stability. ProteinMPNN takes the backbone coordinates, a list of immutable positions (catalytic residues), and generates 100 diverse candidate sequences, each predicted to fold into the target shape.

Industry observers note that step 3: Verify (ESMFold). Refold all 100 candidates with ESMFold to confirm they still adopt the correct shape. Filter for high mean pLDDT (>80), correct topology (RMSD to original), and low clash scores.

It has been revealed that step 4: Optimize (CodonRoBERTa). Take the best amino acid sequences and use CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 to generate optimal DNA sequences for expression in the target organism (E. coli, yeast, or mammalian cells). The model scores synonymous codon choices based on learned biological preferences, identifies contextually optimal codons rather than just globally frequent ones, and produces sequences with high CAI correlation.

It has been revealed that step 5: Synthesize and Test. Order the DNA from a synthesis firm, clone it into an expression vector, and test expression and activity in the lab.

According to recent reports, this loop, from hypothesis to synthesis-ready DNA, replaces what once took months of iterative wet-lab trial and error. A researcher arrives at the bench with 5-10 computationally vetted candidates instead of one or two educated guesses. The success rate improves, the cost drops, and the design cycle compresses from months to days.

For a full ecosystem overview, tool selection guide, and license reference, see Part I.

OpenMed is not working in isolation. Two recent models push the codon/mRNA modeling frontier further:.

mRNABERT (Xiong et al., Nature Communications 2025): 86M-param BERT with a dual tokenization scheme (single nucleotides for UTRs, codons for CDS) and cross-modality contrastive learning against frozen ProtT5-XL protein embeddings. Trained on 18M sequences. Achieves R^2 = 0.66 on full-length mRNA translation efficiency, a 1.6-10x improvement over prior RNA models. Code and weights available (Apache 2.0).

According to recent reports, NUWA (Zhong et al., bioRxiv 2026): Three domain-specific RoBERTa encoders (Bacteria, Eukaryota, Archaea) with curriculum MLM and supervised contrastive learning. Trained on 115M sequences across ~25,000 species. Beats CodonBERT on 11/13 BEACON benchmark tasks. No code or weights released.

In a recent development, both models train on 50-300x more data than OpenMed used. That is the primary gap, and we are transparent about it.

Here is what OpenMed does that neither of them offers:.

Species-conditioned single model. mRNABERT has no species conditioning at all. NUWA trains three separate models (one per domain of life). We put 25 species tokens into one 94-token vocabulary and train a single model that can be prompted for any organism. More parameter-efficient, more flexible.

Recent findings suggest that transfer learning to low-resource organisms, validated. We showed that fine-tuning the multispecies base on just 8.5k E. coli sequences improves over the base model. Neither mRNABERT nor NUWA demonstrates this.

Industry observers note that full open-source pipeline. ESMFold + ProteinMPNN + CodonRoBERTa, end to end, with training code, configs, eval scripts, and model weights. All Apache 2.0. mRNABERT releases code but not the pipeline. NUWA releases nothing.

OpenMed is running a proof-of-concept for a fundamentally different approach: Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) for codon sequences.

Standard MLM predicts masked tokens. JEPA predicts masked embeddings. The hypothesis: if the model is forced to predict in embedding space rather than token space, it should learn that synonymous codons (different DNA, same amino acid) are functionally equivalent. MLM cannot achieve this because it is trained to distinguish every token.

Early results from our evaluation suite (JEPA vs. MLM baseline, same data, same hyperparameters, 15k steps each):.

The synonymous robustness result is the one that matters most for our hypothesis. JEPA embeddings are nearly identical (99.97% cosine similarity) for sequences that differ only in synonymous codon choices. MLM embeddings shift significantly (94.14%). This means JEPA does learn that synonymous codons are interchangeable, exactly as predicted.

In a recent development, the open challenge: JEPA currently suffers from dimensional collapse (91.78% of variance concentrated in one component). This is a known failure mode for self-supervised methods and suggests the VICReg regularization weights need tuning. The architecture works; the training dynamics need more iteration.

It has been revealed that this is early-stage research, not production-ready. But if the collapse problem can be solved, JEPA could produce codon embeddings that are inherently amino-acid-aware, something that MLM, by its token-level prediction objective, fundamentally cannot achieve.

A brand-new phone that doesn’t connect to the internet has been rolled out in Japan, and it looks like the classic Nokia phones that you might remember.

For years, smartphone customers have been trying to find creative solutions to cut down their screen time, especially as phones have started doing weekly reviews of app usage and screen time.

Some have opted to set time limits on the apps they can use, while others have created heavyweight cases that will quite literally force you to work out in order to use your smartphone.

According to recent reports, in other cases, some people have taken a step back in time, ditching their smartphones for flip phones and devices that don’t actually connect to the internet. These throwback phones have popped up across Europe and the United States, and now Japan is getting in on the act with a new device.

As per The Japan Times, Japan’s KDDI Corporation has introduced a mobile phone with “minimal functions.”.

According to recent reports, named the Infobar Zero, it will be available to pick up on Christmas Day, and is limited to calls, text messages, and other basic features. Owners won’t have the ability to connect to the internet, but it will have a camera and a music player.

While it isn’t a complete recreation of Nokia’s iconic 3310 phone, the Infobar Zero does strike up plenty of comparisons to that classic device.

Additionally, the ‘dumbphone’ isn’t aimed at replacing your smartphone, but rather providing a break from the smartphone life.

It has been planned by KDDI for quite some time, just as a way of relieving the reliance to live life on apps.

Owners will be able to register their phone numbers on the Zero and a smartphone as part of KDDI’s “two numbers” system – sort of like using an eSIM in some parts of the world.

Microsoft outage brings fax machines back into action across Japanese offices.

$499 flip phone that blocks all social media revealed by console maker Commodore.

This latest phone is built to break your social media addiction.

You will be able to keep your smartphone at home when you go to school or work, and then return to using it later in the day, if that’s how you choose to live.

Elsewhere, a latest app called Island has been debuted, and the farming simulator-like game will actually punish you for spending too much time on it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

In a recent development, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Sources indicate that A self-hosted LLM gateway sits between your app and the model provider, so every call pays for one extra hop. We measured that cost for three open-source gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each one ran on the same machine, in front of the same OpenAI model. LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to every non-streaming call. AcruxCore added 15 to 24 ms. Langfuse's number could not be told apart from zero.

It has been revealed that the bigger lesson was about the measurement itself. Before we controlled for it, one OpenAI network address moved our results by more than any gateway did.

Industry observers note that each number is the median time a gateway added to a direct OpenAI call, with its 95% interval in brackets. A gateway can log each call, and logging takes time, so we ran the test three times with three logging levels.

According to recent reports, the direct call took 781 to 831 ms at the median, so even LiteLLM's cost is under 9% of a short call. Read the tables this way:.

The obvious test is to time 100 calls through the gateway, time 100 direct calls, and compare the two medians. That test gives the wrong answer, for two reasons.

Sources indicate that the first reason is noise. OpenAI's own response time moved by hundreds of milliseconds between calls in our runs. The direct call's p95 was 1,047 to 1,233 ms against a median near 800 ms. A gateway that adds 20 ms is hidden inside that spread unless the test removes it.

The second reason is the network path to OpenAI. It does not stay the same between a direct client and a gateway, and that difference can be larger than the gateway itself.

Industry observers note that api.openai.com resolves to more than one address. From our network, DNS returned two Cloudflare addresses, and one was much farther away than the other. We measured both with a script that pins one address at a time:.

It has been revealed that on a connection that is already open, both addresses answer in the same time. On a new connection, the far address adds about 250 ms, because the TCP and TLS handshakes take that much longer.

A gateway keeps its connection to OpenAI open between calls. It pays the setup once and then stays on whichever address it reached first. A client that opens a new connection for each call pays the setup again on every call. How much it pays depends on which address DNS returns that time.

In a recent development, node's built-in fetch closes an idle connection after about 4 seconds. So a test client that calls OpenAI every few seconds reconnects on almost every call. In our first, uncontrolled run, the Langfuse gateway came out 43 ms faster than calling OpenAI directly. A gateway cannot be faster than the call it forwards. The direct client paid for newly introduced connections, and the gateway did not.

The fix has two parts. First, pin api.openai.com to one address on every path. In Docker, that is an extra_hosts entry on each gateway container:.

It has been revealed that second, let the direct client keep its connection open, as a gateway does. With undici, the HTTP client behind Node's fetch, that is a custom Agent:.

We then listed each container's open connections to confirm that every path used the same address. The edge-check script is in the repository linked at the end, and it takes about a minute to run from your own network.

It has been revealed that this advice also applies outside benchmarks. If your app calls OpenAI directly from Node, keep the connection open between calls. Otherwise some of your calls pay the handshake, and on a far address that costs about 250 ms.

Industry observers note that each test sent 150 rounds after 5 warm-up rounds. One round calls OpenAI directly and through each gateway, once without streaming and once with streaming. The order rotates every round, so no path always goes first or last.

For each round, the script takes the gateway's time minus the direct call's time in that same round. Calls in one round are made within a few seconds of each other, so a slow moment at OpenAI hits all four paths together and cancels out of the difference. The script then reports the median of the 150 differences.

Industry observers note that the interval comes from a bootstrap. The script draws 150 differences at random, with replacement, and takes their median. It repeats that 2,000 times, and the middle 95% of those medians is the interval. This is a shortened version of the script's function:.

An interval that includes zero means the test could not separate the gateway's cost from zero. That is what the Langfuse rows show. It does not prove that the cost is zero.

Every call used OpenAI gpt-6-luna with reasoning_effort: "none", the same short prompt and a cap of 5 output tokens. A short answer keeps the model's own time small, so more of the measured time belongs to the path. Each streamed call measured the time to its first token. Each non-streamed call measured the time to the full response.

All three gateways did real work on every call, which made the comparison fair:.

The three logging levels mapped to these settings:.

The machine was an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X with 62 GB of RAM, running Fedora Linux and Docker 29.9. All three stacks ran on it at once, and the test was run on 10 November 2026.

Industry observers note that liteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to the full response, but only 9 to 43 ms to the first streamed token. The first token arrives as soon as the model starts to answer, so time spent before that point shows up in both numbers. The larger cost without streaming suggests that most of LiteLLM's extra time is spent after the model has answered. We did not profile LiteLLM to confirm this.

Sources indicate that logging level made no clear difference for any gateway. Adding LiteLLM's Langfuse callback did not raise its cost. AcruxCore's median rose from 15 ms with logging off to 24 ms with full logging, but its intervals overlap across all three runs. AcruxCore's median is 16 to 24 ms above Langfuse's, and those intervals overlap too, so this test does not rank the two of them.

Industry observers note that if 60 ms per call matters to you, as in a chat app that makes several model calls per user message, LiteLLM's cost is real and repeatable. Langfuse and AcruxCore stayed near or within the noise. If your calls take several seconds, any of the three costs less than OpenAI's own variation from one call to the next.

It has been revealed that before you trust a gateway number, your own or anyone else's, check two things. Was each gateway compared with a direct call in the same round? And did the direct client keep its connection open on the same OpenAI address as the gateway? Without both, the result measures the network path and not the gateway.

The scripts, Compose files and raw results are on GitHub: scripts/comparison/langfuse-gateway-vs-litellm-vs-acruxcore.

Google Voice is a wonderful service that’s often neglected, but with RCS supposedly on the way, a newly introduced app redesign is now rolling out on Android that might as well have a significant neon sign that says “RCS is coming.”.

Google Voice is a US-only service that operates a phone number over the internet. No normal carrier, just an app tied to your Google account that gets a phone number with the ability to make calls and send/receive text messages. The latter, though, has been a point of contention for the past few years as Voice was excluded from Google’s huge push into RCS.

Industry observers note that that might finally be changing, though. Recent updates brought mention of RCS in the app’s code.

Now, a slightly newer version (v2026-11-01-1019342246) of Google Voice has debuted a redesign for the app on Android.

Industry observers note that the fresh look isn’t a drastic restructuring, but a huge coat of paint on an app that hasn’t seen any meaningful updates since 2023. The new look feels more modern and very much influenced by Google Messages. The text field at the bottom has a rounded design with the same “+” and camera icons found in Messages, as well as a new long-press gesture that is, again, similar to Google’s primary messaging app. The main page hasn’t been updated beyond a new, rounded search bar up top and some subtly bolder fonts.

According to recent reports, material You colors are hit or miss now. On a Pixel with an orange theme, that color influenced the entire UI, but on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 with a coral/blue theme, the only sign of themeing was a blue message field.

The most important thing here is the “SMS” icon on the send button, which looks just like the button in Google Messages. In that app, it’s used as an indicator as to what type of message you’re sending – SMS or RCS. Combined with code in that other recent revision directly pointing to “RCS” being used on a send button, you can absolutely tell Google Voice is finally adding this long-overdue functionality.

A timeline for RCS support in Google Voice is still unclear, but this redesign going live now certainly suggests it’s coming sooner rather than later.
