💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we're excited to announce Granite 4.0 3B Vision, a compact vision-language model (VLM) designed for enterprise document understanding.
  • In a recent development, the model ships as a LoRA adapter on top of Granite 4.0 Micro, our dense language model, keeping vision and language modular for text-only fallbacks and seamless integration into mixed pipelines.
  • Granite 4.0 3B Vision’s performance is the result of three key investments: A purpose-built chart understanding dataset constructed via a novel code-guided data augmentation approach, a novel variant of the DeepStack architecture that enables high-detail visual feature injection, and a modular design that keeps the model practical for enterprise deployment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we're excited to announce Granite 4.0 3B Vision, a compact vision-language model (VLM) designed for enterprise document understanding. It’s purpose-built for reliable information extraction from complex documents, forms, and structured visuals. Granite 4.0 3B Vision excels on the following capabilities:.

In a recent development, the model ships as a LoRA adapter on top of Granite 4.0 Micro, our dense language model, keeping vision and language modular for text-only fallbacks and seamless integration into mixed pipelines. It continues to support vision-language tasks such as producing detailed natural-language descriptions from images (e.g., “Describe this image in detail”). The model can be used standalone or in tandem with Docling to enhance document processing pipelines with deep visual understanding capabilities.

Granite 4.0 3B Vision’s performance is the result of three key investments: A purpose-built chart understanding dataset constructed via a novel code-guided data augmentation approach, a novel variant of the DeepStack architecture that enables high-detail visual feature injection, and a modular design that keeps the model practical for enterprise deployment.

It has been revealed that charts present a challenge for vision-language models (VLMs) because understanding them requires jointly reasoning over visual patterns, numerical data, and natural language, a combination most VLMs cannot handle well, especially when spatial precision matters—such as reading exact values off a line chart. To close this gap, we’ve developed ChartNet: a million-scale multimodal dataset purpose-built for chart interpretation and reasoning, described in detail in our upcoming CVPR 2026 paper.

In a recent development, chartNet uses a code-guided synthesis pipeline to generate 1.7 million diverse chart samples spanning 24 chart types and 6 plotting libraries [see Figure 1]. What makes it so distinctive is that each sample consists of five aligned components—plotting code, rendered image, data table, natural language summary, and QA pairs—providing models a deeply cross-modal view of what a chart means, not just what it looks like. The dataset also includes human-annotated and real-world subsets, filtered for visual fidelity, semantic accuracy, and diversity.

The result is a training resource that moves VLMs from merely describing charts to genuinely understanding the structured information they encode—with consistent gains across model sizes, architectures, and tasks.

Figure 1: ChartNet’s synthetic data generation pipeline.

Sources indicate that most VLMs inject visual information into their language model at a single point, which forces the model to handle both high-level semantics and fine-grained spatial detail simultaneously. Granite 4.0 3B Vision takes a different approach with DeepStack Injection: abstract visual features are routed into earlier layers for semantic understanding, while high-resolution spatial features are fed into later layers to preserve detail. The result is a model that understands both what is in a document and where—which is critical for tasks like table extraction, chart understanding, and KVP parsing where layout matters as much as content. For a full technical breakdown, see the Model Architecture section of the model card.

Granite 4.0 3B Vision is packaged as a LoRA adapter on top of Granite 4.0 Micro, rather than as a standalone model. In practice, this means the same deployment can serve both multimodal and text-only workloads, automatically falling back to the base model when vision isn’t required. This keeps enterprise integration straightforward without sacrificing performance.

According to recent reports, charts: Evaluated on the human-verified ChartNet benchmark using LLM-as-a-judge, Granite 4.0 3B Vision achieves the highest Chart2Summary (86.4%) score among all evaluated models, including significantly larger ones [see Figure 2]. It also ranks second on Chart2CSV (62.1%), behind only Qwen3.5-9B (63.4%), a model more than double its size.

Figure 2: Granite 4.0 3B Vision performance on chart2csv and chart2summary, compared against peer vision-language models using LLM-as-a-judge.

Tables: We evaluate table extraction in two settings: cropped tables (isolated regions) and full-page documents (tables embedded in complex layouts) [see Figure 3]. The benchmark suite includes TableVQA-extract (cropped table images), OmniDocBench-tables (full-page documents), and PubTables-v2 (both cropped and full-page settings). Models are tasked with extracting tables in HTML format and scored using TEDS, a metric that captures both structural and content accuracy. Granite 4.0 3B Vision achieves the strongest performance across benchmarks, leading on PubTablesV2 on both cropped (92.1) and full-page (79.3), OmniDocBench (64.0), and TableVQA (88.1) scores among all evaluated models.

Figure 3: Granite 4.0 3B Vision’s table extraction performance across cropped and full-page benchmarks (TableVQA-extract, PubTables-v2, OmniDocBench-tables), measured by TEDS.

Sources indicate that semantic KVP: VAREX is a benchmark specifically designed to discriminate between small extraction models, comprising 1,777 U.S. government forms spanning simple flat layouts to complex nested and tabular structures. Models are evaluated using exact match (EM), a strict metric that requires the model’s extracted key-value pairs to match the ground truth. Granite 4.0 3B Vision achieves 85.5% EM accuracy zero-shot.

Granite 4.0 3B Vision can operate either as a stand‑alone visual information extraction engine or as part of a fully automated document‑processing pipeline with Docling. The model is designed to support scalable, accurate extraction across diverse document types and visual formats.

1. Stand‑Alone Image Understanding Granite 4.0 3B Vision can run directly on individual images, making this option useful for applications with existing workflows that need targeted visual extraction without modifying upstream systems. This offers easy integration into existing automation workflows and is suitable for lightweight, task‑specific tools (e.g., form parsers, chart analyzers, etc.).

2. Integrated Document Understanding Pipeline With Docling Granite 4.0 3B Vision can also be integrated seamlessly with Docling to support complete end‑to‑end document understanding. This mode can offer:.

Granite 4.0 3B Vision is available now on HuggingFace, released under the Apache 2.0 license. Full technical details, training methodology, and benchmark results are available in the model card. We’d love to hear what you build with it—share your feedback in the community tab.

While many GTA 6 fans across PlayStation and Xbox are enjoying their time in Leonida, it’s not all sunshine and rainbows for everyone trying to explore Rockstar’s latest installment.

Since its November 19 release, players have reported game-breaking crashes that prevent them from progressing through the main story and even playing altogether.

In a Reddit post, one PS5 player mentioned the game had worked flawlessly until they reached Pipework, one of the game’s early missions, where you are introduced to Mandy.

Recent findings suggest that “It crashes every time I use the plunger or stand around the sink with it,” they wrote, adding that they can no longer progress through the story. “You would think the plane flying was intensive, but it crashes every time I use the plunger or stand around the sink with it. I just paid $125 for my PS5 to be repaired and $100 for the game, this is ridiculous.”.

Others are running into problems much earlier, with a PS5 Pro owner revealing the game crashes as the opening prologue begins.

“Game keeps crashing at the exact same point during the opening prologue. I’m using a PS5 Pro and have been unable to play since launch. The game crashes immediately as the startup prologue begins, either at the exact same point or a couple of seconds into it, displaying error code CE-108255-1.”.

When checking the PlayStation Support page, error CE-108255-1 prompts players to simply “try updating your game”. However, GTA 6 fans who have encountered this issue on PS5 have reported that clearing the console’s cache, rebuilding its database, factory resetting the PS5, and downloading the game three times has done nothing to alleviate the problem.

GTA 6 forces you to take your time with the main story instead of speedrunning it.

PS5 users are reporting crash issues when booting from rest mode.

Crazy GTA 5 footage highlights NPC ‘drunk driver’ cause huge accident.

“Despite all this, the issue persists. It crashes at the same point every single time,” they wrote. “I’m honestly extremely disappointed and frustrated at this point. I’ve exhausted almost every troubleshooting step available online and still haven’t been able to play.”.

According to recent reports, the reports are not limited to PlayStation, either, as some Xbox Series X players have also reported crashes within minutes of play. “The game sometimes even crashes after only 15 minutes. The first crash happened about 2 hours after I started playing, and ever since that it kept crashing,” added another player.

Rockstar’s GTA 6 troubleshooting page right now directs players experiencing console errors to PlayStation or Xbox support, but hopefully a patch will fix this concern sooner rather than later.

📅 01 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A few weeks ago, we wrote about one-shotting full web apps with gr.HTML: building rich, interactive frontends entirely inside Gradio using custom HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  • What if you want to build with your own frontend framework entirely like React, Svelte, or even plain HTML/JS, while still benefiting from Gradio's queuing system, API infrastructure, MCP support, and ZeroGPU on Spaces?
  • Industry observers note that that's exactly the problem gradio.Server solves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A few weeks ago, we wrote about one-shotting full web apps with gr.HTML: building rich, interactive frontends entirely inside Gradio using custom HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. That unlocked a lot. But what if that's not enough?

What if you want to build with your own frontend framework entirely like React, Svelte, or even plain HTML/JS, while still benefiting from Gradio's queuing system, API infrastructure, MCP support, and ZeroGPU on Spaces?

Industry observers note that that's exactly the problem gradio.Server solves. And it changes what's possible with Gradio and Hugging Face Spaces.

It has been revealed that text Behind Image : an editor where you upload a photo, the background gets removed using an ML model, and then you place stylized text between the foreground subject and the background. The text appears to sit behind the person or object in the image.

There's no way to express this UI in Gradio components. It's a full web application. But We still wanted the backend power of Gradio: queuing, concurrency management, ZeroGPU support, and hosting on HF Spaces without infrastructure headaches.

gradio.Server extends FastAPI. It gives you the full power of FastAPI (custom routes, middleware, file uploads, any response type) while adding Gradio's API engine on top: queuing, SSE streaming, concurrency control, and gradio_client compatibility.

Here's the entire backend for Text Behind Image:.

That's it. ~50 lines of Python. The model loads at startup, @spaces.GPU handles ZeroGPU allocation, and gradio.Server manages queuing and concurrency. Let's break down what's happening.

Recent findings suggest that if this were a regular FastAPI app, you'd define a @app.post() route for background removal. That works, until two owners hit it at once. Without concurrency management, both requests fight for the GPU, and the app crashes or returns garbage.

It has been revealed that @app.api() solves this. It wraps your function with Gradio's queuing engine: requests are serialized, concurrency is controlled, and on ZeroGPU Spaces, GPU allocation is handled automatically via @spaces.GPU. As a bonus, any @app.api() endpoint is also callable via gradio_client, so other apps or scripts can use your Space programmatically:.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, @app.get("/") is a standard FastAPI route that serves the HTML page. Both coexist naturally because Server is a FastAPI app.

The index.html in this example is a self-contained ~1300-line web application. No React, no build step, no bundler. Just vanilla HTML with:.

The frontend talks to the backend using the Gradio JS Client:.

Recent findings suggest that this is the key part: by using the Gradio JS client rather than a raw fetch() call, the frontend goes through Gradio's queue. That means concurrency is managed, GPU requests don't collide, and you could even show queue position or progress to the user. Everything else, text rendering, layer compositing, export, happens in the browser.

Here's what was not possible before gradio.Server:.

With gradio.Server, Gradio doubles as a backend framework, use its UI system when you want it, bring your own frontend when you don't.

Industry observers note that if you want Gradio's UI, you can use gr.Blocks, gr.Interface, gr.ChatInterface. If you want your own UI, use gradio.Server and bring whatever frontend you like. Either way, you get Spaces hosting, API queuing, gradio_client access, the full HF ecosystem, and more.

The app is live on Spaces: ysharma/text-behind-image.

Upload any photo with a clear subject, and start layering text behind it. Try the 3D extrusion, perspective tilt, and stroke effects, they combine nicely.

Industry observers note that this post covered the core idea: gradio.Server lets you pair any frontend with Gradio's backend. There's more to explore, including MCP tool registration with @app.mcp.tool(), SSE streaming for real-time updates, batch processing, and patterns for building multi-page apps with shared state.

It has been revealed that we'll dig into those in a follow-up post. Stay tuned.

Animal control was forced to respond to a call about an alligator on the loose, but it turned out to be just a pool floatie. Seriously.

Over the years, plenty of people have rushed to call emergency services to report something that, when investigated, turned out to be totally false.

This was the case over in Sugar Land, Texas, on November 12 when animal control received a call about an alligator being on the loose. As per Sugar Land Animal Services, they were told that the gator appeared to be feeling a bit sick and in need of some assistance.

Industry observers note that yet, when they reached it, it wasn’t all it seemed. “When ASO Perez arrived on the scene to investigate, she was in for a big surprise. What looked very real from a distance turned out to be a runaway pool floatie!” they posted on Facebook.

“While this call definitely gave our team a good laugh, we always take every report seriously,” Animal Services added.

According to recent reports, in the photo, the inflatable gator had its mouth stuck open with teeth on show, so if you see it from a distance, you might be confused. However, up close, you can tell it’s meant to be lounged on, not hunted or scared of.

Industry observers note that “Remember: if you ever spot wildlife that looks sick or injured, please keep a safe distance and call the experts to handle it. You never know if it’s the real deal!”.

Naturally, commenters saw the funny side of things too. “Well, that was a rather inflated story then,” one joked. “She is very brave! Thank you, Officer Perez, for all you do,” another added. “Wow. It looks so realistic! Crazy,” another replied.

As noted, it isn’t the first instance of floaties being reported as real, nor is it the wildest.

Chipotle is bringing back its Thanksgiving BOGO promotion, giving customers a chance to score a free meal ahead of the holiday.

The fast food chain confirmed on November 20 that its Back Home BOGO deal will return for one night only, allowing Rewards members to get two meals for the price of one at participating US restaurants.

The promotion first launched in 2025 and became Chipotle’s largest sales-driving campaign of the year. Its return comes as millions of Americans prepare to travel home and reconnect with friends and family over Thanksgiving weekend.

Recent findings suggest that on Wednesday, November 25, Chipotle Rewards members can receive a free meal when purchasing another one of equal or greater value between 5 p.m. and 9 p.m. local time.

To redeem the offer, customers must visit a participating US Chipotle restaurant and scan their Rewards membership card at checkout.

The promotion is available exclusively in restaurants, meaning orders placed through the Chipotle app, website, delivery services, or third-party platforms will not qualify.

Customers can receive up to five free meals per check, provided they purchase an meal of equal or greater value for each free item. Kids’ meals do not count toward the promotion.

“Thanksgiving Eve is when the hometown group chat comes to life,” said Stephanie Perdue, Chipotle’s Senior Vice President of Brand Marketing.

“Whether Chipotle is the first stop of the night or where the crew ends up later, we’re giving friends a place to get together over real food. The response last year showed us how much our guests embraced the occasion, and we’re excited to bring it back as another reason for hometown crews to reconnect before Thanksgiving.”.

Chipotle is giving away free food to anyone with a tattoo for one hour only.

Chipotle is offering $6 entrees on Halloween to customers who wear costumes.

Chipotle rolls out School Spirit BOGO with free entrees for back-to-school season.

The company cited Morning Consult research showing that 76% of Gen Z consumers visit restaurants to socialize with friends and family, highlighting the role dining out plays in holiday gatherings.

Chipotle is also offering a separate promotion following Thanksgiving, giving customers a $0 delivery fee on qualifying orders from November 27 through November 30.

Recent findings suggest that to claim the delivery offer, customers must enter the code CYBER26 when ordering through Chipotle’s app or website. The deal requires a minimum purchase of $10 in the US or $12 in Canada, excluding taxes and fees.

Although the delivery fee will be waived, customers may still face higher menu prices and additional service fees.

Both promotions are available for a limited time at participating locations, with the Thanksgiving BOGO ending at 9 p.m. local time on November 25.

Industry News: Falcon Perception

📅 01 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, TL;DR — Falcon Perception is a 0.6B-parameter early-fusion Transformer for open-vocabulary grounding and segmentation from natural language prompts.
  • We also relase Falcon OCR, a 0.3B-parameter model which reaches a score of 80.3 and 88.6 on the olmOCR benchmark and OmniDocBench respectively, while having the highest throughput of any open source OCR model.
  • This post is a brief, practical write-up of what we built, why we built it this way, and what we learned along the way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, TL;DR — Falcon Perception is a 0.6B-parameter early-fusion Transformer for open-vocabulary grounding and segmentation from natural language prompts. The model processes image patches + text in one sequence using a hybrid attention mask, and produces variable numbers of instances with a small, structured token interface and lightweight output heads. On SA-Co, Falcon Perception reaches 68.0 Macro-F1 (vs. 62.3 for SAM 3) with the main remaining gap being presence calibration (MCC 0.64 vs. 0.82). We also introduce PBench, a diagnostic benchmark that breaks down performance by capability (attributes, OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, relations) and by dense long-context crowded scenes.

We also relase Falcon OCR, a 0.3B-parameter model which reaches a score of 80.3 and 88.6 on the olmOCR benchmark and OmniDocBench respectively, while having the highest throughput of any open source OCR model.

This post is a brief, practical write-up of what we built, why we built it this way, and what we learned along the way.

In a recent development, many open-vocabulary perception systems are built as modular pipelines: a (often frozen) vision backbone extracts features, a separate fusion/decoder stage combines them with language, and additional components handle matching and post-processing. This family of designs works well in many settings, but it comes with trade-offs: it can be hard to scale cleanly, hard to attribute improvements to the right component, and easy to accumulate complexity as we add a new fix for each failure mode.

We asked a simpler question: can a single early-fusion Transformer backbone handle both perception and language modeling, if we choose the right attention pattern, output interface, and training signal?

In our experiments, the answer is largely yes. The rest of this post describes the main design choices and the evidence behind them.

According to recent reports, A single autoregressive Transformer processes a unified sequence of image patches, text, and task tokens. The model predicts object properties in a fixed order: → → . Bounding box coordinates and sizes are decoded via specialized heads and re-injected as Fourier features. High-resolution segmentation masks are generated by a dot product between the token and upsampled image features.

According to recent reports, at its core, Falcon Perception is a dense Transformer that processes image patches and text tokens in a shared parameter space from the first layer. Instead of a separate vision backbone followed by a late-fusion decoder, we keep a single backbone and rely on masking and a lightweight output interface to make the dense prediction problem tractable.

In a recent development, images and text have different structure: pixels are 2D and benefit from bidirectional context, while the prediction interface is naturally sequential. We address this with a hybrid attention mask:.

This allows the same backbone to behave like a bidirectional visual encoder on image tokens, while still supporting autoregressive prediction over task tokens.

Dense perception is not a fixed-size prediction problem: an image may contain zero instances or hundreds. Autoregressive generation gives a clean variable-length interface, but fully autoregressive dense generation (e.g., polygons or high-resolution masks token-by-token) quickly becomes expensive.

We use a small structured interface, Chain-of-Perception, which decomposes each instance into three steps:.

This ordering is deliberate. Committing to geometry first reduces ambiguity (“which instance?”), and makes the mask prediction step closer to pixel refinement conditioned on the resolved object.

The backbone is shared, while decoding uses lightweight heads tailored to the output type:.

In a recent development, coordinate & Size Heads use Fourier feature encoding : mapping continuous coordinates through a random Gaussian projection into a high-dimensional sinusoidal space. This overcomes the spectral bias of neural networks, yielding more precise localization than discrete binning alone. Decoded coordinates are re-injected into the sequence as conditioning for subsequent tokens.

Segmentation Head computes a dot product between the token’s hidden state and content-aware upsampled image features. Because the token is produced after geometry and has access to early-fused visual context, we can avoid the separate mask-query machinery and Hungarian matching that often appears in decoder-based instance segmentation training.

Existing referring-expression benchmarks like RefCOCO are saturated — models routinely hit 90%+ — and they conflate what went wrong. Did the model fail because it can't read text? Can't understand spatial relationships? Can't handle a crowd?

We introduce PBench, a diagnostic benchmark that separates samples by the dominant capability required:.

Each sample targets one dominant capability: OCR prompts avoid spatial qualifiers, and spatial prompts avoid in-image text disambiguators. This yields a capability profile rather than a single opaque score, and makes it easier to decide where to invest next (data, training curriculum, or post-training).

Industry observers note that rather than training from random weights (which in our ablations was unstable for segmentation), Falcon Perception initializes via multi-teacher distillation. Two strong vision teachers contribute complementary signals:.

The distilled initialization achieves 74.25% zero-shot accuracy on ImageNet-1k and 85.11% linear-probe mIoU on Pascal VOC, providing a strong visual foundation before perception-specific training.

We build the training set through a multi-stage pipeline:.

We maintain a strict 1:1 ratio of positive to negative samples. This makes presence calibration a first-class target: the model should reliably say “absent,” not only draw masks when confident.

Recent findings suggest that stage 1 — In-Context Listing (450 GT): The model learns to autoregressively list scene inventories — predicting text expressions and their locations. Full causal attention between queries enables learning of object co-occurrence ("fork, then knife, then plate"). This builds broad scene understanding.

Stage 2 — Task Alignment (225 GT): The attention mask is modified so queries can no longer see each other, simulating independent queries at inference time. Loss on text tokens is masked, focusing gradient signal entirely on presence classification and localization. This stage transitions from "scene understanding" to "answer this specific question.".

Stage 3 — Long-Context Finetuning (10 GT): A short phase with the mask limit raised to 600 per expression and a minimal constant learning rate. This adapts the model for extreme crowd density without forgetting earlier capabilities.

Key design choices validated through ablations:.

Sources indicate that on the SA-Co open-vocabulary segmentation benchmark, Falcon Perception (0.6B parameters) achieves 68.0 Macro-F1, compared to 62.3 for SAM 3, with large gains on attribute-heavy (+8.2), food & drink (+12.2), and sports equipment (+4.0) splits. At the same time, Falcon Perception lags SAM 3 on presence calibration (MCC: 0.64 vs 0.82), which is the clearest remaining improvement axis.

Here's an example output — the prompt "Falcon" produces precise instance masks:.

Falcon Perception also performs well for reffering expressions, able to correctly segment the burger with a black bun in each frame of the video:.

This is where the early-fusion design indicates the largest differences:.

According to recent reports, on simple objects, the gap is modest. As prompts become more compositional—requiring OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, or relational binding—the gap widens.

In our PBench Dense split, Falcon Perception (0.6B) substantially outperforms generalist VLM baselines (e.g., 72.6 vs 8.9 for Qwen3-VL-30B in our evaluation setup), and matches or exceeds the 8B model on spatial and relational tiers.

As prompts grow more compositional — requiring OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, relational binding, or scaling to hundreds of instances — the early-fusion advantage becomes visually clear:.

It has been revealed that "168 wine bottles": Falcon Perception identifies the bottles labeled "168", while SAM 3 highlights every bottle. "Honolulu direction sign": Falcon reads the text to find the right sign.

Recent findings suggest that "Lower meat skewer on left grill," "black car to the right of red car at bottom," "Belgian flag on the left" — Falcon Perception resolves the correct instance from spatial constraints. SAM 3 predicts false positives for multiple candidates.

It has been revealed that "Pastry next to brown round bread," "person using phone," "person holding helmet in hand" — Falcon Perception identifies the interacting instance. SAM 3 highlights all instances of the object class, ignoring the relational constraint.

"Snow goose," "pigeon," "colorful canned drinks" — Falcon Perception autoregressively segments hundreds of instances. SAM 3's fixed-size decoder runs out of query tokens beyond ~200 instances.

In a recent development, modern OCR has moved well beyond extracting text from clean scans. Today's systems must handle multi-column layouts, mathematical formulas, tables, charts, and multilingual content — all in one pass. Most competitive OCR VLMs tackle this with a familiar recipe: a vision encoder feeding a separate text decoder, plus task-specific glue. These systems work, but they tend to be large (1B–3B+ parameters).

In a recent development, we took a different path: reuse the same early-fusion dense Transformer from Falcon Perception, but train a smaller 0.3B-parameter variant from scratch specifically for OCR. The result is Falcon OCR — a single backbone that processes image patches and text tokens in a shared parameter space with the same hybrid attention mask (bidirectional for image tokens, causal for text tokens), and switches tasks through prompts rather than additional modules.

We trained from scratch (no multi-teacher distillation) because the visual features OCR needs — fine-grained glyph recognition, stroke-level discrimination — differ substantially from the object-level features useful for segmentation. Starting fresh lets the backbone develop text-optimized representations from the ground up.

In a recent development, we train on a curated English-language mixture spanning three core tasks: general document text parsing (digital PDFs, old scans, typewritten documents), mathematical and scientific formula recognition, and table structure recognition. The mixture also includes handwriting, real-world scene text, and synthetic samples generated from rendered LaTeX and HTML sources. The training objective is pure next-token prediction on structured text outputs.

Training proceeds in two phases: a long pre-training phase at constant learning rate where the model learns core OCR capabilities across all element types, followed by a short cosine-decay finetuning phase where the learning rate is annealed to near zero.

In a recent development, we evaluate on olmOCR (binary correctness checks across diverse inputs) and OmniDocBench (continuous metrics over full-page parses). All comparison models are significantly larger and/or use proprietary infrastructure. At 80.3% on olmOCR with only 0.3B parameters, Falcon OCR is within 1.7 points of the top system and leads all models on Multi-Column (87.1%) and Tables (90.3%). On OmniDocBench it scores 88.64 overall, ahead of DeepSeek OCR v2, GPT 5.2, and Mistral OCR 3.

At 0.3B parameters, Falcon OCR is roughly 3x smaller than 0.9B-class OCR VLMs, which translates directly into higher serving throughput. Measured on a single A100-80GB with vLLM at high concurrency:.

The compact footprint and vLLM integration (continuous batching, PagedAttention, optimized CUDA kernels) make it practical for large-scale document digitization where millions of pages need processing.

More broadly, these results suggest that the early-fusion single-stack Transformer is a viable alternative to the "vision encoder plus text decoder" recipe for OCR. One backbone, shared parameter space, one decoding interface, and better data and training signals rather than increasingly complex pipelines. We hope this encourages more work in this direction.

Falcon OCR processes images captured under challenging real-world conditions with varying lighting, diverse text semantics (mathematical formulae, structured tables, handwritten notes), and complex document layouts, to produce structured text output.

Click each category below to expand.

Falcon OCR extracts text from handwritten documents and real-world photographs with variable lighting, orientation, and content complexity.

Falcon OCR accurately reproduces cell entries and structural layout from tables of varying formats and complexity.

Falcon OCR correctly transcribes mathematical expressions ranging from simple equations to multi-line derivations with nested operators.

Falcon OCR preserves reading order and structural fidelity when extracting text from documents with multi-column layouts, figures, and footnotes.

The release includes an inference stack built on PyTorch’s FlexAttention, which makes it practical to express the custom attention patterns and efficiently serve packed variable-length sequences.

It has been revealed that in our setup on an H100, typical latencies are on the order of ~100ms prefill, ~200ms upsampling (0ms if cached), and ~50ms decode for a handful of instances. (These numbers depend on resolution, sequence length, and the number of predicted instances.).

For the Falcon-OCR model, we also provide a vLLM docker server for fast deployment and MLX integration for Apple-Silicon.

Please check out the github repo for details.

Falcon Perception is intentionally minimal: one backbone, one objective family, and small heads only where outputs are continuous and dense. The working assumption is that most gains should come from data, compute, and training signals, rather than continually expanding the pipeline with specialized modules.

The architecture doesn't block any obvious scaling path: add more images and harder prompts for better grounding, mix in text-only data for better language, increase context length for denser scenes. It's still just one sequence model.

Falcon Perception is developed by the Falcon Vision Team at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII), Abu Dhabi, UAE.

If you use Falcon-Perception, please cite.

It has been revealed that the pages of a site form a graph. Think of it as many nodes connected to each other via edges. Each of the edges are the links between the pages, and the nodes themselves are the pages. Now if you start to visualize this as a graph, you will promptly see that there are multiple ways to traverse this graph and reach a particular endpoint.

A search crawler usually uses one of these pages as a starting point and crawls through all of the pages (especially when pages are not fully covered in a sitemap).

Sources indicate that if a page lies very deep from the home page, it means that it's not an vital page. It's an indication to the search engine that this is not something that you yourself consider important, and the search engine has a lesser incentive to rank this page over pages that are linked better within your site.

In a recent development, the key metric here is link depth. That is the number of clicks it takes to reach a particular page from your home page.

In a recent development, another key metric is broken links. If you have too many broken links, it indicates to the search engine that your site is outdated and not well maintained, and the search engine will then not want to rank your site.

The way to identify both these problems is the same: to actually walk through your site, do a crawl of your site outside in, and try to figure out what the link depth is and if there are broken links on your website.

Seed the crawl with the home page and all URLs mentioned in the sitemap. Technically, the sitemap is not required if you're doing a crawl, but going from the sitemap will allow us to detect orphaned pages as well.

Fetch the pages and follow redirects as required. Record when you're following a redirect: we do not let fetch follow it silently, we record each hop and add its target to the crawl. Record HTTP errors as they occur.

Drop URL fragments and tracking parameters. Keep trailing slashes because sometimes there can be mismatches around expectation of trailing slashes in different URLs of a site.

In order to navigate from the home page, we can use BFS. So we know that the first time we reach a page, that is the page's shortest path.

We can cut off the depth over a certain threshold, say 5, to indicate that pages beyond that are too far or too deep to be reached.

According to recent reports, noindex pages will still be crawled. However, we need to make a record of them being not indexed, to reflect that they will not be present in the search engine.

Sources indicate that the desired page depth is as close to the home page as possible. Important pages should be close to the home page. The deeper you go from the home page, it signals to the search engine that the page is less important.

The suggested fix for this is that we link the pages from as close to the home page as possible:.

You can use some of the code over here to create your own crawler and identify internal linking complications; the full script is in this gist. Alternatively, we can use a free internal link visualizer to identify these issues and focus only on the fixes to improve our site's internal linking.

As previewed at I/O 2026, you can text — via Google Messages and iMessage — or email directly with Gemini.

Instead of using the Gemini app, you can now reach the AI assistant to “start tasks and get updates” using your preferred method of communication. To get started, go to gemini.google.com/channels.

You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries.

Text with Gemini works via Google Messages and iMessage. Google does note that this method is “not end-to-end encrypted and may be accessible by your carrier.” The setup process involves verifying a phone number. Afterward, you’ll receive a text from Gemini via RCS Business Messaging that offers a pretty straightforward chat experience. Before sending, booking, or other “major actions,” Gemini will ask for 1-tap confirmation.

…you can text a request, snap a photo of a school flyer to add dates to your Google Calendar, or get scheduled check-ins in a private 1:1 thread. If your intends change while Gemini is working, simply reply to the text to steer the task mid-run without starting over.

(Amusingly, Text with Gemini coexists with the existing Google Messages integration, which you can distinguish by the old blue/purple icon.).

It has been revealed that email with Gemini lets you “start tasks and get updates by emailing” gemini@google.com. Google explicitly names Gmail, Apple Mail, or Outlook as supported clients, while emails from Gemini are always “1:1 to you (never “Reply-All”) with a link to review and confirm your results.”.

Forward a batch of school emails to add key dates to Google Calendar, spot schedule conflicts, or send over threads and PDFs to sort out medical bills and track insurance renewals.

You can manage phone numbers and turn off both options from this latest Channels page. If you’re more familiar with using your email client or phone’s messaging app, Text and Email with Gemini might boost your assistant usage. This is available first in the US.

Meanwhile, when announced in May, these two options were intended for Gemini Spark, which has since been integrated into the main Gemini experience as “tasks.”.

#34900. Playing GTA 6 this weekend? Here's 16 spoiler-free tips for your first playthrough

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1805 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

Playing GTA 6 this weekend? Here's 16 spoiler-free tips for your first playthrough

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's launch weekend for GTA 6 - in case you hadn't noticed - and since I've played the best part of a hundred hours of this thing, I thought it might be useful to share a few pieces of advice from my time with it.
  • Many of these are most applicable for the early game, but there are a few that'll be worth bearing in mind throughout.
  • The below list is spoiler-free, so you can relax if you're anxious about going through the story entirely fresh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's launch weekend for GTA 6 - in case you hadn't noticed - and since I've played the best part of a hundred hours of this thing, I thought it might be useful to share a few pieces of advice from my time with it.

Many of these are most applicable for the early game, but there are a few that'll be worth bearing in mind throughout. After last night's driving around I would also maybe add in a quick bonus one, come to think of it: watch out for cyclists making last-minute left turns. Or don't, actually. Half of this lot deserve it….

The below list is spoiler-free, so you can relax if you're anxious about going through the story entirely fresh. Though naturally I do explain the way some parts of this game work, taking away some of the sense of discovery. You can take my word for it that there's plenty more to discover beyond this though, so worry not.

If you'd like even more help navigating Leonida, then check out our wonderful guide team's GTA 6 walkthrough.

Recent findings suggest that the number one thing I'd tell people to do in GTA 6 is to create lots of save files and, as you progress and start needing to overwrite them, to try to keep a roughly even spread of files through each chapter. There are various reasons for this - for one, while the game autosaves, it doesn't seem to do that successfully if you suddenly lose power to the console or witness a rare game crash, so it'll preserve your progress. More than that: GTA's story and missions are surprisingly, perhaps mysteriously reactive. Quite a lot can differ, and so being able to go back and make different choices, or play the game differently, will be something 'future you' likely appreciates.

It has been revealed that in the very early game you won't have access to a bank account, but once you do: you should put every bit of cash you have in there as soon as you can. Cash is lost on death or arrest - which can happen quite often in GTA 6, funnily enough - and there's no real benefit to carrying it around. Just about everything, besides in-game strippers, can be paid for via your BuckMe account directly. And there's a relatively low $20,000 limit you really don't want to hit in the middle of raiding a gang hideout, either.

According to recent reports, GTA 6 has a luxurious range of customisation settings, from hiding notifications about your relationship to reinstating the old 'tap to sprint' control scheme. The accessibility settings - while crucially I'm not an expert - seem considerable. And there are somewhat disguised difficult settings here around enemy damage taken and encounters with the police.

Fairly early in the game you'll gain access to the Scooter Bros. App, which lets you repair or summon your owned vehicles at will. Crucially, there's also an option to pay a one-off fee to unlock three free uses of the app per day. At $12,000, in the early game this is a lot of dosh, but once you rack up that kind of money after advancing through the game a little, it's well worth the initial cost. The sooner you unlock it, the more value it provides over time on a cost-per-use basis. And trust me when I say: as the game's intensity ramps up, you will probably find yourself needing to repair and recover your vehicles quite often. (Also, in Chapter 1, before you get access to the app, you can access the same service by going to your phone's contacts and calling Joey - handy!).

Sources indicate that rockstar has somewhat disincentivised it by adding a cost and putting it in your phone's apps rather than the main map screen, but you can fast travel around Leonida if you ever want or need to. This is done via the RideMe Uber-like app. It's not cheap - you'll need to pay both the fee for the journey and an additional $100 to skip that journey and instantly arrive at your destination, but in certain scenarios it might prove useful. To skip the journey, hold L2/LT once in the cab, and then hold down Triangle/Y when the option is shown. However….

Recent findings suggest that while it's possible to journey-skip your way around this world, having tested that first hand I'd advise against it. It might be obvious, but GTA 6 is genuinely designed around you manually travelling around, typically in the car. If you skip all your commutes between missions or locations, you'll miss out on the game's dozens and dozens of emergent events, which lead to anything from one-off jokes to entire mission chains. The car is also, in a way, kind of the heart of the entire game. Relish the intentional slowness!

Industry observers note that again, avoiding spoilers here, but in the mid game the 'true' loop of GTA 6 gameplay will properly reveal itself, in all the many methods of earning money and the increased emphasis on doing so. You can of course play the game however you like, but having reached the end and looked back from that point, I found that if there was a particular moment to set aside as the time for aimlessly exploring the world, it was from around Chapter 3 onwards. You'll have enough tools to be able to see it at more or less its fullest then, but also won't have missed anything essential by waiting until that point to take your foot off the pedal either.

A handy early-game tip here that even I missed when I was playing, but have since discovered: two islands in the small cluster of them to the south-west of Jason's early game home each house a really useful weapon, in a silenced pistol and a handy shotgun. You'll own these permanently once found, and so they can be incredibly helpful for navigating missions with maximum or minimal violence. Look for shipwrecks on those islands to find them. The pistol is hidden under a little hatch on the deck of a shipwreck on the southernmost point of the south-easternmost island. The shotgun is next to a small wooden wrecked boat around the middle of the northernmost island.

Sources indicate that A mechanic I slightly underused at first was the ability to 'save' a given outfit to your car. You can do this either from your car's trunk or from the wardrobe, and it's hugely useful as you start to get into more elaborate scrapes with the police (and also if you just like to role-play a bit and don the right outfit for the right occasion).

Industry observers note that there are lots of reasons for this, from the moments of intimacy it affords you with your partner, to the extra buffs you can get from resting. Sleep at home, for instance, and you can then immediately pet your snake (ahem), down a coffee or drink from the fridge, grab an apple and take a shower for a range of buffs across health, stamina, and focus. Each of these will last quite some time, so it's worth the few minutes of time to do them. Eating and drinking regularly also helps you maximise gains in the gym.

Rockstar seems to enjoy the concept of a game within a game, and that's exemplified well by the in-game phone. You can find missions via scrolling Snapmatic, it's in-game social media, or from texting various contacts you pick up as the game progresses. It's worth checking it every now and then just to see if anything interesting - or just funny or absurd - might pop up.

Sources indicate that car trunks, both those belonging to the public and the police, are often well worth a look. Even if you're quickly nabbing a car for a short-term dash, take a moment to check the boot for anything worthwhile. We've found everything from sellable narcotics to very useful weapons in there. In cop cars, that goes up several notches, too.

A small thing, but in-mission checkpoints are relatively generous in GTA 6. If you really wanted to complete a mission a certain way - undetected or non-violent, say - then don't be afraid to rapidly re-load rather than feeling you need to manually load up an earlier save, or give up on your goal entirely. It's also helped me out with a few minor progress-jamming bugs along the way too.

Industry observers note that this might seem obvious, but it's worth emphasising for early-game players: it's very, very rare that you actually need to kill anybody in GTA 6. Enemies are fully incapacitated when you see a yellow hit marker over your crosshairs, even if that just comes from blasting away at their toes. If you make a habit of navigating combat this way then that also makes it much easier to recover your 'Professional' criminal status if you ever do decide to go full rampage. Though you can, of course, ultimately play this game however you like. Just be aware there may be consequences, known and unknown, as you go. Also: don't forget to click the right analog stick to aim down sights - it's an easy thing to forget when playing a third-person shooter like this, and not always the best way to operate, but incredibly helpful in select circumstances.

Industry observers note that throughout the game you'll have a 'family savings' goal to hit. As you progress you'll find more ways to earn money much faster, and so it's easy to make up for lost time here if, later on, you decide that actually you do want to think about the future after all. But that grind will be a fair bit less painful if you chip away at the target as you go. As long as you save yourself some fun money - a few hundred in the early game, few thousand in the mid game, and a few tens of thousands late on - then you'll have enough to do key things like buying fresh garages to register vehicles, or paying to register them themselves.

Sources indicate that throughout your time with GTA 6 you'll encounter moments when you need to make a choice. Interestingly, I noticed at least a few occasions where a scenario changed when I just waited, doing nothing at all. Sometimes that might mean a choice is made for you - so waiting is a risk - but on other occasions latest options become available. Sometimes they might mean a genuinely different consequence, others they might just lead to characters reacting in a certain kind of way. But it's worth experimenting - your first options aren't always your only ones.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Gemma 4 family of multimodal models by Google DeepMind is out on Hugging Face, with support for your favorite agents, inference engines, and fine-tuning libraries 🤗.
  • These models are the real deal: truly open with Apache 2 licenses, high quality with pareto frontier arena scores, multimodal including audio, and sizes you can use everywhere including on-device.
  • We collaborated with Google and the community to make them available everywhere: transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, WebGPU, Rust; you name it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Gemma 4 family of multimodal models by Google DeepMind is out on Hugging Face, with support for your favorite agents, inference engines, and fine-tuning libraries 🤗.

These models are the real deal: truly open with Apache 2 licenses, high quality with pareto frontier arena scores, multimodal including audio, and sizes you can use everywhere including on-device. Gemma 4 builds on advances from previous families and makes them click together. In our tests with pre-release checkpoints we have been impressed by their capabilities, to the extent that we struggled to find good fine-tuning examples because they are so good out of the box.

We collaborated with Google and the community to make them available everywhere: transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, WebGPU, Rust; you name it. This blog post will show you how to build with your favorite tools so let us know what you think!

Recent findings suggest that similar to Gemma-3n, Gemma 4 supports image, text, and audio inputs, and generates text responses. The text decoder is based on the Gemma model with support for long context windows. The image encoder is similar to the one from Gemma 3 but with two crucial improvements: variable aspect ratios, and configurable number of image token inputs to find your sweet spot between speed, memory, and quality. All models support images (or video) and text inputs, while the small variants (E2B, E4B) and the 12B Unified model support audio as well.

Gemma 4 comes in five sizes, all base and instruction fine-tuned:.

Gemma 4 leverages several architecture components used in previous Gemma versions and other open models, and leaves out complex or inconclusive features such as Altup. The combination is a mix designed to be highly compatible across libraries and devices, that can efficiently support long context and agentic use cases, whilst being ideal for quantization.

As shown in the benchmarks above, this feature mix (combined with the training data and recipe) enables the 31B dense model to achieve an estimated LMArena score (text only) of 1452, while the 26B MoE reaches 1441 with just 4B active parameters 🤯. As we'll see, multimodal operation is comparatively as good as text generation, at least in informal and subjective tests.

These are the main architecture characteristics in Gemma 4:.

One of the most distinctive features in smaller Gemma 4 models is Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which was introduced previously in Gemma-3n. In a standard transformer, each token gets a single embedding vector at input, and the same initial representation is what the residual stream builds on across all layers, forcing the embedding to frontload everything the model might need. PLE adds a parallel, lower-dimensional conditioning pathway alongside the main residual stream. For each token, it produces a small dedicated vector for every layer by combining two signals: a token-identity component (from an embedding lookup) and a context-aware component (from a learned projection of the main embeddings). Each decoder layer then uses its corresponding vector to modulate the hidden states via a lightweight residual block after attention and feed-forward. This gives each layer its own channel to receive token-specific information only when it becomes relevant, rather than requiring everything to be packed into a single upfront embedding. Because the PLE dimension is much smaller than the main hidden size, this adds meaningful per-layer specialization at modest parameter cost. For multimodal inputs (images, audio, video), PLE is computed before soft tokens are merged into the embedding sequence — since PLE relies on token IDs that are lost once multimodal features replace the placeholders. Multimodal positions use the pad token ID, effectively receiving neutral per-layer signals.

Recent findings suggest that the shared KV cache is an efficiency optimization that reduces both compute and memory during inference. The last num_kv_shared_layers layers of the model don't compute their own key and value projections. Instead, they reuse the K and V tensors from the last non-shared layer of the same attention type (sliding or full).

In practice, this has a minimal impact on quality while being much more efficient (in terms of both memory and compute) for long context generation and on-device use.

The Gemma 4 12B Unified model has no separate vision or audio encoder. Instead, raw image patches and audio waveforms are projected directly into the LLM's embedding space through lightweight linear layers, and all modalities flow into a single decoder-only transformer. This reduces multimodal latency and allows the whole model to be fine-tuned in one pass. The checkpoint size makes it deployment-friendly on consumer hardware.

We saw in our tests that Gemma 4 supports comprehensive multimodal capabilities out of the box. We don't know what was the training mix, but we had success using it for tasks such as OCR, speech-to-text, object detection, or pointing. It also supports text-only and multimodal function calling, reasoning, code completion and correction.

Recent findings suggest that google has released Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) drafters for the Gemma 4 family: small assistant models that accelerate inference via speculative decoding. The drafter proposes several future tokens at once, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass. You get the same outputs as the target model, just faster — no quality loss, no changes to reasoning behaviour. Reported end-to-end speedups go up to ~3x depending on hardware, batch size, and workload.

In a recent development, assistants are available for all four Gemma 4 sizes (E2B, E4B, 26B A4B, 31B). They share the KV cache with the target model to avoid recomputing context, and the smaller edge variants additionally use an embedder clustering trick to keep memory and compute low on-device.

Find the checkpoints in the Gemma 4 collection and the mlx-community collection.

Recent findings suggest that alongside the autoregressive Gemma 4 family, Google DeepMind is releasing DiffusionGemma, a multimodal model that generates text using discrete diffusion instead of token-by-token autoregression. It's built on the same 26B A4B Mixture-of-Experts foundation (25.2B total / 3.8B active parameters, 8 active experts out of 128 plus 1 shared), takes text and image inputs, generates text, and supports up to 256K context — all under the same Apache 2.0 license.

Where a standard causal LM emits one token at a time, DiffusionGemma denoises whole blocks of tokens in parallel. The architecture is encoder-decoder: an autoregressive encoder prefills the prompt and builds the KV cache, while a decoder applies bidirectional attention over a "canvas" of 256 tokens. During multi-canvas sampling, the model iteratively denoises a full canvas with a diffusion sampler; once a canvas is finalized it's encoded and appended to the KV cache, then the next canvas begins. This block-autoregressive approach increases generation speed.

The headline benefit is throughput: parallel denoising generates roughly 15–20 tokens per forward pass, reaching per-user generation speeds exceeding 1100 tokens/second at low batch sizes (H100, FP8). Inference compute is adaptive too — simpler prompts and structured tasks like code need fewer denoising steps, so tokens-per-second scales with task complexity. It keeps the broader Gemma 4 toolkit: thinking mode, function calling, long context, native system prompts, and image understanding (OCR, document parsing, object detection, pointing) at variable aspect ratios and resolutions.

Benchmarks show an expected trade-off between speed and evaluation metrics — DiffusionGemma trails the autoregressive 26B A4B on most tasks (e.g. MMLU Pro 77.6% vs 82.6%, AIME 2026 69.1% vs 88.3%, GPQA Diamond 73.2% vs 82.3%) in exchange for its large speed advantage, while edging ahead on a few (HLE no tools 11.0% vs 8.7%).

Getting started looks just like the rest of Gemma 4, via the dedicated diffusion class:.

For best results, Google recommends the Entropy-Bounded (EB) sampler with adaptive stopping (up to 48 denoising steps, a temperature schedule decaying from 0.8 → 0.4, and an entropy bound of 0.1 for token selection). As with Gemma 4, place image content before text in your prompt, and toggle reasoning with the <|think|> control token.

Gemma 4 models are ideal for fine-tuning in your favorite tools and platforms and at any budget.

According to recent reports, gemma 4 is fully supported for fine-tuning with TRL. To celebrate, TRL has been upgraded with support for multimodal tool responses when interacting with environments, meaning models can now receive images back from tools during training, not just text.

In a recent development, to showcase this, we've built an example training script where Gemma 4 learns to drive in the CARLA simulator. The model sees the road through a camera, decides what to do and learns from the outcome. After training, it consistently changes lanes to avoid pedestrians. The same approach works for any task where a model needs to see and act: robotics, web browsing, or other interactive environments.

In a recent development, additionally, we have prepared an example on how to fine-tune Gemma 4 with TRL on Vertex AI using SFT, to showcase how to extend the function calling capabilities, whilst freezing both the vision and audio towers. The examples include how to build a custom Docker container with latest Transformers, TRL, etc. with CUDA support on Google Cloud, and how to run it via Vertex AI Serverless Training Jobs.

In a recent development, one gap worth flagging for anyone building on Gemma 4's function calling for real-world deployments: when the model generates a function call, there's at the moment no verifiable record that a human principal authorized that specific action. a compromised system prompt or injected instruction produces a call that's indistinguishable from legitimate delegation at the tool interface.

i opened a PR on the gemma-cookbook repo today that adds a drop-in HDP middleware layer to address this, sits between Gemma 4's function call output and tool execution, verifies Ed25519-signed delegation tokens, classifies actions by irreversibility (Class 0–3), and blocks unauthorized calls pre-execution.

for edge/robotics deployments (E2B on Jetson Nano / Raspberry Pi directing actuators), there's a companion HDP-P extension covering the physical layer.

Running an AI agent on your own GPU sounds simple: point it at Ollama and stop paying per token. I set up OpenClaw, an open-source AI assistant, with a 9B model in Ollama on one RTX 3090 and connected it to Discord. Then I read the Ollama log for every request.

Industry observers note that the agent worked. The numbers were not what I expected, though. A one-line question turned into a prompt of more than 18,000 tokens, the first reply took over a minute, and the small model sometimes guessed instead of using its tools.

This article covers what I measured and what each number means if you proposal to run an agent on local hardware.

OpenClaw ran in Docker and reached Ollama on the host at http://host.docker.internal:11434. Discord was the chat interface, and OpenClaw's web panel showed the sessions and context use.

This article is about the results, not the installation. The full step-by-step setup is in a separate guide to running OpenClaw in Docker with Ollama and Discord. That guide covers the Compose file, the Discord bot and how to keep the ports off your network.

All timings below come from the Ollama log on the test machine. Ollama loaded the model with a 32,768-token context.

My first message in Discord was short: "Which model are you running on, and what is 17 * 23?" The bot answered correctly: it ran on ollama/qwen3.5:9b, and 17 × 23 is 391.

According to recent reports, the Ollama log demonstrated what that question cost. The model processed 18,415 prompt tokens and generated 33 tokens.

Sources indicate that the extra tokens come from the agent itself. With every request, OpenClaw sends:.

It has been revealed that on the RTX 3090, reading that prompt took 10 seconds at 1,838 tokens per second. A slower GPU, or a CPU, needs much longer to read the same prompt.

According to recent reports, prompt tokens per model call, from the Ollama log. Only the first message had to process the whole prompt.

It has been revealed that openClaw counts tokens with its own estimate, which was higher than the Ollama count. The gateway log estimated the prompt at 24,608 tokens, against a prompt budget of 24,576 tokens for this model. By OpenClaw's own count, the base prompt alone used up the budget before any conversation history.

The web panel highlighted a similar figure: 68 to 69 percent of the context window was in use for the Discord sessions after only a few messages.

The first message arrived while the model was not loaded in GPU memory. That reply took 1 min 10 s:.

The next requests were much faster:.

Recent findings suggest that reply times on the test machine. Loading the model took most of the first reply.

It has been revealed that the speed-up comes from prompt caching. The system prompt, tool definitions and workspace files at the start of the prompt stay the same between requests. Ollama kept that part cached and processed only the latest tokens. The model wrote at 91 to 96 tokens per second in every test.

In a recent development, ollama's documentation indicates models stay in memory for 5 minutes by default before they are unloaded. After that, the next message pays the load time again. You can change this with the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE environment variable on the Ollama server, or with the keep_alive parameter per request. A negative value, such as -1, keeps the model loaded. I did not change this setting in the test.

If you run Ollama in Docker, pass the variable with -e OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1 or in the environment: section of your Compose file.

Two things used the GPU besides my chat messages.

A heartbeat. OpenClaw's web panel listed one scheduled automation, heartbeat-main, which runs every 30 minutes. The agent wakes on that schedule, so the model gets called even when nobody chats. With Ollama's 5-minute default, the model is unloaded between heartbeats unless someone chatted recently, so a heartbeat most likely starts with a model load. I did not measure this.

Recent findings suggest that an embedding model. During the first message, OpenClaw also called Ollama's /api/embed endpoint twice to index its memory. It used qwen3-embedding:4b, which was already installed on the Ollama server. I did not set OpenClaw to use that model; it picked it on its own.

That is 11.4 GB for the models alone, almost half of the RTX 3090's 24 GB.

The rest of the stack was light:.

What this means for you: proposal GPU memory for the chat model, the embedding model and the context, not the chat model alone. If the GPU also runs other models, the heartbeat can compete with them.

The first two tests in Discord: a question, then a file written with a tool. The user name is blurred.

Sources indicate that the fix for the first problem was simple. When I wrote "use your read tool to open homelab-test.md", the model opened the file and listed all three points correctly. Naming the tool made it check instead of guess.

The model listed four files and missed the test file and a folder, because it answered from its prompt.

Based on this test, a local 9B model on one consumer GPU works for:.

If you need better answers, OpenClaw also works with hosted models, but then your prompts leave your machine.

According to recent reports, in this test, qwen3.5:9b used 6.3 GB and the qwen3-embedding:4b memory model used 5.1 GB. Together the two models needed 11.4 GB.

The model had to load into GPU memory first, which took 59 seconds of the 70-second reply. Ollama keeps a model loaded for 5 minutes by default, and the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE setting changes that.

Every request includes OpenClaw's system prompt, its tool definitions and its workspace files. A one-line question became an 18,415-token prompt in this test.

#34895. I completed GTA 6's indie game darling pastiche, Tenebrae Lux, and all I got was this lousy sense of accomplishment

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1288 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

I completed GTA 6's indie game darling pastiche, Tenebrae Lux, and all I got was this lousy sense of accomplishment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, "We are but Promethean wanderers on the fringes of oblivion, clinging to a semblance of light amidst the vast abyss of our own ignorance.
  • Developed, seemingly single-handedly, by an eccentric developer called Johannes Zuch - auteur, pseud, charlatan - you first get introduced to this curious little experiment in one of GTA 6's earliest missions, where protagonist Jason is forced to play it during a 'lad's night in' with buddy Cal.
  • The first thing I notice about Tenebrae Lux is the name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, "We are but Promethean wanderers on the fringes of oblivion, clinging to a semblance of light amidst the vast abyss of our own ignorance. Voyaging uncharted waters may appear foolish to some, yet folly and heroism can often appear the same to the undiscerning eye," so claims the voice of Johannes Zuch - creator, writer, director, composer, and 'perceptual architect' behind Leonida's latest favourite indie darling art game, Tenebrae Lux. It's pretentious, it's deeply up its own arse, and it's awkward and off-putting to play. A must-review for Eurogamer.

Developed, seemingly single-handedly, by an eccentric developer called Johannes Zuch - auteur, pseud, charlatan - you first get introduced to this curious little experiment in one of GTA 6's earliest missions, where protagonist Jason is forced to play it during a 'lad's night in' with buddy Cal. Jason is quick to dismiss Tenebrae Lux in organization, but once Cal slinks off home - hungover and dreary - I slide the disc back into my JoyStation console and sink my teeth back into it. Jason loves this stuff, really. He only keeps Time Jackers: Rewind installed so his mates don't judge him.

The first thing I notice about Tenebrae Lux is the name. It's Latin for 'darkness and light', or something similar. Is this riffing on Clair Obscur, which is French for 'light dark'? No, it's too cerebral for that - too plodding and navel-gazey. Sandfall Interactive wouldn't be this pretentious. Maybe it's a pastiche of Dear Esther, then, drawing on the tenets and schema of the 'walking simulator' genre and using that washed-out film noir aesthetic. But then, it's too wordy for that, with too many interactive and puzzle-adjacent elements. Ah, it must be mocking The Witness, instead - there's the telltale lighthouse, the 'I'm definitely not telling you where to go and what to do' internal narration, and of course the fingerprints of Johannes Zuch are all over it. Johannes Zuch, Jonathan Blow - see how they braided them together? (Sorry).

Whilst this has been created by Rockstar as a pastiche - as much loving send-up as it is withering take down - and designed to make a quick joke in the early 'Feng Shui' mission, the game is playable from start to finish if you so desire. You boot it up by inserting a physical disc, too, which is funny given the context. And it's good! Well, not good good, but it's a proper brainteaser, and ribs 2016's The Witness with such knowledge and (I think?) respect that it's hard not to be charmed by Rockstar's game-within-a-game. There are collectibles to be found that riff on Mark Z. Danielewski's House of Leaves, too, a knowing nod to the most try-hard of all try-hard literature.

Within seconds of the title screen, too, you're presented with a game-within-a-game-within-a-game. You must clear four boards filled with puzzle pieces as the protagonist mutters something mysterious and weird in his posh voice. Do so, and you unlock the door to the next location. Head up to a bunker, and you'll see a room filled with various clues - maybe it's a flashing lamp flickering in morse code, maybe it's a malfunctioning clock presenting a maths puzzle, maybe it's a pricetag on a record that changes on every visit, maybe it's a photograph with anomalous elements, maybe it's a "Developed Using Zuchworks Engine" easter egg hidden in the environment. You need to keep your wits about you, because one of these clues changes every time you enter - and the clue corresponds to a date that changes on a calendar on the wall.

Sources indicate that you can look up a guide if you need to, or you can spend far too long figuring out how all this relates to the telephone you can find in the room on your own, like muggins here, before opening up the path to the next puzzle. Look at the image below to see the level of record-keeping and brainteasing this bizarre little game prompted from me. I will say, the sense of achievement you get from playing around with this stuff is pretty remarkable, given - let's not forget I'm actually playing Grand Theft Auto 6 whilst I'm wandering around in the black and white murk trying to complete a puzzle game for no actual reward.

The bunker room is, by far, the hardest part of Tenebrae Lux. From here, things ease up: you need to figure out the right sequence of glyphs on a bridge, and then put some distance between yourself and a curious and rather creepy suited man that's seemingly figuring things out ahead of you in a location inspired by, I think, The Backrooms (or Portal, or Superliminal, or maybe something else entirely. Who knows what Zuch was thinking?).

"With the last enigma finally mastered," the narrator drones in his bumbling monotone, "I step forward into the void, the shadows swallow, consuming all, and then finally the sweet embrace of darkness of which there is no end." 'You have just experienced a Johannes Zuch experience', Tenebrae Lux tells me, before cutting to the best joke of the whole thing: the credits roll much akin to something Hideo Kojima would produce.

So, what do you get out of all of this? Well - just like real puzzle games in the real world - nothing, really. If you've not completed one of the other three fully playable games in GTA 6, you will get a trophy/achievement. But given the main game is all about Jason and Lucia's desperate scramble to escape the poverty trap, to try and break free of the cycle of debt, violence, and consequence that keeps them clinging to Leonida's seedy underbelly, there's no monetary reward. There's no 'progress' in the sense of the protagonist's shared story.

According to recent reports, even in terms of your own cold, hard, mathematical 'completion' you only need to boot each of the four games up once in order to work towards GTA 6's 100% completion. So what's the point of all this? Why did I spend the better part of 90 minutes trying to figure out how to find a sliver of light in the dark in Tenebrae Lux? The game is a wonderful pastiche in that, essentially, it's not really saying anything. You can probably project some vague meaning onto it if you wish - I'm pretty certain the protagonist literally 'finds himself' at the end - but glib little readings like that are ten-a-penny in this genre.

It has been revealed that I think the most impressive thing about Tenebrae Lux is that it exists. You're teased with it in an early mission - Rockstar may as well say 'look, we put a game in a game, lol' - but it's more than that. This is what happens when Rockstar's 4700-plus developers are given the room to… develop. Tenebrae Lux could very easily have been a non-interactive experience, a quick, cheap joke shown over-the-shoulder taking a drive-by pop shot at Johnathan Blow, Hideo Kojima, Dan Pinchbeck, or any and all of the above. Or maybe it could be a 'vertical slice', an incomplete demo, a teaser. But it's not, because nothing about GTA 6 is quick or cheap.

Sources indicate that GTA 6, in every single conceivable way, is a premium experience - part-sandbox, part-simulation, part-otherworld. To create not just one, but four fully playable and completable games within that framework is showboating, sure, but to make that game actually good and - perhaps controversially - even better than some of the games it's pastiching… Well, it's just rubbing salt in the wound, really.

A code for the game was provided by Cal Hampton.
