💡 Key Takeaways
  • Are you wondering how connected the worlds of GTA 5 and GTA 6 are?
  • Right, if you're reading from this point onwards, you're clearly here for the tea.
  • Called 'Body Copy' - a joke I appreciate as a former magazine editor, naturally - this publication features a few different articles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Are you wondering how connected the worlds of GTA 5 and GTA 6 are? Well, I've got some news for you. Keep on reading below if you'd like some very minor spoilers for the early game of GTA 6, spoilers for GTA 5, as well as some information about how the new game links to GTA 5 and other Rockstar games.

Right, if you're reading from this point onwards, you're clearly here for the tea. In the first hour or so of GTA 6, when you finally get control of Jason and head to your first property (the green stilted house) in the Leonida Keys, you will be able to explore a little. On my way to do a workout - you need to keep Jason a peak physical instrument for his work's sake, right? Right? - I happened upon a fitness magazine resting on a table on the decking out front.

Called 'Body Copy' - a joke I appreciate as a former magazine editor, naturally - this publication features a few different articles. There's Morning Glory, where Nolan Crockett jacks you with his early workout; Skindecent Exposure, a photo spread about why beaches are 'crazy' places to work out; Shrediquette, a piece dedicated to proper in-gym decorum; and Twilight Tantra, an interview feature and yoga masterclass with 'gerontophile' Fabien LaRouche.

Hang on, Fabien LaRouche… isn't that the French wellness guru and shyster that was a "close friend" to Amanda De Santa in Grand Theft Auto 5? Yes, yes it is. In fact, Fabien played quite a large role in that game, acting as the antagonistic force that eventually fractured Michael and Amanda's relationship. After conducting an affair under the guise of 'yoga lessons', Amanda left our protagonist, and moved in with Fabien, taking Michael's kids - Jimmy and Tracy - with her. In a totally healthy and normal way, you could follow their new life via updates posted to GTA's Facebook surrogate, LifeInvader. It's clear the kids never liked the pretentious, annoying man - but for Amanda, the penny is a little slower to drop. Eventually, Amanda and Michael reconcile their differences - with the latter whalloping Fabien in the process. The married couple pledge to resolve their differences, and Fabien is never seen again.

Until GTA 6, at least. Here, in what we assume is supposed to be 2025 or 2026, it's been about 13 years since we last saw the character (it is widely agreed that GTA 5 is set in 2013 - the game's original launch year). And it seems that the events surrounding Michael and his family really did a number on Fabien. Which - of course - he blamed on the universe, rather than taking any personal responsibility. Naturally.

In a recent development, "Ever since the karmic decay of Los Santos was made perfectly clear to him in the early 2010s, yoga instructor Fabien LaRouche has been on an epic pilgrimage of enlightenment through the remotest ashrams and finest 5-star resorts and plastic surgery retreats of The East," reads the Body Copy article. "Having completed his chakric education and returned to the United States, we meet with him on the final week of his six-month residency at Dwindle Wood Retirement Community.".

Here, the article goes on to explore Fabien's penchant for older women - he seems to like their nature, their desire to learn about self-improvement and wellness, and (perhaps most importantly) their bank accounts. "Being over the hill doesn't necessarily mean you have nothing left to live for," he opines in the article. Thanks for that, Fabien.

It's interesting to see - very early in the game and quite plainly telegraphed - that Rockstar is willing to reintroduce us to people from previous games. This isn't a megaton addition by any means - Fabien was never a 'main character' - but I love that a nod to him, in a feature tucked away at the back of a magazine, sets the scene for more cameos, perhaps, later in the game. It reveals us, nice and early, that GTA 5 and GTA 6 are indeed connected. By inference, then, we know that GTA 4 is included in that same picture; there were recurring characters in GTA 5 that appeared in GTA 4, after all - Patrick McReary, Johnny Klebitz, Rocco Pelosi and more come to mind.

It may seem like a small thing, but it's just another example of Rockstar using its expansive toolset, ridiculous budget, and well-established legacy to inject a sense of scale into the world of Grand Theft Auto 6. There are other nods to the universe out there, too. I won't spoil them here, but I've been a little bit dewy-eyed to hear rumours of some of the other nods to Rockstar titles hidden in the world of Leonida: it makes all the experiences I've had in past games, the emotional response I've had to previous Rockstar worlds, feel in some way valid and meaningful here, too. I'm looking forward to seeing what other little secrets await me across the keys and into the glowing neon promise of Vice City proper.

Astra, meanwhile, is tuned for the highest-quality work in professional use cases such as documents, slides, coding, and more:.

GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new quality bar for AI in complex professional work. Its slides, spreadsheets, and documents read less like AI, and more closely follow the templates you provide and the conventions of your field. It writes cleaner code and builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming, and 3D design.

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu consumers in ChatGPT Work and Codex, with Astra being significantly more affordable compared to GPT-6 Astra. Pricing for Astra per million tokens lands at $8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output. Sol matches its predecessor at $2 for input, $0.10 for cached input, and $10 for output, again per million tokens.

Safetensors is Joining the PyTorch Foundation

📅 08 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we're announcing that Safetensors has joined the PyTorch Foundation as a foundation-hosted project under the Linux Foundation, alongside DeepSpeed, Helion, Ray, vLLM, and PyTorch itself.
  • Safetensors started as a Hugging Face project born out of a concrete need: a way to store and share model weights that couldn't execute arbitrary code.
  • The format we built is intentionally simple: a JSON header with a hard limit of 100MB, describing tensor metadata, followed by raw tensor data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we're announcing that Safetensors has joined the PyTorch Foundation as a foundation-hosted project under the Linux Foundation, alongside DeepSpeed, Helion, Ray, vLLM, and PyTorch itself.

Safetensors started as a Hugging Face project born out of a concrete need: a way to store and share model weights that couldn't execute arbitrary code. The pickle-based formats that dominated the ecosystem at the time meant that there was a very real risk you’d be running malicious code. While this was an acceptable risk when ML was still budding, it would become unacceptable as open model sharing became central to how the ML community works.

The format we built is intentionally simple: a JSON header with a hard limit of 100MB, describing tensor metadata, followed by raw tensor data. Zero-copy loading that maps tensors directly from disk. Lazy loading so you can read individual weights without deserializing an entire checkpoint.

What we didn't fully anticipate was how broadly it would be adopted. Today, Safetensors is the default format for model distribution across the Hugging Face Hub and others, used by tens of thousands of models across all modalities in ML. It has become the preferred way for the open source ML community to share models.

We want Safetensors to truly belong to the community. The project has always been open source, but code contributions are just one part of its evolution. By bringing more companies and contributors into the governance of the project, we make sure that progress reflects the breadth of the community building on top of it. Joining the PyTorch Foundation means Safetensors now has a vendor-neutral home. The trademark, the repository, and the governance of the project sit with the Linux Foundation rather than any single company. Hugging Face's two core maintainers, Luc and Daniel, remain on the Technical Steering Committee and continue to lead the project day-to-day, but Safetensors now formally belongs to the community that depends on it.

We believe safety is best guaranteed when every contributor can build on what already exists; a principle now embedded in the project's governance itself.

For the vast majority of customers, nothing changes. The format is the same, the APIs are the same, the Hub integration is the same: no breaking changes. Models stored in Safetensors format today will continue to work exactly as they do now.

For contributors, the path to becoming a maintainer is now formally documented and open to anyone in the community. The project's governance lives in GOVERNANCE.md and MAINTAINERS.md in the repository. For organizations building on top of Safetensors, neutral governance under the Linux Foundation provides a stable, long-term foundation, entirely community-driven.

Safetensors is a well-established project, adopted by the ecosystem at large, but we're still convinced we're at the very beginning of the project.

We're working with the PyTorch team so that Safetensors may be used within PyTorch core as a serialization system for torch models.

Sources indicate that the coming months will see significant growth, and we couldn't think of a better home for that next chapter than the PyTorch Foundation. The roadmap ahead includes device-aware loading and saving, so tensors can load directly onto CUDA, ROCm, and other accelerators without unnecessary CPU staging.

Industry observers note that we're also building first-class APIs for Tensor Parallel and Pipeline Parallel loading, so each rank or pipeline stage loads only the weights it needs. And as the ecosystem's quantization landscape continues to evolve, we'll be formalizing support for FP8, block-quantized formats like GPTQ and AWQ, and sub-byte integer types.

These are problems the whole ecosystem has a stake in solving, and being inside the PyTorch Foundation means we can work on them in collaboration with the other hosted projects rather than in parallel.

Safetensors is open source and contributions are welcome at every level, from bug reports and documentation to new features and participation in governance.

If you're a developer, researcher, or organization that builds on Safetensors and want to be more involved in shaping its direction, open an problem, start a discussion, or reach out to the maintainers directly. The project has always belonged to the community that uses it. The governance now reflects that too.

Sources indicate that will there be a concerted effort now to get newer (and older) LLM models to adopt the more secure safetensors format rather than allowing AI developers to continue with pickle files as they did in the past? And what would some of the objections be, if any, for a developer to not transition to safetensors format?

Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a new built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free.

Industry observers note that spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp for Android is adding its own cloud backup option. Prior to this, the app relied on Google Drive backup for transferring chats between devices or keeping a backup in case of accidental deletion.

It has been revealed that “WhatsApp cloud storage” is showing up in the WhatsApp for Android v2.26.46.4 beta enhancement, rolling out now, and includes 2GB of free storage for cloud backups. Everything is still end-to-end encrypted. Beyond the first 2GB, WhatsApp Plus ($2.99/month) adds 100GB, and Meta One ($7.99/month+) offers up to 4TB of cloud storage. WhatsApp will keep your backup for at least 4 months after the subscription ends, even if you are over the 2GB gap.

You can still choose to use Google Drive backups instead of the built-in option, but those using devices without a Google account or who are running low on Google storage may appreciate the option to switch.

It’s unclear exactly when this will be available to all WhatsApp customers.

Waypoint-1.5: Higher-Fidelity Interactive Worlds for Everyday GPUs

📅 09 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Waypoint-1.5 is Overworld’s next real-time video world model, built to bring interactive generative worlds to the hardware people actually own.
  • Recent findings suggest that the first release of Waypoint highlighted that real-time generative worlds were possible.
  • Waypoint-1.5 builds directly on that foundation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Waypoint-1.5 Weights on the Hub.

Waypoint-1.5 is Overworld’s next real-time video world model, built to bring interactive generative worlds to the hardware people actually own.

Recent findings suggest that the first release of Waypoint highlighted that real-time generative worlds were possible. It proved that interactive world models could be more than passive video demos, and that locally runnable systems could begin to close the gap between generating a world and actually stepping into one.

Waypoint-1.5 builds directly on that foundation. This release improves visual fidelity, expands the range of hardware that can run the model locally, and takes another step toward interactive world simulation without datacenter-scale compute.

In a recent development, on desktop hardware including RTX 3090 through 5090, Waypoint-1.5 can generate real-time environments at up to 720p and 60 FPS. This release also introduces a 360p tier designed to run smoothly across a much broader range of consumer hardware, including gaming laptops, and (soon) Apple Silicon Macs.

The biggest change in Waypoint-1.5 is accessibility.

Recent findings suggest that with Waypoint-1, we proved the core experience. With Waypoint-1.5, we wanted to make that experience available on more machines without giving up real-time interactivity. That meant building two model tiers: a 720p model for higher-performance hardware, and a 360p model optimized for broader deployment.

We also scaled training dramatically. Waypoint-1.5 was trained on nearly 100x more data than Waypoint-1, which significantly improves the model’s ability to generate more coherent environments and more consistent motion over time.

Under the hood, Waypoint-1.5 also incorporates more efficient video modeling techniques to reduce redundant computation across frames. That matters because real-time world models are not judged only by how a single frame looks. They are judged by whether the world responds instantly, stays coherent as you move through it, and remains usable on local hardware.

Sources indicate that A lot of recent progress in generative video and world models has focused on visual fidelity. Those results matter, but fidelity alone is not what makes an interactive world feel real.

It has been revealed that what people remember is responsiveness. They remember whether the environment reacts to them, whether motion stays coherent, whether the world holds together as they explore it, and whether the whole experience feels immediate instead of delayed.

That is the gap we care about most: the difference between watching a generated scene and actually being inside one.

Industry observers note that if world models only run on large GPU clusters, they remain impressive demos. If they run locally on consumer hardware, they become something much more useful: a foundation for interactive entertainment, creative tooling, simulation, and AI-native environments people can actually explore.

Waypoint-1.5 is designed around that idea: not just better videos, but more responsive and explorable worlds that remain accessible on consumer hardware.

There are two ways to play Waypoint-1.5.

According to recent reports, the first is local execution through Overworld Biome. This release is designed to run across a wide range of hardware configurations, and the updated Biome runtime makes local setup much simpler. With the upcoming installer flow, owners can go from download to running the model locally in minutes.

The second is Overworld Stream, which lets you try Waypoint-1.5 instantly in the browser with no local setup required.

Whether you want immediate access or full local control, Waypoint-1.5 is built to support both.

Additionally, we provide World Engine, our flexible, easy to use, core inference library powering our official clients, along with nearly a dozen third party clients and libraries.

Waypoint started with a simple question: what would it take for generative worlds to become truly interactive?

Early generative systems demonstrated that models could produce convincing images and videos. But building environments that people can explore, control, and interact with in real time is a different challenge entirely.

Waypoint-1.5 is another step in that direction, improving fidelity and expanding hardware accessibility while continuing to push real-time interactive generation onto local machines.

We think the future of world models will not be defined only by what they can render, but by whether people can actually inhabit and interact with them in real time.

Download Waypoint-1.5, run it locally with Biome, or jump in instantly on Overworld.stream.

And if you build something fun, strange, or unexpectedly immersive with it, we’d love to see it.

Google Home is constantly rolling out latest updates and, today, the manufacturer is detailing some of its latest updates including a faster Gemini for Home experience and an upcoming Nest Thermostat upgrade.

In a post today, Google details several Google Home updates that are widely rolling out to users.

According to recent reports, the first was announced last week – home keys in Google Wallet. This leverages compatible NFC and UWB (Aliro) locks on newer Pixel and select Samsung Galaxy smartphones, letting you unlock your door by simply tapping your phone.

Cameras are also getting an upgrade for Activity Zones:.

…we’ve tightened Activity Zone boundary precision on our newest wired cameras to significantly reduce false alerts from passing cars, animals, and motion just outside your zone borders. We also redesigned the camera settings page to put Activity Zones front and center, and added a confirmation prompt on iOS when exiting an edited zone so you never accidentally lose your custom boundaries.

The Google Home website also gets faster scrubbing and new keyboard shortcuts – Left or Right arrow keys skip back or forward in 5-second increments, rapidly to jump 30 seconds or more.

Gemini for Home continues to get faster, with Google saying that the latest updates have resulted in an overall speed improvement of 20% on “everyday requests.” Gemini for Home has also expanded to six fresh countries including India, Taiwan, Singapore, Colombia, South Korea, and Brazil starting “next month.”.

Finally, Google is also preparing some useful upgrades for Nest Thermostat.

According to recent reports, the first is a dashboard for Nest Thermostat customers in the US and Canada that indicates “estimated cumulative savings” spurred by their thermostat. You’ll be able to see these savings in “the Climate space, thermostat controller, and Favorites widget.” The second is the abiltiy to use third-party room temperature sensors with the 4th-Gen Nest Learning Thermostat. Google has its own sensor for this that sells for $40, but there are more affordable alternatives that often bring more functionality too, so this is a really nice addition. Compatible brands will include IKEA, Eve, and Aqara.

In a recent development, starting in December, Nest thermostat owners in the U.S. and Canada can check the app to see estimated cumulative savings. And they can also balance hot and cold spots with compatible third-party room sensors with their 4th-gen Nest Learning Thermostat.

Sources indicate that A third patch is to the Dynamic Farsight faces on the latest Nest Learning Thermostat. “Upcoming” faces are coming with “designs to match your aesthetics,” while a new Lunar face will track moon phases.

Dynamic Farsight already lets you see the time, temperature, weather, and air quality from across the room, and starting this December, we’re rolling out latest Dynamic Farsight faces with designs that match your aesthetics. Keep an eye out for seasonal animations on the Temperature face, or switch to our new Lunar face to track the phases of the moon right on your wall.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Industry observers note that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

It has been revealed that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Industry observers note that picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

In a recent development, shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that blueprint. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

Recent findings suggest that whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide demonstrates how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

WooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

BigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and plans auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

In a recent development, medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the organization states you can export your data and self-host at any point.

According to recent reports, saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we built one of the most powerful computer-use AIs in the world.
  • Building something powerful is one thing; making it accessible and easy to use is another.
  • According to recent reports, holoTab is a Chrome extension that navigates the web just like a person would.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we built one of the most powerful computer-use AIs in the world. And made it directly accessible from your browser. On March 31st, we released Holo3, our most advanced computer-use model to date.

Building something powerful is one thing; making it accessible and easy to use is another. We’re doing both.

According to recent reports, holoTab is a Chrome extension that navigates the web just like a person would. It automates tasks across any website with zero setup or technical skills required. You describe what you want, and the agent handles it directly inside your browser, navigating interfaces, filling fields, and making decisions the same way you would. The vision models, the action planning, the interface understanding, all of it is running underneath, working for you, and all you ever see is the result.

Industry observers note that some tasks are quick and forgettable, but others are long and repetitive, the kind that reliably eat up your afternoon. You might find yourself cross-referencing competitor pricing across twenty different e-commerce tabs to revision a master spreadsheet, or filtering through a dozen job boards and organization career pages to find upcoming listings, painstakingly porting the details into a tracking doc to manage your applications.

That's where routines come in. You start a recording, and HoloTab captures what you do in your tab in real time while you click or narrate along the way, demonstrating what you're doing and why. Your screen and your actions give HoloTab everything it needs, enriching the routine with enough context to actually understand the goal.

Once the recording stops, a routine is generated. From then on, you can re-run your routine or schedule it whenever you need to, and HoloTab will handle the rest on its own.

Computer-use AI is going to change how people work, research, and get things done, both in their professional and personal lives, and that shift is already closer than most people realize. But it shouldn't require a technical background to access, and the benefits shouldn't accrue only to teams with engineers who know how to wire these systems together.

HoloTab is free and ready for everyone to use today: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/holotab/hlaoiikljjgcjdhkakedfngifaopbcop.

YouTube ‘Co-Views’ try to guess how many people are watching your TV, rolling out now

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following a change in how it counts views earlier this year, YouTube is now announcing “Co-Views” as a way for the platform to try and guess how many people are watching a YouTube video on a TV, and it counts towards the video’s total view count.
  • In a recent development, view counts on YouTube are still settling from the change earlier this year where YouTube now counts a view after the very first frame of a video plays.
  • Now, YouTube states it might count more views with a fresh “Co-Views” setup on TVs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following a change in how it counts views earlier this year, YouTube is now announcing “Co-Views” as a way for the platform to try and guess how many people are watching a YouTube video on a TV, and it counts towards the video’s total view count.

In a recent development, view counts on YouTube are still settling from the change earlier this year where YouTube now counts a view after the very first frame of a video plays. But, even with that, YouTube only counts a single view for each time the video is played.

Now, YouTube states it might count more views with a fresh “Co-Views” setup on TVs.

According to recent reports, in a post, YouTube explains that “Co-Views” include “the estimated number of people watching together on TV” in the view count of a video. This only applies to TVs, with views from a mobile device or desktop still only ever counting as a single video. It applies to long-form videos as well as Shorts and Live videos, and only applies going forward – historical data won’t change.

YouTube states it is making this change to reflect the “over 1 billion hours” spend on YouTube through their TVs “every day” and that the added data will assist creators in channel strategy or brand pitches, while also providing a “more complete picture of how audiences are engaging with’ content, aligning with TV industry standards – including how traditional broadcast and streaming networks estimate the total number of people exposed to content.” But “Co-Views” won’t count towards earnings on the platform, as they’re not “Qualified Views.”.

How is YouTube figuring out what to count here? “Guessing” is not exactly an inaccurate summarization, but Google stresses that it is not using cameras or microphones, but rather a “statistical mode.”.

YouTube doesn’t use devices, cameras, microphones or anything like that. Co-views are estimated using a privacy safe statistical mode, developed by Google research scientists, based on factors like demographic patterns and viewing times, calibrated against ground-truth data sources like industry panels.

This change is rolling out now.

#34882. Inside VAKRA: Reasoning, Tool Use, and Failure Modes of Agents

📅 15 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2152 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Inside VAKRA: Reasoning, Tool Use, and Failure Modes of Agents

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2152 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • VAKRA Dataset | LeaderBoard | Release Blog | GitHub | Submit to Leaderboard.
  • We recently introduced VAKRA, a tool-grounded, executable benchmark for evaluating how well AI agents reason and act in enterprise-like environments.
  • Unlike traditional benchmarks that test isolated skills, VAKRA measures compositional reasoning across APIs and documents, using full execution traces to assess whether agents can reliably complete multi-step workflows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VAKRA Dataset | LeaderBoard | Release Blog | GitHub | Submit to Leaderboard.

We recently introduced VAKRA, a tool-grounded, executable benchmark for evaluating how well AI agents reason and act in enterprise-like environments.

Unlike traditional benchmarks that test isolated skills, VAKRA measures compositional reasoning across APIs and documents, using full execution traces to assess whether agents can reliably complete multi-step workflows.

VAKRA provides an executable environment where agents interact with over 8,000+ locally hosted APIs backed by real databases spanning 62 domains, along with domain-aligned document collections. Tasks can require 3-7 step reasoning chains that combine structured API interaction with unstructured retrieval under natural-language tool-use constraints.

As can be seen below, models perform poorly on VAKRA - in this blog, we include additional dataset details about the tasks in VAKRA and present an analysis of failure modes we observed on different tasks.

As shown below, the VAKRA benchmark comprises of four tasks, each testing a different set of capabilities.

Fig 1: Representative examples of each capability in the VAKRA benchmark.

According to recent reports, this capability includes 2,077 test instances across 54 domains, requiring the use of tools from the SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD collections (Elder et al., 2026). Compared to the setup in Elder et al., the tool universe in SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD is expanded through the inclusion of a larger number of domains. Each domain is restricted to one tool collection, and tasks involve chaining 1–12 tool calls to arrive at the final answer.

Fig 2: Data sample from SEL-BIRD collection.

According to recent reports, as shown above, each instance has an associated JSON data source from which the answer must be derived. The MCP servers supporting this task include a special tool, called get_data(tool_universe_id=id), which must be called at the beginning of each instance. This tool initializes the data source, returns a lightweight preview of the data (see below Figure 3), and stores the full dataset server-side to avoid large data transfers. This prevents the inefficient transfer of large data over the MCP protocol. The call also configures the MCP server to expose the appropriate tool set based on the tool_universe_id and aligns the data source with the domain-specific database for the instance.

Sources indicate that the SLOT-BIRD collection provides a global set of 7 tools for generic data manipulation (e.g., filtering, sorting), inspired by systems like Tableau and Google Analytics. The SEL-BIRD collection extends this by introducing more specialized tools: some are shared with SLOT-BIRD, while others are derived by flattening categorical arguments into separate functions (e.g., sort_data with argument ascending: bool = False becomes sort_data_ascending and sort_data_descending). Additionally, the generic (retrieve_data) function from SLOT-BIRD is replaced with query-specific getters. Every key in the data for a given instance has an associated get function (get_KEY_NAME) for an average of 4 get functions per instance.

Fig 3: Data preview obtained from `get_data` function.

Recent findings suggest that this capability includes 1,597 instances across 17 domains, requiring tools from an expanded REST-BIRD collection (Elder et al.). These use endpoint-style interfaces that provide highly specific, query-aligned endpoints that encapsulate most computation. They are served as REST APIs running in a FastAPI server, which is wrapped by the MCP server. This task requires selecting the correct APIs from the domain-specific tool set (as shown in the example in Figure 1). Each domain contains a minimum of 6 to a maximum of 328 tools (with an average of 116 tools). Similar to the previous task, the get_data tool configures the MCP server to expose only the relevant domain-specific APIs.

In a recent development, the OpenAI API Specification restricts the tool list input to a maximum length of 128 tools. This restriction requires an agent builder using this API to manage the length of the tool list directly via a shortlisting mechanism. In the baseline agents in our repository, a simple shortlisting capability handles this challenge.

Sources indicate that the Capability 3 segment of the benchmark has 869 test instances drawn from 38 subject domains. These instances rely again on the REST-BIRD API collection, but add multi-hop reasoning to the challenge (refer to example in Figure 1). Multi-hop questions require multiple pieces of supporting evidence to be extracted and combined to reach an answer. The instances in this section require between one and five logical hops to answer a query. The question types distribution for queries within the test dataset is shown below in Figure 4.

Fig 4: API Hop-Type distribution for Capability 3 (MultiHop) and Hybrid Hop-Type distribution for Capability 4 (MultiHop MultiSource Reasoning).

Capability 4 includes 644 instances across 41 domains and is also built on the REST-BIRD API collection. Figure 4 above demonstrates a distribution of hybrid hops for test queries without policies. It contains the most complex queries with the following characteristics:.

It has been revealed that multi-Source: This segment adds document indices per domain. Queries in this capability could require information from these document indexes as well as API calls. Similar to Capability 3, this task also has Multi-Hop queries. The required information source applies at the per-hop level, so, for example, a question may entail three logical hops with sources: API - RAG (Document Retrieval) - API. To enforce correct reasoning, sources are decontaminated during data generation, i.e. information required for a given hop is available in only one source. For example, if a hop is to be answered using APIs, the document index is built by removing documents that likely contain the information needed to answer the question.

Multi-Turn: This segment of the dataset also adds multi-turn conversations to the setting. Each instance is a dialog with multiple turns. The data is released as context-response pairs, where the context encodes the current dialog history and the agent is only responsible for answering the current turn.

Tool-usage Policies: A subset of these instances includes tool-use policies that the agent is required to follow. These policies take the form of plain-text instructions about the knowledge sources that the agent is allowed to access and under which circumstances. For example:.

The baseline agent in the project repo imposes adherence to these policies through a simple addition to the prompt: "You are a helpful assistant with access to tools.\n Tool Usage Constraint: {additional_instructions}.". Of course, agent builders are free to choose any constraint enforcement mechanism.

Recent findings suggest that VAKRA evaluates agents in tool environments where success depends on both the ability to execute coherent, multi-step workflows and answer correctness. We introduce an execution-centric evaluation framework that assesses not only final outputs but also the full tool-execution trajectory that includes tool calls, inputs, and intermediate results.

Sources indicate that the VAKRA Evaluator operates over two key inputs for each sample: a predicted final response and the corresponding tool-call trajectory. The tool calls from the predicted trajectory are executed in the same environment as the ground truth to verify intermediate tool outputs.

The evaluation follows a waterfall-style pipeline (Figure 6), where later stages are conditioned on earlier success:.

Fig 6: Waterfall-style Evaluation Pipeline.

Tool-Sequence Comparison Due to the presence of an executable environment, agents can explore the environment and sometimes return the answer by invoking a different set of APIs than the ones identified by us. In order to support alternative but valid tool invocations and reasoning paths, correctness is assessed by executing each predicted tool and comparing the set of tool responses against those from the ground truth (rather than enforcing strict step-level matching).

It has been revealed that specifically, we first perform a programmatic check, verifying whether all information present in the ground-truth tool responses is recovered by the predicted tool responses. This check may be inconclusive in cases involving partial matches, semantic equivalence, or differences in representation (e.g., ordering, aggregation, or formatting). In such cases, we apply a secondary LLM-based evaluation, adapted from the CRAG framework Yang et al., 2024, to determine whether the predicted trajectory retrieves all required information despite structural differences. This step uses an adapted prompt to determine whether the predicted trajectory captures all required information, even if obtained through a different sequence of tool calls.

According to recent reports, final Response Evaluation For trajectories that pass the previous check, the final response is evaluated using an LLM-based judge. This step ensures that the response is (i) grounded in the predicted tool outputs, and (ii) factually consistent with the ground truth answer, accounting for potential variations in phrasing or structure.

This design ensures that agents are rewarded not only for producing correct answers, but for obtaining them through valid and complete reasoning processes.

Every capability is equally weighted to obtain a final leaderboard score.

To obtain a capability score, every sample within a capability is equally weighted for capabilities 1 through 3.

For capability 4, we weight heterogeneous queries higher:.

We now present detailed error analysis across the four VAKRA capabilities. To facilitate our analysis, we adopt stage-wise error categorization to assign each failure to the first point of breakdown. Specifically, we evaluate, in order: (i) whether the correct tool(s) were selected, (ii) whether the required arguments were provided without omissions or hallucinations, (iii) whether argument values were correct, and (iv) whether the final response is both accurate and grounded in the tool outputs.

Industry observers note that since a single sample may exhibit multiple errors across different steps, we sequentially classify each instance to the earliest failing stage (e.g., tool selection errors take precedence over argument errors). This avoids double-counting and allows error categories to be interpreted as disjoint fractions of the dataset. While more granular metrics (e.g., precision/recall over tool usage) are possible (Elder et al., 2026), we find this formulation provides a simple and interpretable breakdown of agent failures.

According to recent reports, the instances in this part of the benchmark required selecting and sequencing multiple tools to solve a single task. We have 2077 samples in this capability. This was challenging for all models, but GPT-OSS-120B performed best on this segment of the benchmark.

Fig 7: SEL-BIRD vs SLOT-BIRD Error Types Analysis.

Recent findings suggest that the Business Intelligence (BI) API capability contains two sets of APIs, from the SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD tool collections. The SEL part of this benchmark had 600 samples, while the SLOT part of the benchmark had 1477 samples. These two collections are grouped under the BI API capability, but have slightly different characteristics. The SLOT-BIRD collection has a smaller number of generic tools with a large number of parameter values to fill, while the SEL-BIRD collection has a larger set of tools and fewer parameters per tool. This focus is reflected in the relative errors made by models using these two tool collections.

Fig 8: Comparison of Accuracy Across Models by Hop Depth.

According to recent reports, multi-hop reasoning increases the difficulty of the original task by requiring models to successfully answer multiple implicitly coupled questions, each of which requires selecting and calling the correct API. As expected, all models performed best on the questions with only a single logical hop, and saw performance degradations on 2-hop and again on 3+ hop questions.

Fig 9: Model Accuracy Rates by Interaction Type (API, Document-Retriever, Hybrid).

Sources indicate that the final segment of the dataset includes document sources in addition to the tool/API sources in the other segments. This leads to instances that require single or multiple API calls, single or multiple document searches, or some combination of API calls and document searches.

Fig 10: Model Accuracy Rates by Policy Type.

Policies introduce an additional layer of difficulty on top of multi-hop, multi-source reasoning. When policies align with the required source for answering i.e. they do not affect the tool list required for models to answer the question, we refer to it as "No Updates to Answer" -- as shown in Figure 10, all models except for Granite-4.0-h-Small-32B experience a clear drop in performance under policy constraints that restrict access to the most relevant information source (i.e. "Policy updates the answer").

In general, we find that models either violate constraints or fail to retrieve sufficient information, where they sometimes understood the policy but could not answer the question correctly, or they exhibit one of the previously analyzed failure modes.

Overall, tool-use policy-constrained settings suggest that while models can reason over tools and sources, they struggle to incorporate external constraints into that reasoning - often a key requirement for reliable real-world deployment.

VAKRA exposes a critical gap between surface-level tool competence and robust, end‑to‑end agent reliability. Although modern models can increasingly select APIs and execute isolated tool calls, VAKRA highlights that these abilities alone are insufficient for real‑world deployment. In practice, models often break down when required to perform compositional reasoning under execution constraints—spanning APIs, documents, dialog context, and policy requirements.

Think your agent is solid? Put it to the test.

Run it on VAKRA and see where it falls apart—tool selection, multi-hop reasoning, or policy constraints.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alongside the huge list of new updates Google detailed yesterday, the tech giant also declared that a “faster and more natural” version of Gemini Live is coming to speakers and smart displays “soon.”.

Google explains this is from Gemini Live moving to the “latest speech-to-speech architecture” and brings “significantly faster response times.” Gemini Live isn’t the default experience when you start a “Hey Google” command, rather hiding behind a “let’s chat” or other similar command to start a session.

It has been revealed that initially, Live sessions were purely for brainstorming or longer conversations and lacking support for commands and other functions mid-session, but Google now claims that this upgrade will add support for actions such as smart home controls, setting timers, and more without leaving a Live session. That’s a significant deal.

Coming soon – A faster and more natural Gemini Live experience: Available with a Google Home Premium subscription, Gemini Live is being upgraded to our latest speech-to-speech architecture for significantly faster response times and a smoother experience. Just say, “Hey Google, let’s chat” to brainstorm dinner ideas or strategy a trip out loud, interrupt naturally to change topics, and perform actions mid-conversation—such as, setting a timer, adding a reminder,or controlling a smart home device—without stepping out of the chat³.

The “catch” is that you’ll still need a subscription to use this. Gemini Live has always required a subscription on Google Home speakers and smart displays, with the functionality looped into Google Home Premium aims which start at $10/month (or bundled into Google One AI Pro). That’s the same subscription that gives you Nest storage.

In a recent development, one of the biggest features here is App Lock, which has been overdue for a launch on Galaxy devices. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial.
  • Sources indicate that every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Sources indicate that every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan. Following the latest upgrade from the CA/Browser Forum, the maximum lifetime of a certificate has fallen from 398 days to 200, and it will drop to 100 days in March 2027 and 47 days in 2029. Renewal is no longer an annual chore. It’s an ongoing task that only stays manageable with automation.

So what does this mean if you already look after sites with SSL certificates, and will it bring drastic changes? For many setups, very little will change. For others, one missed renewal can mean an outage. This article explains what’s changing and what to do if you’re in the second group.

Sources indicate that today, an SSL certificate is valid for 200 days at most. The limit applies when a certificate is issued, so the ones you already hold keep their original expiration date.

According to recent reports, where you feel it depends on how your certificates renew. Sites on managed hosting platforms or behind a content delivery network (CDN) usually renew automatically already, often every 90 days, so the upcoming limit changes little. The pressure lands on setups where someone buys a certificate once a year and installs it by hand. At 47 days, that becomes about 12 renewals a year.

According to recent reports, A certificate is a promise from a certificate authority that a key really belongs to a domain, and that promise gets less reliable the longer it runs. If a private key leaks, or a certificate is issued by mistake, it stays usable until it expires. Cutting the lifetime shrinks that window, so a problem that once lingered for over a year is now fixed in weeks.

Shorter lifetimes also make revocation, the process for canceling a bad certificate, far less critical. Revocation has never worked perfectly, but a certificate that expires within weeks matters much less if a cancellation doesn’t reach every browser.

According to recent reports, another reason is about people. A task done once a year is easy to forget and hard to check from outside. Browser makers have pushed for years to move the industry onto automatic renewal, on the logic that a process that runs every few weeks gets tested constantly. If it breaks, you notice promptly instead of discovering it on the day the certificate expires.

For most people, the first effect is simply more work. A certificate that once needed attention every year will soon need it every few weeks. Plus, each renewal is a small chance for something to go wrong. Multiply that by dozens of sites, mail servers, and devices, and the chance of one slipping through grows rapidly.

The safety nets are also thinner. If you relied on the renewal emails, nothing is watching your certificates now. Additionally, with a shorter life, there’s less time between this should have renewed and this has expired.

An expired certificate doesn’t make a site slow or dated. It makes it unreachable for most visitors. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all show a full-page warning that the connection isn’t private, and most people leave instead of clicking through. If the site uses HSTS, a setting that tells browsers to connect only over secure links, there is often no way to click through at all, and visitors are blocked outright until the certificate is fixed.

The damage doesn’t stop at the home page. Checkouts, contact forms, and logins that depend on the secure connection fail along with it, often without an error message that points at the real cause. Other systems break, too, because apps and integrations that call your site over a secure link refuse to connect to an expired certificate.

Sources indicate that nothing about your site has to change for any of this to happen. A date passes, and a site that worked on Friday is down on Monday. In a 47-day lifetime, that date comes around about every six weeks.

According to recent reports, automatic renewal tools do the heavy lifting well. The failures happen around them:.

Industry observers note that look at the five failures above and you’ll see what they share. Each one happens quietly. The renewal job ran, or looked like it did, and nobody checked what the server was actually serving afterwards. Automation can tell you it tried. It can’t tell you the result reached your visitors.

What closes that gap is a check that never relies on your server’s own account of events. Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring does exactly that. It reads the certificate installed on your web server from the cloud, the way a visitor’s browser would, and alerts you before it expires, using thresholds you choose. If a renewal fails quietly, you hear about it from the monitor and not from a customer.

According to recent reports, for each certificate, it records the issuing authority, the owner, the concern date, the expiration date, and the days remaining, including on servers that host several certificates behind one address. That last number matters more as lifespans shrink. When a certificate lasts 47 days, the days left is the figure that tells you a renewal is overdue, and you can set your warning against it using the quarter-of-the-lifetime rule covered next.

Once a monitor is watching your certificates, the next question is when it should speak up.

In a recent development, most expiration alerts are set to a fixed number of days: warn at 30 days left and escalate at seven. That works for a certificate that lasts a year and renews with a month to spare. It breaks when the whole certificate lasts for a limited number of days.

In a recent development, here’s why: a healthy certificate renews with about a third of its life still left. If your alert appears earlier than that, it goes off on certificates that are doing nothing wrong, and soon everyone ignores it. As lifespans shrink, a fixed 30-day alert will start doing exactly that.

Industry observers note that the fix is to set the alerts based on lateness, not on how close the expiry date is. Warn when a quarter of the lifetime is left, since a renewal is overdue by then, and escalate when a tenth is left. Because these are shares of the lifetime, they keep working, however short lifespans get.

The next cut lands on March 15, 2027, so a few checks now will save you from scrambling later:.

Shorter lifespans won’t break your site, but a missed renewal will, so fix the quiet failures now while a mistake still costs an afternoon to fix, not a Monday morning outage affecting lots of customers.

Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more.
  • According to recent reports, as a practical example, I'll walk through finetuning Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B for Visual Document Retrieval (VDR), the task of retrieving relevant document pages (as images, with charts, tables, and layout intact) for a given text query.
  • If you're newly introduced to multimodal models in Sentence Transformers, I recommend reading Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers first.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. In my previous blogpost, I introduced the latest multimodal capabilities, showing how to use embedding and reranker models that handle text, images, audio, and video. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to train or finetune these multimodal models on your own data.

According to recent reports, as a practical example, I'll walk through finetuning Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B for Visual Document Retrieval (VDR), the task of retrieving relevant document pages (as images, with charts, tables, and layout intact) for a given text query. The resulting tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr demonstrates how much performance you can gain by finetuning on your own domain. On my evaluation data, the finetuned model achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.947 compared to the base model's 0.888, and outperforms all existing VDR models I tested against, including models up to 4x its size.

If you're newly introduced to multimodal models in Sentence Transformers, I recommend reading Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers first. For training text-only embedding, reranker, or sparse embedding models, see the Prior Blogposts section at the end.

According to recent reports, general-purpose multimodal embedding models like Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B are trained on diverse data to perform well across a wide range of languages and tasks: image-text matching, visual question answering, document understanding, and more. But this generality means the model is rarely the best choice for any specific task.

Consider Visual Document Retrieval: given a text query like "What was the company's Q3 revenue?", the model must find the most relevant document screenshot from a corpus of thousands. This requires understanding document layouts, charts, tables, and text, which is a very different skill from e.g. matching pictures of shoes with product descriptions.

By finetuning on domain-specific data, the model can learn these specialized patterns. In my experiment, finetuning improved NDCG@10 from 0.888 to 0.947, ahead of every recent multimodal model I tested, including ones up to 4x larger.

Training multimodal Sentence Transformer models involves the same components as training text-only models:.

According to recent reports, the multimodal training pipeline uses the same SentenceTransformerTrainer as text-only training. The key difference is that your datasets contain images (or other modalities) alongside text, and the model's processor handles the image preprocessing automatically.

Let's walk through each component, using Visual Document Retrieval (matching text queries to document screenshots) as a running example.

Recent findings suggest that the most common approach is to finetune an existing multimodal embedding model, or to start from a Vision-Language Model (VLM) checkpoint. The Transformer module automatically detects supported modalities from the model's processor.

In a recent development, to finetune an existing multimodal embedding model (e.g. one that already has a modules.json file), you can pass processor_kwargs and model_kwargs to control preprocessing and model loading respectively. processor_kwargs are passed directly to AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(...) (e.g., image resolution bounds: higher max_pixels means higher quality but more memory), while model_kwargs are passed to the appropriate AutoModel.from_pretrained(...) call (e.g., precision, attention implementation):.

Recent findings suggest that you can also start from a fresh VLM checkpoint that hasn't been trained for embeddings yet. Sentence Transformers will attempt to recognize the architecture, infer the supported modalities from the processor, and set up the appropriate forward method and pooling. If the automatic detection doesn't work perfectly for a particular model, the configuration in the saved sentence_bert_config.json can be edited to adjust modality settings, forward methods, and output handling:.

In both cases, the Transformer module inspects the processor to determine which modalities are available, and Pooling is added automatically if needed. You can verify the supported modalities:.

Instead of using a single VLM backbone, you can compose separate encoders for different modalities using the Router module. This lets you combine any existing encoders and route inputs to the appropriate one based on detected modality:.

Since Router-based multimodal models use separate encoders per modality, their embedding spaces are initially unaligned. Training is required to align the spaces for meaningful cross-modal similarity. The Dense projection layer shown above helps map embeddings from different encoders into a shared space.

Sources indicate that this approach is useful when you want to use lightweight, specialized encoders rather than a large VLM. You can also combine Router-based multimodality with task-based routing (e.g. different encoders for queries vs. documents) using route_mappings. See the Router documentation for advanced routing scenarios.

In a recent development, for this example, I use the tomaarsen/llamaindex-vdr-en-train-preprocessed dataset, a preprocessed English subset of llamaindex/vdr-multilingual-train. The source dataset was released alongside the Visual Document Retrieval Goes Multilingual blogpost by LlamaIndex, and consists of ~500k multilingual query-image samples collected from public internet PDFs, with queries synthetically generated using VLMs (gemini-1.5-pro and Qwen2-VL-72B). My preprocessed version filters to the 53,512 English samples and resolves 4 of the 16 ID-based hard negatives per sample into actual document screenshot images, so it can be used directly for training without further preprocessing:.

It has been revealed that the train config contains the first 10,000 samples, and the eval config contains the next 300 samples (a full config with all 53,512 samples is also available). For training, I select query, image, and negative_0 to form (anchor, positive, hard negative) triplets. Including additional hard negatives would likely improve the training signal, but each extra negative also increases memory usage and training time, so I stick with one. For evaluation, I keep all four hard negatives per query to build a more challenging retrieval corpus (more on that in the Evaluator section).

Just like text-only training, the dataset format must match your chosen loss function. The rules are the same:.

For multimodal datasets, the inputs can contain:.

The data collator automatically calls model.preprocess(), which detects the modality of each input and applies the appropriate preprocessing. No manual tokenization or image processing is needed.

Many Hugging Face datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers, allowing you to easily find them at https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers.

It has been revealed that for this training, I use CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, a common choice for retrieval tasks. It accepts (query, positive) pairs with any number of additional hard negative columns, from 0 up to n, as long as each sample has the same number of negatives. During training, the loss pushes each query's similarity to its positive up and its similarity to every negative down. The negatives come from two sources:.

Industry observers note that more negatives per query means a stronger training signal, so a larger batch size directly improves training quality. Beyond that, the "cached" variant of the loss uses gradient caching to make large effective batch sizes feasible even when GPU memory is limited.

Industry observers note that the mini_batch_size parameter controls how many samples are processed at once during the cached forward passes. For large multimodal models, setting this to a small value (e.g., 1) is crucial to avoid out-of-memory errors without sacrificing the benefits of large effective batch sizes:.

Recent findings suggest that to produce embeddings that work well at multiple dimensionalities, I wrap the base loss with MatryoshkaLoss. This trains the model so that truncating the embedding to a smaller number of dimensions still yields good performance:.

This is especially useful for multimodal models, where embeddings can be large (2048 dimensions for Qwen3-VL). With Matryoshka training, you can use truncated embeddings (e.g., 256 or 128 dimensions) at deployment time for faster search with minimal quality loss. As I'll show in the Results section, the finetuned model achieves near-peak performance even at 512 dimensions.

The SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments class lets you control training hyperparameters. Here's the configuration used for the VDR finetuning:.

A few things to note for (multimodal) training:.

To track retrieval performance before, during, and after training, I use the InformationRetrievalEvaluator. It computes standard retrieval metrics like NDCG@10, MAP, and Recall@k:.

Recent findings suggest that the evaluator takes text queries, a corpus of images (including hard negatives), and a mapping of which documents are relevant to which queries. Note that the corpus contains a mix of positive and hard negative document screenshots, making this a challenging evaluation. Using batch_size=1 prevents out-of-memory challenges during evaluation of the large VLM.

It has been revealed that the SentenceTransformerTrainer brings everything together. Here's the complete training script:.

Sources indicate that the training script is nearly identical to a text-only training script. The only differences are:.

Everything else (the trainer, training arguments, dataset loading) works exactly the same as text-only training.

In a recent development, after training for just 1 epoch, the finetuned tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr model achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.947 on the evaluation set (300 queries, 1500 corpus documents, cosine similarity). This is a significant improvement over the base Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B model's 0.888, and outperforms all existing VDR models:.

It has been revealed that the finetuned 2B model outperforms even the 8B Qwen3-VL-Embedding model, demonstrating the power of task-specific finetuning. Finetuning on your own domain is often worth considering, even when a larger general-purpose model is available!

Industry observers note that the comparison above uses full-size 2048-dim embeddings. Thanks to the Matryoshka training, the finetuned model also holds up well when truncated to fewer dimensions, letting you trade off embedding size and retrieval quality at deployment time:.

The finetuned model's peak is at the full 2048 dimensions (0.948), but it stays within 0.3% of peak all the way down to 512 (4x smaller), and retains over 92% of peak even at 64 (32x smaller). Matryoshka training concentrates the most important information in the earlier dimensions, so moderate truncation costs very little performance.

The gap between 1024 and 2048 dimensions is small (0.946 vs. 0.948), so I've saved the model with truncate_dim=1024 set in its configuration. This means that SentenceTransformer("tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr") produces 1024-dimensional embeddings by default, halving the storage footprint compared to the full 2048. If you want a different dimensionality, pass truncate_dim=N when loading to override it.

You can also finetune multimodal Cross Encoder (reranker) models using the same training infrastructure. The key difference is using CrossEncoderTrainer and Cross Encoder-specific loss functions. This section provides a brief overview; see the full training examples for complete, runnable scripts with dataset preparation and evaluation.

Here's a simplified example based on the doodles training script, which trains a reranker to match images with text captions:.

There are multiple valid architectural choices for multimodal rerankers, including:.

Both approaches are demonstrated in the multimodal cross encoder training examples.

The two scripts linked above split the training data into two datasets, one per direction (image-to-text and text-to-image), with a task-specific prompt for each that tells the model how to score in that direction. Each positive pair is then expanded with randomly sampled negatives so the loss sees a balanced mix of matches and non-matches.

Your best people are training your AI. Pay them for it

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills.
  • Early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills.
  • Recent findings suggest that when we looked into which AIs brought the most value, there was an obvious pattern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills. Within months, we were running five agents for every employee, which felt like a transformation until we looked at the actual output and efficiency. In my own finance org, only 30% of employee-built agents and skills actually moved the needle. When we looked into which AIs brought the most value, there was an obvious pattern. The successful agents were created by employees who understood where a process in their work typically tends to break, and could turn that knowledge into clear rules and processes for artificial intelligence. We went from treating AI skill-building as an open invitation and instead focused on the people who were building AI agents that moved the needle. That fixed the quality problem, but handed us a harder problem to solve. When you take your best talent’s craft and turn it into an AI agent, what does that employee get in return for their expertise and labor? As more companies have the best employees train their AI, leaders must have a response to this question. Define the bar, then pay against it When we changed our AI skill-building process, eligibility depended on a manager’s recommendation and a strong performance review. But identifying the right people is half the work. Companies also need to establish what qualifies as a high-value skill, and what it is worth, before anyone starts building one. We created a framework that categorizes skills, assigns value, and determines the reward. It’s simple but makes it clear what employees should aim for and gives us a consistent way to reward them. At ClickUp, every skill falls into one of four categories, and each category has its own measure of success. One, revenue acceleration skills are measured by the pipeline or bookings they add, and two, cost elimination skills are measured by the spend they remove, like canceling a software we no longer use. Time compression skills, three, are measured by how much faster a core process runs, like closing the books or responding to a customer. And executive bounties, four, are specific problems our leadership team has identified, each with a reward attached. The category tells employees what type of skills to build with AI, but the proof of impact is what determines how much the AI skill is worth. Before creating a newly introduced AI skill, employees must record where the measure stands today, like how many sales meetings aren’t rebooked each month or how long it takes to close the books. Then they can build, and once the AI skill has been running long enough to show a consistent pattern of value, finance compares the new numbers against the starting point. Finance then subtracts the cost of running the AI skill, including tools and maintenance, and what remains is the value the employee created. We then look at what we would have paid to get the same result a different way. Hiring even a few experienced sellers is a major expense, so when one person’s AI skills deliver that same capacity, a standard raise no longer reflects what their work is worth to the business. To determine the reward, we also consider how long the value will last. A skill that solves a single, contained problem earns a bonus. A skill or system the employee will keep running and improving earns a permanent raise, since the company will keep benefiting from that work every year. Together, these steps give us a dollar amount for each AI skill created, which we can use to determine the compensation ranging from a one-time bonus to becoming part of our “unicorn” group. Unicorns are employees whose AI work changes what an entire team can do, and they receive a merit increase of more than 30% along with eligibility for compensation up to $1 million at the top of the band. For example, one growth operations manager identified 17 places where we were regularly losing potential sales and built 11 AI skills to address them. Those skills recovered hundreds of thousands of dollars in pipeline and increased the number of sales prospects by 25%. They also saved every sales rep about 90 minutes in their day, which is equivalent to seven sellers’ worth of capacity. Because the results were large, verified, and directly tied to revenue, this employee joined our “unicorn” group. Reward your talent for making their expertise reusable Your best people are already training your AI. They are handing over the part of themselves that made them hard to replace, and the company can keep using that knowledge long after they have moved on. Hoarding what only one person knows feels like job security, but it is ultimately a ceiling. The people thriving in this model build the skill, hand over their knowledge, and move to the next problem. Each handoff allows them to take on a bigger, more interesting challenge. This is the model companies should build toward as AI moves deeper into knowledge work—rewarding people for making their expertise reusable. That judgment is intellectual property, and paying for it is how you build AI that works while retaining top talent.
