The PR you would have opened yourself

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Making transformers models available in mlx-lm using a Skill and test harness.
  • We provide a Skill and a test harness to help port language models from transformers to mlx-lm, so they become (almost) instantly available the moment they are added to transformers.
  • In a recent development, in 2026, code agents started to actually work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Making transformers models available in mlx-lm using a Skill and test harness.

We provide a Skill and a test harness to help port language models from transformers to mlx-lm, so they become (almost) instantly available the moment they are added to transformers. The Skill is designed to support contributors and reviewers as an aide, not an automation. We explain why we did it, how, and comment about how to meaningfully contribute to open source in the age of agents.

In a recent development, in 2026, code agents started to actually work. What used to be auto-completion at the side of your editor turned into a system that one-shots reasonable solutions from brief specifications. The generated code usually works out of the box, covers what you asked for, and makes reasonable assumptions about details you didn't specify. This is great. As Jensen Huang puts it, we've instantly gone from 30 million to one billion coders in the world. Creative minds are unleashed.

But it forces us to rethink open source.

Sources indicate that take the transformers library as an example. It has hundreds of contributors, is used in thousands of projects, has been downloaded over a billion times. Suddenly, anyone with an agent can instruct it to find some open problem, fix it, and submit a PR. And that's exactly what's happening. Those people feel happy because they are contributing to a great library, but the sad reality is that, most of the time, they don't realize they are not.

Why not? There are two assumptions that agent-generated PRs usually miss.

Recent findings suggest that codebases like transformers care deeply about the code. It's cool to build projects where it doesn't matter what the code looks like, but transformers is not one of them. Being used by thousands of people, transformers is primarily built as a human-to-human communication method, through code. Model files read top to bottom, because we want practitioners to understand them without jumping through complex abstractions. This permeates throughout the library design and is the reason why, for example, we favor flat hierarchies.

Sources indicate that agents don't have that context. Because design decisions are not explicit, agents suggest refactors to "improve" the codebase by following "best practices", without realizing they are breaking implicit contracts between the library and its owners. They are verbose, generalize too early, don't notice when a change affects other areas, introduce subtle bugs, break performance. They are also sycophantic, and accept any idea as good and follow it through diligently, including ones a maintainer would have pushed back early on with a terse comment.

According to recent reports, A small number of maintainers still has to read every PR, understand it, decide if the design direction is right, identify side effects, and write feedback. PR volume has gone up tenfold, but the amount of maintainers has not (and cannot, because team coordination does not scale).

Transformers is one of the first projects to feel this pressure because of sheer volume, but the same dynamic is happening everywhere. As an example from a different domain, App Store reviewers are swamped because anyone can now build and submit an app, so many do.

Industry observers note that the same logic applies to MLX: their maintainers care deeply about the code and read every PR carefully. We wanted to see whether agents could help contributors land high-quality model ports fast, and at the same time support reviewers in their work. Not only do we aspire to produce PRs that could have come from a careful human submission, but we also provide additional artifacts to increase the signal: generation examples, numerical comparisons, and a separate non-agentic test harness for reproducibility.

Recent findings suggest that another connection between transformers and MLX is that, most times, mlx-lm models are ported from transformers implementations. Because transformers focuses on clarity and readability, it has become the source of truth for model definitions. Downstream contributors wait until the transformers implementations are ready before they port to other frameworks. As a side effect, this is an excellent environment for an agent because it naturally limits the scope: rather than creating an implementation from scratch, the agent relies on transformers code as the source of truth.

This approach supports our goal: when a model lands in transformers, it should be available on MLX shortly after.

We built a Skill that mlx-lm contributors can use to port a model from transformers to MLX. Given a prompt like "convert the olmo_hybrid architecture to MLX", the Skill sets up a virtual environment to work on, discovers and downloads the relevant models from the Hub, reads the transformers modeling code, writes the MLX implementation, and runs a battery of tests. If results don't look right, it debugs and iterates, and does not declare success until it's satisfied.

We designed it to be useful to reviewers as much as contributors.

It has been revealed that for the contributor, the Skill of course handles all the scaffolding: finding model variants on the Hub, diffing their configs to spot parameters that vary across model variants, downloading checkpoints, setting up editable installs of both mlx-lm and transformers. But it also handles the more difficult modeling tasks. It pays attention to salient architecture details and verifies sensitive areas, like RoPE configurations, that may result in hard-to-find bugs. It detects when the config doesn't declare a dtype and infers it from the safetensors metadata header. It runs per-layer comparisons between transformers and MLX to pinpoint exactly where divergence occurs. These are the kinds of checks that only someone with porting experience would think to run.

In a recent development, for the reviewer, the Skill produces a PR that is upfront about being agent-assisted, but does look like a careful human submission. Reviewers will see that the code follows mlx-lm conventions: idiomatic solutions, no unnecessary comments, no speculative abstractions, no modifications to shared utilities without explicit approval. Given that the code is agent-assisted, we try to include more data than the median PR, to provide as much signal as possible. The PR body includes a report with a summary of the variants and their architectural differences, generation examples, numerical comparisons, dtype verification, per-layer comparisons against the transformers baseline. The PR always discloses that it was agent-assisted, and the Skill will not open it until the contributor has accepted the results.

For verification, the Skill generates a test manifest for a separate, non-agentic test harness that is, by design, easily reproducible and not subject to LLM hallucinations or complacency (more on this below).

According to recent reports, skills are recipes for agents: simple text files with guidelines that steer the model through a complex task. They are not magic; you can achieve the same results via prompting and iteration. But they provide consistency (every run follows the same process, whereas different people would prompt differently), minimize ambiguity and serve as documentation: anyone can read the Skill to understand what it does, identify missing cases and suggest improvements.

We bootstrapped the Skill by porting a model ourselves, in conversation with Claude. I asked it to port GLM 4.7 from transformers to mlx-lm, giving instructions as I would during a normal session. One trick: I pointed Claude at a checkout of mlx-lm from which I had deleted the already-existing implementation, so I could compare the output against the ground truth. After a few iterations I had a working implementation, a conversation that revealed how Claude approached the problem, and the first draft of the Skill, which Claude created as a summary of the process. I edited it heavily, and incorporated the learnings from @gabegoodhart, who kindly shared their own porting conversation for a different model 🙌.

We repeated this loop several times and the Skill grew. On the technical side, we covered stuff such as RoPE bugs that may produce plausible output that degrades with long sequences, float32 precision contamination that silently kills inference speed (you'd be surprised how frequently these things happen!), config fields that vary across model variants in ways the implementation must handle, distributed inference for super large models that don't fit on a single machine. We taught it how to invoke the hf CLI to discover and download models. Most importantly, we instructed it to run the tests that experienced porters would, and to not declare success until they pass.

On the cultural side, we covered softer characteristics and explained the conventions that make a PR easy to review: don't use comments to explain code (the reviewer has to parse the comment and the code 🤦‍♂️), never propose refactors, don't touch shared utilities without asking. These rules cost the agent nothing but save the reviewer lots of time.

The end result: the contributor types a prompt, and the Skill produces a PR like this one, plus a test manifest for the external test harness.

According to recent reports, the Skill shares a comprehensive results report as part of the PR. All these come from tests the agent runs during conversion, but we didn't want the reviewer to take a leap of faith to accept them. To go a step forward, we created a separate, non-agentic test harness that runs systematic tests on the converted code. This brings a couple of benefits:.

It has been revealed that the test harness is not a CI gate. Some checks are straightforward (is the output dtype correct?), but most are qualitative. Is it normal that a pre-trained model repeats itself in long sequences? Is a 4% relative logits difference against the transformers baseline acceptable? These are judgement calls based on experience with similar architectures. The harness provides useful signal, but it's the reviewer and contributor who still have to make the call.

According to recent reports, the Skill is designed for the people who are already opening mlx-lm model PRs, or who would do it manually on their own. It's not meant for mass consumption, because PRs to mlx-lm are rarely accepted on sight. The typical cycle is: contributor opens a PR, reviewers point out improvements, both sides iterate until the quality bar is met. If this is true for expert submissions, it will remain true for agent-assisted ones.

If you're not prepared to engage in that cycle, you probably shouldn't be opening a PR. The reviewers will make an effort to understand your code (even knowing it was agent-assisted), so you should do the same. Own the code, and be ready to incorporate their feedback. In particular, don't hand reviewer comments back to an agent and post whatever it produces. LLMs double down on their decisions, go on tangents, and don't push back effectively. Once you engage with the reviewer, this becomes a person-to-person conversation, so it's your turn to discuss and be respectful of the time they put in.

Recent findings suggest that you can also use the Skill to learn; you don't need to submit anything until your confidence and experience build. Read the Skill to identify problem areas you weren't aware of: it contains nearly 15 thousand words among the skill file, reference docs and utility scripts. Point it to your own fork of mlx-lm, try a conversion, and compare your output against the accepted implementation once it lands in the official repo. If you do this a few times, you'll learn a lot about transformers, MLX, and language model architectures.

In a recent development, we developed and tested the Skill using Claude Code. The same approach would work with Codex or other coding agents, but we haven't tested them. If you try the Skill in a different environment, please let us know how it goes!

The Skill works well for LLMs in mlx-lm, but there's plenty of room to grow.

The bottleneck in open source is not typing speed: it's understaning the codebase to change it without breaking the implicit and explicit contracts with users. Agents can help in this process, if we teach them what matters. We explored what this looks like in the context of mlx-lm, and hope it's useful for contributors and reviewers to land high-quality model conversions faster!

Thanks a lot to Ben, Shaun, Aritra for reading previous versions of this post and making it so much better 🙌.

We are incredibly indebted to Apple for making MLX an open-source project, and to the community for instantly recognizing its value and contributing enthusiastically 🙏.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While many services are turning to AI in place of an actual human being, Pebblebee’s fresh Alert Dispatch brings the help of a real person into an emergency situation, and it all starts with your Find Hub tracker.

Pebblebee rolled out its Alert feature in 2025 as a way to use a Clip 5 tracker for Find Hub as a siren in an emergency. The firm later added an optional live location-sharing feature to this, and also released “Halo” as an emergency siren first, tracker second with a special design.

Now, “Alert Dispatch” takes the whole system up a notch.

Instead of relying solely on location sharing and the siren, Pebblebee’s Alert Dispatch assigns an actual human being to the situation, with a trained dispatch agent reaching out first over SMS or a call, then pulling in emergency responders if the situation calls for it. The feature works with Clip 4, Clip 5, and Halo.

Sources indicate that alert Dispatch connects Pebblebee people with a trained dispatch agent when they trigger an Alert, starting with a text and escalating to an Emergency call if they don’t respond. With an attempt to send help when users cannot confirm they’re safe, plus live location sharing and private Check-In calls on Clip 5 and Halo, it adds another layer of support when calling for help isn’t an option.

Pebblebee Alert Dispatch runs in partnership with Noonlight, with an alert triggered by disconnecting Halo or rapidly pressing the button on Clip trackers. Pricing is as follows:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

In a recent development, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Picture this. A customer writes to your support chatbot: "Hi, I'm Asha, my card ending 4111 was charged twice, call me on 98400 12345." Your Java service wraps that message in a prompt, sends it to a model, and logs the whole thing so you can debug it later. Congratulations, you now have a customer's name, phone number and card details sitting in a plain text log file that half the engineering team can open.

Recent findings suggest that this happens more often than people admit. Logging AI calls is genuinely useful, but prompts and responses are some of the most personal text your application ever touches. Here's how to keep the usefulness and drop the risk.

It has been revealed that A regular web request is easy to log: URL, status code, time taken. AI calls are messier.

The output changes from run to run. If a user says "your bot gave me a wrong answer yesterday", the only proof of what happened is what you sent and what came back at that moment. You can't just replay it and expect the same result.

Prompts are also built, not typed. The final text is usually a template, a few retrieved document chunks, some chat history and the user's message stitched together. When something looks off, the bug could be in any of those pieces, and only the assembled prompt demonstrates you which one.

Sources indicate that then there's cost. You pay by the token, so without per-call records you can't say which feature is burning money. And quality drifts over time as models get upgraded and templates get edited. Old logs are your only baseline.

So yes, you need these logs. The real question is what goes into them.

In a recent development, before writing any masking code, agree on what counts as sensitive. In most business apps that means:.

Names, emails, phone numbers and home addresses.

Card numbers, bank details and government ID numbers.

Passwords, API keys and bearer tokens.

Health, legal or job-related details people mention in free text.

Internal material like contract wording, pricing rules or source code.

It has been revealed that the first three groups follow patterns, so they're easy to catch. The last two don't, and that's where most teams get caught out. Keep that in mind, because it shapes the design below.

The safest sensitive value is the one that never reaches the log. So split what you record into two buckets.

In a recent development, the first is metadata: a request ID, a hashed user or tenant ID, model name, prompt template name and version, token counts, latency, retry count, error type and estimated cost. None of this is personal, and it answers most day-to-day questions.

Sources indicate that the second is content, meaning the actual prompt and response text. You only need this when you're investigating quality, and even then you rarely need all of it. A sensible default is to log metadata for every call and masked content for a small sample, maybe five percent, plus every failed call.

Sources indicate that here's a mistake that's easy to make: letting the log appender clean things up afterwards. By then the raw text may already be in a buffer, an async queue or a crash dump. Mask first, then log.

The cleanest way is one small component that every AI log call has to pass through:.

public interface PiiMasker {     String mask(String input); }.

Sources indicate that nothing else is allowed to write raw prompts. One chokepoint is much easier to review and test than masking sprinkled across fifty classes.

For structured data like emails, cards and tokens, regular expressions do the job well:.

public class RegexPiiMasker implements PiiMasker {     private static final Map RULES = new LinkedHashMap<>();     static {         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("[A-Za-z0-9.%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"), "[EMAIL]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\+?\d{1,3}[ -]?)?\d{10}\b"), "[PHONE]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("(?i)bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9.~+/=-]+"), "Bearer [TOKEN]");     }     @Override     public String mask(String input) {         if (input == null || input.isBlank()) return input;         String result = input;         for (var rule : RULES.entrySet()) {             result = rule.getKey().matcher(result).replaceAll(rule.getValue());         }         return result;     } }.

A few small choices matter here. The patterns are compiled once, not on every call. The order is fixed, because a card number can otherwise get half eaten by the phone rule. And the replacement labels such as [EMAIL] keep the sentence readable, so whoever debugs it later can still follow what the user was asking.

Regex won't catch a name like "Asha Raman" or an address buried mid-sentence. For those you have a few options, and they work best together.

You can run a named-entity recognition model that tags people, places and organisations, then mask anything above a confidence threshold. You can do exact replacement of values you already know, such as the customer's name from the current session. Or, best of all, you can mask at the field level while building the prompt. If your code knows that customer.getEmail() is going into the template, swap in a placeholder right there instead of trying to spot it afterwards. Knowing beats guessing every time.

Plain redaction can remove too much. If the same email indicates up five times in a conversation, five identical [EMAIL] tags hide the fact that it was one person.

According to recent reports, the fix is consistent pseudonyms. Turn each real value into a short token using a keyed hash, so the same email always becomes something like EMAIL_7f3a. You can still follow the thread, but nobody can read the original from the log. Use an HMAC with a secret from your secrets manager. A plain unkeyed hash of a phone number can be brute-forced in minutes, because there just aren't that many phone numbers.

One warning: if you also store a lookup table to reverse the tokens, that table is now sensitive data too. Most teams are better off with one-way tokens.

Free-text log lines are hard to search and easy to leak through. Write one JSON record per AI call with clearly separate fields:.

log.info("ai_call",     kv("requestId", requestId),     kv("model", model),     kv("promptVersion", "support-reply-v4"),     kv("inputTokens", usage.inputTokens()),     kv("outputTokens", usage.outputTokens()),     kv("latencyMs", elapsed),     kv("promptMasked", masker.mask(prompt)),     kv("responseMasked", masker.mask(response)));.

Now dashboards for cost and latency never need to touch the text fields at all. You can also keep the two kinds of data for different lengths of time: metadata for a year, masked content for a couple of weeks. Put the request ID into your logging framework's MDC so every line belonging to one call, including retries and tool calls, carries the same ID.

According to recent reports, streaming trips people up. Tokens arrive in tiny pieces, and a card number can be split across two chunks, which means masking each chunk on its own will miss it. Collect the full response in a buffer, mask it once the stream ends, and log that. If the stream dies halfway, run the partial buffer through the same masker.

Tool calls are the other trap. When the model calls one of your Java methods, the arguments and return values are often the most sensitive thing in the whole exchange: order details, account balances, addresses. Treat them as part of the prompt and response. Log the tool name, duration and outcome by default, and log arguments only after masking.

Masking lowers the risk but never removes it, so surround it with some ordinary discipline:.

In a recent development, give content fields a short retention period. Old prompt archives are liabilities.

Limit who can read AI logs. Debugging a model doesn't mean someone needs to read customer messages.

Encrypt log storage and the pipeline that feeds it.

Log the hashed user ID so you can find and delete one person's records when they ask.

Allow verbose logging in development with fake data, and enforce strict settings in production through configuration, not through people remembering.

In a recent development, A masker that quietly stops working is worse than having none, because everyone assumes the logs are clean. Write tests for it:.

@Test void masksEmailAndCardNumber() {     String raw = "Contact me at asha@example.com, card 4111 1111 1111 1111";     String safe = new RegexPiiMasker().mask(raw);     assertFalse(safe.contains("asha@example.com"));     assertFalse(safe.contains("4111"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[EMAIL]"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[CARD]")); }.

Build a small set of messy, realistic samples: numbers with odd spacing, mixed languages, addresses inside sentences, text pasted from spreadsheets. Run them in your CI pipeline, and add a new case every time a leak turns up. A scheduled job that scans stored logs for patterns that should never appear makes a good safety net too.

In a recent development, A few I'd watch for. Logging raw text at debug level and assuming production never enables it; debug flags get switched on during incidents, so mask at every level. Masking only the user's message while forgetting retrieved documents, system prompts and tool results. Letting SDK exceptions carry the full request body into the logs. Leaving wire-level HTTP logging on in production, which bypasses your masker completely. And treating masking as finished once it ships, when every new prompt template can bring new kinds of data.

Every AI call writes a structured metadata record with a request ID.

All prompt and response text goes through a single masker first.

Streams are masked after assembly, and tool arguments are masked too.

Content logging is sampled, short-lived and access-controlled.

Tests cover the masker, with a regression case for every past leak.

Client libraries aren't dumping raw payloads into the logs.

In a recent development, good logs turn an AI feature from a black box into something you can actually debug, price and improve. The same logs can also expose the people who trusted you with their details. The way through is fairly plain: record metadata for every call, push all content through one well-tested masker, use pseudonyms when you need to follow a conversation, handle streams and tools carefully, and keep retention short. Set that up before launch, not after the first incident, and you get visibility without regret.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The smart glasses race is heating up as Meta and Samsung are about to go head-to-head, but could a new Meta glasses style fix the privacy stigma, or are things too far gone?

According to recent reports, meta debuted its own-branded smart glasses this summer (read: with no Ray-Ban or Oakley branding), and they seem to have done well for a number of reasons. Some models are much cheaper than Ray-Ban-branded pairs, while other Meta glasses carry Kylie Jenner or LISA names, bringing in a unique note of fashion, but none of these models changed the look of the camera LED indicator on the front.

Meta has come under fire over the past two years as people have abused the organization’s smart glasses, giving them the unfortunate term “perv glasses” on social media because some people disabled the camera LED, which is supposed to illuminate when the camera is recording. Meta has issued several different software patches to disable the glasses’ camera when the LED is tampered with, but many have begun to feel like having a camera on smart glasses just feels wrong after people have abused the technology.

Meta glasses product lead David Woodland posted a render of the Gentle Monster cateye style glasses in a now-deleted Tweet on X on November 17, simply saying “I plead the fifth.” Presumably, he was calling out how similar these glasses look to the Meta Starfire Kylie Jenner style, but we’ll likely never know now.

Samsung and Google’s Warby Parker and Gentle Monster glasses certainly resemble Meta’s glasses, but they also do something noticeably different: the camera LED doesn’t look like the camera on the other side.

So this begs the question: can Meta do anything to salvage the unsavory association its glasses now have attached to them? We covered this topic on episode 125 of our Pixelated podcast, and Woodland’s post further highlights the question. A camera LED that’s obviously different from the camera on the other side would likely prompt people to ask about your glasses, while Meta’s design is purposefully stealthy because of its symmetry.

Does this design difference help Samsung’s Gentle Monster/Warby Parker glasses feel more private, and would a similar redesign help Meta’s glasses? I think it would help a lot, but I also want to know what our readers think. What say you, folks?

Ecom-RLVE: Adaptive Verifiable Environments for E-Commerce Conversational Agents

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1431 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR — We extend the RLVE framework from single-turn reasoning puzzles to multi-turn, tool-augmented e-commerce conversations.
  • This project originated in the Pytorch OpenEnv Hackathon and is still evolving, follow us for updates 🔥.
  • Large language models can hold fluent conversations, yet deploying them as shopping assistants reveals a persistent gap: fluency ≠ task completion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR — We extend the RLVE framework from single-turn reasoning puzzles to multi-turn, tool-augmented e-commerce conversations. EcomRLVE-GYM provides 8 verifiable environments — product discovery, substitution, cart building, returns, order tracking, policy QA, bundle planning, and multi-intent journeys — each with procedural problem generation, a 12-axis difficulty curriculum, and algorithmically verifiable rewards. We train a Qwen 3 8B model with DAPO over 300 steps and present early results demonstrating that environment scaling and adaptive difficulty transfer to agentic, real-world task completion.

This project originated in the Pytorch OpenEnv Hackathon and is still evolving, follow us for updates 🔥.

Large language models can hold fluent conversations, yet deploying them as shopping assistants reveals a persistent gap: fluency ≠ task completion. A customer who asks "find me a USB-C charger under $25 that ships in two days" needs an agent that invokes the right catalog search, filters on three hard constraints, avoids hallucinating product IDs it never retrieved, and handles follow-ups when the top result goes out of stock.

Supervised fine-tuning can teach surface-level tool use from demonstrations, but it cannot scale to the combinatorial space of constraint configurations, partial-information dialogues, and multi-step transactional workflows that real e-commerce demands.

Sources indicate that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) offers an alternative: the agent optimises for outcomes — did the products satisfy the constraints? Was the cart correct? Was the return initiated for the right order line? The challenge is constructing reward functions that are both verifiable (no LLM-as-a-judge subjectivity) and adaptive (difficulty that grows with the policy's capability).

RLVE-Gym provides 400 environments for sorting, multiplication, Sudoku, and other algorithmic-reasoning tasks; however, those are all single-turn, text-in / text-out puzzles — extending to agentic domains was left as future work.

EcomRLVE-GYM fills that gap: we stay in the verifiable regime (e-commerce outcomes can be checked algorithmically) while extending to multi-turn, tool-augmented, agentic conversations — environments where the agent must act (call tools, modify world state) rather than merely reason (produce a text answer) and compensates for the deficiency of the search system.

EcomRLVE-GYM transforms customer-service outcomes structurally verifiable:.

It has been revealed that every signal above can be evaluated by a program with access to the hidden ground-truth goal. No human annotation or LLM-as-a-judge is needed.

Before we explain the framework, here is what a single EcomRLVE episode looks like at difficulty d = 4. The environment generates a hidden goal, a simulated user opens the chat, and the agent must use tools to satisfy the request. Every action is verified algorithmically — no LLM judge required.

Recent findings suggest that the reward is fully computed by code: F1 over (product, variant, qty) tuples, an efficiency bonus for finishing in fewer turns, and a hallucination check that every recommended product ID was actually retrieved. If the agent had picked the Lightning variant instead of USB-C, the simulated user would have corrected it mid-dialogue — and the F1 would have dropped.

In a recent development, each environment covers a distinct real-world shopping scenario. The agent must complete the task using tools (catalog search, cart operations, order lookups, policy queries) and is scored by a program — not a human or another LLM.

Every environment uses the same three-part reward signal:.

Invalid outputs (malformed JSON, illegal tool calls) trigger an immediate failure score, creating a strong incentive for well-formed responses from step one.

A single difficulty number d controls 12 independent aspects of a task simultaneously. This is key because e-commerce conversations are hard in many different ways at once — not just along one dimension.

Here are four representative difficulty axes:.

The other eight axes cover turn budget, input noise (typos, slang), context switches, retrieval depth, order-history size, policy complexity, and tool budget. The full breakdown is in the technical report.

It has been revealed that adaptive scheduling. Each environment tracks the agent's success rate independently and only advances to harder problems once the agent is passing the current level reliably. This keeps every environment training at the agent's capability frontier — avoiding both "too easy to learn from" and "too hard to make progress on".

Cart building is a good showcase because it requires the full search → inspect → clarify → act loop, has a binary ground truth, and introduces a challenge absent from most recommendation benchmarks: variant selection.

To succeed, the agent must develop five distinct skills:.

The agent uses six tools to accomplish this:.

Industry observers note that the generator samples 1–5 target products (scaling in difficulty with d), each potentially requiring a specific variant (USB-C vs Lightning, Matte vs Glossy) and a quantity > 1. The agent must:.

Real product catalogs have sparse variant data — many products have none, and those that do typically vary only by colour or size. To create a richer discrimination task, we synthesize variants at episode initialization:.

Recent findings suggest that at d = 0 the agent adds a single product with no variant complexity — learning the basic catalog.search → cart.add workflow. At d = 6 it juggles 3 items, nearly all requiring a specific variant, with half needing qty > 1.

The cart must be exactly right — correct product, correct variant, correct quantity. Partial credit is given for partially correct carts, but a perfect score requires every item to match. If the agent adds the wrong variant, the simulated user corrects it mid-dialogue ("that's the Lightning version, but I need USB-C"), giving the agent a chance to self-correct before the episode ends.

Two real E_CART episodes from a Qwen 3 8B agent. Same environment, same agent — difficulty alone changes the game.

In a recent development, at d=1 the agent solves the task in 3 clean turns. At d=8 it spirals — picking Bamboo instead of Charcoal, XL instead of XS, never fixing the air fryer despite two user corrections, then hallucinating that the variant doesn't exist. This is exactly the kind of multi-step error cascade that the difficulty curriculum surfaces, and that adaptive training should teach the agent to recover from.

A verifiable environment needs a user simulator that behaves realistically. We use Qwen3.5 (9.7B) to generate natural, varied user messages rather than canned templates — covering everything from typo-filled requests to mid-conversation topic switches.

Two design choices matter for training quality:.

Preferences match stated constraints. Each simulated user has a hidden set of preferences (price sensitivity, brand loyalty, shipping speed, etc.). These are deliberately biased toward whatever constraints the user communicated — so if the user stated "under $25", the reward function actually cares about price. Without this, an agent could be penalised for correctly following the user's instructions.

Strategic omission. The LLM deliberately withholds some constraints from the opening message to force the agent to ask clarifying questions. The system tracks exactly what was and wasn't mentioned, so the agent is never penalised for information it was never given.

Following RLVE's methodology, we define nested environment collections:.

We hypothesise — consistent with RLVE's findings — that C8 agents outperform single-environment specialists, even on the specialist's own task.

We trained Qwen 3 8B with DAPO on C1 (Cart Building) for 300 steps as an initial viability study.

We saw progressive growth in difficulty reached, confirming that adaptive scheduling produces a steady learning signal rather than the saturation (static-low) or starvation (static-high) patterns predicted by the RLVE paper.

#34866. AI and the Future of Cybersecurity: Why Openness Matters

📅 21 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1099 w)

AI and the Future of Cybersecurity: Why Openness Matters

📅 21 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following the announcement of Mythos and Project Glasswing, institutions throughout the world are grappling with the potential dawn of a latest era of cybersecurity.
  • Mythos is a “frontier AI model”, a large language model (LLM) that can be used to process software code (among many other things).
  • What Mythos demonstrates is that the following system recipe is powerful:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following the announcement of Mythos and Project Glasswing, institutions throughout the world are grappling with the potential dawn of a latest era of cybersecurity. In this post, we break down the current situation, discuss the role of openness, and situate the future of cybersecurity within the larger AI ecosystem.

Mythos is a “frontier AI model”, a large language model (LLM) that can be used to process software code (among many other things). This follows a general trend in LLM development, where LLM performance on code-related tasks has recently skyrocketed. What’s particularly significant about Mythos is the system it’s embedded within: It's the system, not the model alone, that has enabled Mythos to rapidly find and patch software vulnerabilities. Understanding this distinction is key to understanding the current landscape of AI cybersecurity.

What Mythos demonstrates is that the following system recipe is powerful:.

Together, these ingredients can uncover software vulnerabilities, find exploits, and build patches. It’s in this recipe — not in any one model — that both the benefits and the risks come in.

In a recent development, this matters because others can build comparable systems. Smaller models embedded in systems built with deep security expertise could potentially produce similar outcomes more cheaply, which is particularly promising for defense. AI cybersecurity capability is jagged: It doesn’t scale smoothly with model size or general benchmark performance. The system the model is embedded within matters a lot.

So what Mythos has demonstrated is that it’s possible to build an AI system that finds and addresses software vulnerabilities. We already knew this was possible and there has been increasing work on this, but we’re just beginning to explore what it means in the context of agentic AI: Systems that can rapidly and autonomously take action.

As autonomous systems that identify software vulnerabilities proliferate (and they will), open code and tooling can help level the playing field. Software security has become a speed race across four stages: detection, verification, coordination, and patch propagation. Open ecosystems distribute these across a community, where more closed-source projects centralize knowledge and action across all four stages inside a single vendor, representing a single point of failure where only one organization can see and fix the code. The distributed nature of open development is robust to such constraints, and can be especially powerful in communities with dedicated security professionals, like the Linux kernel security team, the Open Source Security Foundation, and the team at Hugging Face working on model and supply-chain security.

Sources indicate that A common argument for more closed systems is proprietary obscurity, where the code underlying a system is inaccessible. Unfortunately, this provides less protection than it used to. AI systems are increasingly able to assist with reverse engineering of stripped binaries, which matters because most legacy firmware and embedded code is closed, binary-only, and no longer maintained. That code represents a huge attack surface, and it’s becoming more legible and accessible as AI tools improve.

According to recent reports, there’s also a risk created by how AI is being used inside closed codebases. When companies adopt AI coding tools under the wrong incentives (for instance, evaluating engineers by the volume of features shipped rather than code quality) AI-accelerated development can introduce more vulnerabilities into proprietary code than traditional development would. Those vulnerabilities then sit inside a closed codebase where only one organization can find and fix them, while AI-enabled attackers are increasingly capable of discovering them from the outside. The combination of more vulnerabilities produced more rapidly, behind a single-organization firewall, is exactly the kind of imbalance that open ecosystems are positioned to avoid.

According to recent reports, underlying all of this is capability asymmetry between attackers and defenders. Open models and open tooling narrow that gap by giving defenders access to the same class of capabilities attackers can reach for — capabilities that would otherwise be concentrated within a small number of well-resourced entities.

Recent findings suggest that cybersecurity defense is where open source and AI agents can play a key role together. Based on the System Card, it appears that Mythos is capable of operating with close to full autonomy, something we’ve advised against due to the potential loss of control. AI agents that are instead semi-autonomous, where the types of actions they can take are prespecified and certain steps require human approval, hit a sweet spot of benefit and risk. In semi-autonomous systems, people remain in control, and the AI agent is responsible for specific subtasks. This is possible to do with open code that organizations can run privately within their own institutions, specifying allowable tools, skills, and system access privileges. With this setup, AI agents can be deployed defensively, finding vulnerabilities and assisting with patching under an organization’s own controls.

In a recent development, the semi-autonomous approach depends on humans being able to actually understand what an AI agent did and why. That’s much more possible when the system is built on open components, such as open agent scaffolding, open rule engines, and auditable decision logs and traces, than when it’s a black box. The “human in the loop” is only meaningful if the human can see into the loop.

In a recent development, companies don’t have to build these capabilities entirely from scratch. There’s a rich open-source ecosystem of security tooling, including vulnerability scanners, intrusion detection systems, log analyzers, and fuzzing frameworks, that AI agents can be integrated with.

Recent findings suggest that for high-stakes organizations, starting from open, auditable foundations means security teams can actually inspect how their monitoring works, rather than trusting a single vendor’s claims. This is particularly key where sensitive data and processes are involved, and where sensitive material should generally not be flowing through external AI providers. Open systems can be rigorously analyzed by in-house security professionals, fine-tuned on an organizations’s own secure data, modified to produce organization-specific oversight mechanisms, and run entirely within an organization’s own infrastructure, keeping everything behind appropriate firewalls.

Attackers will develop models that take advantage of vulnerabilities. A significant part of the answer is leaning into transparent practices: open security reviews, published threat models, shared vulnerability databases, and open tooling that any team can adopt. The alternative of each organization trying to secure itself in isolation with proprietary tools doesn’t scale against attackers who are coordinating and sharing techniques in their own communities.

Recent findings suggest that the future of AI cybersecurity will be shaped less by any single model and more by the ecosystems that surround them. Openness provides defenders with the visibility, the control, the community, and the shared infrastructure to stay ahead.

Industry observers note that A visitor clicks a search ad, submits a quote request, and calls your sales team ten minutes later. The form integration creates a CRM contact. The phone platform records a call. By Friday, the marketing report reveals two leads, while sales remembers one conversation that turned into a deal.

Industry observers note that both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

According to recent reports, this tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

Industry observers note that before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a new purchase.

Use separate identifiers for these different things:.

Sources indicate that this separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

For this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

According to recent reports, keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

It has been revealed that campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

Recent findings suggest that google's campaign URL documentation explains the roles of utm_source, utm_medium, and utm_campaign. The following helper reads those fields and a few optional ones, without copying the entire query string:.

The browser's URLSearchParams interface handles query parsing and decoding. It saves you from writing string-splitting code that breaks on encoded characters.

Industry observers note that run this helper through your site's existing consent and attribution flow. Where storage is permitted, associate the result with an opaque attribution reference in your backend and retain that reference through the visit. A later form submission sends the reference; the server resolves it within the correct tenant and visitor session. The form must still work when attribution storage is unavailable.

In a recent development, keep first-touch and current-touch records separately if you need both. Overwriting the first campaign every time someone returns makes the eventual report answer a different question.

Treat campaign labels as untrusted input. Visitors can edit query strings and hidden fields. Validate them on the server, escape them when displayed, and never use them as authorization or as the sole evidence for commission payments. Avoid putting names, email addresses, or other personal information in UTM values.

According to recent reports, missing tags also need careful handling. An empty UTM object only tells you that no accepted UTM values were captured. Classifying a visit as direct, organic, or referral requires additional evidence and an explicit attribution rule.

Industry observers note that forms carry browser context naturally. Phone calls need a bridge between the number dialed and the marketing interaction that prompted the call.

There are two useful levels of precision. A number assigned to one campaign can identify that campaign. Dynamic number insertion can support a more detailed association by displaying tracking numbers according to a visitor or session mapping. That association depends on the provider's number allocation and expiry rules.

Providers differ in how they implement this, and in what they expose beyond it, such as keyword-level reporting or conversation analysis. If you are still choosing one, this comparison of attribution software with call tracking is a useful starting point. At the integration boundary, check which event identifiers, attribution fields, delivery mechanisms, and authentication options your configured product exposes.

Sources indicate that keep that provider-specific work in an adapter. Its job is to turn an authenticated notification into your event contract and resolve any attribution reference supported by the provider's data. The application schema below is an internal contract; each provider adapter translates its documented payload into that contract.

Store the basis of a match with the attribution record. For example, session_match, campaign_number, and unknown make different levels of evidence visible to reporting. If a number has been reassigned, use the mapping valid when the call occurred, not whichever mapping happens to be current when the callback arrives. If the evidence is ambiguous, leave the association unresolved.

Caller ID is a separate issue. A shared office number, a withheld number, or an outdated contact record can make automatic identity matching unreliable. A confirmed CRM contact ID or an authenticated account provides a stronger link. Treat a matching phone number as a candidate for reconciliation rather than proof that two records belong to the same person.

Recent findings suggest that A shared event envelope lets the rest of your application work with a small, predictable vocabulary. Here is an illustrative call event:.

"occurred_at": "2026-11-06T10:14:00.000Z",.

"data": { "status": "completed" }.

In a recent development, the event ID identifies this occurrence. The interaction ID groups it with other events for the same call. contact_ref can remain empty until you have enough evidence to connect the interaction to a contact.

Sources indicate that keep contact details in a controlled contact store and campaign details in an attribution store. The references above point to those records; they are not credentials and must not grant access on their own.

The following factory checks the shared envelope. Each adapter still needs its own validation for provider fields and the contents of data.

Resolve trusted from server configuration and the authenticated integration. Never let a submitted tenant_id choose whose records a webhook can write. Resolve contact and attribution references within that same tenant.

According to recent reports, for a form, problem a submission ID and reuse it when retrying the same submission. Generate a upcoming one when the visitor deliberately starts another inquiry. Preserve the originally accepted timestamp as well. For a phone event, prefer the provider's stable event ID. If the provider documents a sequence number, a call ID plus that sequence can identify an occurrence within a provider account.

Industry observers note that twilio's call resource documentation provides a concrete example: call progress callbacks include a SequenceNumber, and separate HTTP requests can arrive out of order. Preserve that sequence in the adapter. A late “ringing” event should remain in the history without replacing a newer terminal state.

Industry observers note that authenticate before calling this factory. Use the provider's supported validator and the exact request representation it requires. Twilio's webhook security guide describes signature validation, including the importance of the request URL and payload. Other providers may use different mechanisms. Public form endpoints need their own input limits, abuse controls, and appropriate CSRF protection.

It has been revealed that consider a failure between these two operations: the application saves an event, then crashes before scheduling its CRM update. The event exists, but nothing is waiting to deliver it.

A transactional outbox addresses that gap. Save the event and a delivery task in the same database transaction, then let a worker process the task. AWS explains this dual-write problem in its transactional outbox guidance.

According to recent reports, here is a compact schema. received_at records ingestion time, while the envelope retains the event's original occurred_at value.

FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id).

REFERENCES lead_events (tenant_id, source, event_id).

The ingestion function below accepts a pg pool and a normalized event. Install pg in your Node.js project, save the function as persist.mjs, and initialize the pool using your application's database configuration.

Sources indicate that postgreSQL's INSERT documentation defines the conflict handling used here. The unique key makes duplicate detection hold across application processes. A duplicate with the same normalized payload creates no second task; reuse of the key with different data raises a conflict for investigation.

Recent findings suggest that this depends on immutable event bodies. Do not add a fresh receipt timestamp, random identifier, or current CRM status to the normalized payload on each delivery. Store later enrichment separately or emit a fresh event. Otherwise an ordinary retry will appear to be a conflicting event.

The function deliberately uses one database client throughout the transaction, as required by the node-postgres transaction documentation. Parameter values are passed separately from SQL, following its parameterized query guidance.

After this function commits, acknowledge the notification using the response expected by the sender. An identical duplicate should also receive a successful acknowledgement. If persistence fails, return the appropriate failure response and rely on the configured retry or reconciliation process. A success response sent before durable storage can turn a temporary database failure into a missing event.

For voice integrations, distinguish an informational status callback from a request asking your application how to handle a live call. They can require different response bodies, as explained in the Twilio webhooks FAQ.

It has been revealed that the outbox gives you durable work to process. It does not make a remote CRM operation happen exactly once.

Imagine the CRM saves an update, but the worker crashes before setting processed_at. When the task runs again, the same request may reach the CRM twice. Design for that case explicitly.

Recent findings suggest that use a stable external identifier for each contact, opportunity, and activity, and check which deduplication guarantees the destination supports. HubSpot's contacts API documentation, for example, describes upserts using unique properties. Support for a contact upsert does not automatically make every associated activity or workflow idempotent. Verify the behavior of each operation you send.

If the destination cannot deduplicate a create request and a timeout leaves its result uncertain, reconcile that operation before repeating it. A local “sent” flag alone cannot prove whether the remote write happened.

The worker should claim due tasks, commit a recoverable lease, and perform network calls outside the database transaction. A lease allows another worker to recover work after a crash. When multiple workers poll the outbox, PostgreSQL's SKIP LOCKED behavior can help claim separate rows, but the lease and its recovery logic still need to be implemented.

Retry transient failures with increasing delays and jitter. Respect the destination's rate-limit instructions. Send persistent validation failures to a review queue with a useful error category, and provide a way to replay them after correction. The schema above is the ingestion foundation; a production worker needs lease fields, failure details, and a retry policy appropriate to its destination.

According to recent reports, also preserve ordering where it changes meaning. If two events enhancement the same contact or opportunity, process them serially or reject stale updates using a stored version. A historical event should not move a won opportunity back to an earlier stage.

Industry observers note that once both channels reach the CRM, connect them to the result the business cares about. A form submission is an inquiry. A completed phone call is a technical outcome. Neither alone establishes that a lead qualified or a purchase happened. If agents record call dispositions, such as whether a call was qualified or transferred to a closer, that field is a richer signal than call completion status alone.

Recent findings suggest that have the CRM or the system that owns the transaction emit explicit outcome events, such as lead.qualified and deal.won. Include the internal opportunity ID and the original outcome time. Model reversals or cancellations explicitly if they affect revenue reporting.

Then choose the unit behind each metric. For a report about opportunities acquired during a particular month, a qualification rate can use qualified opportunities divided by all opportunities in that acquisition cohort. Counting qualification events received during the month would answer a different question and could include older inquiries.

Sources indicate that deduplicate opportunities before calculating channel totals. A person who submits a form and calls about the same purchase should retain both interactions, while the opportunity receives credit according to your chosen attribution rule. Label that rule in the report so first-touch and last-touch numbers are not compared as though they measure the same thing.

Measure data quality alongside performance. Track unresolved attribution, duplicate deliveries, ingestion failures, and the age of the oldest pending outbox task. Once several sources and destinations feed the same reports, a data observability platform can watch these signals across the whole pipeline instead of relying on checks inside a single worker. An apparently quiet campaign may actually have a broken integration.

Operational logs should contain enough context to investigate failures without becoming another customer database. Use internal references and error categories, and avoid dumping webhook bodies into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet provides guidance on excluding or protecting sensitive values.

Recent findings suggest that A successful form submission proves little about retries or missing data. Before connecting production traffic, test the cases that could distort reporting or lose an inquiry.

Sources indicate that run database cases against PostgreSQL with separate connections so the tests exercise actual constraints and transaction behavior. Use the provider's test tools or signed fixtures for webhook authentication. Test CRM retries against a sandbox with the destination's real duplicate-handling rules.

Start rollout with one form and one phone source. Trace a known inquiry from its captured campaign through its interactions to its CRM outcome. Reconcile event totals against the source systems over the same time window, allowing for delivery delays. Expand once that path is explainable and failures are visible.

Sources indicate that the same adapter pattern extends to inquiries that start offline, such as leads collected at a trade show and exported as a CSV or XLSX file. Import each row as a form.submitted event with the event as its source, a stable row identifier as event_id, and the original capture time as occurred_at. Because the outbox treats an identical event as a duplicate, re-importing the same export won’t create a second CRM task.

What is a unified lead tracking pipeline?

Industry observers note that it is a workflow that converts inquiries from different channels into a shared data model, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to business outcomes. Forms and calls keep their own interaction records, while contacts and opportunities provide the relationships needed for reporting.

Can I connect a phone call to a website visit?

Sometimes. Dynamic number insertion can provide a session or visitor association when the provider's mapping is available and valid. A campaign-specific number usually supports campaign-level attribution. If the caller uses a saved number, switches devices, or calls after a mapping expires, the available evidence may be less precise.

How do I prevent duplicate leads?

Handle duplicate delivery and identity resolution separately. Stable event IDs and a database constraint prevent repeated notifications from producing repeated work. Connecting several interactions to one contact or opportunity requires a separate matching policy, with ambiguous cases left unresolved until there is enough evidence.

Should a completed call count as a conversion?

Recent findings suggest that only if that is the conversion your report explicitly measures. A completed call does not establish that a prospect qualified or bought something. Keep technical call status separate from CRM outcomes and use the latter when reporting qualified demand or revenue.

Do I need a message broker for this architecture?

You can begin with PostgreSQL and an outbox worker if that setup meets your throughput and latency needs. A broker becomes useful when several consumers need independent delivery, or when buffering and scale justify the additional operations. In either case, retries still require idempotent consumers.

What happens when tracking consent is unavailable?

Keep the inquiry flow usable and apply your site's existing consent rules to optional attribution collection and storage. Accept permitted form or call data, leave unavailable attribution empty, and avoid reconstructing a visitor identity through fingerprinting. Reports should expose that missing context instead of inventing a campaign match.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • QIMMA validates benchmarks before evaluating models, ensuring reported scores reflect genuine Arabic language capability in LLMs.
  • If you've been tracking Arabic LLM evaluation, you've probably noticed a growing tension: the number of benchmarks and leaderboards is expanding rapidly, but are we actually measuring what we think we're measuring?
  • We built QIMMA قمّة (Arabic for "summit"), to answer that question systematically.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

QIMMA validates benchmarks before evaluating models, ensuring reported scores reflect genuine Arabic language capability in LLMs.

🏆 Leaderboard · 🔧 GitHub · 📄 Paper.

If you've been tracking Arabic LLM evaluation, you've probably noticed a growing tension: the number of benchmarks and leaderboards is expanding rapidly, but are we actually measuring what we think we're measuring?

We built QIMMA قمّة (Arabic for "summit"), to answer that question systematically. Instead of aggregating existing Arabic benchmarks as-is and running models on them, we applied a rigorous quality validation pipeline before any evaluation took place. What we found was sobering: even widely-used, well-regarded Arabic benchmarks contain systematic quality complications that can quietly corrupt evaluation results.

This post walks through what QIMMA is, how we built it, what problems we found, and what the model rankings look like once you clean things up.

Arabic is spoken by over 400 million people across diverse dialects and cultural contexts, yet the Arabic NLP evaluation landscape remains fragmented. A few key pain points have motivated this work:.

Translation problems. Many Arabic benchmarks are translations from English. This introduces distributional shifts. Questions that feel natural in English become awkward or culturally misaligned in Arabic, making benchmark data less representative of how Arabic is naturally used.

It has been revealed that absent quality validation. Even native Arabic benchmarks are often released without rigorous quality checks. Annotation inconsistencies, incorrect gold answers, encoding errors, and cultural bias in ground-truth labels have all been documented in established resources.

Sources indicate that reproducibility gaps. Evaluation scripts and per-sample outputs are rarely released publicly, making it hard to audit results or build on prior work.

Industry observers note that coverage fragmentation. Existing leaderboards cover isolated tasks and narrow domains, making holistic model assessment difficult.

To illustrate where QIMMA sits relative to existing platforms:.

QIMMA is the only platform combining all five properties: open source, predominantly native Arabic content, systematic quality validation, code evaluation, and public per-sample inference outputs.

QIMMA consolidates 109 subsets from 14 source benchmarks into a unified evaluation suite of over 52,000 samples, spanning 7 domains:.

A few things stand out about this design:.

This is the methodological heart of QIMMA. Before running a single model, we applied a multi-stage validation pipeline to every sample in every benchmark.

Each sample was independently evaluated by two state-of-the-art LLMs:.

We chose two models with strong Arabic capability but different training data compositions, so that their combined judgment is more robust than either alone.

Each model scores a sample against a 10-point rubric, with binary scores (0 or 1) per criterion:.

Recent findings suggest that A sample is eliminated if either model scores it below 7/10. Samples where both models agree on elimination are dropped immediately. However, where only one model flags a sample, it proceeds to human review in Stage 2.

Flagged samples are reviewed by native Arabic speakers with cultural and dialectal familiarity. Human annotators make final calls on:.

For culturally sensitive content, multiple perspectives are considered, since "correctness" can genuinely vary across Arab regions.

The pipeline revealed recurring quality concerns across benchmarks; not isolated errors, but systematic patterns reflecting gaps in how benchmarks were originally constructed.

False or mismatched gold indices, factually wrong answers, missing or raw text answers.

Corrupt or illegible text, spelling and grammar errors, and duplicate samples.

Stereotype reinforcement and monolithic generalizations about diverse communities.

Misalignment of gold answers with evaluation protocols.

Code benchmarks required a different intervention. Rather than discarding samples, we refined the Arabic problem statements in 3LM's Arabic adaptations of HumanEval+ and MBPP+, leaving task identifiers, reference solutions, and test suites completely unchanged.

The modification rates were striking:.

Modifications fell into five categories:.

QIMMA uses LightEval, EvalPlus and FannOrFlop as its evaluation framework, chosen for consistency, multilingual community adoption, and reproducibility.

QIMMA standardizes prompting by question format, with six template types:.

According to recent reports, all prompts are in Arabic. For MizanQA and ArabCulture, benchmark-specific system prompts from the original papers are preserved.

Sources indicate that across the full leaderboard (46 models), a clear but imperfect size-performance correlation emerges. However, there are interesting exceptions:.

Fitbit Edge after 30 days: Life in the middle lane [Video]

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1445 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.
  • I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy.
  • The Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that important to me day-to-day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.

I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy. I’ve talked about it multiple times on the Pixelated podcast, here on the site, and it made me switch away from the Pixel Watch 5 because of how easily it fit into my existence without insisting on itself.

The Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that important to me day-to-day. After 30 days of wear, I’m conflicted because maybe I was too hasty to ditch a display on my wrist.

The design is somewhat in a halfway house because it feels like it’s trying to be both a classic Fitbit while integrating some of the Pixel Watch features we know and love. Initially, I loved it, but it has become something that isn’t quite enough in either direction to suit my own tastes.

My love for the simplicity of the Fitbit Air has colored how I feel, but the Edge has an excellent core design. The display bezels remind me heavily of the original Pixel Watch; yes, they’re there, but you only notice them when the light catches the frame edge.

After a month of daily wear, the display has lost a bit of its luster. The oleophobic coating is just about holding up, but now we’re into the cooler months; it’ll be put through a barrage of jacket cuffs and hoodie sleeves. This is one of the only durability concerns I have had so far.

Despite that admittedly minor concern, the Fitbit Edge is not something you need to baby. I’ve bashed it with weights, caught my wrist on zips (zippers for you, my American friends), and bashed it around with reckless abandon. It’s solid and hasn’t picked up as much as a single scuff. I don’t care too much if a fitness tracker gets a beating, whereas I would be more concerned about damaging my Pixel Watch.

If you come in wanting a smartwatch-like experience from the Fitbit Edge, I think you’ll instantly be frustrated by the UI. It can feel cramped when you see notifications, and the large bezels don’t help all that much, but Google has well optimized almost all of the key sections outside of this.

According to recent reports, tiles are very well implemented; they’re just a smaller, squatter take on the Pixel Watch tile system, and it’s one of the best things about the Fitbit Edge interface. It’s also really snappy, which is something that isn’t the case with cheaper fitness trackers such as this. I’m constantly checking the weather or using the Google Health tile, but I have loved the quick access complication on the default watch face.

In a recent development, I tried a few of the other designs over the past 30 days; a lot of them are great. The default has become my favorite. It’s information-dense without being too overloaded. Tapping the complications takes you to the exact data point. I genuinely love how fuss-free an experience it is, save for a few minor complaints.

We could criticize the accuracy of the data or the lack of tracking for certain types of workouts, but I think that misses the point of the Fitbit Edge. It’s a simple tracker with a screen, and the fact that you get even basic ECG on a device of this size is impressive.

In a recent development, I truly have worn the Edge daily for a full month, and while the bands are comfortable, I have found that they cause me to get a rash on the underside of my left wrist just under the palm. It’s actively stopping me from wearing it all the time now. I hope that the latest connector doesn’t slow down third-party development for bands, because I’m desperate for a fabric band to alleviate this matter.

According to recent reports, this is exacerbated when the rubber band gets wet or sweaty. If you have sensitive skin, you might have the same problem as I have. Using some moisturizer has helped, but it is something I wasn’t prepared to suffer with before the Fitbit Edge turned up. I get that this is likely a “me” problem, but I wanted to note it.

When the screen gets wet or moist, it can bug out quite a lot. Taps don’t register properly, and a few water droplets can activate all the menus and submenus. Luckily, it won’t force your phone to place a call or anything like that, but the water protection mode is a must. I have kept it on extensively.

In a recent development, swimmers will probably get super frustrated; heck, I was on a rainy day as the screen kept bugging out. Overall, though, I have enjoyed the fitness tracking. Unlike on the Fitbit Air, it is nice to have a screen to start a workout rather than head over to my phone. That mentioned, the experience is the same as on your phone, but scaled down to fit the watch face.

I dislike that you don’t get a phone notification to show the current workout progress by default, like the Fitbit Air. I had become accustomed to that. Luckily, you can enable it in the Google Health settings. I like having this as I forget to stop workouts so often without a prompt to hit “stop.”.

With audio playback, you’re also getting the partial benefits of watch-phone controls, but it’s a two-step process unlike on Pixel Watch. You either have to go to the “Media” app or have the tile active and navigate to it to access play/pause and all your other streaming app controls. I tend not to bother using these as it’s finicky.

Industry observers note that this had me thinking about NFC. I think a lot of people would have liked NFC for Google Wallet on the Fitbit Edge, but I think having to enter a PIN on such a small screen would really have been a nightmare. I’ve made wireless payments with my watch less than five times, as it’s just easier to use my phone rather than contort my wrist to a wireless payment terminal. I figure this was something that was thought about and makes a lot of sense given the constraints.

In a recent development, one of my other complaints is that the DND and Bedtime modes from my account haven’t synced or at least don’t appear to sync. Unless I’m mistaken, you need to activate these settings manually every time, which has been super annoying when in bed, as a flick of your wrist can blind you in a dark room. I figure this is something that can be fixed with an upgrade, so here’s hoping.

I’ve been super impressed with the battery life. A week is easily attainable for me with up to three gym visits per week, so I’ve charged 5 times in a month. That, to me, is excellent. I picked up a cheap charging dock, as the Edge uses the same charger for the Fitbit Air, so I figured why not.

It’s not the best-looking dock, but I quite like how it airs off my Edge so it’s not as stinky after gym sessions – as I wipe with an alcohol pad and clean as regularly as possible.

The experience is fine; it’s almost a third of the price of the Pixel Watch and lacks a few features due to the various compromises – compromises I can deal with, as smartwatches have become information overload for me over time, and I like that the app selection is ultra-refined. At no point does the Fitbit Edge give you information overload.

Coming from a Charge 6 or an older Fitbit, this is an amazing replacement. It’s the fresh “default” fitness tracker for people who want all the hallmarks of what makes a great Fitbit.

There is just enough. Nothing more, nothing less. To me, this feels like the perfect middle ground for a lot of people. You want something simple, touchscreen-enabled, and that doesn’t get in the way. As impressed as I have been with the Edge, though, I’ve loved a fuss-free tech accessory so much recently that I’ll probably go back to the Fitbit Air.
