#34792. Breaking: Direct Preference Optimization Beyond Chatbots

📅 03 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2883 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Direct Preference Optimization Beyond Chatbots

📅 03 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In April, we released DharmaOCR, our specialized structured OCR model (available on Hugging Face) along with a paper detailing the methodology behind it and a benchmark demonstrating its superior quality and cost efficiency.
  • Across the tested open-source families, vanilla degeneration rates ranged from below 1% to above 33%.
  • Recent findings suggest that A second training stage - applied after supervised fine-tuning (SFT), on the same documents, using the same model - reduced text degeneration in every family tested.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In April, we released DharmaOCR, our specialized structured OCR model (available on Hugging Face) along with a paper detailing the methodology behind it and a benchmark demonstrating its superior quality and cost efficiency. The paper benchmarked leading vision-language model families - both open-source and commercial - on a structured document extraction task: OCR on Brazilian Portuguese text. Among the reported metrics was text degeneration rate: the frequency with which a model produces a repetition loop instead of a transcription.

Across the tested open-source families, vanilla degeneration rates ranged from below 1% to above 33%. Supervised fine-tuning reduced those rates for most models - but rarely to production-acceptable levels. The pattern points to a structural limitation: SFT optimizes for correct outputs, but does not explicitly penalize degeneration. There appears to be a ceiling on how much task-focused fine-tuning alone can reduce this failure mode (Text Degeneration Article).

Recent findings suggest that A second training stage - applied after supervised fine-tuning (SFT), on the same documents, using the same model - reduced text degeneration in every family tested. No exceptions. Average reduction: 59.4%. Best case: 87.6%.

Figure 1: DPO reduced degeneration relative to SFT in every family tested - average reduction of 59.4%, peak of 87.6% (Nanonets-OCR2–3B: 1.61% to 0.20%). The direction is invariant; only the magnitude varies.

That second stage was Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Almost all published DPO applications target chat alignment - models trained on human judgments about helpfulness or harmlessness (example: Rafailov et al., 2023). OCR carries none of that subjectivity: the task is objective, and there is no conversational context. There is, however, a clear preference signal. A correct transcription is chosen; a degeneration loop is rejected. DharmaOCR used that binary to construct a DPO training set, testing the technique not for alignment, but as a direct mitigation tool for a specific failure mode.

The training signal came from the model itself - specifically from the outputs it produced when it failed. How a failure mode becomes a training signal is a structural question about the failure, not the model.

Sources indicate that why SFT has a ceiling on degeneration is still an open question - but the leading conjecture points to loss granularity. SFT trains token by token: each prediction is evaluated in isolation, and a repetition loop is never penalized as a completion-level failure. DPO inverts that logic. The training signal is the full output - chosen or rejected - which means a degenerated completion can be explicitly labeled as the wrong outcome, not just a sequence of locally probable tokens.

Recent findings suggest that when a training objective maximizes the likelihood of observed sequences, it concentrates probability mass in the regions of distribution space those sequences occupy. A model that enters one of those high-probability attractor regions during inference assigns elevated probability to the same token at the next step - which increases the probability further, which sustains the loop until the sequence hits the maximum token limit. Text degeneration is the output of this geometry: a self-reinforcing repetition loop that an autoregressive model cannot exit without external intervention (Holtzman et al., 2020). It is not purely a decoding artifact. The attractor involves the training objective, the learned distribution, and how probability mass concentrates during inference - a systems-level failure rather than a failure localized to any single component.

The geometry of this failure is visible at the token level.

Figure 2: When a token dominates its own conditional distribution, every sampling step deepens the attractor. The decoder samples from this geometry; it does not determine it.

According to recent reports, inference-layer interventions - repetition penalties, temperature adjustments, early-abort logic - operate on the sampling step. They contain the symptom without touching the distribution that produces it. The attractor persists.

Supervised fine-tuning moves the distribution closer to the task domain. For a structured generation pipeline, this means training on domain-specific documents, in the target language, with the required output format. The model gains fluency with longer sequences, constrained syntax, domain vocabulary. What SFT does not do is attack degeneration directly. Its objective - maximizing the likelihood of observed sequences - has no term that penalizes repetition loops. The failure mode is simply outside the scope of what the training signal optimizes for.

One model family in the DharmaOCR benchmark revealed an unexpected pattern: vanilla degeneration rate of 0.60%, rising to 3.23% after SFT, before a subsequent DPO stage brought it to 1.41%. It is a single data point - an exception, not a rule - and it would be overstating the evidence to treat it as proof of a mechanism. What it does illustrate is that SFT does not reliably reduce degeneration. Capability and degeneration resistance can move independently.

The distinction matters structurally. SFT and DPO are not interchangeable training stages performing the same operation at different intensities. SFT closes the distance between the model's prior distribution and the task domain. What it does not do is target degeneration as an objective - its effect on the failure mode is incidental, and the benchmark results show it is not consistent. The attractor that produces degeneration is not a problem with the model's proximity to the task - it is a problem with the shape of the distribution space the model now occupies.

According to recent reports, addressing that geometry requires a training signal built specifically to point the model away from its own failure modes. For a structured, non-conversational task with no human preference labels and no conventional "helpful versus harmful" distinction, constructing that signal is a design decision.

The DharmaOCR pipeline's contribution to DPO methodology is specific: it used the SFT model's own degenerate outputs as the rejected examples - not as noise to remove, but as the negative training signal the optimization needed.

DPO requires preference pairs: a chosen output and a rejected output for the same input, with a quality difference clear enough for the optimization to learn from. In chat alignment, human annotators produce those judgments - rating responses as more or less helpful, accurate, or safe. Structured generation tasks have no equivalent annotation source. An OCR pipeline either produces a correct transcription or it does not. Quality differences exist, but they are not produced by human preference rankings - they are produced by the task's own criteria for correctness.

In a recent development, the DharmaOCR pipeline identified a preference signal that structured generation tasks already produce: the range of outputs the SFT model generates in inference. A model capable of performing a structured task is also capable of failing at it in characteristic ways. Those failures - outputs that enter the degeneration attractor - are not noise to filter. They are the most informative negative signal available.

The paper implemented this on 23,726 training documents, generating multiple candidate responses per document with the SFT model and scoring each with an automated LLM judge. The pipeline is shown below.

Figure 3: The critical design decision is not in the pipeline's structure - it is in what the pipeline preserved: outputs displaying text degeneration were deliberately labeled as rejected examples, not filtered out as low-quality noise.

The conventional response when degenerate outputs appear in training data is to remove them. They are low-quality signal; filtering produces a cleaner dataset. The DharmaOCR approach inverted this logic. Degenerate outputs were deliberately retained as the rejected examples in each (chosen, rejected) pair, because they represent exactly the failure mode the DPO stage was designed to suppress. Removing them would have discarded the clearest target available.

Industry observers note that the paper describes this as "preference-guided implicit unlikelihood" - the model is trained not only toward better outputs but away from a specific class of failure. Where SFT maximizes the likelihood of high-quality outputs, the DPO stage simultaneously penalizes outputs displaying the degeneration attractor geometry. The direction of the optimization is explicit in a way SFT alone cannot achieve.

Degenerate outputs are particularly well-suited as rejection examples because they represent a consistent failure mode rather than varied low-quality outputs. A transcription that misses words is low quality, but its failure is case-specific. Repetition loops, by contrast, appeared persistently across documents and model families even after SFT - a pattern consistent with a failure mode that likelihood-based optimization does not reliably correct. DPO applies its loss differently: at the completion level, with explicit rejection signals. The post-hoc analysis cannot establish causality, but the evidence suggests that what SFT's objective leaves unresolved, DPO's may address.

Sources indicate that this approach requires no specialized annotation infrastructure - only a model capable of producing both acceptable and identifiable-failure outputs, and a scoring model to label preference pairs. A rule-based mechanism could detect repetition loops mechanically - but it could not identify which outputs represented high-quality transcriptions worth preserving as chosen examples.

The scoring model does both: it flags degeneration as the rejected output and validates clean extractions as the chosen one, keeping the model's extraction capability intact while the DPO signal penalizes the failure mode. Whether the resulting training signal successfully moves the distribution in the intended direction - and whether it does so consistently across architectures - is the evidence question.

The DPO stage reduced text degeneration in every model family tested - with reductions ranging from 37% to 88% and an average of 59.4% relative to SFT alone. The result held across architectures, parameter scales, and starting degeneration profiles that differed by more than one order of magnitude. One case in the dataset saw degeneration increase after the SFT stage before DPO corrected it. That case does not complicate the consistency. It confirms the mechanism more directly than any of the others.

Figure 1 shows the three-stage degeneration rate for each of the five model families tested: Vanilla, SFT, and SFT+DPO. In four of the five families, degeneration falls at each stage. The fifth family's bars move differently - and that difference is the most analytically notable data point in the study.

According to recent reports, the Qwen2.5-VL-3B result, read carefully, is not a complication. It is a confirmation. The model's vanilla degeneration rate was 0.60% - not because it was stable, but because it was too generic to produce long structured outputs at all. The model was not entering the degeneration attractor because it was not attempting the task seriously enough to find it.

Industry observers note that SFT changed that. After domain adaptation, Qwen2.5-VL-3B became capable of the task - producing longer, more structured outputs with the domain vocabulary and format the pipeline required. That capability brought it into proximity with the degeneration attractor for the first time. Its degeneration rate rose to 3.23%.

Industry observers note that this is the mechanism made empirically visible: SFT moved the model toward the task and toward the task's failure geometry simultaneously. These are not necessarily the same operation. A training stage that increases task capability can increase failure-mode exposure as a side effect - particularly when the failure mode lives at the edge of the capability frontier. Treated as the same operation, the Qwen2.5-VL-3B result looks like an error. Treated as distinct operations - which is what the SFT + DPO pipeline formally does - the result is consistent with the hypothesis that SFT and DPO address different failure dimensions.

The DPO stage then brought the degeneration rate to 1.41%. It did not restore the vanilla baseline because it was not designed to: the model after SFT was more capable than it had been, and a return to 0.60% would have required undoing that capability. What the DPO stage did was address the failure geometry the SFT stage had introduced.

The remaining four model families add quantitative weight to the same conclusion. Figure 1 highlights the SFT-to-SFT+DPO comparison for all five.

Industry observers note that figure 1: DPO reduced degeneration relative to SFT in every family tested - average reduction of 59.4%, peak of 87.6% (Nanonets-OCR2–3B: 1.61% to 0.20%). The direction is invariant; only the magnitude varies.

No model family showed degeneration increasing after DPO. No family was immune to its effect. The consistency extends to gemma-3–4b-it, which entered the benchmark with the highest vanilla degeneration rate by an order of magnitude - 33.96%, compared to the next highest at 2.62% - and still reached a 75% reduction after the DPO stage. The reduction range - 37.3% to 87.6% - reflects differences in starting configuration and architecture, not inconsistency in the intervention's direction.

This is not a proof of universal applicability. DPO may not transfer to every domain, failure mode, or model family. What the DharmaOCR benchmark provides is evidence across five OCR architectures that the core hypothesis holds: optimizing over complete preference pairs - rather than maximizing token-level likelihood - addresses a failure mode that SFT structurally cannot target. The result was consistent in direction across every model family tested. That consistency, within the scope of this benchmark, is what the evidence supports.

The DharmaOCR approach was possible because this pipeline satisfied a set of structural conditions that allowed a DPO training stage to function as designed - conditions whose presence or absence determines whether the same methodology applies elsewhere (Dharma OCR Paper on ArXiv). It was not possible because OCR is a unique domain.

The first condition is that the failure mode be identifiable as a distinct class of output, not just a point on a quality continuum. Text degeneration qualifies because a repetition loop is categorically different from a transcription that misses words or misreads a character. The output is not merely suboptimal - it is broken in a specific, behaviorally recognizable way. That categorical distinctness is what allowed the pipeline to construct preference pairs where the rejected examples represented a coherent failure geometry, not noise. A task whose failure modes blend into its range of acceptable variation lacks this property.

The second condition is that a scoring mechanism can reliably distinguish acceptable outputs from failure-mode outputs without requiring human annotation. In the DharmaOCR pipeline, an automated LLM judge scored candidate responses against four task-specific criteria. The scoring did not need to be perfect - it needed to be consistent enough to produce preference pairs with a meaningful quality gap between chosen and rejected. Pairs with ambiguous quality differences contribute noise to DPO training, not signal. The judge's consistency was a design requirement, not an incidental feature.

The third condition is sufficient volume - enough inference outputs to generate a preference dataset with meaningful variance in quality. This is not an extraordinary requirement by fine-tuning standards, but it is a real one.

When all three conditions are present, the methodological move is structurally available. The design decision at the center of the DharmaOCR pipeline - treating the model's own failure outputs as the rejected examples rather than filtering them - applies wherever a model's failures are categorically identifiable, scoreable, and sufficiently numerous.

In a recent development, the practical implication for ML engineers building structured generation pipelines is direct. SFT is necessary - it closes the distance between a generalist model and a task-capable one. It is not sufficient for structured output reliability, because task capability and degeneration resistance are different properties of the distribution. A DPO stage after SFT is a one-time training investment. In the DharmaOCR results, the degeneration reduction did not come at the cost of extraction quality - the paper's benchmark results show both moving together (Specialization Beats Scale article).

Recent findings suggest that what makes a failure mode usable as training signal is not the domain - it is whether the failures are consistent enough, identifiable enough, and numerous enough to constitute a legible signal. In the DharmaOCR pipeline, they were. Whether the same holds in another context is a structural question about the task's failure mode, not a question about the model family or the domain.

The DharmaOCR result does not depend on the domain being special. It depends on the failures being useful.

According to recent reports, text degeneration qualifies as useful because it is categorically distinct from acceptable outputs, consistently produced across inference runs, and reliably scoreable without human annotation. Those three properties - not the OCR context, not the model family, not the language - determined whether the preference dataset was tractable. A failure mode that satisfies them is not noise to remove. It is the most direct evidence available of where the distribution should not go.

Recent findings suggest that the DPO stage used that evidence. Degeneration fell in every model family tested - in models that entered the benchmark with vanilla rates below 1% and in models that entered with rates above 33%. The direction held. The pipeline did not discard its failures. It trained on them.

In a recent development, interesting explanation of how Direct Preference Optimization can improve model alignment beyond traditional chatbot applications. I think techniques like this are important for making AI systems more reliable and better at understanding user intent. This is particularly relevant when building a customer service chatbot, where accurate, relevant, and helpful responses can make a massive difference in the user experience. Consistency and understanding context are just as important as generating natural-sounding answers. I recently came across this article that shares some useful insights into how businesses can use AI chatbots to improve customer service: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-chatbot-for-customer-service. It adds another useful perspective to the discussion.

# My First Step into Machine Learning: Understanding Linear Regression.

I've recently started exploring Machine Learning, and honestly, there are so many algorithms and concepts that I want to understand.

Instead of jumping directly into advanced algorithms, I decided to start with the basics.

My first topic is Linear Regression.

I had heard this name several times while studying Machine Learning, but I wanted to understand what actually happens behind the algorithm rather than just memorizing its definition.

So, here's what I've understood so far.

Let's understand it with a simple example.

Industry observers note that imagine you want to buy a house. You visit different properties and notice something interesting: houses with larger areas generally cost more than smaller ones.

"If a house has an area of 1,500 square feet, what would its approximate price be?".

You might look at the prices of other houses and try to estimate the answer.

This is basically the kind of problem Linear Regression helps us solve.

In simple words, Linear Regression is a supervised Machine Learning algorithm that predicts continuous numerical values by learning the relationship between input features and an output.

When I first saw the equation, it looked quite familiar from school mathematics.

The interesting part is that the algorithm learns the values of m and c from the training data.

For multiple input features, we use:.

Industry observers note that y = b0 + b1x1 + b2x2 + ... + bnxn.

This allows the model to consider multiple factors while making predictions.

This was the part I wanted to understand properly.

Think of a graph containing several data points.

The algorithm tries to find a straight line that fits the data as closely as possible.

Sources indicate that initially, the predictions may not be accurate. The model calculates the errors between actual values and predicted values and tries to reduce them.

One commonly used error measurement is Mean Squared Error (MSE).

It calculates the average squared difference between actual and predicted values.

A smaller MSE generally means the predictions are closer to the actual values on the evaluated dataset.

Recent findings suggest that this is also where concepts like Gradient Descent become important. I'll explore that in more detail in another article.

After understanding the basic idea, I wanted to see how Linear Regression works in practice.

I want to understand each algorithm step by step, implement it using Python, experiment with datasets and gradually work on real-world projects.

#34790. Designing the hf CLI as an agent-optimized way to work with the Hub

📅 04 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2208 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Designing the hf CLI as an agent-optimized way to work with the Hub

📅 04 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • hf is the official command-line entrypoint to the Hugging Face Hub.
  • Recent findings suggest that the hf CLI has been primarily built for our people over the years.
  • We started tracking agent usage of the Hub in April 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

hf is the official command-line entrypoint to the Hugging Face Hub. Anything you can do on the Hub from the Python SDK, you can do from your terminal: download and upload models, datasets and Spaces; create and manage repos, branches, tags and pull requests; run Jobs on HF infrastructure; manage Buckets, Collections, webhooks and Inference Endpoints.

Recent findings suggest that the hf CLI has been primarily built for our people over the years. But it's now increasingly used by coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more. So we rebuilt it to make it work for both audiences at once. This blog post summarizes what we did, and how we benchmarked it. We found that on complex, multi-step tasks the no-CLI baseline (an agent hand-rolling curl or the Python SDK) uses up to 6× as many tokens as the hf CLI.

We started tracking agent usage of the Hub in April 2026. The hf CLI (and the huggingface_hub Python SDK it's built on) detects when a coding agent is driving it by reading the environment variables agents set: CLAUDECODE/CLAUDE_CODE for Claude Code, CODEX_SANDBOX for Codex, plus Cursor, Gemini, Pi, and the universal AI_AGENT. That single signal does two jobs: it shapes the CLI's output (more on that below) and it tags each Hub request with an agent/ user-agent, so we can attribute traffic to the agent driving it. The two largest by distinct users are Claude Code and Codex, well ahead of everything else, and they're the two agents we benchmark later in this article.

Recent findings suggest that the bars count distinct customers per agent; request volume is the sub-label. Claude Code alone is ~40k users and nearly 49M requests, with Codex close behind. These are early numbers (we only began attributing agent traffic in April 2026), but the scale is already significant, and we expect it to keep growing as coding agents become a standard way to work with the Hub.

In a recent development, humans and coding agents expect different outputs for the same hf commands. A human wants rich terminal output: ANSI color, padded tables truncated to fit the screen, a green ✅ on success, ✔ for booleans, progress bars, prose hints. An agent wants the inverse: no ANSI, nothing truncated, every value in full since an agent can handle far denser output than a human, kept compact and structured to stay light on tokens. It also can't answer a CLI prompt and will happily re-run a command after a timeout. The rest of this section is how hf gives each side what it needs. We introduced agent-mode output in hf v1.9.0 and have been migrating the rest of the CLI to it gradually in the following releases.

In a recent development, when hf auto-detects agent use (via the environment variables mentioned above), it renders the same command differently. It optimizes output format for humans or agents without passing a flag:.

Industry observers note that A human gets an aligned table, truncated to fit the terminal, plus a hint on how to see more, with color cues for status (a green ✓ on success, red on error). An agent gets the complete record as TSV: full repo ids, full ISO timestamps, every tag, no ANSI codes, nothing truncated, clean to parse and light on tokens.

According to recent reports, in practice, we've implemented logging methods like .table(...), .result(...), .json(), etc., which take raw data as input and handle the formatting. In addition to human and agent modes, we've introduced --json and --quiet options to make it easier to pipe commands together. The default mode is automatically chosen based on context, but owners can always force the format of their choice with --format human | agent | json | quiet.

In a recent development, CLI commands rarely run in isolation: one step usually implies the next (git add, then git commit). Many hf commands now end with a hint: the exact next command to run, pre-filled with the IDs you just used, so a user or agent can chain straight to the next step instead of working it out from scratch. Start a Job in the background and it points you to its logs; create a Space and it points you to its boot status:.

Industry observers note that for a human that's a convenience. For an agent it's a rail: the next action is named, parameterized with the right ids, and ready to run, so it takes fewer steps working out what to do. Errors behave the same way, naming the fix instead of just failing:.

Hints, warnings and errors all go to stderr while data goes to stdout, so none of this guidance pollutes the output the agent is parsing.

Sources indicate that hf never sits on an interactive prompt waiting for a key an agent can't press. A destructive command still asks a human to confirm, but in agent mode it fails fast with the fix in the message (Use --yes to skip confirmation.), and -y/--yes skips it. And because agents retry on timeouts and lost context, operations are built to be safe to repeat: hf repos create --exist-ok is a no-op if the repo already exists, and re-running an upload re-commits cleanly. Separately, the commands that move real data take a --dry-run that demonstrates exactly what they'll transfer before they run, which proves handy for humans and agents alike, since neither has to commit to a long download or blind sync:.

hf is built to be probed: run hf to see the resource groups, run --help on the one you need, and every --help ends with real, copy-pasteable examples (which an agent matches against far faster than it parses a description):.

Recent findings suggest that the command tree is consistent, resource + verb with the obvious aliases (hf models ls, hf repos create, hf jobs ps, hf collections delete; list/ls, remove/rm), so once an agent learns one command it can guess the rest. And the output composes: -q prints one id per line to pipe into the next command, --json gives you something to hand to jq.

Sources indicate that to find out whether the hf CLI is really more efficient for agents, we measured it. We built a small evaluation harness and ran the same set of Hub tasks through each way of driving the Hub, many times over, grading every run against the live Hub. Here's the headline before the methodology: across both agents the hf CLI comes out ahead, most clearly on complex, multi-step tasks where it uses far fewer tokens.

(self-report error = the agent reported success on the 17 solvable tasks but the Hub noted otherwise. The hf CLI rows are the CLI with its skill installed; what the skill adds on top of the bare CLI (chiefly fewer tool calls) is broken out in the skill section below. Representative transcripts are published in this bucket.).

We defined 18 non-trivial Hub tasks. Not "download a file", but the kind of thing you'd actually ask for: aggregate a trending org's models, inspect a repo's files and their sizes, upload a folder with include/exclude rules, delete files, copy files across repos, open a PR that adds a license, create a repo with a branch and a tag, sync and prune a bucket, build a collection. Each task goes to a fresh coding agent with exactly one way to talk to the Hub:.

Industry observers note that we run the hf CLI in two configurations, with and without its skill (a generated command reference we come back to in its own section). But the headline comparison below is simply hf CLI vs curl / the SDK; the skill's incremental effect is small enough that we break it out on its own rather than crowd it into the main results.

The config is deliberately clean: a fresh instance per run, no custom MCP servers, no CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, nothing in context to nudge behavior. The task and the tool go into a single prompt, and the agent finishes with a TASK_COMPLETE or TASK_FAILED marker, but we don't trust that marker (an agent will report success on work that never landed), so we grade every run independently by re-querying the live Hub: did the branch really get created, is the file actually gone, does the bucket exist? Each task/tool combination is run 10 times, since coding agents are non-deterministic, about 520 runs per agent (18 tasks × 3 tools × 10 reps, minus a cap on one billable Jobs task) and ~1,000 graded runs in total. We ran the whole thing twice, on the two most popular coding agents (Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6 and OpenAI Codex with GPT-5.5).

In a recent development, the two charts below unpack the table above. First, task success on Sonnet, the agent where curl and the SDK struggle most:.

Without the CLI, curl and the SDK trail by ten points, because on Sonnet they simply can't finish parts of the job (the writes, mostly), while the hf CLI clears them.

The second image shows token impact on GPT-5.5, broken down per task. Each bar is the curl/SDK tokens divided by the CLI's on the same task, so 2.4× means the non-hf version burned 2.4 times as many tokens to do the same thing:.

Sources indicate that on a one-shot read (count dataset rows, batch metadata) curl and the SDK are fine, and sometimes lighter. But as tasks get more complex and involve several dependent steps, the agent has to hand-roll the entire chain of REST calls (or dig through the SDK) and the cost blows up: 2.4× to 6× the CLI's on creating a repo with a branch and tag, deleting files, copying across repos, or syncing a bucket. The hf CLI lets the agent express the task as a few higher-level commands, rather than crafting a complex workflow.

It has been revealed that hf ships a skill: a compact reference of the whole command surface that an agent loads as context. It's auto-generated from the live hf command tree, one line per command (its signature, a one-line description, and the flags that matter), grouped by resource, with a short glossary of common options. It deliberately skips the self-explanatory flags so it stays terse and light on context, and it's regenerated every release. Run hf skills preview to print it, or install it with:.

Industry observers note that what does it buy you? Mostly, the agent stops guessing. The clearest single view is how many commands each run takes, with the skill and without:.

According to recent reports, on both agents that's about ten commands per task down to about seven, roughly 30% fewer tool calls. That's because the agent isn't probing --help to find the right command and argument. The skill won't cut your token bill, because it prepends a fixed slice of info to the context, so tokens remain about the same or slightly tick up for the same task. The Skill won't make the CLI more reliable either, but it will help the agent spend time running your task rather than finding out how the tool works. This could be particularly helpful when using hf with local models.

We ran each task in a fresh session, so the skill pays its context cost on every task. In a real multi-task session that cost amortizes (the agent learns the command surface once), so the token picture likely improves there; we didn't measure that case.

We benchmarked all this because we think it matters. Agents are becoming real users of the Hub: they train models, build and clean datasets, and ship demos as Spaces, almost always on behalf of a person. A Hub that works well for agents is also a Hub that works better for the people using them. The better an agent's tools are, the more it can do for you.

If your agent interacts with the Hugging Face Hub, we recommend giving it the hf CLI:.

Then hand it the skill, so it knows the whole command surface from the first turn:.

Then point your agent at the Hub and let it work. Make sure you're logged in (hf auth login), then hand it a prompt like:.

It'll work out the commands on its own and come back with something useful.

The full command reference lives in the hf CLI guide.

Sources indicate that building an agent harness? Get it registered! That's how hf learns to detect it, and how the Hub attributes its traffic to your harness. You simply need to open a small PR adding an entry to agent-harnesses.ts. Read the Register your agent harness guide for more details.

Giving AI agents access to command-line tools can make them more capable because they can interact with real development resources instead of relying entirely on generated text. The key part is setting appropriate permissions, defining task boundaries, and checking the results of commands before allowing consequential changes. I also think repeatable workflows make these integrations easier to manage, especially when the same development tasks occur frequently. This guide onhttps://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-development/ai-workflow-automation-cursor-claude-commands is relevant to that idea, as reusable commands can help standardize routine coding activities. Combining tool access with clear safeguards is key to building dependable AI-assisted workflows.

#34789. Breaking: IPv6-First Container Networking on AWS: PrivateLink vs VPC Lattice vs VPC Endpoints, Measured

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2815 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: IPv6-First Container Networking on AWS: PrivateLink vs VPC Lattice vs VPC Endpoints, Measured

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2815 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when you connect containers over IPv6, should you use PrivateLink, VPC Lattice or VPC endpoints?
  • Industry observers note that this article is a deeper write-up of my English talk "IPv6-first container network design practices" at JAWS-UG Yamanashi #14 on November 21, 2026.
  • This is for engineers who connect containers on Amazon ECS or similar platforms across several VPCs or accounts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when you connect containers over IPv6, should you use PrivateLink, VPC Lattice or VPC endpoints? I was not sure either, so I put the same container behind all three paths and measured speed and security under the same conditions. The short answer: choose a path less by speed and more by whether the provider needs to know who is calling.

Industry observers note that this article is a deeper write-up of my English talk "IPv6-first container network design practices" at JAWS-UG Yamanashi #14 on November 21, 2026. It includes background and lessons that did not fit into the 20-minute slot. All numbers were measured in the Tokyo Region (ap-northeast-1) on November 19, 2026.

This is for engineers who connect containers on Amazon ECS or similar platforms across several VPCs or accounts. If every team owns its own VPC and you keep asking yourself how services should talk to each other, I hope this gives you something concrete to decide with.

According to recent reports, it is also for teams that started thinking about IPv6 because of the public IPv4 charge. You may know the names PrivateLink and VPC Lattice but have never compared their actual speed or how you secure them. That is exactly the gap this article tries to fill.

By the end, you should be able to explain how to decide IPv6 per subnet tier and apply it to your own setup, without moving everything to IPv6-only at once.

Recent findings suggest that you will also be able to explain the speed and security differences between the three paths with real numbers and raw logs. The article ends with a top-down checklist for choosing a path, which you can bring straight into a design review.

Internet egress and Transit Gateway matter a lot for IPv6 too, but each could fill an article of its own. Here I focus on private traffic between services.

I assume you know VPC subnets, route tables and security groups, and Amazon ECS tasks. You will see the term "dual stack" (having both IPv4 and IPv6) many times.

According to recent reports, three changes made IPv6-first design realistic. In February 2024, public IPv4 addresses started to cost $0.005 per IP per hour. In September 2025, Amazon ECS added support for IPv6-only tasks and services. In November 2025, Amazon S3 gateway and interface VPC endpoints added IPv6 support. With all three in place, the question is no longer "can we use IPv6?" but "how do we design for it?".

Sources indicate that adding an IPv6 range to a VPC takes a few clicks. The hard part comes next: connecting services. When every team or account creates its own VPC, many of them end up with 10.0.0.0/16, and overlapping IPv4 ranges cannot simply be routed. AWS gives us three building blocks that work even when ranges overlap: PrivateLink, VPC endpoints for AWS services, and VPC Lattice. The documentation alone did not tell me which to pick, so I built a lab and measured.

I deliberately gave both the consumer VPC and the provider VPC the same range, 10.0.0.0/16. There is no internet gateway and no NAT gateway, so the only way out is the path being measured. That way, nothing can quietly take another route.

It has been revealed that on the provider side, the same container runs twice: one copy behind PrivateLink and an internal Network Load Balancer, the other behind VPC Lattice. On the consumer side, k6 runs on an EC2 instance and calls each path over IPv6. S3 is read through both a gateway endpoint and an interface endpoint.

The baseline is a direct call to the NLB from inside the provider VPC. Subtracting it demonstrates only what each path adds. The lab is an AWS CDK app; I deployed the four stacks with cdkd in about 14 minutes (852 seconds) and deleted everything the same day.

According to recent reports, IPv6-first does not mean IPv6-only everywhere. My recommendation is to decide IPv6 per subnet tier rather than per VPC, because each tier has a different role and can move at its own pace.

Industry observers note that the edge tier, with load balancers and endpoints, is called over both IPv4 and IPv6, so it stays dual stack. The workload tier starts dual stack too, and moves to IPv6-only once every dependency is reachable over IPv6. For that, I created dual-stack endpoints for ECR, CloudWatch Logs, Systems Manager and S3.

One real pitfall was the ec2messages endpoint. In the Tokyo Region it supports IPv4 only, and my deploy failed when I tried to create it as dual stack. Supported IP types differ by service and Region, so check before you create. I created only that endpoint as IPv4. SSM Agent 3.3.40 or later works with ssm and ssmmessages alone, so Session Manager still works on IPv6-only workloads.

In a recent development, before the numbers, here is the mental model in one picture. All three let you call something outside your VPC from inside it, but they work at different layers and expose different things.

PrivateLink works at layer 4 and exposes one NLB port; the provider accepts each consumer. VPC endpoints use the same technology to reach AWS services, and the endpoint policy is the main control. VPC Lattice is a layer 7 application network with IAM authentication. Please keep the last row in mind: does the provider know who is calling? It drives both the security results and the final recommendation.

Recent findings suggest that first, latency with connection reuse at 500 requests per second over IPv6. The baseline median (p50) was 1.84 ms.

According to recent reports, privateLink added only 0.13 to 0.30 ms. VPC Lattice added about 2.3 to 2.9 ms as an L7 proxy. Up to 1,000 requests per second, p99 did not get worse on any path. Across three runs the spread was small (PrivateLink 1.93 to 1.99 ms, Lattice HTTP 4.24 to 4.32 ms), so the roughly 2.3 ms gap comes from the path itself, not from noise.

Another finding from the report: with connection reuse, Lattice HTTPS was only 0.04 to 0.19 ms slower than HTTP. There is no reason to avoid TLS for performance, so I recommend HTTPS with Lattice too. A few milliseconds matter for chatty, latency-critical calls, where PrivateLink is a good fit. For most API calls, how you handle connections matters more, as the next result reveals.

Next, the same test with a newly introduced connection for every request, which is what happens when an app does not reuse connections or runs as a short-lived process.

Sources indicate that on PrivateLink, the TCP connect alone took 2.5 to 2.8 ms, because the handshake travels through the NLB to the task and back. VPC Lattice terminates TCP close to the client, so the connect took about 0.5 ms, but TLS added about 1.8 ms for HTTPS. In total, a latest connection costs about 2.3 to 2.6 ms per request, as much as the gap between paths. Before debating paths, check that your app reuses connections.

One caveat when reading k6 results: http_req_duration does not include connect and TLS time, so it hides this cost. The report adds connect, TLS and request time together; at 300 requests per second the totals were 4.59 ms for PrivateLink and 6.63 ms for Lattice HTTPS, the same trend.

Is IPv6 slower? I measured the same paths over both protocols with the same load.

The p50 values were 2.01 vs 2.04 ms for PrivateLink, 4.24 vs 4.34 ms for Lattice, and 24.96 vs 24.75 ms for the S3 gateway endpoint. The differences of 0.03 to 0.21 ms were within run-to-run variation. VPC Flow Logs confirmed that the test traffic really used IPv6: about 3.16 GB over IPv6 versus about 36 MB over IPv4.

I also checked throughput by fetching 1 MiB objects with 64 virtual people.

According to recent reports, privateLink reached about 1,475 MiB/s, the network limit of the c7i.xlarge client (12.5 Gbps), even with two small 0.5 vCPU tasks. VPC Lattice leveled off around 1.1 GiB/s, and doubling the load only doubled latency. One run cannot tell whether that is a Lattice limit or a target-side limit, so I will retest with more and larger tasks. Also note that one-minute tests may use the instance's burst bandwidth, which is higher than its sustained baseline.

For S3, the gateway and interface endpoints had nearly the same p50, but p99 was 41 ms versus 57 ms in favor of the gateway endpoint. It has no extra charge and now supports IPv6, so I recommend it as the default for S3.

Sources indicate that speed is not only milliseconds. How long does a fresh team wait before its first successful call?

The S3 gateway endpoint was ready in 4 seconds and the interface endpoint in 247 seconds. The PrivateLink endpoint was created in 6 seconds and became available 38 seconds after the provider accepted it. The VPC Lattice VPC association took 74 seconds and needed no approval. On the provider side, the NLB took 127 seconds, the endpoint service 2 seconds, and the Lattice service and its association 10 seconds each.

On machine time alone PrivateLink wins, but a human approval is added in practice. And there is a trap that makes the wait much longer. If you resolve the PrivateLink DNS name before acceptance, the VPC resolver caches the negative answer. In my lab I accepted at 11:09:32 and the name resolved only at 11:19:16, about 584 seconds later. If a name resolves from outside but not from inside the VPC, suspect this, and check DNS only after the endpoint is available.

I tested security as three layers, so that one mistake does not open everything.

The network layer is the security group on the endpoint or the Lattice association. The connectivity layer is PrivateLink acceptance, the Lattice auth policy and endpoint policies for AWS services. The resource layer is, for example, an S3 bucket policy. I changed one condition at a time to see whether each layer really works.

Same instance, same DNS name, one change per column: trusted, untrusted security group, PrivateLink not yet accepted, and Lattice with IAM required.

Sources indicate that with an untrusted security group, PrivateLink, Lattice and the S3 interface endpoint all timed out. Before acceptance, the PrivateLink name did not even resolve. With IAM required on Lattice, unsigned calls got 403 and SigV4-signed calls got 200. In every case both VPCs kept the same 10.0.0.0/16 and all three paths worked. The PrivateLink endpoint service only allows my own account and requires acceptance.

The surprise was the S3 gateway endpoint: it still returned 200 with the untrusted security group, over both IPv6 and IPv4. The raw data explains why.

According to recent reports, through the gateway endpoint, the client connected to public S3 addresses over both IPv6 and IPv4. Through the interface endpoint, it connected to the address of a network interface in my VPC. VPC Flow Logs marked the gateway traffic as traffic path 7. A gateway endpoint is a route in the route table, not a network interface. Security groups attach to network interfaces, so they cannot protect it. Use the endpoint policy and the bucket policy instead.

With IAM required, unsigned calls were logged as 403 with authDeniedReason Service, so you can see why they were denied. Signed calls were logged as 200 together with the caller's IAM role. Before IAM was required, about 1.34 million anonymous calls were all logged with their source VPC. Getting this audit trail without touching your application is a real advantage; just remember to configure a log destination on the service network or service.

According to recent reports, this was my favorite slide in the talk. What does the provider's container actually see about the caller?

Sources indicate that behind PrivateLink, the task sees only the NLB's IPv4 addresses (one per AZ) and cannot tell who called. Behind VPC Lattice, the x-amzn-source-vpc header shows the source VPC, and with SigV4 you also get the caller's IAM principal. If your provider must decide per caller, PrivateLink pushes that logic into your application, while Lattice hands it to you from the network. This is why I recommend choosing by caller identity rather than by speed alone.

Industry observers note that the client connected over IPv6, but the task received IPv4: the NLB's IPv4 address with PrivateLink, and a link-local IPv4 address with Lattice. With dual-stack workloads, IPv6 stops at the edge. A fun detail: the last 32 bits of the Lattice IPv6 address, a9fe:ab61, are 169.254.171.97 in decimal, exactly what the IPv4 lookup returned. For IPv6 end to end, the workload itself has to be IPv6-only.

Sources indicate that even though an outside bucket allowed my endpoint, my endpoint policy did not list that bucket, so the request got 403. From the internet, the data bucket returned 403 because its policy only accepts requests through my endpoints. The endpoint policy controls where data can go; the bucket policy controls where requests can come from. Two policies facing opposite directions catch each other's mistakes, which matters most for the gateway endpoint.

Industry observers note that every path has strengths and weaknesses. VPC Lattice tells you the caller but adds a few milliseconds and leveled off around 1.1 GiB/s for large objects. PrivateLink is fast, but you build caller identity yourself and wait for approval and DNS. The S3 gateway endpoint is free and stable but cannot use security groups. Rather than one path for everything, I recommend choosing per type of traffic.

I measured with k6 on a c7i.xlarge instance: 1 KiB responses, a 20-second warm-up, then one minute per load level. PrivateLink and Lattice ran three times in rotating order; the others ran once. All 59 runs had zero errors and zero dropped requests.

Industry observers note that I wrote down my expectations before measuring. Most held, and some held only with conditions. In particular, the cost of latest HTTPS connections turned out to be about the same as the gap between paths, not larger.

According to recent reports, building the lab took four deploy attempts, and I fixed four challenges along the way, adding tests to prevent regressions (from 30 to 32). The first deploy failed because a security group's IPv6 rule read the VPC's IPv6 range without waiting for it to be associated. Then came the ec2messages endpoint. A non-root k6 container could not write to a Fargate bind volume; I fixed it with a locked-down init container that keeps only the CHOWN capability and uses a read-only root file system. The last glitch was the DNS negative cache described above.

Deploying took 852 seconds, switching the Lattice auth mode took about 27 seconds, and deleting took about 990 seconds with no leftover resources. These numbers come from short runs; please measure with your own workload before deciding. The code and the full report are in ContainerNetwork-Research-handson.

Here are the key parts of the AWS CDK app used in the lab, written with aws-cdk-lib L1 constructs as of November 2026. L1 lets you set newer options such as ipAddressType and dnsOptions exactly as in CloudFormation.

First, dual-stack interface endpoints for dependencies, with ec2messages as the IPv4-only exception in the Tokyo Region.

Next, an S3 gateway endpoint whose policy allows reading only the buckets you need. In a real environment, remember to also allow the buckets that hold ECR image layers and OS packages.

The data bucket only accepts reads through the two endpoints. A policy restricted with aws:SourceVpce is not treated as public by S3, so Block Public Access can stay on.

Industry observers note that finally, a VPC Lattice auth policy that allows only signed callers from this account coming from the consumer VPC. A coarser policy on the service network adds a second layer.

Recent findings suggest that in operations, write security group rules for both IPv4 and IPv6; writing only one can block or allow traffic unexpectedly. Include pkt-srcaddr and traffic-path in VPC Flow Logs so you can later confirm which path and which IP version traffic actually used.

Sources indicate that with IPv6-only ECS tasks and IPv6 for S3 VPC endpoints, AWS now has the pieces for IPv6-only workloads. As long as workloads stay dual stack, though, IPv6 stops at the edge. Next, I want to run the same tests with IPv6-only workloads, find out what limits Lattice throughput, and remeasure with five two-minute runs. I will write it up when it is done.

According to recent reports, ensemble Engineer (@mob_engineer) is the pen name of an SRE and project lead at a systems integration company. He works across AWS, Azure and OCI, with a particular interest in containers, virtual networking, and running observability with Dynatrace. Outside of work, he helps organize tech communities and conferences, and shares what he learns through talks and blog posts.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years.
  • Recent findings suggest that swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years.
  • Swapping sugary drinks for water is linked to less weight gain over time, according to a study of more than 140,000 adults.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

Recent findings suggest that swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

Swapping sugary drinks for water is linked to less weight gain over time, according to a study of more than 140,000 adults.

Replacing them with diet drinks demonstrates much the same pattern.

Switching from diet drinks to water was linked to a much smaller difference in weight.

Both swaps could make a difference by cutting the calories people get from their usual soft drinks.

A diet version can also preserve the familiar sweet taste, which may make the change easier for some people to stick with.

The findings suggest that the drink someone gives up may matter more for their weight than which of these two alternatives they choose.

The researchers drew on three long-running US studies that followed nurses and other health professionals for a typical period of 28 years.

Participants regularly reported what they drank and how much they weighed, allowing researchers to see how their drinking habits and weight shifted over four-year periods.

The researchers estimated about 1.4 kg less weight gain over four years when three sugary drinks a week were replaced with either water or diet drinks.

The estimated difference for replacing three diet drinks a week with water was only about a tenth of a kilogram over the same period.

People who cut back on sugary drinks tended to gain less weight whether or not they increased their intake of diet drinks.

The researchers estimated the swaps from changes in people’s reported habits, so the study can show associations but cannot establish how much weight any individual would gain or lose after making the switch.

Replacing a regular soft drink with its diet version changes the calories while keeping much of the experience of having a sweet drink.

Switching to water also removes the sweet taste, which may change how much sweetness people prefer over time.

In a separate year-long randomised trial, people assigned to replace sugary drinks with unsweetened ones showed a greater drop in their preferred level of sweetness than those assigned to artificially sweetened drinks (Ebbeling et al., 2020).

That change in taste preference offers a possible reason why an unsweetened choice might become more appealing with time.

The study was published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (Espinosa et al., 2026).

Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety: Customizable Multimodal Safety for Global Enterprise AI

📅 04 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1642 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the last two years have seen NVIDIA's content safety stack grow from a focused English text classifier into a family of specialized models—each extending coverage to new modalities, languages, and inference modes.
  • This post covers what changes in 3.5, the design decisions behind each latest capability, and how to integrate the model into production safety pipelines.
  • In a recent development, nemotron 3 introduced image understanding; Nemotron 3.5 deepens the multimodal integration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the last two years have seen NVIDIA's content safety stack grow from a focused English text classifier into a family of specialized models—each extending coverage to new modalities, languages, and inference modes. Nemotron 3 Content Safety, released in March 2026, combined multimodal and multilingual capabilities for the first time in a single 4B-parameter model. Today, we are releasing Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety, which completes that arc: a single model that unifies multimodal input, multilingual reach, custom enterprise policy enforcement, and auditable reasoning into one inference call.

This post covers what changes in 3.5, the design decisions behind each latest capability, and how to integrate the model into production safety pipelines.

In a recent development, nemotron 3 introduced image understanding; Nemotron 3.5 deepens the multimodal integration. The model takes a user prompt, an optional image, and an optional assistant response as a single context window and produces a coherent safety verdict over the combined input. Evaluating all three together—rather than scoring each independently—closes a well-known gap in multimodal safety scenarios: policy violations that only emerge from the interaction between text and image, or between request and response, are now caught in a single pass.

Recent findings suggest that nemotron 3.5 maintains the 12-language explicit training coverage of its predecessors—English, French, Spanish, German, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, Hindi, Russian, Portuguese, and Italian—while also inheriting strong zero-shot generalization across approximately 140 languages from the Gemma 3 base model. This means deployments in markets where training data is sparse (e.g., Southeast Asian languages, Scandinavian languages, less-resourced African languages) benefit from base-model multilingual transfer without requiring separate fine-tuning.

In a recent development, this is the most significant architectural addition in 3.5 relative to Nemotron 3. Production deployments rarely operate under a single universal safety taxonomy. A healthcare platform has a different risk profile than a financial services chatbot, a developer tools IDE, or a children's education app. Nemotron 3.5 accepts a custom policy specification alongside the input. The model reasons over that policy when producing its verdict rather than deferring entirely to the built-in taxonomy. This extends the work first introduced in Nemotron Content Safety Reasoning 4B to the full multimodal, multilingual setting.

Every safety verdict in Nemotron 3.5 can be accompanied by an auditable reasoning trace via an optional think mode. When enabled, the model outputs its step-by-step reasoning before delivering a final safe / unsafe label and, optionally, the violated categories.

When latency is the primary constraint, THINK mode can be disabled to return to the same low-latency binary verdict available in Nemotron 3.

It has been revealed that with Nemotron 3.5, we are releasing our safety dataset. This is an important milestone since most OSS safety models don't generally provide the training or evaluation sets. This problem is worse for the multimodal space where artifacts such as images or videos are often derived from resources with restrictive licensing terms. The Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety Dataset is multimodal, multilingual, and includes safety reasoning traces that were used to train the model. These reasoning traces were generated in a 2-step manner to make them concise, similar to the Nemotron Content Safety Reasoning 4B model.

Industry observers note that nemotron 3.5 Content Safety is built on Google Gemma 3 4B IT (4B parameters), providing a 128K context window, strong vision-language reasoning, and broad multilingual coverage. NVIDIA fine-tunes this base with a LoRA adapter that installs targeted safety classification behavior while keeping the model compact enough for real-time deployment on 8GB+ VRAM GPUs.

The inference interface supports three output modes:.

Mode 1 — Low-latency binary verdict:.

Mode 2 — Binary verdict with categories:.

Mode 3 — THINK mode (reasoning + verdict):.

According to recent reports, the safety taxonomy follows the Aegis 2.0 framework: 13 core categories aligned with the MLCommons safety taxonomy, plus 10 fine-grained subcategories. This alignment allows direct comparison with other open and closed guard systems benchmarked on Aegis-taxonomy datasets.

Reasoning is a supercharger for content safety classification because it provides the necessary context, customization, and accountability required for production AI systems, especially in enterprise and regulated environments.

Enables Custom and Contextual Policy Enforcement.

Reasoning allows a content safety model to dynamically interpret and enforce custom, domain-specific policies defined in natural language at the time of inference. This is necessary because production deployments rarely operate under a single, universal safety taxonomy. A financial services chatbot has a different risk profile than a children's education app which may have a lower tolerance for profanity. This capability supports:.

Provides Auditable and Documented Justification.

In a recent development, the reasoning traces show the model's step-by-step logic before it delivers a final safe or unsafe verdict. This documented justification serves several purposes:.

Sources indicate that while reasoning can introduce latency, the Nemotron model addresses this by condensing reasoning chains into concise summaries to limit output tokens and increase efficiency. This is done in a 2-step process similar to what was done in the predecessor model Nemotron-Content-Safety-Reasoning-4B. In the first step, we use larger, more powerful models such as Qwen 397B to generate chain-of-thought reasoning traces based upon provided prompts, images, and responses. We also provided the ground-truth labels of the samples to avoid any misclassification that can find its way into the reasoning traces. In step 2, we make these reasoning traces more concise by using another large model such as Qwen 80B. We specifically instruct this model to rephrase the original traces (from step 1) so that it fits in no more than 3 sentences. Based on our experiments, most reasoning traces generated are under 3 sentences.

The efficient reasoning traces optimization allows for low-latency custom policy enforcement. Furthermore, the reasoning traces provide a valuable training signal that can be used for training specialized moderator models. Developers can choose a dual-mode operation, disabling reasoning for minimal latency in generic tasks or enabling it for complex policies.

The dataset driving Nemotron 3.5 is an evolution of the multimodal, multilingual blends used for Nemotron 3, with additions targeting the reasoning and custom-policy capabilities. We have used the following sources of data:.

In a recent development, nemotron 3.5 Content Safety was evaluated across multilingual, multimodal, and custom-policy safety benchmarks, including VLGuard, MM-SafetyBench, PolyGuard, RTP-LX, Aya Redteaming, XSafety, MultiJail, Aegis, Dynaguardrail, and CoSA. These evaluations reflect the core production challenge for enterprise safety: applying consistent guardrails across global languages, text and image inputs, and domain-specific policies without adding significant latency.

Nemotron 3 set a strong baseline with 84% average accuracy on multimodal harmful-content tests and roughly half the latency of LlamaGuard-4-12B. Nemotron 3.5 maintains that compact 4B efficiency while adding custom policy support and reasoning traces.

Industry observers note that across multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks, Nemotron 3.5 delivers strong harmful-content classification accuracy while maintaining a compact footprint. This matters because many safety models remain English-first, text-only, or too costly to run repeatedly in production pipelines. Nemotron 3.5 is designed to combine multilingual coverage, multimodal classification, custom-policy support, and low-latency deployment in one model.

It has been revealed that figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety delivers strong harmful-content classification accuracy across multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks, averaging about 85% across the evaluated benchmark set.

The language-level results highlight why multilingual safety matters for global enterprise AI. On Multilingual Aegis, Nemotron 3.5 averages 96.5% harmful-content classification accuracy across 12 languages. On RTP-LX, it averages 88.8%, for a combined Aegis and RTP-LX average of 92.7%. This consistency helps teams apply the same safety posture across customer, employee, and partner-facing workflows instead of relying on English-only moderation or separate regional safety models.

Figure 2. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety averages 97% harmful-content classification accuracy on Multilingual Aegis Cultural + Adapted (prompt classification) (harmful-f1) across 12 languages.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety averages 89% harmful-content classification accuracy on RTPLX (prompt classification) (harmful-f1) across 12 languages.

Recent findings suggest that accuracy alone is not enough for production guardrails. Safety models must also be efficient enough to run before content is processed, returned, or routed downstream. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety's compact 4B design helps reduce the cost and latency of repeated safety checks, making multilingual and multimodal guardrails practical for real-world AI applications.

According to recent reports, the latency profile is unchanged from Nemotron 3 in the default (no THINK) mode. THINK mode adds inference time proportional to trace length, but this overhead is predictable and can be budgeted separately from the synchronous moderation loop—for instance, by running THINK-mode evaluation asynchronously as part of an audit pipeline while the default mode handles real-time decisions.

Figure 4. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety achieves 3x lower end-to-end latency on a multimodal benchmark compared to an alternative multimodal safety model.

Compared to another reasoning safety model, our model generated up to 50% fewer tokens when reasoning is enabled, making it efficient in terms of cost and latency.

A recurring theme in multimodal safety research is the gaps in existing evaluation infrastructure. Nemotron 3.5's development encountered the same gaps documented in the broader literature:.

NVIDIA's multimodal training data—with real images and culturally nuanced multilingual prompts—is designed to fill some of these gaps for model training. The benchmark gap for evaluation remains an open problem for the broader safety research community.

Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety is available on Hugging Face under the NVIDIA Open Model License for research and commercial use, along with the training dataset. It supports transformers, vLLM, and SGLang, and is available as a production-grade NVIDIA NIM on build.nvidia.com for teams that need a pre-packaged, GPU-optimized inference microservice.

Developers can also access the model through inference platforms including Baseten, Eigen AI, DeepInfra, OpenRouter, and Vultr.

According to recent reports, for custom policy workflows, NVIDIA provides a Claude- and Codex-compatible skill for generating custom policies, along with cookbooks showing how to use the model. Custom policies and reasoning traces help teams adapt safety behavior to domain-specific rules while keeping decisions auditable.

  • In a recent development, then I saved a second results page with a different query and ran it through the same parser.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I built MiniSERP to learn how a search results API works underneath. It's a small Rails 8 API that takes a Google results page and turns it into clean JSON: title, link, snippet, position.

Sources indicate that the first version worked on the first page I tested. I wrote the specs and they passed, and I thought the parser was done.

In a recent development, then I saved a second results page with a different query and ran it through the same parser. I got back an empty array with HTTP 200.

It has been revealed that an empty array with a 200 looks exactly like "Google found nothing for this query." Nothing crashed and nothing demonstrated up in the logs. If I had shipped this, every search would have come back empty, and the API would have reported success every time.

The cause turned out to be simple. I ran a quick check on the latest page:.

In a recent development, my parser looked for results inside div.g. On this page, Google had moved results into div.MjjYud, rearranged what was inside them and rotated its obfuscated class names. My one selector matched nothing, so the parser happily returned nothing.

Instead of trusting one selector, the parser now goes through a list of container strategies in order and uses the first one that finds usable results:.

That covers the layouts I've seen, but Google will change it again, and a list of class names will always fall behind eventually.

If every selector misses, the parser stops looking at class names completely and uses the page structure instead. It finds every , then walks up to the nearest that also contains a link, and treats that as one result.

To make sure this really doesn't depend on class names, one spec wraps the results in a made-up container called div.totally-upcoming-class. The parser still pulls the results out.

Two smaller filters keep the output clean:.

This was the most notable change, and it's the rule I'd keep even if I deleted everything else.

There are two very different situations that used to produce the same response:.

The second case is my bug, not the user's empty search, and it should look like one. A 502 indicates up in monitoring and someone can go fix the parser. A silent 200 just hides the problem until a customer notices their data is missing.

Industry observers note that that last point is why I have so much respect for search APIs that do this at scale. I hit one markup change on one engine in a side project. They deal with this across many engines, every day, behind a single API call.

MiniSERP is open source if you want to look at the parser and the specs: https://github.com/Divyanshu-2907/MiniSERP.

The Open Source Community is backing OpenEnv for Agentic RL

📅 08 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that openEnv is a tool for creating an agentic execution environment like terminals, browsers, or anything an agent can interact with.
  • Starting today, OpenEnv will be coordinated by a committee that so far includes Meta-PyTorch, Reflection, Unsloth, Modal, Prime Intellect, Nvidia, Mercor, Fleet AI, Microsoft, Hugging Face, and RadixArk.
  • OpenEnv project is supported and adopted by some of the leading organizations in the AI ecosystem, including PyTorch Foundation, vLLM, SkyRL (UCB), Lightning AI, Axolotl AI, Stanford Scaling Intelligence Lab, Mithril, OpenMined, Scaler AI Labs, Scale AI, Patronus AI, Surge AI, Halluminate, Turing, Scorecard, Snorkel AI, SGLang, and Miles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that openEnv is a tool for creating an agentic execution environment like terminals, browsers, or anything an agent can interact with. And today, we’re excited to announce that OpenEnv is becoming even more open, to make the future of training agents open source.

Starting today, OpenEnv will be coordinated by a committee that so far includes Meta-PyTorch, Reflection, Unsloth, Modal, Prime Intellect, Nvidia, Mercor, Fleet AI, Microsoft, Hugging Face, and RadixArk. OpenEnv now lives at huggingface/OpenEnv.

OpenEnv project is supported and adopted by some of the leading organizations in the AI ecosystem, including PyTorch Foundation, vLLM, SkyRL (UCB), Lightning AI, Axolotl AI, Stanford Scaling Intelligence Lab, Mithril, OpenMined, Scaler AI Labs, Scale AI, Patronus AI, Surge AI, Halluminate, Turing, Scorecard, Snorkel AI, SGLang, and Miles.

It has been revealed that agent harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, and Hermes just keep improving. One reason for their improvement is that models like GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 are trained to use their respective harnesses.

We want those gains with open source models too: training local models that use harnesses effectively, and saving compute by specializing models for specific tasks.

Frontier labs train models and harnesses that, for the most part, work like hand in glove. The model is trained to use the harness and optimised for its characteristics. Models can generalise beyond these harnesses, to some extent, but nothing beats the efficiency of training.

It has been revealed that in the open, this isn’t the case. Developers use any harness, any model, any inference engine, on whatever use case they value. This is fundamental to the community, but it’s also a challenge that requires infrastructure and tooling to tackle.

That’s where OpenEnv comes in. It’s a library to interface between harness, environment, and trainer, which works on any model. For this to stick, it will need to be owned by all the major stakeholders.

Alongside the governance change, we're tightening what OpenEnv is.

In recent releases, OpenEnv has become an interoperability layer for RL environments. Its job is to standardize how environments are published, deployed, and consumed by agents. It will not dictate how rewards are defined or how training loops work. Reward definition, scoring rubrics, and trainer-specific logic belong in the libraries that specialize in them. OpenEnv is the common socket they can all plug into.

According to recent reports, one interface, many environments which all expose the familiar Gymnasium-style API (reset(), step(), state()) running on a client/server architecture. A trainer that speaks OpenEnv can drive any compliant environment without bespoke code.

Familiar protocols and canonical packaging. Environments are served over standard protocols like HTTP and WebSocket and packaged with Docker. MCP is a first-class citizen, so OpenEnv environments are instantly compatible with MCP servers and the same environment behaves consistently in both simulation (train/eval) and production modes.

Sources indicate that interop across env libraries. You can define and consume environments across different ecosystems (verifiers, harbor, and others) and on the infrastructure and hub of your choice. OpenEnv is the deployment and interface layer underneath them, rather than a competitor to them.

Over the coming months we will focus on the things that turn OpenEnv from a fast-growing project into a dependable standard:.

OpenEnv is community-centric by design, and it's still early — expect rough edges, and help us smooth them. Check out the code and RFCs: github.com/openenv/OpenEnv.

Thanks to everyone who helped make this transition happen. Let's build the common substrate for open-source agentic RL together.

According to recent reports, there is some excellent work here to check. https://a2eprotocol.github.io/docs/.
