Running a video-by-code agent on one RTX 4090: the context budget is the real limit

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that run an open model as a long agent (a model that calls tools in a loop on its own) on one card and the weights are rarely what stops you.
  • In a recent development, we learned that with SenseNova 6.8 Code2Video, SenseTime's open 27B model that makes video by writing code.
  • In a recent development, the SenseNova team publishes a Claude Code skill called code-video and six complete production runs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that run an open model as a long agent (a model that calls tools in a loop on its own) on one card and the weights are rarely what stops you. The budget around them is: how much the agent can keep in view, and how long one answer may be.

In a recent development, we learned that with SenseNova 6.8 Code2Video, SenseTime's open 27B model that makes video by writing code. We drove it with Claude Code on one 24 GB RTX 4090 on our cloud. Ten minutes in, it had a full 12-second clip. Forty minutes in, it had no finished film. The logs and frames are in the full research write-up on running Code2Video on one RTX 4090. Here I focus on the settings.

In a recent development, the SenseNova team publishes a Claude Code skill called code-video and six complete production runs. They serve the full-size model across four GPUs. Their context window (the text the model can see at once, counted in tokens, which are word pieces) is 512K tokens, and one answer may run to 64K. Their films needed between 261 and 876 turns each.

We used bartowski's 4-bit GGUF, a compressed copy of the weights (17.2 GB) for the llama.cpp server, plus a 0.93 GB vision part so the model can see images. Three Claude Code variables encode the gap:.

Without the first one, Claude Code assumes 200K for a model it does not recognize.

Recent findings suggest that compaction is how Claude Code survives a full context. Once the window passes 80%, it has the model write a recap, throws the old history away and continues from the recap alone. The recap is a normal reply, so the output cap applies to it too.

Our 98,304-token window was full after about 19 minutes. Three recap requests followed. All three ran into the 16,384-token ceiling, none produced a usable summary, and together they ate 21 minutes until our 40-minute limit killed the run with no final film.

According to recent reports, compaction can work: four of the authors' six runs cleared contexts of 167K to 492K tokens, under a 64K cap. On our side two settings are under suspicion. One is the 16,384-token cap. The other is hidden reasoning, the thinking the model writes before its visible answer, which we left on and which draws from the same cap. The logs cannot tell them apart, though in a separate single request the same 4-bit file burned all 8,192 output tokens thinking and wrote no page. A bigger window, a bigger cap or reasoning off might fix it; we tried none of them.

So when you size a single-card agent, measure two things before you trust it: when the context will hit the compaction threshold, and whether one summary fits under your output cap with reasoning on.

Self-review did its job. The model opened 21 of its own stills as images, spotted two bugs and fixed both. All on-screen text matched the brief word for word.

The one fact that mattered was still wrong. The brief asked for 30 dots in a 5 by 6 rectangle. We located each dot centre in the 7.2-second frame with numpy and scipy and got 5 rows of 7 columns, one cell empty per row. The skill's file check still said yes. It only looks at resolution, frame rate and duration, never at what is drawn.

Add a check that knows what the clip should show.

Industry observers note that claude Code speaks Anthropic's Messages API format, so whatever sits in front of the model has to translate it. Ours lost the frames: each image either vanished or arrived as a block of text, and the model reviewed its work blind. Fixed in our test build, not yet on the hosted service. With any gateway, send one PNG first and check the model describes it.

Second, time. Our first call waited for the full answer instead of streaming it piece by piece. The worker, the process on the GPU machine that forwards requests to the server, gives up after 120 seconds, and the model was still thinking. Raising that to 30 minutes fixed the run, and the example now streams.

The 4-bit run peaked at 20.9 GiB. Smaller copies, one short request each:.

These ran on the 4090, not real 16 or 12 GB cards, with one sample each. The memory ladder, launch command and step-by-step setup for the Code2Video test have the rest. See also our earlier test of another SenseTime model, SenseNova-Loop-9B.

The SenseNova team at SenseTime built the model, the skill, the prompt template and the production runs, starting from the Qwen team's base model (model card, skill repository). bartowski made the GGUF quants and the llama.cpp maintainers made the server. Anthropic made Claude Code and Claude Opus 5.5, which drafted the brief from the authors' template. We first saw the model in an AI Search news video. We handled the deployment, fixed the image path, ran the sandboxed agent and counted the pixels.

Sources indicate that this was one attempt at one brief under tight limits we chose. Logs, timings, the full VRAM table and the SDK example are in the complete Code2Video research post on inferencekey.com.

Tech Report: Migrating Your GitHub CI to Hugging Face Jobs

📅 09 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you have a GitHub repository and you have GitHub Actions enabled, you probably use GitHub-hosted runners for CI.
  • That default is convenient, but it also has limits.
  • So built an alternative: keep GitHub Actions in charge of CI, but run the jobs on Hugging Face Jobs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you have a GitHub repository and you have GitHub Actions enabled, you probably use GitHub-hosted runners for CI. That is the default for many projects because it is simple: add a workflow, write runs-on: ubuntu-latest, and GitHub gives you a machine.

That default is convenient, but it also has limits. GitHub Actions can be slow or down for maintenance, the hosted machines are generic, and GPU access is not something most open-source projects can just turn on. For Trackio, those limits started to matter. We wanted both reliable CPU CI for basic unit tests and frontend checks, but also GPU CI for tests that need to run on actual CUDA hardware.

So built an alternative: keep GitHub Actions in charge of CI, but run the jobs on Hugging Face Jobs.

The result: Trackio's CI now runs on Hugging Face Jobs and streams back real-time logs, cutting our CI time for CPU jobs by about 30% and enabling a whole latest test suite that runs on GPU machines!

Sources indicate that in this article, we explain step-by-step how to recreate the same setup for your GitHub repo. If you are using an agent, you can point it to this article, since we provide CLI instructions alongside browser-based instructions for us humans.

Let's start with a quick intro to Hugging Face Jobs!

Hugging Face Jobs lets you run commands or scripts on Hugging Face's serverless infrastructure with almost any hardware flavor. A Job is essentially:.

Recent findings suggest that that makes Jobs a natural fit for CI. CI jobs are already command-driven, already run in clean environments, and often benefit from choosing exactly the right hardware. For ML libraries, the GPU case is especially compelling: you can run a test suite on real GPU hardware without maintaining your own always-on runner.

The key step is connecting GitHub Actions to HF Jobs, which we describe below.

For this setup, we created huggingface/jobs-actions, a small bridge that turns a GitHub Actions job into an ephemeral self-hosted runner running inside an HF Job.

The complete flow looks like this:.

From GitHub's point of view, this is just a self-hosted runner. From Hugging Face's point of view, it is just a Job that launches a container to run the workflow steps from the repo’s GitHub Actions.

Sources indicate that the first thing you need is the dispatcher. This is a small Docker Space that receives GitHub workflow_job webhook events and launches HF Jobs in response.

Industry observers note that create this first because the GitHub App needs a webhook URL, and that URL comes from the Space. This Space should be under your own namespace or under a Hugging Face org that you have write access to.

Go to huggingface/jobs-actions-dispatcher and click Duplicate this Space.

Use cpu-upgrade for real CI so the dispatcher stays available for GitHub webhooks. cpu-basic is fine for testing and will probably work, but it can sleep after inactivity; if GitHub's webhook arrives while it is waking up, the workflow may stay queued forever.

After it builds, open the duplicated Space. You will see a section that says "Required Space secrets," which you can ignore for now. The landing page should display the GitHub App webhook URL you need in the next step. It will look like this:.

If you'd prefer to set up the dispatcher Space with an agent or use a CLI workflow:.

Next, create and install the GitHub App from the dispatcher Space itself. This App needs permission to listen for queued workflow jobs and create ephemeral self-hosted runner registration tokens.

Open your duplicated dispatcher Space:.

In the setup form, enter the GitHub repo whose CI should run on HF Jobs:.

Then click the button to create the GitHub App. GitHub will ask you to choose a name for the App; the name can be anything, as long as it is available in your GitHub account or org. After you submit, the final screen tells you exactly how to upload the App credentials to the dispatcher Space with the hf CLI.

It has been revealed that important note: you will need to provide an Hugging Face token that has permissions to launch Jobs, corresponding to your personal account or an org under which Jobs should be charged. This token should be saved as the HF_TOKEN secret in your dispatcher Space.

Recent findings suggest that finally, you will install the App on the same GitHub repo you entered in the Space. In the Trackio setup, we installed it on gradio-app/trackio.

The GitHub App manifest flow is still browser-based, but an agent can follow the same Space-driven path:.

Paste $GITHUB_REPO into the Space, click the GitHub App creation button, choose any available App name, and follow the generated GitHub instructions.

Sources indicate that after the App exists, install it on your repo from the App settings page. For a GitHub org, the installation settings are under:.

At this point, the dispatcher Space should be configured. The GitHub App setup flow generated the commands that upload the App credentials, webhook secret, and Hugging Face token to the Space.

By default, HF Jobs are launched under the same namespace as the dispatcher Space. Optionally, set HF_NAMESPACE as a Space variable if you want to bill jobs to a different Hugging Face user or org:.

The token you set in Step 2 should correspond to this namespace.

In a recent development, the actual workflow change is small. Instead of:.

use one of the labels handled by the dispatcher:.

For GPU tests, use a GPU label:.

For any GitHub Action you'd like to run on HF Jobs, this 1-line change is all you need!

To add a minimal smoke-test workflow from the CLI:.

You should be able to see logs just like a regular GitHub Action—for example, in this Trackio PR #565.

Note on choosing the right Docker image.

Our first CPU setup used ubuntu:22.04 and installed missing system packages during every run. That worked, but it was slower than it needed to be. GitHub's ubuntu-latest image includes a lot of developer tooling by default; a bare Ubuntu image does not.

In a recent development, for Trackio, the UI tests need Playwright browsers, Node, ffmpeg, sqlite, git, and normal Linux build dependencies. Hugging Face Jobs supports using any Docker image, so we switched to the Microsoft Playwright image, which worked well:.

Here are the numbers from the Trackio CI:.

The biggest win was GPU CI. The Trackio GPU check ran on HF Jobs and passed in 45s, costing less than a cent at the t4-small rate for that duration.

It has been revealed that the CPU result was also encouraging. With the right image, the Linux test job was faster than the GitHub-hosted baseline. That suggests HF Jobs can be a practical CI backend, especially for ML projects that need custom images or accelerators.

Logs were another pleasant surprise. GitHub Actions logs are useful, but the web UI can be heavy for large logs. HF Jobs logs are easy to fetch from the CLI:.

Finally, although we didn't need them for Trackio's CI, HF Jobs also supports mounting volumes, which can be very helpful if you need to load datasets or models from Hugging Face rapidly as part of your CI.

Hopefully, this gives you all you need to try HF Jobs for running your GitHub Actions!

Claude May Have Just Proved the Riemann Hypothesis. Here's Why You Shouldn't Celebrate Yet

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that on Friday, November 20, 2026, a mathematician at Anthropic posted a four-page note on his personal website.
  • Industry observers note that levent Alpöge is a number theorist on Anthropic's technical staff, formerly of the Harvard Society of Fellows.
  • That "if" is doing an enormous amount of work, and this article is mostly about the "if".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that on Friday, November 20, 2026, a mathematician at Anthropic posted a four-page note on his personal website. The claim inside it is the kind of sentence that stops you mid-scroll: "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.".

Industry observers note that levent Alpöge is a number theorist on Anthropic's technical staff, formerly of the Harvard Society of Fellows. The Riemann Hypothesis is the most famous unsolved problem in mathematics — open since 1859, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, worth $1 million if it ever gets solved properly. If this claim holds up, it is one of the biggest moments in the history of mathematics, and an AI system helped do it.

That "if" is doing an enormous amount of work, and this article is mostly about the "if". The claim has not been independently verified. No outside expert has reviewed the proof. The man who wrote it states he has not yet mastered all of it himself. So: excitement, yes. Celebration, not yet. Here's what actually happened, what it would mean, and what to watch next.

Prime numbers — 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and so on — are the building blocks of arithmetic. They get rarer as numbers grow, but not in a smooth, predictable way. Their distribution has irregularities, and mathematicians have spent generations trying to understand the pattern behind them.

The Riemann Hypothesis, first proposed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, says something remarkably precise about that pattern. Technically, it says that all the "nontrivial" zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie on a single vertical line in the complex plane, the line with real part equal to one-half. You don't need to follow the complex analysis to get the stakes: a proof would give mathematicians far tighter control over how primes are distributed, and it would remove an assumption from a huge body of mathematical results that currently depend on the hypothesis being true.

Alpöge's claim goes further than the original problem. His note states the method also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, which extends the same idea to a broader family of mathematical functions, and he expects the Extended Riemann Hypothesis to follow with more work. That last part is an expectation, not a result.

In a recent development, here's the unusual part: there is no conventional paper. Nobody has published a written argument explaining the complete proof, because — by Alpöge's own account — the full written argument would run to more than 250,000 pages, and he has not yet mastered all of the mathematics involved. He intends to write it up properly.

What he released instead is a formalization in Lean 4, the programming language and proof assistant that checks mathematical reasoning step by step, spread across 14 archive parts and reported to run to around 17 million lines of Lean code. That is the whole public record of the proof right now: a four-page note saying "I believe I have discovered a proof," plus a mountain of machine-checked code.

That format is both the strength and the strangeness of this announcement. It means the claim is checkable in a way a 250,000-page manuscript never could be — a computer can verify each logical step. It also means that, as of today, no human being fully understands the argument, including its author.

It has been revealed that lean is worth understanding, because it's doing a lot of the heavy lifting in how seriously people are taking this. A proof written in Lean's formal language can be checked against explicit definitions and logical rules. Researchers can inspect what the final theorem actually states, and which assumptions it depends on.

That gives the mathematical community a concrete, fast first check: does it compile? Kevin Buzzard, a mathematician at Imperial College London known for his work with Lean, gave the suitably practical response to New Scientist: "Let's see if it compiles first.".

But compiling is only the first of several checks, and the later ones are harder:.

In a recent development, that last point is the one that makes this story different from a normal breakthrough. If the proof survives, mathematicians could have strong formal evidence for a result while still working to understand the ideas that make it true. As IBM's coverage put it, the unusual presentation leaves mathematicians with two tasks: determining whether the computer-checked proof establishes the claimed result, and understanding the mathematical ideas behind it.

Industry observers note that extraordinary claims need more than a four-page note. This one has several things going for it.

According to recent reports, first, the person. Alpöge is a serious number theorist, not a crank with a website. Second, the track record on the same territory. In August 2026, Anthropic reported that an experimental version of Claude had improved a long-standing result about the zeta function, raising the proven lower bound on the proportion of zeros lying on the critical line from 41.6% to 67.25%. That was not the Riemann Hypothesis being "two-thirds solved" — the full hypothesis concerns every relevant zero, and closing the remaining gap requires a proof that covers them all — but mathematicians examined the earlier result, and Anthropic released both a paper and a formalization. And in July 2026, Alpöge announced a Claude-assisted counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture, another long-standing problem. This claim arrives against a background of substantive, checked work on the same mathematical ground.

Industry observers note that third, the early reactions from people qualified to judge. James Maynard, the Regius Professor of Mathematics at Oxford and a 2022 Fields Medal winner, told IBM Think: "If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics, establishing one of the great mysteries of the subject." He added: "I suspect that the proof will turn out to be correct, although even checking the Lean verification will take some time.".

Lamzouri, who developed a shorter, simpler proof of the earlier 67.25% result without AI, told IBM Think he was astonished: "I don't have words to describe what I am feeling right now. I am just in awe. If this claim happens to be true, it will be a huge achievement." And Brian Conrey, a leading specialist on the Riemann Hypothesis, told AFP: "It's a monumental moment in human history. It's really the biggest thing I think that's ever happened in mathematics." He was careful to add that he had not yet seen a manuscript, only Alpöge's remarks, and had asked for a copy.

In a recent development, that mix — genuine excitement from the top of the field, paired with open admissions that nobody has checked anything yet — is exactly the right posture. It is also the posture this article is taking.

It has been revealed that hours after Alpöge's announcement, there was a second claim. Stanford mathematics professor Ravi Vakil said a postdoctoral researcher in the same department had independently submitted a proof of the hypothesis. Neither Vakil nor the researcher immediately responded to requests for comment, so almost nothing is known about that second claim yet — not the method, not the format, not whether it overlaps with Alpöge's. But it means the verification story now has two threads to follow, and possibly a priority question if both survive scrutiny.

You can't write about this announcement without writing about its timing, because Alpöge himself raised it. The announcement came the day after Anthropic's record stock-market debut — an IPO with roughly $93.5 billion in gross proceeds, shares closing their first day at $97.17, about 17% above the IPO price. Alpöge stated he had consulted Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei before announcing, and acknowledged that the timing could be viewed cynically, without elaborating. Anthropic declined to comment.

The honest way to handle this: the timing is genuinely awkward, and noticing that doesn't make you a cynic. It also doesn't make the proof wrong. A Lean formalization either compiles and states the theorem or it doesn't, and no IPO changes that. The right response is to hold both thoughts at once — the timing invites questions, and the mathematics will answer them on its own schedule.

There is also recent history worth knowing. Two months ago, OpenAI stated an AI model had solved another Millennium Prize Problem, on the equations that govern how fluids move. Mathematicians say that proof appears correct but has yet to be fully vetted. Alpöge, who had worked on related fluid problems with NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, was at the center of a dispute over credit for that work; OpenAI denied wrongdoing. One observer told AFP he was glad that "this time there might not be any of the same corporate controversy," and praised Alpöge for being open that he did not yet fully understand the proof — the back-and-forth, he said, indicated AI working "more like a tool" and helped dispel "this idea of the machine god.".

If verified, this solves one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems and earns the $1 million Clay Mathematics Institute prize. But the prize itself is slow: the Clay Institute's rules require publication in a qualifying outlet, at least two years after publication, and general acceptance by the global mathematics community before it will consider a proposed solution. Nobody is collecting a cheque this year.

The mathematical consequences would be far larger than the money. A proof of the Riemann Hypothesis would tighten our understanding of how primes are distributed and settle thousands of results that currently rest on the assumption that it's true. The Generalized version would extend that to a whole family of related functions.

Sources indicate that one thing it would not do, at least not directly: break your encryption. The Riemann Hypothesis is about the distribution of primes, not about factoring large numbers, and the leap from "we understand primes better" to "RSA is broken" is not one any serious mathematician is making. If you see that claim in the next few days, treat it as a sign the writer hasn't done the reading.

Industry observers note that the bigger question, for people who build software rather than prove theorems, is what this notes about AI as a research partner. Alpöge describes a collaboration in which he directed the effort toward a promising approach and Claude supplied major advances as the argument developed — including, by his account, pulling ahead near the finish. His sketch draws on a technique used in another mathematical setting where an analogue of the Riemann Hypothesis is already known; the difficulty is carrying the useful idea across to ordinary integers. According to the note, Claude helped find a workaround involving a long chain of transformations called theta lifts. Specialists will have to assess that explanation. For everyone else, the important detail is that Alpöge attributes mathematical ideas to Claude, including a central step in the proposed argument.

Recent findings suggest that if that holds up, it is a specific, inspectable example of a human mathematician and a model reaching a result that generations of researchers couldn't — and a case study in how the human direction and the model's contributions fit together. That is worth studying even if you never touch number theory.

This is the most exciting unproven claim in mathematics in living memory, and also the most honestly uncertain one. The ingredients for taking it seriously are all there: a credible mathematician, a checkable formalization, a track record on the same problem, and early optimism from Fields Medalists. The ingredients for proof are not there yet, and won't be for a while — possibly months, possibly years, possibly never, if a flaw turns up in the formalization.

The correct position right now is excitement plus scepticism, held at the same time. Don't dismiss it because an AI was involved, and don't celebrate it because a headline told you to. The mathematics will decide, and the Lean files are public — which means the deciding is already underway, in the open, by people who know what they're looking at.

The next report worth reading isn't another announcement. It's the first one from a researcher who has checked the files and can begin explaining what Claude and Alpöge actually found.

Engineering Indian Government Payroll: 7th CPC, a 63% DA Scenario, FR 22 and the 8th CPC Challenge

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Writing a salary calculator looks simple until the salary belongs to an Indian government employee.
  • The obvious formula is straightforward: basic pay plus allowances minus deductions.
  • A small change to Dearness Allowance (DA) can affect several payroll components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Writing a salary calculator looks simple until the salary belongs to an Indian government employee.

The obvious formula is straightforward: basic pay plus allowances minus deductions. But implementing that formula correctly requires understanding multiple layers of government rules, effective dates, employee classifications, pay-matrix levels, promotion histories and retirement systems.

A small change to Dearness Allowance (DA) can affect several payroll components. A promotion may require a different calculation depending on the employee's increment date and applicable service rules. An 8th Central Pay Commission (CPC) estimate introduces another challenge because projections must never be confused with legally effective pay structures.

It has been revealed that the real engineering challenge is not arithmetic. It is translating changing administrative rules into accurate, traceable and maintainable software.

This distinction matters to developers building payroll products, HR technology teams maintaining compensation systems, and government employees using digital tools to understand their salaries.

Most conventional salary calculators assume a fairly straightforward compensation structure.

Indian Central Government payroll is more complex because several elements have independent governing rules.

These variables cannot always be treated as interchangeable numerical inputs.

For example, a 7th CPC salary calculation uses a notified pay matrix, while future 8th CPC modelling requires assumptions that may not yet have legal effect.

A reliable system must distinguish an enforceable rule from a forecast.

It must also distinguish what a user has selected from what the employee is actually eligible to receive.

A particularly useful example is the revision of Dearness Allowance.

Industry observers note that for covered Central Government employees under the 7th CPC framework, the Department of Expenditure issued Office Memorandum No. 1/2(i)/2026-E.II(B), dated 29 October 2026, providing a 63% DA rate effective from 1 July 2026.

That combination of dates is vital.

The order was issued in October, but the revised rate applies from July. A payroll system must therefore distinguish the date an order is published from the date the rule becomes effective.

Consider an employee with monthly basic pay of ₹44,900.

This is a component calculation, not the employee's complete gross or take-home salary.

Now imagine software that still uses a hard-coded 53% DA value.

It calculates DA of ₹23,797, which is ₹4,490 less per month than the 63% calculation.

That difference can propagate into other salary components and contributions wherever the applicable rules use DA.

The correct design is not a permanent variable called CURRENT_DA_RATE.

It is a versioned policy record containing the employee category, applicable rate, effective date, source document and conditions.

A DA calculation interface should ideally support historical payroll periods rather than replacing every previous rate with the newest one.

The engineering lesson is simple: a percentage without an effective date and applicability rule is incomplete data.

Another common mistake is treating government basic pay as a continuously increasing percentage.

Under the 7th CPC, basic pay follows a pay matrix containing defined levels and cells.

For example, familiar entry values include:.

A calculation system must use the officially applicable pay-matrix cells rather than estimate every new value by multiplying the old salary by a fixed percentage.

Because rounding, cell placement and level transitions matter.

A mathematically plausible value may not correspond to an actual permitted cell.

This requires a different software model: an authoritative matrix dataset, explicit lookup rules and validation against government notifications.

For annual progression, an increment calculation tool should also account for the employee's applicable date of next increment and the relevant increment rules.

An engineer cannot safely infer those conditions from salary alone.

Promotion-related pay fixation introduces a deeper problem.

Sources indicate that FR 22 and applicable Central Civil Services (Revised Pay) Rules govern pay fixation in relevant cases. The actual treatment depends on the nature of the promotion, applicable provisions and employee options.

For eligible promotions involving FR 22(I)(a)(1), the broad pay-fixation process can involve:.

Consider a simplified illustration.

An employee at the moment receives ₹35,400 in Level 6. The next cell in that level is ₹36,500. If the applicable fixation route requires one increment before placement in Level 7, the next eligible amount in that higher level is ₹44,900.

It has been revealed that this example illustrates matrix-based placement. It does not establish that every promotion follows exactly this route.

The software must first determine whether the employee qualifies for that fixation method.

A pay-fixation calculator is useful for exploring these questions, but any final result must follow the employee's actual service history and applicable orders.

The critical distinction is between calculating an amount and determining which calculation is legally applicable.

A robust implementation needs both abilities.

The Modified Assured Career Progression Scheme (MACP) creates another important distinction.

MACP financial upgradation and regular promotion are not identical administrative events.

Although the scheme broadly refers to financial progression over qualifying service periods, actual eligibility must account for applicable guidelines, earlier promotions and prior financial upgradations.

Consequently, a system should not simply increment an employee's pay level every ten years without evaluating the required conditions.

An MACP eligibility and calculation reference demonstrates why employee history belongs in the calculation model.

At the data-model level, promotion date, effective pay level, previous upgradations and qualifying service should be maintained as distinct fields.

Combining them into a single variable labelled "years worked" is not sufficient.

Government salary calculations are interconnected.

Consider a simplified dependency chain:.

Basic Pay → Dearness Allowance → Applicable Allowances and Contribution Bases → Gross Pay → Deductions → Net Pay.

Transport Allowance, where applicable, can include a DA-linked component under the relevant orders.

For eligible Central Government NPS employees, employee contributions are based on Basic Pay plus DA, subject to applicable contribution rules.

The amount ultimately deducted must follow the governing payroll and rounding instructions.

This dependency matters when generating a monthly salary statement. If the DA component is updated but the contribution calculation still uses an earlier rate, the resulting statement becomes internally inconsistent.

Retirement calculations require even greater care.

For instance, the Unified Pension Scheme has separate eligibility, contribution and assured-payout provisions. An UPS pension calculation reference therefore requires a different ruleset from a simple monthly salary calculator.

Not every DA-dependent concept applies to every employee or pension scheme.

A well-designed engine must model these boundaries explicitly.

Future-pay modelling introduces uncertainty.

The 7th CPC provides an established framework for relevant existing calculations. However, an 8th CPC salary forecast must not assume that a particular proposed fitment factor, matrix or allowance structure has already been approved.

Consider a hypothetical employee with basic pay of ₹35,400.

These figures result from multiplication only.

They are not officially notified 8th CPC salaries.

A completed government implementation may involve a different matrix, rounding method, effective date and allowance treatment.

It is also incorrect to assume that a percentage increase in basic pay produces the same percentage increase in take-home salary.

DA treatment, HRA, Transport Allowance, pension deductions and income-tax liability may all influence the final outcome.

Software should therefore separate:.

These categories should be visible in both the software interface and its generated output.

The most useful engineering principle is to separate policy from calculation logic.

Instead of scattering rates across interface components, every rule can be represented through a structured record.

A rule model should include fields such as rule_id, employee_category, effective_from, effective_to, source_document, calculation_method and rounding_policy.

The calculation engine can then:.

This is a proposed engineering architecture, not a claim that a particular website already implements every element.

Such separation makes statutory changes easier to maintain and audit.

When a DA order changes, the responsible team should be able to introduce a newly introduced effective-dated record and run regression tests across every dependent calculator.

Historical results should remain reproducible under the rules that applied to their original periods.

Traditional unit tests often verify whether the expected number emerges from a known formula.

Statutory payroll needs additional types of testing.

Boundary-date tests: Check the day before and after a latest rate becomes effective.

Pay-matrix tests: Verify that every returned cell exists in the applicable official dataset.

Promotion-option tests: Evaluate eligible fixation options and relevant increment dates.

Eligibility tests: Confirm that a rule does not apply to employees outside its designated category.

Dependency tests: Verify that changes to DA flow correctly into every component that uses it.

Historical regression tests: Ensure updates do not silently rewrite calculations for previous payroll periods.

A particularly valuable approach is to maintain a collection of officially sourced reference cases, often called golden test cases.

Each case should record the input, expected output, government authority and applicable date.

This turns administrative guidance into reproducible software evidence.

It also exposes the difference between a calculator that produces numbers and one that can explain those numbers.

Government payroll tools handle financially sensitive information.

Consequently, a trustworthy product needs more than a polished interface.

Every crucial result should ideally identify its governing source, applicable employee category, calculation period, rounding assumptions and limitations.

The user should be able to see where the result came from.

Product teams must also distinguish privacy promises from verified technical behaviour.

A website can state that calculations happen locally, but that claim should be supported by source-code inspection, network testing and an accurate privacy disclosure.

For example, the published FreePayCalculator provides a starting point for understanding the site's stated practices. Independent technical verification is still necessary before treating any no-transmission claim as proven.

The broader principle applies to salary calculators, tax tools, pension systems and other financial software.

Trust is earned through verifiable rules, reproducible calculations and accountable maintenance, not through confident product descriptions.

Indian government payroll exposes a fundamental challenge in financial software engineering.

The arithmetic may be simple, but its correctness depends on choosing the right rule, for the right employee, at the right point in time.

In a recent development, the 63% DA revision demonstrates the importance of effective-date versioning. The 7th CPC pay matrix indicates why discrete official datasets matter. FR 22 promotion cases reveal the need for eligibility-aware decision logic. The 8th CPC introduces a final requirement: modelling uncertainty without disguising it as law.

For founders and developers, the most valuable engineering investment is not another formula or interface.

It is a system that can answer three questions about every result:.

Which rule was applied? Why did it apply? Can the result be independently reproduced?

When software can answer those questions reliably, it becomes more than a convenient calculator.

It becomes a transparent decision-support tool.

A simplified gross salary calculation combines basic pay, DA and applicable allowances. Net salary is obtained after relevant deductions. Actual calculations depend on pay level, employee category, location, payroll period and statutory eligibility.

Industry observers note that no. The 63% DA rate effective 1 July 2026 applies to the Central Government employee categories covered by the relevant Department of Expenditure order. State employees and other categories require their own applicable orders.

Sources indicate that DA equals eligible basic pay multiplied by the applicable DA percentage. For example, ₹44,900 × 63% equals ₹28,287 per month before considering other salary components.

It has been revealed that FR 22 can govern pay fixation following an eligible promotion. The calculation may involve an increment in the existing pay level followed by placement in the promoted level. Applicable options, eligibility and dates must be checked.

No final 8th CPC fitment factor was established in the available research as of 21 November 2026. Online values such as 1.92 or 2.28 must be treated as hypothetical unless supported by a subsequent official notification.

For eligible employees whose NPS contribution base includes Basic Pay plus DA, a DA increase can increase the contribution amount. The applicable contribution rate, rounding and eligibility rules determine the final deduction.

Recent findings suggest that FR 22 addresses pay-fixation treatment in applicable service situations, including eligible promotions. MACP provides financial upgradation under separate eligibility guidelines. A financial upgradation is not automatically equivalent to a functional promotion.

Industry observers note that A reliable calculator should use official rules, effective-dated rates, applicable pay-matrix values, transparent assumptions, appropriate eligibility checks and reproducible test cases. The result should be clearly presented as an estimate unless confirmed by the competent payroll authority.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An agent built a 3D Paris gallery from two Hugging Face Spaces.

I asked a coding agent to build a beautiful website showcasing the monuments of Paris as 3D Gaussian splats. I never opened an image generator. I never touched a 3D reconstruction tool. The agent produced every asset (the images and the 3D splats) by calling two Hugging Face Spaces directly, then wired them into a cinematic viewer.

Here's the result, live as a static Space:.

This post is about how that's possible now, and why I think it's a preview of how a lot of multimedia software gets built from here on.

Industry observers note that mitchell Hashimoto recently described a shift he calls the building block economy: the most effective path to software is no longer a polished monolith, but small, well-documented components that others (increasingly agents) can assemble. His key observation: AI is okay at building everything from scratch, but it is really good at gluing together proven pieces.

It has been revealed that that thesis has mostly been told with code libraries. But the same forces are hitting multimedia AI. The hard part of using a state-of-the-art image model, a video model, a TTS model, or a 3D reconstruction model was never the model. It was the integration: SDKs, weights, GPUs, input formats, polling. If each model were instead a documented, callable block, an agent could glue them together the same way it globs together npm packages.

That's exactly what Hugging Face Spaces have quietly become.

The Hub hosts thousands of state-of-the-art models (a huge share of them open-weights), and most are deployed as interactive Spaces. As of now, every Gradio Space also exposes a plain-text agents.md that tells an agent exactly how to call it:.

returns everything needed in one shot: the schema URL, the call and poll templates, how to upload files, and the auth hint:.

No client library. No hardcoded integration. An agent reads that, and it can drive the Space end to end. Set an HF_TOKEN and you're going. You can find these instructions on any Gradio Space via its Agents button:.

The real unlock is chaining: the output of one Space becomes the input to the next. Prompt → image → 3D. That's the whole pipeline behind this gallery.

The six source images the agent generated, all isolated on black, ready for single-image 3D reconstruction:.

Recent findings suggest that from there the agent did the "glue" work too. It noticed TripoSplat outputs are Y-down and flipped them upright, auto-framed each monument, compressed the .ply files to .ksplat (~3× smaller, so they load fast), built a Three.js viewer with a scroll-to-switch and drag-to-rotate UI, and deployed the whole thing as a static Space. The only human inputs were taste-level: "make it zoomed out," "replace the obelisk with something better for splatting," "the transition lingers too long.".

Several of those steps were the agent reacting to reality. A wide glass pyramid splats poorly. A thin obelisk is dull. A single-view reconstruction infers the back. That is exactly the "outsourced R&D, fast iteration" loop the building-block economy predicts, except the R&D was a conversation.

The real test of a building block is how cheaply you can reuse it. Once this pipeline existed, spinning up entirely new galleries cost about one sentence each. "Create a similar Space with splats for Japan," then the same for Egypt, and the agent did the rest: six monument images, six splats, compression, a viewer, and a deployed Space, per country.

Check the audio stream before assembling AI video clips

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (267 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI video exports can mix clips with audio and clips with no audio stream at all.
  • Run this on one input before it enters the assembly queue:.
  • Check the command's exit status first.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI video exports can mix clips with audio and clips with no audio stream at all. If your assembly job maps an audio stream for every shot, an otherwise playable clip can fail before the edit is rendered.

Run this on one input before it enters the assembly queue:.

Check the command's exit status first. A failed probe means the file could not be inspected. A successful probe with an empty streams array means the selected audio stream is absent. A successful probe with a stream gives you its codec, sample rate, and channel count. It does not tell you whether that track contains silence.

To reproduce the missing-stream case without using production material, generate a one-second input without audio:.

Then run the probe on silent-shot.mp4. Use a filename that does not already exist, or FFmpeg will prompt before replacing it.

Industry observers note that for narration that will be mixed in later, a video-only shot may be fine. For a shot that is supposed to retain dialogue, send it back for review. If your assembly needs each input to have matching audio streams, normalize deliberate silence and real audio to the chosen sample rate and layout before concatenating. Make the policy explicit so that missing dialogue never gets silently replaced with silence.

Keep the probe result next to the shot ID. When a render fails, the person reviewing it can see whether the input was unreadable, missing a stream, or incompatible with the assembly settings.

Industry observers note that disclosure: I’m part of the AlphaDrama team. AI assisted with drafting this article.

Profiling in PyTorch (Part 2): From nn.Linear to a Fused MLP

📅 11 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the second post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.
  • According to recent reports, in the first part of this series "Profiling in PyTorch", we used torch.add(torch.matmul(x, w), b) to learn how to read PyTorch profiler traces.
  • Sources indicate that in the second iteration (this blog post), we climb one rung up the ladder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the second post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.

According to recent reports, in the first part of this series "Profiling in PyTorch", we used torch.add(torch.matmul(x, w), b) to learn how to read PyTorch profiler traces. We also discussed several other topics that came our way - the CPU dispatch chain, launch overhead, the difference between an overhead-bound and a compute-bound regime, and some internals of torch.compile.

Sources indicate that in the second iteration (this blog post), we climb one rung up the ladder. We replace the hand-written matmul-add pair with an nn.Linear (with bias=True). This is the building block every deep learning model uses. We then stack three of them (specific to our example), with an activation in between, to form a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) block.

Recent findings suggest that the scripts for this blog post live here: 02_linear.py, 03_simple_mlp.py, and 03_kernels_mlp.py. Like before, it helps to open them in a separate tab and walk through the code as you read. We use an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU to run the scripts. It is really easy to set up a GPU on the Hugging Face infrastructure and experiment with the scripts using Dev Mode with Spaces. One could also run the scripts with the Hugging Face Jobs pipeline.

Before we begin, a quick recap of two ideas we will lean on repeatedly:.

Recent findings suggest that nn.Linear is a module wrapper around the same matrix multiplication and addition we already profiled in Part 1. The only difference is that it owns its weight and bias as parameters and exposes a forward method that PyTorch users have grown familiar with.

The operation at hand can be written as:.

Recent findings suggest that where x is the input, w is the weight and b is the bias. Let's run 02_linear.py and check the profile.

trace-util is a utility that will sync your traces to a Hugging Face bucket and then provide the Preffeto URLs on your terminal.

Figure 1 reveals the profiler trace of a forward call of the linear layer. We trace the forward call of the linear layer with a similar schedule setup as the previous traces, with wait=1, warmup=1 and active=3. This is why we see three Profile Steps in the CPU and GPU lanes.

Sources indicate that if we zoom into the profiler trace, as we do in Figure 2, we notice an aten::t (transpose) op before the aten::addmm (multiplication and addition) op. We can already figure out that nn.Linear transposes the weight parameter and then multiplies it with the input. This is the reason we see an aten::t op.

An important thing to notice is that aten::t does not really copy or reorganize data: it only rewrites tensor metadata (shape and stride) on the CPU to represent the transposed matrix. It does not launch a kernel on the GPU. One can verify this two ways: by looking at the GPU lane in the trace, or by checking the aten::t row in the profiler table and the time it took on CUDA.

There is no aten::add (the bias addition) in the dispatch chain of the linear layer, as seen in Figure 3. This is because the bias addition has been folded into the matrix multiplication kernel, using what is called an epilogue.

Sources indicate that an epilogue is a small computation that a GEMM (GEneral Matrix Multiply) kernel does at the very end, just before it writes its result back to HBM (High Bandwidth Memory, the GPU's main memory). Adding a bias, applying an activation, or scaling by a constant are all classic epilogues. The point of an epilogue is to avoid loading or writing to HBM a second time, since memory traffic makes an operation expensive.

nn.Linear calls torch.nn.functional.linear, which, in turn, calls aten::linear. aten::linear looks at the inputs, notices that a bias was passed, and dispatches aten::addmm(bias, x, weight) instead of doing a matmul and an add separately. addmm computes:.

The cuBLAS GEMM kernel that runs on the GPU has a bias-add variant built in, and that's the kernel aten::addmm picks. The add never appears as a separate kernel because it is part of the matmul kernel's writeback, which is exactly what an epilogue is.

It has been revealed that this is the moment to notice something subtle. The kernel you saw in Part 1 under --compile (addmm) is the kernel that eager nn.Linear already uses. There is nothing left for torch.compile to fuse here, which is the next thing we will verify.

According to recent reports, let's compile the forward call and look at the profiler trace. (The profiler trace is visualized in the next section).

If you compare the eager and compiled traces for a single nn.Linear's forward, you will find:.

This is worth internalizing. A common reflex is to reach for torch.compile whenever a model feels slow. For a single GEMM-with-bias, compile has very little to do. This is not a bug, this is just that compile needs more than one operation to possibly do any fusing. Let's prove that by looking at an MLP.

A careful reader of the two traces (eager vs compile) will notice that the eager CPU dispatch chain has more in it than the compiled one.

According to recent reports, the eager CPU dispatch chain inside aten::linear is aten::t followed by aten::addmm (Figure 4). To understand what aten::t actually does, we need a quick detour into strides and views.

Sources indicate that A tensor stores its data as one flat, contiguous run of numbers in memory. The shape and stride are metadata that sit on top of that run and tell PyTorch how to walk it: a stride of (s0, s1) means "step s0 elements to move one row, step s1 to move one column". Change the metadata and you get a different view of the same raw data, with no copy:.

M.t() did not move a single number. It returned a new view whose strides are swapped, so reading it row-by-row now walks the original buffer 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in transposed order. The underlying data is identical; only the metadata differs.

This is exactly what aten::t does inside the linear layer: it does not allocate a newly introduced tensor or copy any data, it produces a view of the weight with rewritten strides.

Sources indicate that as we can see in Figure 5, compile did not remove a GPU kernel: it removed the CPU overhead of dispatching that view. Inductor traced through the view chain at compile time, computed the resulting strides once, and emitted a direct aten::addmm call with those strides hard-coded. A few microseconds of CPU work disappear while the GPU does identical math.

As one would expect, when the input data violates the strides precomputed by the compiler, it will throw an error.

If you look at the GPU lane in both traces, there is exactly one kernel per forward, and it is the same kernel both times:.

It has been revealed that if no transpose kernel ran, who taught the GEMM to read the weight matrix in transposed order? The answer is in the kernel's name. Look at the suffix:.

Industry observers note that that tn is the layout descriptor. cuBLAS and CUTLASS precompile a separate kernel binary for each combination of input layouts.

It has been revealed that n (non-transposed) and t (transposed) describe how a kernel walks its input during the inner loop. The dispatcher's job is to look at the input strides, decide which suffix combination matches, and pick the right precompiled kernel.

The kernel name in a profiler trace is a hash dump of the kernel's identity. If two runs show the same kernel name, the GPU is doing the same work. If they differ (e.g., _tn_ vs _nn_, bf16 vs fp16, or s16816gemm vs s161616gemm) then the GPU is doing different work, and the dispatcher took a different branch. Learning to read this name is one of the most useful habits when comparing traces.

It has been revealed that in this section, we will profile a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). To make this more interesting, we will profile a feed-forward network with the GeGLU activation variant (which is quite heavily used in practice). This is also our way of paying tribute to one of the greatest lines ever written in the history of deep learning research (Figure 6).

You will find the entire script here: 03_simple_mlp.py. Execute it like so:.

Before we open the trace, let's think together about what we should expect to see. The forward function does a fair amount of computation, but most of it is already familiar to us.

We should expect three aten::linear dispatches, one for each nn.Linear layer. We should also expect two pointwise kernel introduces, one for the GeLU and one for the multiplication. Forming this expectation before looking is the single most useful habit in the profiling journey: you read the trace to confirm or break a guess, not to form one from scratch.

From Figure 7 we can pat ourselves on the back, as our intuition was correct. Per forward pass (one mlp_fwd), the GPU runs exactly 5 kernels. Figure 8 highlights the "occupancy query" as seen in the CPU lane for the linear projection layers.

The three GEMMs each do an extra cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor call before the launch. We have a separate section on this in Part 1, you can find it here. That is cuBLAS sizing the grid. The pointwise ops (GeLU and mul) launch directly, with no occupancy query. So "a linear" is actually query + launch, while "a pointwise op" is just launch.

Recent findings suggest that the aten::t, aten::transpose, aten::reshape, aten::view, aten::as_strided, and aten::_unsafe_view ops launch zero kernels. They show 0.000us of CUDA time in the table (Figure 9) because they only rewrite tensor metadata (shape and stride) on the CPU. A reader scanning the table sees around six op names per linear, but only one of them (mm) ever reaches the GPU.

The MLP flattens [batch, seq, dim] to [batch * seq, dim] for the matmul. In our command-line invocation we used 64 for batch and 128 for seq, so that's where the 8192 (batch * seq = 64 * 128) below comes from.

In a recent development, all three GEMMs have the same FLOP count, 2·8192·768·3072 ≈ 38.7 GFLOP each, yet down_proj is about 10% faster. Same work, different shape (N=768 instead of 3072), so cuBLAS picks a different tile (128×256, with a deeper stages_64x3 pipeline) that gets better reuse for that shape.

If you want to learn more about tiling in depth, here is a great resource to get started with.

This is exactly why the table had two GEMM rows (Figure 9): the 128x128 row is gate+up and the 128x256 row is down.

Sources indicate that before compiling the forward method and visualizing it, let's do the mental exercise again of asking ourselves what we expect to see in the trace. This is a fun experiment, and an important one to repeat every time you profile something yourself. Always build on your intuition, and the moment something does not match, stop and figure out why.

In eager mode, each nn.Linear was expanded into a chain of dispatcher ops (aten::linear → aten::t → aten::transpose → aten::matmul → aten::reshape → aten::mm). Those are the high-level wrappers that ATen walks through before reaching the real GEMM. torch.compile removes that chain.

By the time the compiled graph runs, there is no linear, no matmul, no transpose or reshape and those metadata ops were folded into how mm is called. We can see three bare aten::mm external calls (Figure 10). The proof that it is the same GEMM is that the kernel names are byte-for-byte identical to eager: ...128x128...stages_32x5_tn for gate and up, and ...128x256...stages_64x3_tn for down.

This is the headline of the whole compile lesson. The two eager pointwise kernels (GeLU and mul) plus a reshape collapsed into one kernel, triton_poi_fused__unsafe_view_gelu_mul_0 (Figure 11). Let's decode the name:.

In a recent development, why is this a win? In eager mode, the intermediate h = gelu(g) is a full [8192, 3072] bf16 tensor (around 50 MB) that the GeLU kernel writes to HBM and the mul kernel immediately reads back. Fusion keeps it in registers (memory that resides inside the chip and are closer than the HBM). The Triton kernel reads g and u once, computes gelu(g) * u, and writes the result once. One whole round trip of the intermediate through global memory is gone.

So far we have let PyTorch (eager) and the compiler (torch.compile) pick our kernels. Now we plug in a kernel that a human expert wrote and tuned by hand. We use the LigerGEGLUMLP layer, that we can easily fetch from the Hugging Face Hub with the kernels library.

The full script is here: 03_kernels_mlp.py.

Figure 12 reveals the profile for the LigerGEGLUMLP layer using the Liger kernels from the Hub.

Sources indicate that writing kernels in Triton or CUDA is one problem and shipping them is another. The kernel has to be compiled for your exact combination of GPU architecture, CUDA version, and PyTorch version. This is the step that usually breaks ("works on my machine", missing nvcc, wrong Triton version).

The kernels library moves that build step off your machine. get_kernel("kernels-community/liger-kernels", version=1) downloads a pre-built, version-pinned kernel package from the Hugging Face Hub and caches it locally (here under ~/.cache/...kernels-community--liger-kernels). The benefits are:.

When we say "tuned", we mean two concrete things, and both are visible in the trace.

Recent findings suggest that the fusion is baked in. The LigerGEGLUMLP forward is down_proj(LigerGELUMulFunction.apply(gate_proj(x), up_proj(x))). The LigerGELUMulFunction runs a single Triton kernel, _geglu_tanh_forward_kernel, that computes gelu(gate) * up in one pass. This is exactly what we saw from torch.compile, where the intermediate never makes a round-trip through HBM. We get it here without the compiler, as shown in Figures 13 and 14 (no Dynamo guards, no compile latency, no recompilation risk).

In a recent development, the launch parameters were chosen for the hardware. The kernel does not guess its block size at random. Liger's calculate_settings picks them from the column count.

In a recent development, it is worth being honest about the trade-off here, because the raw numbers can be misleading. The Liger kernel runs in 92.8 µs, while Inductor's fused kernel from the compile run was 89.4 µs. At first glance the hand-written kernel looks slightly slower, but that comparison hides the cost that makes it worthwhile.

torch.compile specializes for a static shape. Inductor's 89.4 µs kernel is fast precisely because it was generated for this exact [8192, 3072] problem. Change the batch size, the sequence length, or the hidden dimension, Dynamo re-traces, and you pay the compile cost all over again to get a latest specialized kernel.

Recent findings suggest that so the real choice is not "slow human kernel vs fast compiled kernel". It is a fast generic kernel vs a kernel specialized for one particular input shape. The Liger kernel takes one set of launch parameters and runs them for any shape with no recompilation. It gives up the last few microseconds that per-shape specialization would buy, in exchange for being robust to changing shapes.

The table below collects what each step changed on the GPU and what it left untouched.

In a recent development, if there is one habit to carry forward, it is the one we practiced before every trace: guess first, then look. State what you expect the trace to contain, open it, and treat any mismatch as the most interesting thing on the screen.

It has been revealed that this was the second stop in the Profiling in PyTorch series. In the next post we will keep climbing the ladder, moving from this MLP block towards the attention block and, eventually, a full model.

#34775. CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1468 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Krebsonsecurity ↗ Open Full Page

CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1468 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
  • A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.
  • The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”.

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the organization’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

Recent findings suggest that the indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim manufacturer and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

In a recent development, the following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Industry observers note that paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their organization and client data.

Ihme remarked RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”.

It has been revealed that A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”.

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Recent findings suggest that ihme stated RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the manufacturer’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

Sources indicate that A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

Sources indicate that “The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme remarked. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”.

In a recent development, indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

In a recent development, the Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”.

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a upcoming negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”.

According to recent reports, ihme stated RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme remarked. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”.

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

According to recent reports, around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.
