Browser Use in DSH Agent Enhancer: Click, Debug, and Replay Saved Flows

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that dsh-agent-enhancer is a desktop plugin for DSH.
  • Industry observers note that you do not need scripting or API knowledge.
  • The practical rule: if you click through the same web admin every day or every week, it is worth handing over.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that dsh-agent-enhancer is a desktop plugin for DSH. Its Browser Use layer gives your agent a dedicated browser. It can click, type, and submit. Login state stays in its own profile, so your everyday browser is left alone.

Industry observers note that you do not need scripting or API knowledge. Do the task once in the dedicated window, and the agent can follow the same steps. Save the recording as a flow, rerun it by name, and hand it to a scheduled task without approving every action.

The practical rule: if you click through the same web admin every day or every week, it is worth handing over. Here are scenarios that work right after install:.

Three patterns cover most of these:.

This post starts with what it can do, then walks through six areas: operation, troubleshooting, demo recording, saved flows, scheduled tasks, and boundaries. Each section ends with a concrete use case.

Multiple tabs. The sidebar lists every tab; click one to switch. When navigating, you can choose to open a latest tab. If a task needs to compare orders, inventory, and shipping, you do not have to cram everything into one page.

Read-only tabs. One click in the sidebar makes a tab read-only: the agent can look, but it cannot click, type, or navigate within that tab. Opening a new tab and scrolling still work. Check-only pages — reports, order details — are the safest place to use it. Even a saved flow replay is blocked by this restriction.

Idle cleanup. Idle tabs can close automatically after 10, 30, or 60 minutes, or never. The tab you are at the moment viewing, session-bound tabs, and the last remaining tab are never closed. The dedicated window does not pile up.

Recent findings suggest that use it for: reconciling orders across three admin pages. Open orders, inventory, and shipping in separate tabs; make inventory read-only so nobody accidentally clicks "Adjust stock"; come back from lunch and idle tabs are gone, but the login is still there.

It has been revealed that when the Export button does nothing, guessing is the worst approach. Turn on Debug & Page Emulation in settings (off by default):.

Startup failures do not require digging through logs either. The status bar and sidebar show the reason and the next step: feature not enabled, browser not started, WebKit missing, no usable browser on the machine, profile directory locked, and so on.

In a recent development, use it for: a dead Export button. Check whether the network call returns 500 or times out, then look for console errors. Switch to a narrow viewport to rule out an overlay covering the button. Once you know the cause, change the agent's action instead of trying blindly.

Some admin tasks are easier to show than to describe. Turn on Demo Recording in settings (off by default), click "Start demo" in the sidebar, and use the dedicated window normally. When you are done, click "End and view steps".

In a recent development, it records clicks, typing, Enter presses, and page navigations. It can record across tabs, and other tabs opened during the demo are captured. When finished, you can copy the steps or click "Send to agent" to insert them into the input box (the current conversation needs at least one message first, otherwise it asks you to send one). You can also say "let me show you" in the chat, and the agent can start a recording itself.

Industry observers note that password, CAPTCHA, token, and card-number fields are stored as *** only. It does not take screenshots or record network requests.

In a recent development, use it for: handing over monthly reconciliation. Ask a teammate to demo it once: open the reconciliation page, pick the month, export, download, and check the three tables. Send the steps to the agent, and next month nobody has to ask "where do I click first?".

Recent findings suggest that after recording, click "Save as flow" and give it a name, such as "Weekly report export". There are three ways to run it:.

It works across sessions and restarts. If the current page is not the page where recording started, it returns there first. Data stays local and only redacted steps are stored; password fields remain ***.

The sidebar row keeps only Run and "⋯"; rename and delete live in the menu, and delete asks for confirmation. Expanding the row indicates editable values, run mode, and steps. Replay supports dropdowns and checkboxes. If several controls share a name and cannot be distinguished, it stops and lists the candidates instead of clicking the first one by name.

In a recent development, after saving, values worth changing — dates, email addresses, search terms — are detected automatically. Parameter names come straight from the page labels ("Start date"), so you do not have to invent variable names.

Industry observers note that date fields get a date picker. You can also say "last week", "this month", or "last quarter", and the agent converts it to a real date. When a value is missing, it asks in plain language: "Which start date should I use this time?".

Each value's default and display name can be changed; it can be set to "Ask me each time" or switched back to a fixed value. Every change goes into version history, and the last change can be undone.

Recent findings suggest that if the site renames a control or inserts an extra dialog, the flow gets stuck. The agent finishes the task, then offers a suggestion:.

"The control in step 4 changed; it is now called 'Start date'. Remember this for next time?".

Repair changes only how the control is located. It does not change values or step order. Password fields do not participate, and are never stored in the flow. Every write-back creates a version that can be undone.

Each saved flow records its last run: time, success / stopped at step N / failure. If it did not finish, the row shows a "Last run incomplete" badge. It stores counts and the reason it stopped, not page content.

Recent findings suggest that use it for: a weekly report export. Record once, save "Weekly report export", set "Start date" to Ask me each time, say Run "Weekly report export" with last week's start date on Monday morning, and check the run result. If the site changes, repair it once, remember it, and the next run uses the fix.

First, a common misconception: a saved flow is not an asset you drag into a scheduled task. When the schedule fires, the task only claims one sentence.

Sources indicate that the built-in Automation Tasks scheduler creates a newly introduced session with fixed permissions: Workspace Modify with approval prompts. The task itself cannot change permissions. So when our flow runs, an approval prompt will appear — and nobody is there to click it. The task stalls.

Recent findings suggest that the fix is not to loosen global permissions. Turn on Unattended for that one flow. It applies only to the site recorded in that flow, with a default budget of 20 minutes / 30 actions. When time or actions run out, it goes back to per-action approval. It is off by default; it cannot be enabled if the flow has no recorded site; password fields still stop and wait; it does not apply to another site or another session; if a run is denied, the site grant is revoked immediately.

These two numbers can be changed in Settings → Agent Enhancer → Features → Browser Agent: authorization duration 5–60 minutes, action limit 10–200. Defaults stay unless you change them.

Recent findings suggest that use it for: an automatic weekly report at 8:00 on Monday. Enable unattended only for "Weekly report export", tune the budget to that flow, and check the run result afterward. Other tasks and other sites still require approval each time.

If the session already uses Full Access, actions no longer prompt one by one; Auto Review goes through the built-in reviewer; View Only is refused with an explanation.

It can act, but it does not have unlimited permission. By default, every action that changes external state needs approval. It stops at a login wall and waits for you to click "I'm done, continue"; it does not bypass it.

It has been revealed that the dedicated window does not label itself as an automation environment, so sites with login bot checks, such as Bilibili, no longer reject it for that reason. This is not a generic anti-detection patch; sites that check more signals still need a separate look.

In a recent development, use it for: hand a read-only report page to the agent for checking; when a submission is needed, let it stop and wait for you; give a scheduled task one flow and a limited window. Narrow permissions are what make it safe to let go.

Command line (installs the latest version by default):.

Compatible with DSH desktop 0.2.2.x.

Recent findings suggest that start by walking it through one demo recording. After that, it remembers the run for you.

#34773. Industry News: MySQL secure_file_priv limits paths, not the FILE privilege

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (713 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: MySQL secure_file_priv limits paths, not the FILE privilege

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • FILE is one of the most consequential privileges in MySQL.
  • Sources indicate that the MySQL 8.4 manual defines three states for the variable.
  • An account with FILE can read files that the MySQL server process can read, subject to the secure_file_priv directory boundary.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FILE is one of the most consequential privileges in MySQL. It allows a user to perform import and export operations, including LOAD DATA, SELECT ... INTO OUTFILE, and LOAD_FILE(). secure_file_priv narrows where those operations can touch the server filesystem. It does not make an account that holds FILE safe, and it does not grant or remove the privilege.

Sources indicate that the MySQL 8.4 manual defines three states for the variable. An empty value has no effect and is explicitly described as insecure. A directory value limits import and export operations to files in that directory, which must already exist. A NULL value disables import and export operations. The server checks the setting at startup and logs a warning when a non-NULL value is empty, points at the data directory or one of its subdirectories, or points at a directory accessible by all users.

An account with FILE can read files that the MySQL server process can read, subject to the secure_file_priv directory boundary. That makes the server's operating-system identity part of the database security model. A file that is unreadable to the database user stays unreadable through SQL. A file that is readable to the database user may become an import source if the path rules permit it.

According to recent reports, the write side has the same shape. A directory allowed by secure_file_priv can receive exported data if the server can write there. Do not point it at the data directory, a web root, a plugin directory, a backup target, or a directory writable by an unprivileged local user. A dedicated directory with restrictive ownership and no executable content is easier to reason about.

The variable is global and not dynamic. Changing it requires a configuration change and restart, which makes drift detection crucial. An operator may set the value in one configuration file while another file supplies a later override. Check the effective value and the startup log, not just the intended template.

Start with the accounts that hold FILE. Routine application accounts should not need it. A migration or reporting account may need a narrow import path, but it should be a separate identity with an expiration date, a controlled source directory, and logging. Avoid granting FILE to a shared administrator account that many people use.

Recent findings suggest that check for indirect paths to elevated file operations. An account that can create or modify stored programs with DEFINER privileges, or an account with broad SUPER-style authority, may be able to make another module perform work. The exact privilege set depends on the MySQL version and deployment. Review the effective grants and the program definitions rather than assuming a single system variable covers every path.

Recent findings suggest that also inspect the server's operating-system account. A database process that can read private keys, application configuration, or backup credentials has a larger blast radius even when SQL file paths are constrained. File permissions, mount options, and container volumes are part of the same boundary.

Record the effective secure_file_priv value and classify it as disabled, restricted, or insecure. Confirm that a restricted directory exists, is owned by the database service identity or a dedicated service group, and is not inside the data directory or a world-writable location. Verify that the directory is not mounted into a web server or a container that hosts application code.

List the accounts with FILE. For each one, capture the owner, purpose, connection path, and the operational reason for the privilege. Remove it from accounts that cannot demonstrate a current need. For the remaining accounts, test the allowed import and export path in a lab with a harmless file. Confirm that an attempt outside the directory fails and that the failure is logged.

It has been revealed that monitor changes to grants and to the effective startup configuration. A schema migration tool or a temporary support account can reintroduce the privilege. If the organization uses managed MySQL, verify how the provider exposes the setting and whether the value is guaranteed across failover nodes.

secure_file_priv is useful because it turns a broad filesystem capability into a smaller one. It is not a substitute for least privilege, service-account separation, filesystem permissions, or monitoring. Treat the variable and the grant list as one control package.

#34771. The upload works in the office and dies at 80% on the train. Making large uploads survive mobile networks.

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (574 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

The upload works in the office and dies at 80% on the train. Making large uploads survive mobile networks.

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (574 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The bug: owners attach a video or a batch of photos, the progress bar gets most of the way, and then the upload fails and starts again from zero.
  • It has been revealed that A single POST with the whole file in the body has no way to recover from any of them.
  • Before changing the client, check the path the upload takes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The bug: owners attach a video or a batch of photos, the progress bar gets most of the way, and then the upload fails and starts again from zero. On office Wi-Fi it never happens. On a phone it happens a lot, because a long upload on a mobile network is very likely to hit at least one of these: a network switch (Wi-Fi to cellular), a dead zone, the user leaving the app, or a timeout somewhere between the phone and your server.

It has been revealed that A single POST with the whole file in the body has no way to recover from any of them. Here's what does.

Before changing the client, check the path the upload takes. A few limits are hit only by large or slow uploads, and they look like network failures from the phone:.

According to recent reports, test by uploading a file just over each limit from a fast connection. If that fails, the problem isn't the mobile network.

According to recent reports, on iOS, URLSessionConfiguration.timeoutIntervalForRequest (default 60 s) is an idle timeout: it fires when no data moves for that long, not when the whole request takes longer than 60 s. timeoutIntervalForResource (default 7 days) is the total limit. Setting the request timeout to a few minutes "because uploads are slow" mostly delays the error. Leave it, and make the upload resumable instead.

On Android with OkHttp, writeTimeout is also per write, not for the whole body. callTimeout is the total, and it's off by default. If someone set callTimeout to 30 seconds for the whole app, every upload that takes longer than 30 seconds fails, and that only happens on slow networks.

The fix that actually solves it: upload in pieces, and let the client ask the server how much it already has.

Recent findings suggest that you don't need to design this yourself. Common options:.

Whatever you use, the client has to store the upload ID and the part list on disk, not in memory, so it can continue after the app is killed.

Industry observers note that iOS: use a background URLSession (URLSessionConfiguration.background(withIdentifier:)) with uploadTask(with:fromFile:). Background sessions only upload from files, so write the data (or each part) to a file first. The system carries on with the upload while your app is suspended or terminated by the system, and relaunches the app in the background when it's done. (If the user force-quits the app, iOS cancels its background transfers, which is another reason to keep the upload state on disk and resume on the next launch.) Implement application(_:handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession:completionHandler:) and call the completion handler after processing the events. Each part of a multipart upload can be its own background upload task.

Android: use WorkManager with a NetworkType.CONNECTED constraint so the work waits for a network and retries with backoff. For long uploads the user started, run it as a foreground worker with a progress notification (setForeground); on Android 14 and later that foreground service needs the dataSync type declared. Android 14 also added user-initiated data transfer jobs in JobScheduler, made for exactly this case.

The cheapest fix: a 12-megapixel photo doesn't need to go up at full size if the server shrinks it anyway. Resize and recompress on the device first. For video, check whether the server transcodes it anyway, and if it does, upload a lower bitrate version.

#34769. The 10-Step Self-Audit to Run Before You Apply for Permanent Residency in Japan

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1350 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

The 10-Step Self-Audit to Run Before You Apply for Permanent Residency in Japan

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1350 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shortly before applying for permanent residency (PR), a man in my research took out a home loan and bought an apartment.
  • Buying the apartment did not cause the refusal.
  • So before you apply, run the same audit the examiner will.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shortly before applying for permanent residency (PR), a man in my research took out a home loan and bought an apartment. He had lived in Japan for more than ten years, and he was confident. The application was refused.

Buying the apartment did not cause the refusal. What it shows is the mistake underneath almost every refusal story I have collected: he trusted his memory of his own record instead of auditing it. Immigration does not review the life you remember. It reviews documents — tax certificates, a pension record read month by month, reports you filed or forgot, days you spent outside the country, and what happens in your life while the review is running.

So before you apply, run the same audit the examiner will. Ten steps, documents in front of you, nothing from memory. If a step produces a "not sure," that step is your application risk. Fix it now, while fixing is cheap.

The standard route is ten continuous years in Japan, including five or more years on a work visa or a residence-based visa. The shorter routes are the points system (70 points kept for three years, or 80 kept for one year) and the spouse route.

If you are using points, the question is stricter than "do I have the points today?" Did you have them at the start of the period, and have you kept them the whole time, with documents to prove every item?

According to recent reports, then check your period of stay. PR requires the longest period of stay for your status. A three-year period of stay has long been treated as the longest in practice, but that treatment ends at the 2027 changeover — March 31, 2027 is the last day to apply under the old treatment. If you hold three years, your dates are part of your eligibility.

Collect your resident tax certificates for the past five years. Then find the dangerous periods: any time in those five years when resident tax was not deducted from your salary — a gap between jobs, self-employment, a period after arriving in Japan. For those periods, immigration wants proof that you paid by each deadline: receipts or bank records showing the dates.

This is the single most common trap in the refusal stories. People paid. They just could not prove when, years later, because the convenience-store slips were thrown away. Also collect your national tax certificates while you are at it.

Open your pension record online through the Japan Pension Service and read it month by month, for at least the past two years and ideally longer. Gaps cluster around job changes. If you ever paid national pension or national health insurance yourself, do you still have the receipts?

And check your employer, not just yourself. One applicant's premiums were deducted from his salary every month while his firm handled the social insurance incorrectly. The record was in his name, so the refusal was too. Your online record highlights you whether your employer did its part.

Sources indicate that immigration examines the household, not the individual. Run Steps 2 and 3 again for your spouse: one applicant with a high income and a clean personal record was refused over his wife's late payments.

In a recent development, work out who counts as your household for the income test, including family members you support outside Japan. Under the revised guidelines, household income is compared with the average for Japanese households of the same size — and it has to stay there, not spike once.

Finally, look forward. The fresh rules add a check on your expected future pension: what will you actually receive in old age, based on your record? If the projection is thin, your savings and investments become part of the answer. People who arrived in Japan later in life, or spent years outside the pension system, need this step most.

List every employer you have had in Japan, with dates. For every job change, resignation and tech giant name change — yes, a name change counts — did you report it to immigration within 14 days? Did you register every change of address with your city or ward office within 14 days?

It has been revealed that if you missed one, file it now, and be ready to explain it honestly in writing. A missed report filed late is a problem you have addressed. A missed report the officer finds first is a different kind of problem.

Recent findings suggest that add up every day you spent outside Japan in the past ten years. Two numbers matter under the revised guidelines: any single trip of six months or more, and a total of two and a half years or more. Either one, without a reasonable reason, can break the continuous-residence requirement.

According to recent reports, for business trips, get proof that your employer sent you. Your employer's records are easiest to obtain now, not after a request from immigration arrives mid-review.

If you are not exempt, is your Japanese at around B1 level — everyday conversation and daily-life reading and writing — and do you know how you will show it? Highly skilled professionals and their families are among the exemptions, which is one more reason the points calculation matters.

Have you read the Guidebook on Living and Working in Japan? And if you have school-age children, are they attending elementary or junior high school? The guidelines treat children's schooling as part of the overall picture of your life in Japan. If they are not attending, take advice on how that will be viewed before you file, not after.

It has been revealed that your review will take a year or more, and it does not freeze your file on the day you apply. Job losses, firm bankruptcies and long trips during the review have all turned good applications into refusals.

It has been revealed that so ask honestly: is anything likely to change — job, income, family, travel? Are you planning a major decision that depends on a yes, like the apartment in the story above? Can it wait? And when does your current period of stay expire — will you need to renew it during the review? Put that date in your calendar now.

According to recent reports, do you have a guarantor — normally a Japanese citizen or permanent resident living in Japan — who has agreed to sign? Line this person up early; it is not a same-week favour to ask.

Then take your document list from the Immigration Services Agency's current official list, not from a friend's experience, an old blog post, or even this article. Lists change, and the 2027 revision changed more than most.

After the audit, you are in one of three positions.

Recent findings suggest that apply now. Your record is clean, your dates work, and nothing massive is about to change.

Wait and repair. You found something. Fix what can be fixed, let time pass where it must — remember the checked windows: five years for resident tax, two years for pension and health insurance — and set a date to run this audit again.

Get help first. Your file includes something complicated: a past violation, a long period abroad, a complex household, the three-year trap. This is when professional advice is easily worth its cost.

Whichever position you are in, you now know more about your own file than most applicants ever do. Under the old rules, learning these things from a refusal cost you a year. Under the newly introduced ones, it costs a year and ¥200,000.

It has been revealed that want the short version? The free one-page checklist version of this audit is here: https://kyshepard-books.github.io/checklist.html.

It has been revealed that ky Shepard writes about living and working in Japan. The refusal stories behind each step of this audit, and what to do when an answer is "no," are in "Why Japan Says No: The Hidden Reasons Permanent Residency Applications Fail, and How to Get a Yes (2027 Edition)," available on Amazon.

Is Water Better Than Diet Soft Drinks For Weight Loss? A Two-Year Trial Put Them To The Test

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (453 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
  • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
  • People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.

Among those who completed the trial, average weight loss was 4.8 kg in the diet drink group and 3.7 kg in the water group (which was not a statistically significant difference).

Both groups took part in a weight management programme and remained lighter a year after regular support ended.

They also reported similar changes in hunger, despite the difference in how sweet their drinks tasted.

Almost 500 adults with overweight or obesity began the trial after being randomly assigned to drink water or commercially available diet drinks each day.

The study included regular diet drink consumers alongside those who rarely or never chose them.

Everyone began with 12 weeks of active weight loss, followed by 40 weeks of support to help them maintain their progress.

Sugar intake fell by similar amounts in both groups.

One theory is that people learn to expect energy when they taste something sweet.

If the expected calories fail to arrive, the theory goes, that mismatch might affect hunger and lead people to make up the difference by eating more later.

Comparing water with a diet soft drink allows researchers to ask whether sweet taste matters during weight management, since both drinks provide little or no energy.

By the end of the trial, hunger ratings had risen slightly in both groups, and the change was similar whether participants drank water or diet drinks.

Professor Joanne Harrold, the study’s first author, said:.

“These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomised trial.”.

When water or a diet drink replaces a sugary soft drink, the swap also cuts the calories in that serving.

A review of 17 randomised trials found small reductions in body weight when people replaced sugary drinks with low- or no-calorie sweetened alternatives, with results broadly similar to those for water (McGlynn et al., 2022).

The two-year trial adds a longer view of what happens when people keep the sweet taste in their drinks while working to maintain weight loss.

The study was published in the British Journal of Nutrition (Harrold et al., 2026).

The Positive Personality Trait Linked To Having A Crush Outside Your Relationship

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (515 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
  • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
  • Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.

The clearest link among the dark traits is with psychopathy, which includes impulsivity and a lack of empathy.

Yet a more positive trait, the tendency to see value in other people and admire their qualities, is also linked to stronger infatuation once other differences are taken into account.

The researchers suggest that impulsivity may make a new attraction more rewarding, while an appreciation of other people may make it easier to form an emotional connection with them.

People who are more open to casual sex or less satisfied with their relationship also report stronger feelings for someone else.

The study involved just over 300 adults in Romania who were in committed relationships.

They completed questionnaires about their personality, their attitudes and experiences around casual sex, and how satisfied they were with their relationship.

The researchers also asked about the thoughts, feelings and desires people had towards someone other than their partner.

Psychologists call this extradyadic infatuation, a preoccupation that can involve repeatedly thinking about someone and feeling unable to tell your partner how strongly you feel.

People who scored higher on humanism, the tendency to value and admire others, generally reported less infatuation outside their relationship.

Of all the factors the researchers examined, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation after the others were taken into account.

The researchers suggest that people high in humanism may be more receptive to forming a close connection with someone new.

Faith in humanity, which reflects a belief in other people’s goodwill, highlighted a different pattern and remained linked to less infatuation.

People who expect others to be dependable may also see their existing relationship as more secure and feel less drawn to alternatives, the researchers suggest.

Machiavellianism, a tendency to approach relationships strategically and manipulate others for personal gain, also revealed a reversal.

It was linked to stronger infatuation when examined on its own and to weaker infatuation once the other factors were considered.

The researchers suggest that someone who takes a calculating approach to relationships may be wary of an outside attachment that demands sustained emotional investment.

Psychopathic traits, by comparison, were linked to stronger infatuation in both analyses.

When the researchers compared all the factors together, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation.

Dissatisfaction with an existing relationship may also make an alternative partner seem more appealing, although the survey leaves open whether dissatisfaction precedes the infatuation or follows it.

The study was published in the journal Psychological Reports (Huţanu & Holman, 2026).

#34759. Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain

📅 04 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1228 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain

📅 04 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1228 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before birth, the human brain is assembled through an enormous series of cellular choices.
  • These cells produce large numbers of the neurons and support cells that make up the cerebral cortex, the brain region involved in thought, memory, and language.
  • "Radial glia are the coolest cells that have ever existed," said Aparna Bhaduri, an assistant professor of biological chemistry at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before birth, the human brain is assembled through an enormous series of cellular choices. At the center of this process are radial glia, a special type of stem cell that helps create many of the features that distinguish the human brain.

These cells produce large numbers of the neurons and support cells that make up the cerebral cortex, the brain region involved in thought, memory, and language. Radial glia are also believed to contribute to the unusually large expansion of the human cortex compared with that of other species. Although most disappear before birth, similar cells can later appear again in brain cancers for reasons scientists still do not fully understand.

"Radial glia are the coolest cells that have ever existed," said Aparna Bhaduri, an assistant professor of biological chemistry at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. "They're really key to making us human. But they're also at the center of many neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders, as well as cancer -- so understanding how they make their decisions is one way to start understanding how those conditions arise.".

According to recent reports, two new studies published in Cell and Science now provide a closer look at how radial glia make those developmental choices. Bhaduri and her colleagues found that the cells respond to two very different kinds of information: the way they process nutrients and direct physical signals from another part of the developing brain. Together, these findings offer new insight into how the human cortex produces its remarkable variety of cell types.

Metabolism helps direct brain stem cells.

In the Cell study, researchers built a detailed map of metabolism in the developing human cortex. The project was a collaboration between Bhaduri's lab and Heather Christofk's lab and was led by co-first authors Jessenya Mil and Jose Soto.

To create the atlas, the team analyzed donated human tissue along with brain organoids grown from stem cells. Their results pointed to an unexpected conclusion: metabolism does not simply support brain development in the background. It can actively influence which kinds of cells are produced.

The researchers found that radial glia depend heavily on the pentose phosphate pathway, a metabolic process that uses glucose to make materials needed by cells that are dividing rapidly.

When the scientists lowered the amount of available glucose or interfered with this pathway, the stem cells changed what they produced. They began generating more inhibitory neurons and other cell types that normally appear later in development.

Sources indicate that "What was surprising is that metabolism isn't just a passive thing that happens in the background," stated Bhaduri, a member of both the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center and the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center. "It can really control how stem cells make decisions.".

The results could help scientists investigate how maternal nutrition, metabolic disorders, and other environmental influences affect the developing brain. The metabolic atlas also provides one of the most detailed resources yet for researchers studying metabolism during human brain development.

A signal arrives early from the thalamus.

The second study, published in Science and led by first author Claudia Nguyen, examined a completely different source of developmental information. This time, the researchers focused on signals coming from the thalamus, a structure deep inside the brain that helps relay information throughout the nervous system.

Scientists have known for years that neurons in the thalamus send long projections toward the cortex. These wire-like fibers eventually form connections with specific cortical neurons. However, anatomical studies have shown that in humans, the projections reach the cortex long before those final connections are established.

That raised an crucial question: Why do the fibers arrive so early?

In a recent development, using human stem cell-derived brain "assembloids," the UCLA researchers found part of the answer. The thalamic projections physically touch radial glia while the brain is still developing.

That contact changed the behavior of the stem cells. It caused them to produce more excitatory neurons, the primary signal-carrying neurons in the cortex. The effect was especially strong for upper-layer neurons, which are particularly expanded in the human brain.

"We already knew that these projections influence how the cortex develops," Bhaduri remarked. "What we specifically found is that this influence comes through an actual physical connection between the projections and the radial glia -- a point of contact that just hasn't been identified before, and one that very likely does not exist in rodents.".

A gene linked to autism enters the picture.

Industry observers note that the researchers connected this physical interaction to NRXN1, a gene already known for helping neurons form connections with one another. Mutations in NRXN1 have previously been associated with autism spectrum disorder.

To investigate its role, the team created assembloids from patient-derived cells carrying an NRXN1 mutation. In these models, the altered thalamic signals behaved differently from signals made by unaffected cells.

Those changes shifted the balance between the number of stem cells and the neurons they generated. The result offers researchers a possible way to study how disturbances early in brain development could influence the formation of the cortex.

The developing brain is in constant communication.

Industry observers note that although the two studies focused on very different mechanisms, they point toward the same broader idea. One examined metabolism, while the other explored neural connections, yet both highlighted that radial glia do not make their decisions in isolation. Their behavior is continuously shaped by signals from the environment around them.

Sources indicate that the studies also demonstrate how dramatically organoid technology has changed the study of human brain development. About a decade ago, scientists had few practical ways to directly investigate how uniquely human neural stem cells behave.

According to recent reports, today, brain organoids and related models allow researchers to recreate key features of human brain development in the laboratory. These systems also make it possible to test questions that cannot be addressed through animal models alone.

Bhaduri hopes the findings will encourage scientists to view metabolism and physical cellular connections as active drivers of development rather than as background processes.

According to recent reports, "Ultimately, these studies give us a glimpse under the hood of how these cells make decisions," she said. "Understanding those decisions is a first step toward understanding normal brain development, disease vulnerability and, potentially, how similar stem-cell programs operate in brain cancer.".

Sloan Foundation, the Rose Hills Foundation, the Esther A. & Joseph Klingenstein Fund, the Simons Foundation, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, the NIH BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network, the International Foundation for Ethical Research, the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center's Stem Cell Research Training Program, and the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center and UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center Ablon Scholars Program.

  • Fast breathing and an elevated heart rate are often linked with rapid decision-making.
  • In a recent development, decision-making has traditionally been viewed as a process centered mainly in the brain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A fresh study suggests that deliberately changing the rhythm of your breathing can influence how you make decisions by altering activity in both the heart and brain. Researchers from the German Institute of Human Nutrition Potsdam-Rehbruecke (DIfE) and Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin found that longer exhalations increased heart rate variability and made the brain more responsive to rewards, which was associated with bolder choices. The findings were published in Neuron.

Fast breathing and an elevated heart rate are often linked with rapid decision-making. Under pressure, people may become more cautious in an effort to avoid losses, whether they are making an investment, handling a tense workplace situation, or choosing a meal rapidly. Slower breathing and a calmer cardiovascular state, by contrast, may encourage a more positive assessment of potential outcomes and make people more willing to take risks.

How Breathing Connects the Body and Brain.

In a recent development, decision-making has traditionally been viewed as a process centered mainly in the brain. The newly introduced research examined a broader possibility: that signals from other parts of the body can change brain activity and influence the choices people make.

According to recent reports, the study was led by Prof. Soyoung Q Park in collaboration with researchers from institutions including the Neuroscience Research Center at Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Freie Universität Berlin, and the German Naval Institute of Maritime Medicine.

It has been revealed that "Our decisions are rarely determined solely by external information. Rather, our judgment emerges from the interplay between cognitive processes and our current bodily state. It was previously unknown how the conscious regulation of our body, for example through targeted breathing, could actively control our decision-making process. We wanted to create a physiological shift using a slow breathing pattern to change the quality of our decisions," explains Soyoung Q Park, head of the Department of Decision Neuroscience and Nutrition at DIfE, summarizing the research question.

Testing Whether Longer Exhales Change Decisions.

It has been revealed that the researchers studied 41 healthy participants while they made risky choices under carefully controlled breathing conditions. Participants followed visual breathing instructions and either breathed at their normal individual pace or slowed their breathing while extending the exhalation phase (2:8 inhale-exhale ratio).

As the participants completed a series of risk-related decisions, the research team measured several aspects of their physical and neurological responses. Functional magnetic resonance imaging was used to track brain activity, while breathing patterns, heart activity, skin conductance, and pupil responses were monitored at the same time.

In a recent development, this combination of measurements allowed the researchers to test whether extending the exhale did more than simply lower heart rate. They also wanted to determine whether the breathing pattern directly changed how the brain processed potential rewards.

Longer Exhalation Shifted Choices Toward Reward.

The results indicated that extended exhalation slowed heart rate and was associated with riskier choices. Importantly, the change appeared to come from greater attention to possible rewards rather than reduced concern about potential losses. Participants still responded to losses in a similar way.

According to recent reports, the researchers also detected stronger activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the precuneus. These brain regions are involved in reward processing and in regulating the timing between heartbeats, a measure known as heart rate variability.

Sources indicate that "Our study thus underscores the transformative role of breath-based interventions. The interplay between breathing and cardiac dynamics makes the brain more receptive to rewards," explains lead author Wenhao Huang, interpreting the results.

What the Findings Could Mean for Breathing Techniques.

The work adds to a growing field focused on body-brain communication and supports neurovisceral models, which propose that a person's physical state can strongly shape cognitive processes.

Park explains: "Breathing techniques have accompanied humanity for millennia across various religions and cultures. With this study, we provide scientific proof that it is a reliable and targeted method capable of controlling our decisions.".

According to recent reports, because controlled breathing is simple, inexpensive, and relatively easy to learn, the researchers say it could have value as a tool for everyday self-regulation. It may also have potential as a supportive, non-pharmacological approach in clinical settings, particularly for conditions such as anxiety disorders or depression, which can involve disrupted autonomic regulation and altered responses to reward.

Could Breathing Influence Eating Behavior?

Recent findings suggest that future studies will need to determine whether the same effects appear in broader clinical populations, including people with overweight. The researchers are particularly interested in whether breathing techniques could influence food-related decisions, since eating behavior is strongly affected by both reward processing and a person's physical state.

"Since dietary decisions are strongly influenced by reward assessment and physical state, targeted breath regulation could also play a role in consciously perceiving and more effectively managing eating behavior," Park summarizes for future research activities.

Ignacio Rebollo was supported by the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Action (MSCA) BRAINSTOM (grant agreement no. 101028203).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A painting by Sandro Botticelli at risk of leaving the UK earlier this year has gone on display at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford where it was first shown in the 1930s.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Virgin and Child Enthroned (1470s) was bought by the London-based private collection Klesch Collection, which declared intends in May to loan the painting to the Ashmolean for three years.
  • According to recent reports, the UK government placed an export bar on the Botticelli painting, valued at £10.2m, in May 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A painting by Sandro Botticelli at risk of leaving the UK earlier this year has gone on display at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford where it was first shown in the 1930s.

Recent findings suggest that the Virgin and Child Enthroned (1470s) was bought by the London-based private collection Klesch Collection, which declared intends in May to loan the painting to the Ashmolean for three years. The painting was previously exhibited at the museum in 1934–35 when it was attributed to Botticelli's workshop.

According to recent reports, the UK government placed an export bar on the Botticelli painting, valued at £10.2m, in May 2025. The UK Department for Culture, Media and Sport noted that the painting had a recommended price of £9,960,000 (plus VAT of £272,000, which can be reclaimed by an eligible institution). The work was sold at Sotheby’s London in late 2024 for £9.7m (with fees).

According to recent reports, the painting underwent conservation over the summer to remove discoloured varnish and later retouching, revealing well-preserved details of the Virgin and Child and restoring the original cooler tones, states an Ashmolean statement. The painting is also unusual for its generous use of gold leaf, “although earlier Italian painters regularly applied gold to the backgrounds of their devotional works, it was less widely used by Botticelli's time”, add the statement.

According to recent reports, the Botticelli painting was housed in the Convent of San Giuliano in Florence in the early 19th century, and was later transported to a small chapel attached to a group of farmhouses in a nearby village. It then passed into the family of Giovanni Magherini Graziani, who sold it in November 1903 to the Italian dealer, Elia Volpi. Harriet Sarah Jones Loyd (Lady Wantage) bought the work in May 1904 for £5,000. The Botticelli painting had been kept at Betterton House, near Wantage, Berkshire, since 1944.

Sources indicate that founders A. Gary and Dr. Anita Klesch started the Klesch Collection with the acquisition of a set of Four Seasons by Giuseppe Arcimboldo in 2014. The collection of 15th-to-17th-century European art, which also includes works by Caravaggio, Sofonisba Anguissola and Rubens, is regularly loaned to museums and institutions worldwide.

#34754. Scientists find a new layer of Alzheimer’s hidden in the genome

📅 13 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1138 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists find a new layer of Alzheimer’s hidden in the genome

📅 13 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University's School of Computer Science, the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and the University of Washington have uncovered a previously underexplored feature of Alzheimer's disease that may help scientists identify newly introduced avenues for treatment.
  • The study, published in Science, found that the three-dimensional organization of the genome differs in certain brain cells from people with Alzheimer's disease.
  • To build this detailed picture, the team combined single-cell technology, spatial mapping of brain tissue, and a newly developed deep learning model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University's School of Computer Science, the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and the University of Washington have uncovered a previously underexplored feature of Alzheimer's disease that may help scientists identify newly introduced avenues for treatment.

The study, published in Science, found that the three-dimensional organization of the genome differs in certain brain cells from people with Alzheimer's disease. Scientists from SCS's Ray and Stephanie Lane Computational Biology Department, Pitt's Department of Neurobiology, and collaborating institutions connected these changes in genome folding with shifts in gene activity and the organization of brain tissue.

To build this detailed picture, the team combined single-cell technology, spatial mapping of brain tissue, and a newly developed deep learning model.

"Alzheimer's disease cannot be understood one layer at a time," noted Jian Ma, the Ray and Stephanie Lane Professor of Computational Biology who led and supervised the study. "The genome's 3D structure is a fundamental regulatory layer that helps to connect DNA sequence to gene activity. By integrating genome folding, cell state, and tissue context, we can move beyond cataloging disease-associated changes toward understanding how they fit together and which mechanisms to test next.".

DNA does not sit inside a cell as a simple straight strand. Instead, it folds into a complex three-dimensional structure that helps determine which genes are accessible and active. Changes in that physical organization can therefore influence how cells function.

The researchers examined postmortem samples from the prefrontal cortex, an area at the front of the brain. The tissue came from people with and without Alzheimer's disease who had taken part in a long-term dementia study and later donated their brains for research.

Sources indicate that the team used GAGE-seq, a technique that can measure both gene expression and three-dimensional genome contacts within the same individual cell. Those measurements were then combined with spatial transcriptomic maps, which preserve information about where gene activity occurs within intact brain tissue.

By bringing these datasets together, the researchers were able to connect the physical organization of the genome with gene regulation while also seeing where Alzheimer's related molecular and cellular changes appeared within the surrounding tissue.

A Latest Layer of Alzheimer's Biology.

It has been revealed that "Our study represents a major advance in understanding what goes wrong in Alzheimer's disease," noted Hansruedi Mathys, assistant professor of neurobiology at Pitt's Department of Neurobiology, who directed the Pitt arm of the study. "We know the classic hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease - accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles - but our results establish higher-order chromatin alterations as a component of the molecular pathology associated with the disease, which at the moment affects seven million Americans, a number that continues to grow.".

Sources indicate that amyloid beta plaques and tau tangles are among the best known biological features of Alzheimer's disease. The upcoming findings suggest that changes in chromatin, the material made of DNA and associated proteins that packages the genome inside cells, should also be considered part of the disease's molecular landscape.

AI Connects Genome Folding to Gene Activity.

Another important part of the research was Hicformer, an artificial intelligence model developed to investigate how genome structure may influence cellular behavior. The model combines DNA sequence information with broad patterns of genome folding and detailed maps showing where different sections of DNA physically contact one another.

Using these inputs, Hicformer predicts gene activity across different types of cells. Xinyue Lu, a doctoral student in Computational Biology who co-led the research, described the system as a computational test bed that can be used to explore how changes in genome folding might alter gene activity.

"Measuring gene activity and genome folding in the same cell allows us to directly connect chromosome structure with disease-related gene programs," stated Yang Zhang, a project scientist in the Computational Biology Department who co-led the research. "Across several kinds of brain cells, this paired view revealed a consistent signature of 3D genome reorganization in Alzheimer's disease and helped us prioritize regulatory regions for future mechanistic and therapeutic investigation.".

DNA Organization Becomes Less Distinct.

The researchers identified several consistent differences in the genome architecture of cells from people with Alzheimer's disease.

It has been revealed that large sections of the genome are normally organized into relatively distinct active and inactive regions known as compartments. In Alzheimer's cells, those boundaries appeared less sharply defined. The researchers describe this pattern as "increased compartment mingling.".

Several kinds of brain cells also indicated fewer interactions between nearby sections of the genome and more contacts between regions located farther apart. Cells with greater compartment mingling tended to have lower overall levels of gene activity.

According to recent reports, the team also observed weaker interactions between genes and nearby regulatory elements that normally help control whether those genes are switched on or off. At the same time, some contacts across intermediate distances became stronger.

In a recent development, these structural differences were associated with reduced activity in programs involved in neurons and synapses, along with changes in metabolism and cellular stress responses. The researchers also found links to senescence-related programs in microglia, immune cells in the brain that play vital roles in maintaining brain health and responding to damage.

Potential Clues for Future Alzheimer's Treatments.

When the researchers mapped these molecular changes across intact brain tissue, they found that the reorganization of the genome was connected not only to altered gene activity but also to differences in how brain cells were arranged within the tissue.

In a recent development, the results establish three-dimensional genome organization as another notable layer of Alzheimer's disease biology. They also provide researchers with a framework for testing which changes in genome architecture might directly contribute to the disease.

Future studies can now investigate whether particular structural changes help drive Alzheimer's progression and whether any of the affected regulatory regions could eventually become targets for new therapies.

It has been revealed that the research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health. Other CMU authors included doctoral students Shahul Alam and Shike Wang and postdoctoral research associate Junjie Tang. Other Pitt authors include doctoral students Alexander K. Kunisky and Jude Baroudi, post-baccalaureate research fellows Sahar and Sahel Ghorbanikalateh, and visiting scholar Shihan Wang. The team included researchers from the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Washington; and the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center.

#34753. Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks

📅 14 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1166 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks

📅 14 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists at the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have uncovered evidence that two neighboring types of brain tissue may work together to support thinking abilities later in life.
  • The study, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, included brain imaging and cognitive testing from 459 adults aged 60 and older living in communities across India.
  • Superficial white matter forms a thin layer of nerve fibers directly beneath the gray matter covering the outside of the brain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists at the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have uncovered evidence that two neighboring types of brain tissue may work together to support thinking abilities later in life. Their findings suggest that the condition of the brain's local communication pathways could influence how strongly gray matter loss affects cognition.

The study, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, included brain imaging and cognitive testing from 459 adults aged 60 and older living in communities across India. The research is among the first to investigate superficial white matter in a community-based population from a low- and middle-income country.

The Brain's Local Communication Network.

Superficial white matter forms a thin layer of nerve fibers directly beneath the gray matter covering the outside of the brain. These short, curved fibers connect nearby regions of the cerebral cortex, allowing them to exchange information. They can be thought of as local roads linking neighboring areas of the brain.

Gray matter serves a different role. It contains many of the nerve cells responsible for processing information. Together, gray matter and the white matter directly beneath it form closely connected systems that may both contribute to cognitive health.

According to recent reports, "Gray matter and superficial white matter are physically close and may play different roles: gray matter processes information, while superficial white matter helps nearby brain regions communicate," said Yingxu Liu, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar at the Stevens INI and first author of the study. "Our findings suggest that cognitive health depends not only on how much gray matter is preserved, but also on the condition of the wiring that connects it.".

Measuring the Brain's Hidden Wiring.

To investigate these local connections, the researchers used an advanced type of diffusion MRI. This imaging technique tracks the movement of water through brain tissue, allowing scientists to examine microscopic features that conventional brain scans may not reveal.

Industry observers note that the researchers focused on measurements related to neurite density and the amount of freely moving water surrounding these structures. Neurites are the small projections through which nerve cells send and receive signals. A lower density of neurites or an increase in free water can indicate damage or disruption in tissue associated with processes including loss of myelin, inflammation, or swelling.

Participants also underwent assessments covering several areas of cognition, including language, memory, executive function, and visuospatial ability.

In a recent development, the most consistent connection between superficial white matter health and cognitive performance involved language. People with healthier superficial white matter tended to perform better on language tests. The strongest associations appeared in frontotemporal regions of the brain involved in recognizing words, speaking fluently, and temporarily holding language information in mind.

Healthy Wiring May Cushion Gray Matter Loss.

Measures of gray matter atrophy were still the strongest overall predictors of cognitive ability. However, the researchers found that the impact of gray matter loss appeared to vary depending on the health of nearby superficial white matter.

When these local connections demonstrated poorer integrity, gray matter loss was more strongly associated with impaired language performance and broader cognitive difficulties. When superficial white matter was healthier, the link between gray matter loss and poorer cognition was weaker.

This raises the possibility that the condition of the brain's local wiring could help explain why two people with similar amounts of gray matter loss do not necessarily experience the same degree of cognitive decline.

"The findings point to superficial white matter as a possible source of resilience," stated Leon Aksman, PhD, assistant professor of research neurology at the Stevens INI and senior author of the study. "Two people with a similar degree of gray matter loss may not experience the same cognitive effects if the local connections surrounding that gray matter differ in health. Following participants over time will be essential to test whether preserving these connections can help maintain cognition.".

Expanding Brain Aging Research Beyond Typical Populations.

According to recent reports, the researchers drew their data from the Harmonized Diagnostic Assessment of Dementia for the Longitudinal Aging Study in India, known as LASI-DAD. More than half of the larger LASI-DAD population has low literacy, while about 60% lives in rural communities.

Populations with these characteristics have historically been underrepresented in brain imaging studies, making the research an opportunity to examine cognitive aging across a broader range of social, educational, and geographic backgrounds.

In this analysis, the association between superficial white matter and language ability was stronger among people who were unable to read or who read incorrectly, those who had received no formal education, and participants living in rural areas.

Sources indicate that the researchers emphasize that the results do not establish that these social factors caused changes in brain tissue. Instead, they suggest that brain aging may be shaped by a complex combination of experiences throughout life, including education, social circumstances, health, and environmental exposures.

What Scientists Still Need to Learn.

Because participants were examined at only one point in time, the study cannot establish which brain changes occurred first. Researchers do not yet know whether deterioration of superficial white matter begins before gray matter loss, develops alongside it, or precedes measurable cognitive decline.

In a recent development, long-term research that follows people as they age will be needed to clarify these relationships. Future studies will also investigate how vascular health, inflammation, Alzheimer's related proteins, and other biological factors interact with changes in gray and white matter.

"A fuller understanding of brain aging requires research that reflects the world's social, cultural, and geographic diversity," noted Arthur W. Toga, PhD, director of the Stevens INI and Provost Professor at USC. "By studying an underrepresented population and looking beyond gray matter alone, this work brings us closer to identifying the biological and social factors that may protect cognition across the lifespan.".

In addition to Liu and Aksman, the study's authors include Kirsten M. Lynch, Miguel Arce Rentería, Emma Nichols, Alden L. Gross, Lindsay C. Kobayashi, Neda Jahanshad, John P. John, Harshita V. Vishwakarma, Pranali Khobragade, Joyita Banerjee, Niranjan Khandelwal, Jyoti Dangwal, Sudhir Saxena, Nirod Medhi, Soumik Das, Prudhvinath Reddy, Pratyaksha Rana, Arjun Narula, Saravanan Kannan, Dinesh Patel, A. B. Dey, Sharmistha Dey, and Jinkook Lee.

The research was supported by the National Institute on Aging (R01AG080473, RF1AG087965, RF1AG088003, R01AG087513), the National Institute of Mental Health (R01MH134004), the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (RF1NS136995), and the Office of the Director of the National Institutes of Health (S10OD032285).

Tech Report: The Depression And Bladder Medicines That May Increase Dementia Risk

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.

These drugs block the action of acetylcholine, a chemical messenger in the brain and body, and are used to treat depression, overactive bladder and symptoms of Parkinson’s disease.

For example, amitriptyline is an antidepressant formerly sold as Tryptizol in the UK and Elavil in the US.

Oxybutynin, used to treat overactive bladder, also has anticholinergic effects and comes in patches known as Kentera in the UK and Oxytrol in the US.

In a study of more than 217,000 people, each additional anticholinergic medicine prescribed at the start was associated with a 15 per cent higher rate of dementia diagnosis in the UK group and about a 6 per cent higher rate in the US group.

Acetylcholine helps the brain pay attention, learn and form memories.

In the bladder, blocking certain acetylcholine signals can help control involuntary contractions.

Blocking those signals in the brain can make it harder to concentrate and may cause confusion.

Other tricyclic antidepressants with anticholinergic effects include clomipramine, known by the brand name Anafranil in both countries, and nortriptyline, known as Allegron in the UK and Pamelor in the US.

Paroxetine, an SSRI antidepressant with anticholinergic effects, has been sold as Seroxat in the UK and Paxil in the US.

Some antipsychotics also have these effects, including olanzapine, known as Zyprexa in both countries and used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

The medicines have different uses, which makes their shared effect easy to overlook when someone takes several prescriptions for unrelated conditions.

Using a list of 88 medicines, the researchers counted how many each person had been prescribed at the start of the study.

They then looked at dementia diagnoses over a median of about 16 years in the UK Biobank and nine years in the US All of Us Research Program.

About a quarter of participants in the British group and just over a fifth of those in the American group had been prescribed at least one medicine on the list.

The increases were relative, and fewer than two in 100 participants in each group were diagnosed with dementia during follow-up.

The percentages describe how the rate of dementia diagnosis varied with the number of medicines prescribed and give no risk estimate for any individual drug.

A prescription can reveal something about a person’s health as well as what medicine they have been given.

Depression and Parkinson’s disease, for example, can lead to anticholinergic prescribing and are themselves associated with dementia risk.

The researchers could account for some differences in health between participants, but the reasons for prescribing and the severity of those conditions could still explain part of the association.

A count taken at the start also gives only a snapshot, since people may change medicines or stop taking them over the years.

For someone taking several prescriptions, a prescriber or pharmacist can review the full list and weigh the benefits and risks of each medicine in context.

The study was published in the journal Age and Ageing (Asiimwe et al., 2025).

#34751. Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice
